=== Page 13 ===
INTRODUCTION

The presentation of a translation of the Mādhavanidāna and its chief
commentary needs some words of introduction in order to explain why
this particular treatise was selected.
Firstly I have to bring to the reader's notice that the three classical
*saṁhitās* of Sanskrit medical literature are available in translations. The
Carakasaṁhitā was twice translated into English (by Kaviraj Avinash
Chandra Kaviratna and by a group of scholars of the Shree Gulabkun-
verba Ayurvedic Society); a third translation (by Ramkaran Sarma and
Bhagavan Das), with extracts from Cakrapāṇidatta's commentary, is in
course of preparation. The Suśrutasaṁhitā was translated into Latin (by
F. Hessler) and into English (by Kaviraj Kunjalal Bhishagratna); there
are also incomplete translations of this text (Sū. 1-14 by Hoernle; Sū.
1-42, 10 by Udoy Chand Dutt; Sū. 42, 10-46, 176 by Aughorechunder
Chattopadhyaya). The Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṁhitā was translated into Ger-
man (by L. Hilgenberg and W. Kirfel); the first five chapters of both
the Sanskrit original and the Tibetan version were translated into Eng-
lish (by C. Vogel). Among the vast mass of medical Sanskrit literature,
apart from the mentioned *saṁhitās*, a restricted number of texts has
been partially translated : Aṣṭāṅgasaṁgraha (BDHM Hyderabad, 1964),
Bhedasaṁhitā (Sū. 16, by Filliozat and by R. F. G. Müller), Hāritasaṁ-
hitā (section 2, chapter 1, by Filliozat), Bhāvaprakāśa (the ophthal-
mological parts, by Esser), Cikitsākalikā with Candrata's commentary (by
Jolly), Todara's Āyurvedasaukhya (BDHM Hyderabad, 1965) and Kalyā-
ṇakāraka (BDHM Hyderabad, 1965), not to mention translations found
in books on Indian medicine in general and articles on special subjects.

The first five chapters of the Mādhavanidāna were already translated
into Italian by Vallauri (GSAI 26, 1913-14, p. 253-290).

The systematic study of the medical compendia and compilations,
which were composed in increasing numbers after the age of the *saṁhitās*
had passed, has scarcely begun; translations and attempts to analyze
their contents are scarce. So it appeared desirable to work at a translation
of the earliest and most important compendium on the section of Indian
medicine that is traditionally called *nidāna*, the Rogaviniścaya by Mā-
dhava, usually referred to as the Mādhavanidāna. Though the first work
of this type to appear in the field of Sanskrit medical literature, it has
remained a classic up to modern times.


=== Page 14 ===
2

                                      INTRODUCTION

      Mādhava set the standard as to the order in which the diseases should
be described. In this he definitely improved upon the earlier *saṁhitās*
in which a restricted number of diseases is dealt with in the section on
*nidāna*, while the remaining ones are found in various other sections.
Collecting his material from the *saṁhitās*, for the greater part at least,
and selecting what was appropriate to the nature of his work and its
scope, he organized the whole in a new way. Mādhava clearly met with
success. The compendia written by subsequent authors (Vṛndakuṇḍa's
Siddhayoga, Cakrapāņidatta's Cikitsāsaṁgraha, Vaṅgasena's Cikitsāsasaṁgraha,
Bhāvamiśra's Bhāvaprakāśa, etc.) faithfully reflect the
scheme of the Mādhavanidāna.
      The almost complete translation of a commentary on a Sanskrit
medical text hardly needs justification, because the only specimen available
so far is the abbreviated rendering of the first part of Candrața's
commentary on Tisața's Cikitsākalikā (Jolly, ZDMG 60, 1906, p. 413-
468). The commentaries on Sanskrit medical texts are of great importance
for a number of reasons.
      The text of a Sanskrit medical treatise is not clear in many instances
and may be interpreted in a number of ways. The commentaries are
indispensable for a correct understanding of the way in which difficult
passages were explained according to tradition. Conflicting views are
often discussed by commentators and variants of the text are recorded.
Quotations from and references to works which have not been preserved
and works which are still extant are frequently found in commentaries.
For this reason they are essential tools in establishing a relative chronology
of medical authors and works. Apart from all this, the way of
reasoning about medical concepts and the tendency to reconcile disagreeing
traditions are interesting in themselves.
      The text of the most important commentary on the Mādhavanidāna,
the Madhukośa, is presented here in an almost complete translation.
Only those parts of it dealing with subjects not connected with medicine,
particularly discussions on grammar, have been left out. The task of
rendering the commentary into English presented many problems. I
have kept rather close to the peculiar style of a Sanskrit commentary,
which has the disadvantage of making difficult reading, but retains the
flavour of the original. On the other hand it does not obscure that it
proved impossible sometimes to arrive at a full understanding of the
allusions to various theories, opinions, conflicting views etc., which may
have been clear in the age in which the commentary was composed, but
are confusing when the sources are not referred to by name or lost to us.


=== Page 15 ===
                           INTRODUCTION                               3

Seeing that many translations of medical Sanskrit texts are unsatis-
factory in certain respects, I tried to elaborate a translating technique
which would render the original as consistently as possible. First of all
it should make clear what is in the text and what is added by the trans-
lator. In this respect Bhishagratna's translation of the Suśrutasaṁhitā
is a bad example of what a translation should be; elements from Ḍalha-
ṇa's commentary are incorporated in the translation without indication,
a practice that results in confusing all those who cannot consult the
Sanskrit text for comparison at every page. Words necessary to com-
plete a sentence or make clear its meaning have been put between brack-
ets in the translation here presented. There are also many versions with
a tendency to overinterpretation, especially by the use of technical terms
borrowed from contemporary medical science (e.g. the Gulabkunverba
translation of the Carakasaṁhitā and Bhishagratna's translation of the
Suśrutasaṁhitā).

Finally, it is my conviction that names of medicinal plants should
remain untranslated whenever their botanical identification is doubtful,
i.e. in the greater number of cases (in this respect Hilgenberg and Kirfel's
translation of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṁhitā shows much more confidence
than is warranted; the Gulabkunverba translation of the Carakasaṁhitā
is a particularly bad example, because it forces the reader to learn by
heart the equivalents used or to consult the list of Sanskrit names with
their equivalents again and again).

The most difficult problem encountered in preparing the translation
of the Mādhavanidāna and the Madhukośa consisted in finding suitable
English equivalents for the great number of technical Sanskrit terms.
Firstly, I generally avoided the use of modern medical terms except in
a few cases where they appeared adequate. Secondly, striving for a trans-
lation that would be as consistent as possible, I decided to render techni-
cal terms by a fixed equivalent whenever the range of meaning of the
Sanskrit word allowed this. As a matter of fact the work went through
a series of stages in order to accomplish this aim, but it proved to be a
method that could be worked out. In this way it becomes easier to find
out which terms are synonymous or convey a related meaning and which
terms have different connotations. A better understanding of the Sans-
krit technical terms used in medical texts is moreover acquired by com-
paring parallel passages from several texts. Those who are not versed in
Sanskrit are unable to do so and will be at a loss when comparing the
existing translations, which are so different from one author to another
that a comparison is not possible at all. That is why I have added trans-


=== Page 16 ===
4

                                       INTRODUCTION

lations of the parallel passages in notes on the respective chapters,
which has the attendant advantage that much material from hitherto
untranslated texts can be presented.

    The volume is provided with a series of Appendices which may in-
crease its usefulness to those who have not made a special study of
Sanskrit medical texts.

    The work would have been incomplete without a concordance of the
Nidāna and lists of the quotations and their sources, found in the com-
mentary (App. 1). The printed editions are not always reliable in this
respect and certainly not complete. The errors of the printed editions
have been corrected; a number of hitherto unidentified passages and
quotations has been traced to their sources, though gaps remain, some
of which may be filled in later.

    As no reliable survey of our present knowledge on the chronology of
Sanskrit medical authors and works is available, I have summarized what
is known to me about the authors and works referred to (App. 2). Some
information on technical terms was thought to be useful, both to medical
historians and Sanskritists (App. 3). The material has been largely col-
lected from Sanskrit medical treatises and nighanṭus; the latter have so
far not been much studied.

    The botanical identifications of plants mentioned in Sanskrit texts is
a field in which almost complete confusion reigns, a fact of which every
Sanskritist is constantly aware. A preliminary survey of the identifica-
tions as found in the literature pertaining to this field seems highly
desirable. The material collected only applies to plant names found in
this volume (App. 4). Decisions regarding the adequacy of the identifi-
cations could not be reached in this way and require much separate
study.

    Identification of the syndromes described, or the clusters of symptoms
enumerated, has been attempted, but proved an exceedingly difficult
task (App. 5). A thorough acquaintance with the diseases prevalent in
India at the present time and with the history of those diseases is ab-
solutely required to solve the problems, and this is lacking in the present
author. I have tried, however, to arrive at a first approximative evalua-
tion of the data presented and can only hope that a great number of
medical colleagues, specialized in the several branches of medicine, will
endeavour to improve on these first attempts.

    The translation is based on the edition of the Mādhavanidāna with the


=== Page 17 ===
INTRODUCTION                                                                       5

Madhukośa and extracts from the Ātaṅkadarpaṇa by Vaidya Jādavji
Trikumji Āchārya (fifth edition, 1955, Nirṇaya Sāgar Press, Bombay).
Several other editions of the Nidāna and the Nidāna with the Ma-
dhukośa were consulted for comparison (see Bibliography). The differences
proved to be of little importance, even with regard to the number of
additional stanzas. Additions to Mādhava's text of the Nidāna are, as
a rule, indicated as such, or have been put between brackets. Words
which complete sentences and are put between brackets are by the hand
of the translator. Untranslated parts of the commentaries are indicated
by three dots. The editions of Sanskrit texts referred to in the notes and
Appendices are those recorded in the Bibliography and, when more than
one edition of a text is found there, it is the first one of the list.

I shall now give a survey of what is known about (1) Mādhava and
his works, (2) the commentaries on the Mādhavanidāna, (3) Vijayarakṣita
and Śrīkaṇṭhadatta, the authors of the Madhukośa, and (4) Vācaspati,
the author of the Ātaṅkadarpaṇa.

MĀDHAVA (KARA).

The author of the Rogaviniścaya does not reveal his name in the text
of the work, but in colophons of manuscripts of the Nidāna and its com-
mentaries he is called Mādhava (Cat.Skt.Mss. BORI, vol. 16, part 1, nr.
149, p. 184), Śrīmādhava (l.c., nr. 151, p. 187, and nr. 153, p. 189) and
Mādhavakāra (l.c., nr. 152, p. 188). In the Madhukośa his name appears
as Mādhava and Mādhavakara. Śrīkaṇṭhadatta refers to him as Mādhava-
kāra in the introduction to the comments on chapter two of Vṛnda's
Siddhayoga. Niścalakara quotes from Mādhava and Mādhavakara
(Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 146 and 153), but it is not clear from Bhaṭṭa-
charyya's indications whether the Nidāna is quoted in Niścalakara's
Ratnaprabhā. Hemādri, who quotes, with mention of the title of the
work, six times from the Rugviniścaya in his commentary on Vāgbhaṭa's
Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā, once cites it (on A.h.Sū. 8, 28) as the work of
Mādhavakara, omitting its title.

Mādhava's name does appear, however, at the end of one of his other
works, granted that this work, the Paryāyaratnamālā, was indeed com-
posed by the same author; in the concluding stanzas it is disclosed that
it was written by Mādhava, the physician (bhiṣaj). From the foregoing
it is clear that we are not quite sure whether the author of the Rogavinīś-
caya was called Mādhava or Mādhavakara.


=== Page 18 ===
6
INTRODUCTION

About Mādhava(kara)'s lineage little information is available. In a
small number of manuscripts his father is mentioned by name, but there
is no agreement among these sources. Mādhava is said to be a son of
Indukara in the colophon of a manuscript of Vācaspati's commentary
on the Nidāna (Cat.Skt.Mss. BORI, vol. 16, part 1, nr. 149, p. 184); his
father's name appears as Candrakara, which may be regarded as a syno-
nym of Indukara, in the colophon of a manuscript of the Mādhava-
cikitsita (l.c., nr. 143, p. 178); at the end of the printed text of Mādhava's
Paryāyaratnamālā (an edition based on nine manuscripts, only one of
which contains the concluding stanzas), the author says that he is a son
of Indrakara (ardhaśloka 1756). Usually it is assumed that Indukara is
the correct form of the name of Mādhava's father (see e.g. S. K. De,
NIA 2, 1939-40, p. 273, footnote 4; the same in R. C. Majumdar, The
history of Bengal, vol. 1, p. 315). The view, held by some, that this
Indukara may be identical with Indu, the commentator on the Aṣṭāṅga-
saṃgraha, is not based on evidence and certainly erroneous (see App. 2:
Indu).

It has been supposed that Mādhavakara and his father, Indukara, be-
longed to the Kara family, mentioned as one of the families of Bengal
physicians by Bharatamallika in his Candrabhā (Candrabha p.
7-9, acc. to Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 128-129; Bharatamallika was a
Bengal commentator who lived about 1800, acc. to Krishnamachariar,
p. 145, footnote 1; see about Bharatamallika : N. N. Dasgupta, The
Bengali commentators on the Amarakośa, IC 2, 1935-36, p. 266). The
only evidence on this point is the ending -kara of the names of Mādhava
and his father, and, as we have seen, there is no certainty in this regard
with respect to Mādhava's name. Therefore it has rightly been pointed
out (S. K. De, NIA 2, 1939-40, p. 273, footnote 4; the same in R. C.
Majumdar, The history of Bengal, vol. 1, p. 315, footnote 3) that it is
doubtful whether -kara really was a cognomen of Mādhava; S. K. De
adds that the name of Mādhava's father, Indukara, is intelligible in it-
self and need not lead to the supposition of a Bengal origin; moreover
he refers, as an example, to Bhānukara, the author of the Rasikajīvana,
who did not belong to Bengal.

A clue with regard to his place of residence has been supplied by Mā-
dhava himself. At the end of the Paryāyaratnamālā (ardhaśloka 1755) he
has clearly indicated that he was an inhabitant of Śīlāhrada. The pro-
blem of Mādhava's provenance can only be settled by the identification
of this locality. Bhattacharyya observes (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 154) that it
appears to have been a famous place at that time, at a considerable


=== Page 19 ===
INTRODUCTION                                            7

distance from Pāṭaliputra, for it is mentioned in an illustration in Vācas-
patimiśra’s Nyāyakaṇikā : “Someone who has obtained a favour at
Pāṭaliputra will certainly not remember it without confusion at Śīlā-
hrada” (Nyāyakaṇikā, Chowkhamba ed., p. 301, acc. to Bhaṭṭ, l.c.,
p. 154; Vācaspatimiśra lived about 850 acc. to Winternitz, vol. 3, p.
436-437). No more is known to me about the location of Śīlāhrada.

Though it is asserted sometimes that there is no conclusive evidence
to assign Mādhava to Bengal (see e.g. S. K. De, NIA 2, 1939-40, p. 273-
274; S. K. De in R. C. Majumdar, The history of Bengal, vol. 1, p. 315-
316), Bhaṭṭācharyya defended the view (l.c., p. 153-154) that he lived
in Bengal and, in order to prove this theory, he drew attention to the
Bengali synonyms of substances of vegetable, animal and mineral origin,
occurring in Mādhava’s Paryāyaratnamālā. N. N. Das Gupta (IC 3,
1936-37, p. 155) also claims a Bengal origin for Mādhava and pays atten-
tion to the vernacular words in the Paryāyaratnamālā, adding that the
substances mentioned in it are for the greater part still known by the
same names in Bengal. Many terms from the popular speech are indeed
given in the work, but their relationship to terms from the contemporary
Bengali language requires careful study.

Summarizing, it may be said that conclusive evidence, enabling us to
assign Mādhava to Bengal, has not been produced so far. The problem
may be brought nearer to its solution by a detailed study of the deśī
words from the Paryāyaratnamālā.

With regard to the identity of Mādhava and his works, confusion was
created by Hoernle in an article about the commentaries on the Suśruta-
samhitā (JRAS, 1906, p. 283-302). He was struck by the observation
that Dalhaṇa, in the introduction to his commentary on the Suśruta-
samhitā, notes that he has studied the glosses (*ṭippaṇa*) of Śrīmādhava
on this work before starting to write his own comments. Hoernle was
puzzled by this statement because it was apparently unknown to him
that references to Mādhava as a commentator are not a particularly rare
occurrence. He made a link between Mādhava, the glossator, and Vṛnda,
the author of the Siddhayoga, after noticing that Śrīkaṇṭhadatta, in his
commentary on the Siddhayoga, repeatedly observes that Vṛnda added
glosses (*ṭippaṇa*, *ṭippaṇikā*) of his own to stanzas of the Siddhayoga,
taken from the Caraka- or Suśrutasamhitā (see e.g. Siddhayoga 12,
24cd; 22, 9-10; 39, 6cd). This led him to assume that Mādhava and
Vṛnda were probably one and the same person (JRAS, 1906, p. 288-290).
To give more force to this assumption he drew attention to the fact that
the Siddhayoga, according to its colophons, is also called Vṛndamādhava;


=== Page 20 ===
8

                                 INTRODUCTION

the author discloses his name as Vṛnda at the end of the work, while
no author's name appears in the Mādhavanidāna. Hoernle came to re-
gard the Mādhavanidāna and Siddhayoga as the two parts of one great
work by Vṛnda. The name Mādhavakara, abbreviated to Mādhava in
the introduction to the Madhukośa, might in that case be forged as a
poetical description, meaning 'maker of honey', in relation to the title
of its commentary, Madhukośa, which means 'store of honey'.
    At the present time it is clear that Hoernle's views do not reflect the
real state of affairs. Mādhava wrote, apart from the Nidāna, a treatise
on therapy which is different from the Siddhayoga and, moreover, he
must have been active as a commentator. The works, partially extant,
which are known to be his, are : (1) Rogaviniścaya, (2) Mādhavacikitsita,
(3) Paryāyaratnamālā, (4) Praśnavidhāna, (5) Yogavyākhyā, (6) Dravya-
guṇa, (7) one or more commentaries.

    (1) The Rogaviniścaya, the title of the work as presented in its text
    (Nidāna 1, 2), also called Rugviniścaya (Śrīkaṇṭhadatta on Siddhayoga
    1, 2; Hemādri in his commentary on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā) and
    Gadāviniścaya (Siddhayoga 1, 2), which are synonyms of Rogaviniścaya,
    is usually referred to as the Mādhavanidāna. Śrīkaṇṭhadatta (on Sid-
    dhayoga 1, 2) also calls it Nidānasaṃgraha.
    (2) Mādhavacikitsita. As already stated Hoernle was unaware of the
    existence of this work by Mādhava, though the description of a manu-
    script of its text (by R. Mitra; see below) was available at the time he
    wrote his studies on Indian medicine. In more recent times S. K. De
    (NIA 2, 1939-40, p. 273, footnote 8; the same in R. C. Majumdar, History
    of Bengal, vol. 1, p. 315, footnote 7) suggested that the Mādhavacikitsita
    is not a separate work, different from the Nidāna. He holds the view
    that the Cikitsā of Mādhava is either identical with the Rugviniścaya
    or represents a version of it. He refers to R. Mitra's Bikāner Catalogue
    (nr. 1413, p. 647-648) and says that the two opening verses, quoted by
    R. Mitra, are nothing else than the third and fourth verse of the Rugvinīś-
    caya, while the only concluding verse cited, which is too corrupt for
    identification, deals apparently with viṣaroganidāna (the origins of dis-
    ease by poison), which forms the subject matter of the concluding chap-
    ter of the Rugviniścaya. S. K. De is right in observing that the manu-
    script, described by R. Mitra, begins in the same way as the Nidāna,
    but it must contain the text of the Mādhavacikitsā or part of it as well,
    for the concluding verse, cited by Mitra, does not occur in chapter 69
    on viṣaroganidāna of the Rogaviniścaya, and, corrupt though it is, it


=== Page 21 ===
                                INTRODUCTION                                  9

does not deal with *nidāna*, but, clearly, with *cikitṣā*. S. K. De probably
thought that it deals with *viṣaroganidāna* because the last word of the
first line of the stanza is *viṣabheṣajam*. This term, literally meaning ‘a
remedy for poison’, is absent from chapter 69 of the Nidāna and may,
taken on its own, already point to a treatise on therapy. The second
*pāda* of the verse quoted by R. Mitra reads : *nagaraṁ viṣabheṣajam*; this
should be corrected into *nāgaraṁ viṣabheṣajam* (i.e. dry ginger is a reme-
dy for poison) or *nāgaraṁ viśvabheṣajam* (both *nāgara* and *viśvabheṣaja*
denote ginger); moreover, *pārada* (mercury) and *bījapūra* (a kind of
citrus fruit) are mentioned in the same stanza. These indications suffice
for me to disagree with S. K. De and to say that it is not open to doubt
that the manuscript contains the Mādhavacikitsā, completely or par-
tially.

        Another manuscript of the *Mādhavacikitsita*, undoubtedly containing
the text of Mādhava’s treatise on therapy, is described by Har Dutt
Sharma (Cat.Skt.Mss. BORI, vol. 16, part 1, nr. 143, p. 177-178). This
manuscript, erroneously catalogued as being probably a manuscript of
the Mādhavanidāna in Aufrecht’s Catalogus Catalogorum (vol. 1, p. 449),
is complete or almost complete. It is said to appear very old, consists of
102 leaves and its total number of verses is 1693. The work follows the
order of diseases as presented in the Mādhavanidāna. Its colophon runs :
*iti candrakarātmajāvaidyarājaviracite* (read : -*viracitam*) *cikitsāsūtraparī-
bhāṣāsūtrasahitaṁ mādhavacikitsitaṁ samāptam*, i.e. : “Thus has been
completed the Mādhavacikitsita, together with the Cikitsāsūtra and
Paribhāṣāsūtra, composed by *vaidyarāja* Mādhava, the son of Candra-
kara”. The meaning of Cikitsāsūtra and Paribhāṣāsūtra, connected in
this way with the Cikitsita, is not clear. The manuscript may contain
sections on general rules of treatment (*cikitsāsūtra*) and on definitions of
technical terms (*paribhāṣā*). If this be so, they are probably found at the
end of the Cikitsita, for it begins with the treatment of fever. A section
on general therapeutic topics also forms part of the Siddhayoga (chap-
ters 69-82) and a section on *paribhāṣā* is included in that on *māna*
(measures), which is appended to Mādhava’s Paryāyaratnamālā (1642-
1754). A manuscript of a work, called Mādhavacikitsā by Mādhavakara,
which may be the Mādhavacikitsita, is present in the collection Cordier
of the Bibliothèque Nationale of Paris (Filliozat, JA, t. 224, 1934, p.
159, nr. 87). No particulars about this manuscript are given, except that
it consists of 81 folios, and it is not clear whether it is an independent
manuscript or a copy. N. N. Das Gupta has stated (IC 3, 1936-37, p.
155) that Mādhava wrote his Cikitsā as a supplement to the Nidāna,


=== Page 22 ===
10                                INTRODUCTION

explicitly setting down in the introduction to the work that he composed
it after the Nīḍāna. N. N. Das Gupta refers to R. Mitra’s Bikāner cata-
logue, which remains unintelligible to me, unless he studied the manu-
script itself and read more of it than the lines quoted by Mitra, and to
G. Bühler’s Gujārāt catalogue (fasc. 4, p. 230; this fascicle was inaccess-

commentary on the Siddhayoga, according to to N. N. Das Gupta (IC 3,

stanza of the Mādhavacikitsita, as presented by the Poona manuscript;
2) probably on 1, 25; Mādhava is said to be the source, but the name
of the work is not mentioned; 3) in the comment on 61, 9; Mādhava is
quoted, but the title of the work is omitted; it may be a quotation taken
from some other work by Mādhava. Mādhava’s treatise on therapy was
also known to Niścalakara, who refers to it as the Mādhavasamgraha

and Ātaṅkadarpaṇa, which I could only trace to the Siddhayoga (see
App. 1), may originally have been taken from the Mādhavacikitsita; this,
however, cannot be verified at the present time, because the Mādhava-
cikitsita has not been edited.
(3) The Pāryāyaratnamālā, or, as Mādhava calls the work himself,
Ratnamālā, has been critically edited by Dr. Tarapada Chowdhury
(Patna, 1946). The work is a synonymous medical lexicon, written in
verse; it also contains a section on homonyms and, as already stated,
a section on measures (_māna_), the latter including the definition of tech-
nical terms (_paribhāṣā_); the vernacular words for the medicinal sub-
stances dealt with are added. Mādhava’s Pāryāyaratnamālā is, after the
Dhanvantarīy anighaṇṭu, the oldest extant medical lexicon (_nighaṇṭu_).
At the end of the work Mādhava mentions his name (Mādhava) and
place of residence (Śīlāhrada), the title of the work (Ratnamālā) and his
father’s name (Indrakara). Eight manuscripts are described by Chow-
dhury in his introduction. In addition to these, he made use of a printed
edition and the material contained in the Śabdakalpadruma and Ume-
śacandra Gupta’s Vaidyakaśabdasiṅdhu, the authors of which often
quote from the Ratnamālā and have had access to independent manu-
scripts. Among the eight manuscripts, which have been made use of by
Chowdhury to establish a reliable text, there is only one that reaches
the end (Cat.Skt.Mss. Calcutta Sanskrit College, vol. 10, nr. 51, p. 41;

Chowdhury must be in error here, for the Ms. is not described in vol. 10);

In my opinion the Ratnamālā can without much doubt be regarded as
an authentic work by Mādhava, the author of the Rogaviniścaya. It is
repeatedly quoted and referred to by later authors and commentators
and appears to have been rather well known. Careful consideration is
required, however, before quotations and references are assigned to
Mādhava’s medical lexicon. There is another Paryāyaratnamālā, written
by Maheśvara Miśra; a manuscript of this work is in the Bibliothèque
Nationale of Paris (see Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, p. 976; Cat.Cat. 1, p. 330).
Govardhana, a prolific medical author and commentator, who is later
than Mādhava, also wrote a Ratnamālā; this Govardhana is one of
Nīścalakara’s most distinguished authorities (Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p.
141). Mādhava’s Ratnamālā is quoted by Vandyaghatīya-Sarvānanda in
his commentary, called Tīkāsarvasva, on Amarasiṃha’s Nāmalingānu-
śāsana. This commentary was composed in 1159, as indicated by the
author himself (on kālavarga 21; see Gaṇapati Śāstrī’s introduction to
the edition of the work). Mādhava is quoted at least five times (vol. 1,
p. 112 : tathā ca ratnamālā = Ratnamālā 1324; vol. 1, p. 203 : iti ratna-
mālāyāṃ mādhavaḥ = Ratnamālā 185-186; vol. 2, p. 81 : iti mādhavaḥ =
Ratnamālā 348; vol. 3, p. 245 : tathā ca ślokārdhaparyāye mādhavaḥ =

Ratnamālā 439; ibid. : *iti ślokaparyāye mādhavah* = Ratnamālā 451

Mādhavakara is clearly referred to by Haricaraṇasena in the introduc-
tory stanzas of his Paryāyamuktāvalī, which was composed at an un-
known date. From these stanzas it can be inferred that the work was
based on that by Mādhava.

The Paryāyaratnamālā is probably quoted once in the Madhukośa (on
2, 10-11); the quotation is introduced by *yad uktam*, without specifica-
tion of the source. The same quotation occurs in the Ātaṅkadarpaṇa (on
the same passage), where it is said to be taken from a work called Abhi-
dhāna, a very vague indication. The quoted words are identical with
Paryāyaratnamālā 1506b, but may be from a different work, because it
is a known fact that lexicographers often took their material from pre-
decessors without specifying their sources. Moreover, there is a medical
lexicon by an unknown author that is called Abhidhānaratnamālā
(Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, nr. 2741 and 2742, p. 976-977).

(4) Praśnavidhāna. This work is once referred to by Vijayarakṣita (on
1, 14cd-15ab) in a discussion about the constitutions. He says that this
subject is extensively dealt with in the Praśnavidhāna, which should be
consulted (a variant, found in two manuscripts, reads Praśnasahasrani-
dāna) and calls it a *suśrutaślokavārtika*, i.e. versified glosses on the Su-
śrutasamhitā, without indicating, however, that it was composed by
Mādhava. The same work is twice referred to by Niścalakara, who calls
it Praśnasahasravidhāna, i.e. 'Exposition on thousand questions' and
instructs us about the author, Mādhava, because he once calls him
*suśrutavārtikakāra*, i.e. the author of the glosses on Suśruta (see Bhatt.,
IHQ 23, 1947, p. 144).


=== Page 25 ===
INTRODUCTION 13

(5) Yogavyākhyā is the title of a work by Mādhava, quoted twice by
Nīścalakara (Bhatt., l.c., p. 146). Bhaṭṭachāryya is in error when he
asserts (l.c., p. 153) that Nīścalakara gives the names of two new works
by Mādhava, viz. the Yogavyākhyā and the Suśrutavārtika. The latter
is, as we have seen, referred to by Vijayarakṣita, a fact noticed by
Bhaṭṭachāryya himself (l.c., p. 144), though it is right to claim that
Nīścalakara is the first authority known to us who assigns the work to
Mādhava. The Yogavyākhyā, however, is quoted as a work by Mādhava-
kara in Śrīkaṇṭhadatta's Kusumāvalī (on Siddhayoga 10, 47cd), though
this may have escaped his attention and that of other scholars. The
Yogavyākhyā may have been a work on medicinal compounds, to judge
by Śrīkaṇṭhadatta's quotation.

(6) Dravyaguṇa. A work of this name by Mādhavakara is referred
by Śivadāsasena in his commentary on Cakrapāṇidatta's Cikitsāsam-
graha (acc. to N. N. Das Gupta, IC 3, 1936-37, p. 155; he refers to p.
155 of the first ed. by Devendra Nath Sen, which was inaccessible to me;
the reference could not be traced in the ed. by Śrījayadeva Vidyālam-
kāra, Lahore, 1928). Nīścalakara also refers to it once in his Ratnaprabhā
(Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 143). An author, called Mādhavakāra, is quoted
seven times by Hemādri in his commentary on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasam-
hitā. Once (on A.h.Sū. 7, 40-41ab; see App. 3 : maireya) he quotes in
this way from the Paryāyaratnamālā (a variant of ardhaśloka 1664), the
other times probably from Mādhava's Dravyaguṇa (on A.h.Sū. 6, 75cd-
78; Sū. 6, 82; Sū. 6, 97cd-98ab; Sū. 6, 99cd; Sū. 6, 137cd-138; Sū. 6,
161cd-163ab). It is not quite clear whether the text of Mādhava's Dra-
vyaguṇa is still available in one or more manuscripts. An edition of a
work, called Dravyaguṇa, by an author whose name is Mādhava, is
planned by P. V. Sharma (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series). For two rea-
sons more information is required about the nature of this text and the
identity of its author. Firstly, there is a work by a later author, also
called Mādhava, which, though usually called Bhāvasvabhāva, is some-
times referred to as Dravyaguṇasamgraha (Cordier, Le Muséon, N.S. 4,
1903, p. 345-346). Secondly, at least one manuscript has been described
of a work, called Dravyaguṇaratnamālā, by an author whose name is
Mādhava (Cat.Skt.Mss. N.-W.P. 1, p. 590-591, nr. 28 : old and incorrect;
not well-known ; procurable with difficulty for copying). This manuscript
is said to contain rules for preparing different medicines and their bene-
fits. If its text really agrees with this description, it must be different
from the Paryāyaratnamālā and from a text on Dravyaguṇa in its proper
sense, but it may be the supposedly lost Yogavyākhyā.

                                          INTRODUCTION

(7) Mādhava's commentary or commentaries. Mādhavakara is once
mentioned by Vijayarakṣita among a series of authors of explanatory
works (Madhukośa on 1, 5d-6 : Jejjaṭa-Vāpyacandra-Mādhavakara-
Kārtikakuṇḍa) in a passage that refers to Su.U. 39, 27, a stanza that
was incorporated in the Mādhavanidāna by Vācaspati (see Āṭaṅkadar-
paṇa on 2, 6). It is unlikely that Mādhavakara should form one of this
company, unless he wrote a commentary himself. Though it may be
argued that he is a member of this group as the author of the Praśnavini-
dhāna, this is improbable because that work was a metrical vārtika. More-
over, Śrīmādhava is mentioned as the author of a ṭippaṇa on the Suśruta-
saṁhitā by Ḍalhaṇa in the introduction to his commentary on that work.
Finally, Vācaspati quotes (on 5, 31-32 = Ca.Ci. 14, 21-22) an explanation
by Mādhava that seems to be taken from a commentary in prose (the
same quotation occurs in the Madhukośa where it is not attributed to
Mādhava in an explicit way). So it is not unreasonable to suppose that
Mādhava wrote a commentary on the Suśrutasaṁhitā, and, may be, on
the Carakasaṁhitā as well.

     As already remarked, there have been, apart from the author of the
Rogaviniścaya, more medical authors, called Mādhava. Two works which
have remained unmentioned so far are sometimes attributed to the
author of the Rogaviniścaya. One of these is the Kūṭamudgara, ascribed
to him in the Cat.Cat. (1, p. 449), New Cat.Cat. (vol. 4, p. 260-261) and
by N. N. Das Gupta (IC 3, 1936-37, p. 155), while S. K. De notes (NIA 2,
1939-49, p. 273, footnote 8; the same in R. C. Majumdar, The History
of Bengal, vol. 1, p. 315, footnote 7) that there is nothing to identify
its author with the author of the Rugviniścaya. The Kūṭamudgara is a
short treatise on regimen of twenty-two verses that would be unintelli-
gible without a commentary. One manuscript has been described by
Jolly (Cat.Skt.Mss. München, nr. 394, p. 62-63), who observed that the
author is called Mādhava and that the anonymous commentary may be
by the same person; no particulars about this Mādhava are given. Six
manuscripts are at Poona (Cat.Skt.Mss. BORI, vol. 16, part 1, p. 63-68,
nr. 51-56); the author of both text and commentary calls himself Mā-
dhava, without adding any information about his lineage. Any judgment
on the authorship of the treatise should be suspended until it has been
thoroughly studied.

     The second work that is sometimes ascribed to the author of the
Rogaviniścaya is called Bhāvasvabhāva. Cordier described it as a
manual of materia medica and hygiene (Le Muséon, N.S. 4, 1903,


=== Page 27 ===
INTRODUCTION                                                                       15

p. 345-346). Two manuscripts were known to him (one in the collection
Hodgson, catalogued by Cowell and Eggeling : Buddhist Skt.Mss.
nr. 74, under the title : *Dravyaguṇasaṁgraha*, and another one
mentioned in the lists of the Bhau Dāji Memorial). S. K. De
noted (NIA 2, 1939-40, p. 273, footnote 8) that a third manuscript is
described in Bühler's *Gujarāt* catalogue (G. Bühler, Catalogue of Skt.
Mss. contained in the private libraries of Gujarāt, Kāṭhiāvād, Kachchh,
Sindh and Khaṇḍeś, fasc. 4, p. 230 ; Cat.Cat. 1, p. 408). There is also
a manuscript in the collection Cordier of the Bibliothèque Nationale of
Paris (Filliozat, JA, t. 224, 1934, p. 159, nr. 79). Haraprasād Śāstrī
discovered an incomplete manuscript (almost complete according to
Cordier : Le Muséon, N.S. 4, 1903, p. 345) of a commentary on the
Bhāvasvabhāva in Nepāl. He wrote about it : "The Bhāvasvabhāva is
a well-known medical work by Mādhavadeva, perhaps the same as Mā-
dhavakara, the author of the *Nidāna*. A commentary to the work, en-
titled *Vaidyavallabhā* (unknown to Aufrecht in his Cat.Cat.), by Megha-
deva, the son of Ravinābha, has been acquired for Government. The
work is incomplete and consists of 68 leaves; it treats of the properties
of the articles of food and drink". Cordier (l.c.) added that Meghadeva
imputes the composition of the work to Mādhavakara and says that his
elucidations are really due to Indumatī. Cordier put forward that this
Indumatī might be identical with Indu, the author of a commentary on
the *Aṣṭāṅgasaṁgraha*. Acc. to N. N. Das Gupta (IC 3, 1936-37, p. 155)
the Bhāvasvabhāva was written by a Mādhava who was later than the
author of the *Rogaviniścaya*. In this case too we have to await more
detailed studies which may throw light on the chronological position
of the text.

Mādhava Upādhyāya, who wrote the medical treatise called *Āyurve-
daprakāśa*, is without any doubt posterior to the author of the *Roga-
viniścaya*. This Mādhava himself stated that he belonged to the Sāras-
vatakula of Saurāṣṭra and was a resident of Benares. The *Āyurveda-
prakāśa* is a rather late work because it quotes from Trimallabhaṭṭa's
*Yogatarangiṇī* (see App. 2 : *Yogatarangiṇī*; see about the *Āyurveda-
prakāśa* : Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, nr. 2696 and 2697, p. 950-951 ; Cat.Skt.Mss.
BORI, vol. 16, part 1, nr. 19 and 20, p. 22-25 and nr. 133 and 134, p.
157-160 ; R. G. Bhandarkar, Lists of Skt.Mss. in private libraries in the
Bombay Presidency, part 1, p. 115, nr. 228 ; Śivaśarmā's introduction
to the edition of the text by Gulrājśarmā Miśra). Mādhava Upādhyāya
also wrote the *Rasasiddhiprakāśa* (Cat.Skt.Mss. BORI, vol. 16, part 1,
nr. 224, p. 279-280).

A work, called Rasakaumudī, has been ascribed to Mādhava, the son
of Indukara, by R. Mitra (Notices of Skt.Mss., vol. 4, p. 178, nr. 1616,
acc. to N. N. Das Gupta, IC 3, 1936-37, p. 156, footnote 1) and Aufrecht
(Cat.Cat. 1, p. 449). P. Rāy (History of chemistry, p. 229) places the work
in the 16th or 17th century. N. N. Das Gupta (l.c., p. 156) and S. K. De
(NIA 2, 1939-40, p. 273, footnote 8; the same in R. C. Majumdar, The
history of Bengal, vol. 1, p. 315, footnote 7) agree that this work is of
a later date than the Rogaviniścaya.
The author of the Ayurvedarasasāstra, also attributed to Mādhava,
the son of Indukara, by Aufrecht (Cat.Cat. 1, p. 449) is probably different
again from the author of the Mādhavanidāna (New Cat. Cat. 2, p. 153;
N. N. Das Gupta, l.c., p. 156; S. K. De, l.c., p. 273, footnote 8).
Apart from these medical authors, called Mādhava, there have been
many others of the same name (see e.g. Śivaśarmā's introduction to the
edition of the Āyurvedaprakāśa by Gulrājsarmā Miśra, p. 2-3). Some
recent authors still confuse a great number of Mādhava's and present
a very composite, but impressive, picture of Mādhava to their readers
(see e.g. Jaggi's Scientists of ancient India and their achievements,
p. 104-106).

Returning now to the author of the Mādhavanidāna, we are faced
with the task of determining his date.
The terminus post quem has to be deduced from the sources Mādhava
employed in the composition of the work. The other treatises are of no
avail in elucidating the lower limit of the period in which Mādhava must
have lived; the sources of the Paryāyaratnamālā have not yet been
subject to research; the Mādhavacikitsita, which will undoubtedly con-
tain much evidence supplementing that of the Nidāna, awaits study of
its contents in almost all respects.
The Nidāna consists, for the greater part, of stanzas borrowed from
the three classical medical samhitās, the Carakasamhitā, the Suśruta-
samhitā and Vāgbhaṭa's Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasamhitā, while a small number
of verses has been taken from the Aṣṭāṅgasaṁgraha, attributed to
Vāgbhaṭa; the remaining ones are from unidentified treatises or were
composed by Mādhava himself (see App. 1). With regard to Mādhava's
sources there has been some disagreement among scholars in the past,
as will presently be explained.
The terminus ante quem of the Nidāna depends, firstly, on the date
or Vṛnda, who explicitly refers to it, and, secondly, on the answer to
the question whether a certain Indian medical treatise, known to early


=== Page 29 ===
                 INTRODUCTION                               17

Arabic authors, is identical with the Mādhavanidāna. Most scholars
assent to the view that Mādhava borrowed from the Carakasaṁhitā, but
it should always be specified whether this holds true with regard to the
Carakasaṁhitā after its completion by Dṛḍhabala, because the latter is
often assigned to a later period than Mādhava (see App. 2 : Caraka,
Dṛḍhabala). It is not open to doubt that the Nidāna contains many
stanzas taken from the Suśrutasaṁhitā, also from its Uttarātantra that
was added later (see App. 2 : Suśruta, Nāgārjuna). Mādhava's indebted-
ness to the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṁhitā and Aṣṭāṅgasaṁgraha is usually
admitted; the priority of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṁhitā has only been
questioned by Hoernle. If we accept that Mādhava lived when the
Caraka- and Suśrutasaṁhitā had been completed and after the compo-
sition of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṁhitā, his date cannot be earlier than
about 600 (see App. 2 : Vāgbhaṭa).

Hoernle is the only scholar who has seriously investigated Mādhava's
sources and has tried to fix his date, and, though his views are anti-
quated now, they deserve to be mentioned, because they have been in-
fluential for a considerable time. He thought that Mādhava had preceded
Dṛḍhabala and adduced two arguments to sustain his thesis. The first
was that Mādhava was not acquainted with the so-called kāśmīrapāṭha
of the Carakasaṁhitā, identified by Hoernle with Dṛḍhabala's recension
of the work. This argument does not bear proof, firstly because there is
evidence that the kāśmīrapāṭha was known to Mādhava, and, secondly,
because there is no certainty that the kāśmīrapāṭha refers to Dṛḍhaba-
la's redaction of the Carakasaṁhitā (see App. 2 : Caraka). Hoernle's se-
cond argument was derived from the number of eye diseases described
in the Carakasaṁhitā, Suśrutasaṁhitā, Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṁhitā, Aṣṭāṅga-
saṁgraha and Nidāna. His line of reasoning was as follows. Seventy-six
eye diseases are enumerated in the Uttarātantra of the Suśrutasaṁhitā
(U. 1, 28-45) ; their number is ninety-four in the Aṣṭāṅgasaṁgraha (see
U. 20, 37), and the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṁhitā (see U. 16, 60cd-61ab) agrees
with it. Mādhava, though abiding by the method of counting of the
Suśrutasaṁhitā, nevertheless increases the total number to seventy-
eight (see chapter 59) by adding two diseases of the eyelashes. Dṛḍha-
bala, attempting to reach a compromise, states the number to be ninety-
six. From these data Hoernle inferred that Dṛḍhabala obtained his total
of ninety-six by adopting the total of ninety-four from the Aṣṭāṅgasaṁ-
graha and adding to it the two new diseases set up by Mādhava, from
which it follows that Mādhava is anterior to Dṛḍhabala. Hoernle's
interpretation of the evidence he collected is rather arbitrary and his


=== Page 30 ===
18

INTRODUCTION

line of reasoning is not convincing. The facts he presents are, when care-
fully considered, both vague and incomplete. He is right in asserting
that seventy-six eye diseases are enumerated in the Suśrutasaṃhitā, but
he omitted to mention that at least seventy-seven eye diseases are de-
scribed; one disease, occurring in children, is added (see Su.U. 19, 8-9).
Moreover, it is not clear what he meant by the two new diseases set up
by Mādhava. He appears to refer to *pakṣmakopa* and *pakṣmaśāta*, but,
if these two entities are really intended, he is in error. *pakṣmakopa* is
not a new disease, described for the first time by Mādhava ; it is already
mentioned in the Suśrutasaṃhitā (U. 3, 29-30). *pakṣmaśāta*, on the other
hand, may be a term borrowed by Mādhava from some unidentified
treatise; Śrīkaṇṭhadatta equates it with *kṛcchronmīla*, described by
Vāgbhaṭa (A.H.U. 8, 3-4); if Śrīkaṇṭhadatta is right, it is not a new
disease but another name of a well-known disorder. It may be, however,
that one of the two diseases meant by Hoernle is *kuñcana* ; this entity
was borrowed by Mādhava from ‘some other treatise’, as Śrīkaṇṭhadatta
says (Madhukośa on 59, 96). It is inadmissible to conclude that Dṛḍha-
bala’s number of eye diseases is a compromise between the numbers of
Vāgbhaṭa and Mādhava. Therefore this piece of evidence concerning
Dṛḍhabala’s posterity to Mādhava, put forward by Hoernle, can be
set aside.

Hoernle was also convinced that Mādhava was later than the author
of the Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha (called Vāgbhaṭa I by Hoernle) and earlier than
the author of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā (called Vāgbhaṭa II by Hoern-
le). The latter point is easily explained. As we have seen, Hoernle re-
garded Dṛḍhabala as posterior to Mādhava. Dṛḍhabala preceded Vāg-
bhaṭa II because a particular chapter from the Carakasaṃhitā (Ci. 26),
redacted by Dṛḍhabala, is referred to in the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā
(U. 40, 84). In addition to this, Aruṇadatta observes in his commentary
on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā that a particular stanza (Śā. 3, 62cd-63ab)
was taken from a chapter of the Carakasaṃhitā (Ci. 15), which was also
redacted by Dṛḍhabala. (See about Hoernle’s views : JRAS, 1908, p.
1016-1018, and the Introduction to his Osteology, p. 14-16). Hoernle was
right in regarding Dṛḍhabala as a predecessor of Vāgbhaṭa who compo-
sed the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā, but he was wrong in assuming Mādhava
to be anterior to the latter. All the available data point to Mādhava as
an author who was acquainted with Vāgbhaṭa’s work. He borrowed
extensively from it, especially in chapters 1, 5 and 7 (see App. 1). There
is no evidence in favour of the supposition that he composed series of
stanzas which were incorporated in the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā at a later


=== Page 31 ===
INTRODUCTION                                                                    19

date. On the contrary, Vijayarakṣita explicitly refers to Vāgbhaṭa when
commenting on passages of the Nidāna which were borrowed from the
Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā (see Madhukośa on 1, 5d-6 and 1, 10). Moreover,
Mādhava expressly states that his work was compiled from 'the words
of various sages' (Nidāna 1, 2). So it may be assumed that Mādhava was
later than the author of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā, i.e. later than about
600 (see App. 2 : Vāgbhaṭa). The complicated way in which Hoernle tried
to establish (JRAS, 1908, p. 1002-1028) that the author of the Aṣṭāṅga-
saṃgraha was anterior to Mādhava is of no importance any more, since it
can safely be admitted that the Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha was gradually elabor-
ated after the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā had been written (see App. 2 :
Vāgbhaṭa).

       Finally we have to consider the date before which the Nidāna was
composed.
       In this respect it should firstly be recalled that the Mādhavanidāna
is referred to to by Vṛnda in his Siddhayoga. So Mādhava is earlier than
Vṛnda, who lived about 800-900 (see App. 2 : Vṛndakuṇḍa). Secondly,
it has already long been common knowledge that various Arabic authors
mention an Indian medical treatise that may well be Mādhava's Roga-
viniścaya. The older material on this subject was collected by A. Müller
(Arabische Quellen zur Geschichte der indischen Medizin, ZDMG 34,
1880, p. 465-556). A number of Indian medical works is recorded by
Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa (who died in 1270, acc. to EI², vol. 3, p. 693) in the
twelfth book of his History of physicians, the ‘Uyūn al-anbā’ fī ṭabaqāt
al-aṭibbā’. The title of one of these treatises is written bdān (a variant
reads ydān); this word is usually vocalized as Badān, though it is equally
admissible to read Bidān. A. Müller prefers the reading bdān to ydān, but
remains neutral with regard to the conjecture ndān, i.e. Nidān, proposed
by Dietz in his Analecta Medica (p. 122), because the name Badān is
already found in al-Rāzī’s Kitāb al-ḥāwī (A. Müller, l.c., p. 475; al-Rāzī
died in 925, acc. to Sezgin, Bd. III, p. 275). Uṣaybiʿa observes (A. Mül-
ler, ibid.) that the signs of 404 diseases are described in the work, without
indicating their treatment. This characterization points to the Mādhava-
nidāna and not to the Nidāna section of one of the classical saṃhitās,
because only a restricted number of disorders is dealt with in the latter
under that heading. The Nidāna is also mentioned by the Arab historian
Ibn Wāḍiḥ al-Yaʿqūbī (M. Z. Siddiqi, Indo-Asian Culture 5, 1957, p. 279).
This author, who is earlier than Uṣaybiʿa and al-Rāzī (he lived in the
second half of the ninth century, acc. to Nicholson, p. 349), describes


=== Page 32 ===
20                               INTRODUCTION

the work in the same way as Usaybi‘a. Important new evidence came
to light in 1928 with the edition of ‘Ali b. Sahl al-Ṭabarī’s Firdaws al-
ḥikma, i.e. Paradise of wisdom. In the so-called Indian books of this
treatise several Indian medical works are mentioned : jrk, ssrd, ndān
and asḥṭānghṛdy, i.e. Caraka, Suśruta, Nidāna and Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya. It is
highly probable that ndān is the Mādhavanidāna, because no other fa-
mous Indian book with a similar title could have spread to the Arab
world at so early a date (about 850). This reference to the Nidāna is the
earliest one known in Arab literature. Because of its importance it is
now expedient to give a summary of the most important facts about the
work and its author. (For fuller accounts see Meyerhof’s articles : ZDMG
85, 1931, p. 38-68 and Isis 16, 1931, p. 6-54; compare the introduction
to the translation of the Indian books by Siggel, who disagrees with
Meyerhof on a number of points; those versed in Arabic may read Siddi-
qi’s introduction to his edition of the Firdaws al-ḥikma).

Abū’l Ḥasan ‘Ali b. Sahl Rabban al-Ṭabarī wrote his Firdaws al-
ḥikma fī ’l-ṭibb in Sāmarrā in the third year of the reign of the caliph
al-Mutawakkil, i.e. in 849-850. It is a work of large scope, giving a survey
of the Greek, Syrian and Indian systems of medicine as known to the
Muslims. Its arrangement is less methodical than in later medical works
in Arabic, but it is often quoted by al-Rāzī and other writers. Particu-
larly important is the thirtieth and last section of the Paradise of wisdom,
which deals with Indian medicine. It describes succinctly in thirty-six
chapters, the majority of which are rather short, the theory and general
therapeutic principles of Indian medicine, while at the end a number
of recipes is found. According to Meyerhof (ZDMG 85, 1931, p. 64) the
translation of Sanskrit medical terms into Arabic is usually correct,
which indicates that ‘Ali b. Sahl made use of the translations of Sanskrit
medical works executed by order of the first ‘Abbāsid caliphs, in particu-
lar Hārūn al-Rashīd (768-809) and the Barmakids. (See also M. Z. Siddiqi,
Indo-Asian Culture 5, 1957, p. 374-378. Siggel holds the view that ‘Ali
b. Sahl based his work on earlier translations of Indian texts into
Syriac or Persian; see the introduction to his translation, p. 1102).

The Nidāna as a separate book is mentioned once in the Indian books
of the Paradise of wisdom (see p. 1110 of Siggel’s translation). The term
Nidāna appears on two other occasions (p. 1116 and 1131 of Siggel’s
translation), where, however, it is not the Mādhavanidāna which is re-
ferred to, but the Nidāna section of some other treatise. No direct trans-
lation of parts of the Mādhavanidāna are traceable, nor of the Caraka-
samḥitā, Suśrutasamḥitā and Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasamḥitā, for ‘Ali b. Sahl
only gives summaries of Indian medical doctrines.


=== Page 33 ===
INTRODUCTION                                            21

Accepting the evidence afforded by ‘Ali b. Sahl and later Arabic
authors, it appears reasonable to suppose that Mādhava’s date is about
700, taking into account the time needed for the work of an Indian
writer to become so famous as to be translated into Arabic in Persia
and to be employed as one of his chief sources by an Arabic author in
849-850.

THE COMMENTARIES ON THE MĀDHAVANIDĀNA

A great number of commentaries has been written on Mādhava’s Roga-
viniścaya, which proves that the work achieved considerable fame. The
following are known to us :

(1) Madhukośa by Vijayarakṣita and Śrīkaṇṭhadatta. Jolly described a
    manuscript (Cat.Skt.Mss. München, nr. 378, p. 52-53) the text of
    which is partially more extensive than the printed editions and
    which also contains more quotations.
(2) Ātaṅkadarpaṇa by Vācaspati.
(3) Siddhāntacintāmaṇi (Cat.Cat. 2, p. 124). Eggeling, who described a
    manuscript of this work (Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, nr. 2670, p. 935-936),
    says that it was written by Narasimha Kavirāja, assistant of Rāma-
    kṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa and son of Nīlakaṇṭha Bhaṭṭa. Eggeling adds that the
    author refers to his commentary on the Carakasamhitā that was
    called Carakatattvaprakāśakaustubhaṭīkā and frequently adduces
    Caraka in illustration of Mādhava’s precepts, whilst quotations from
    Suśruta are much rarer. This commentary appears to be the same
    as the Siddhāntacandrikā by Narasimha Kavirāja, son of Nīla-
    kaṇṭha Bhaṭṭa and pupil of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa, mentioned by Das-
    gupta (H.I.Ph. 2, p. 434, footnote 2), who says that the work,
    though based on the Madhukośa, is an excellent commentary, con-
    taining much that is both instructive and new. Dasgupta (errone-
    ously) supposed that probably the only manuscript available was
    the one belonging to the library of his family; an edition was plan-
    ned by him, but it never appeared. Aufrecht also recorded a manu-
    script of the Siddhāntacandrikā (Cat.Cat. 1, p. 527).
(4) Subodhinī; this work consists of short glosses on difficult portions
    of the Nidāna and was written by Vādeva (Vāsudeva ?) Māthura
    (Cat.Cat. 3, p. 112; Cat.Skt.Mss. München, nr. 380, p. 53-54; Cat.
    Skt.Mss. BORI, vol. 16, part 1, nr. 152, p. 187-188).
(5) Mādhavanidānaṭippaṇi by Bhāvamiśra (Cordier, Le Muséon, N.S. 4,

A work, sometimes said to be a commentary on the Mādhavanidāna
(Cat.Cat. 1, p. 527; R. Mitra's Bikāner catalogue, p. 652; Dasgupta,
H.I.Ph. 2, p. 434) is the Nidānapradīpa by Nāganātha, the eldest son
of Kṛṣṇabhaṭṭa. Eggeling observed (Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, nr. 2671, p. 936)
that it is rather surprising that Mādhava is never once alluded to by
Nāganātha, unless, indeed, the title of the work is meant to imply that
the work is intended to be an exposition or paraphrase of the Mādhava-
nidāna. According to Jolly (Cat.Skt.Mss. München, nr. 381, p. 54-55)
the Nidānapradīpa is an extensive treatise in verse on pathology and
not a commentary on the Nidāna.

VIJAYARAKṢITA is the author of the first half of the Madhukośa. His
share ends with the comments on chapter thirty-two. Why he did not
complete his commentary is a matter of uncertainty, but probably death
intervened. No other works of his hand are known. Nīścalakara affords
information about Vijayarakṣita's death, for he notes (in the fifth stanza
of his introduction to the Ratnaprabhā, acc. to Gode, St. I.L.H. 1, p.
124, footnote 1) that he started writing his commentary after the death


=== Page 35 ===
INTRODUCTION                                                                          23

of Vijayarakṣita, who was his teacher. Taking into account that the
Ratnaprabhā was composed between 1110 and 1120 according to Bhaṭṭa-
chāryya (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 134), Vijayarakṣita's death must have oc-
curred some time before that decade. If Bhaṭṭachāryya is right in stating
that Niścalakara was undoubtedly a native of Bengal (l.c., p. 128-129),
it may be safely assumed that Vijayarakṣita lived there too. The argu-
ments adduced by Bhaṭṭachāryya to prove Niścalakara's Bengal origin
are based on the ending -kara of his name and that of his father, on the
fact that he refers to different localities of Bengal and, finally, on the
local names of medicinal plants recorded in the Ratnaprabhā. Vijayarakṣi-
ta may have been in charge of an *ārogyaśālā* (hospital), for he is called
*ārogyaśālyavaidyapati* in the colophons of some old manuscripts of the
Madhukośa (Cat.Skt.Mss. BORI, vol. 16, part 1, p. 178-179, nr. 144, a
manuscript dated 1363; Bhaṭṭ. also refers to R. Mitra's Bikāner cata-
logue, p. 649).

According to N. N. Das Gupta (IC 3, 1936-37, p. 160) the term *ārogya-
śālīya* is not easy to explain; he observes that it is an epithet of Śākya-
muni (i.e. Buddha) and Avalokiteśvara, but adds that he does not con-
sider this to be a proof that Vijayarakṣita openly professed Buddhism
in the age he lived. N. N. Das Gupta adheres to Hoernle's date of Vi-
jayarakṣita (about 1240), which explains his difficulties, because Bud-
dhism had declined in Bengal at that time. Bhaṭṭachāryya (IHQ 23,
1947, p. 127-134) has contributed a great deal to the elucidation of
Vijayarakṣita's date, which was erroneously fixed by Hoernle at about
1240 (Osteology, Introduction p. 17). He noticed that Niścalakara has
recorded the names of some of his distinguished patients; among these
there was a Buddhist monk and scholar called Śākyarakṣita. This is
only one of a whole series of references to Buddhism in the Ratnaprabhā,
though Niścalakara himself professed Śaivism. Śāntideva's Bodhicaryā-
*vatāra* is referred to and Dharmakīrti is quoted; it is said that a particu-
lar medicine should be taken after paying obeisance to Khasarpaṇa, a
particular manifestation of Lokeśvara, who is, in his turn, an emanation
of Amitābha (see Sādhanamālā, vol. 2, Introduction, p. 152-155); Kha-
sarpaṇa is also the name of a village in the Khāḍimaṇḍala (Sādhanamālā,
vol. 1, p. 42-43), located in lower Bengal by Bhaṭṭachāryya (l.c., p. 129).
At some places Hindu and Buddhist scriptures are mentioned side by
side in the Ratnaprabhā. From these data Bhaṭṭachāryya concluded
that Niścalakara undoubtedly flourished when Buddhism was still
reigning supreme in Bengal and certainly before the Muslim armies
destroyed the Buddhist universities of Bihar. This would place Niścala-
kara in the last quarter of the twelfth century at the latest.


=== Page 36 ===
24                                          INTRODUCTION

This conclusion disagrees with the date assigned by Hoernle to Niścala-
kara's teacher, Vijayarakṣita. Therefore Bhattacharyya argues that
Hoernle's date is not correct. Firstly there is a manuscript of the Mādhava-
nidāna which was written in 1210; it is preserved in the Library of
the Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal at Calcutta (its number is G. 4812).
Though this manuscript only contains the text of the Nidāna with a line
by line Newari translation, the name of the work, given in the colophon,
is Śāstramadhukośa. Bhattacharyya holds the opinion that it is thus
called after Vijayarakṣita's commentary. If this view is correct, Vijaya-
rakṣita lived before 1210.
     A more precise date of Niścalakara was derived by Bhattacharyya
from further indications in the Ratnaprabhā. Niścala describes in a vivid
and flowery way an audience given by king Rāmapāla of Bengal to the
king of Kāmarūpa. Bhattacharyya says there is no doubt that the au-
thor was present on that occasion and that the panegyric epithets prove
that the monarch was still alive when Niścala wrote his commentary.
The date of Rāmapāla's reign is fixed by Bhattacharyya at 1078-1120
(IHQ 3, 1927, p. 571-591; Bhatt.'s method is criticized in R. C. Majum-
dar's History of Bengal, vol. 1, p. 180-181). His conclusion is that Niścala-
kara must have written his Ratnaprabhā within the decade 1110-1120.
This date, which may well be correct, leads to the assumption that
Vijayarakṣita may have written the first part of the Madhukośa between
1090 and 1110.
     Bhattacharyya proved beyond any doubt that the way in which
Hoernle determined his date of Vijayarakṣita was completely wrong
(IHQ 23, 1947, p. 130-133). Hoernle held the erroneous view (Osteology,
Introduction p. 17) that Vijayarakṣita controverts a certain doctrine of
Aruṇadatta concerning the structure of the eye (see Madhukośa 59, 29).
Now this comment on Nidāna 59, 29 was written by Śrīkaṇṭhadatta and
not by Vijayarakṣita. Moreover, the interpretation rejected by Śrīkaṇ-
ṭhadatta is not ascribed to an authority called by name; this authority
cannot be Aruṇadatta because the latter's comment on the correspond-
ing passage of the Aṣṭāngahṛdayasaṁhitā (U. 12, 1) is very brief. In
addition, Aruṇadatta is never quoted in the Madhukośa, either by
Vijayarakṣita or by Śrīkaṇṭhadatta, for the simple reason that Aruṇa-
datta is posterior to both; the references to Aruṇadatta in Śrīkaṇṭha-
datta's Kusumāvali may be regarded as interpolations of Nārāyaṇa (see:
Śrīkaṇṭhadatta). Śrīkaṇṭhadatta's note on Nidāna 59, 29 probably re-
fers to an old interpretation, already rejected by Indu (Śaśilekhā on
A.s.U. 15, 1, Trichur edition, vol. 3, p. 109, acc. to Bhatt.). Another


=== Page 37 ===
INTRODUCTION                                            25

point put to use by Hoernle to establish his date of Vijayarakṣita is
a quotation from Guṇākara in the Madhukośa; with this he was also on
the wrong track (see App. 2: Guṇākara). So Hoernle's date of Vijayarakṣi-
ta can be set aside.

The commentary on the first half of the Mādhavanidāna, as written
by Vijayarakṣita, is not as abounding in quotations from authors and
works referred to by name as Niścalakara's Ratnaprabhā evidently is.
It is, however, an independent work not leaning heavily on earlier com-
mentaries, at least as far as any judgment in these matters dares to go,
because many early medical works and commentaries have not been
preserved.

ŚRĪKAṆṬHADATTA wrote the latter half of the Madhukośa, from the com-
ments on chapter thirty-three up to the end. He was a pupil of Vijaya-
rakṣita, as stated by himself in the introduction to his part of the com-
mentary. Probably he completed the work of his teacher after the latter's
death. Śrīkaṇṭhadatta also wrote a commentary on Vṛndakuṇḍa's
Siddhayoga. Bhaṭṭacharyya (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 131) observes of this work,
called Vyākhyākusumāvalī, that scholars did not generally notice that
the printed text (Ānandāśrama Series Nr. 27, first ed. 1894, second ed.
1943) is really a revision by a later author, Nārāyaṇa, who collected
additional notes from Ḍalhaṇa's commentary on the Suśrutasamhitā,
etc.; quotations from Aruṇadatta, Ḍalhaṇa and Hemādri presumably
belong to Nārāyaṇa's interpolations, for all these interpolated notes are
quite untraceable in Niścalakara's expansive commentary on the corres-
ponding passages from Cakrapāṇidatta's Cikitsāsaṁgraha. At the end of
the printed text of the Kusumāvalī, Nārāyaṇa clearly states that he
completed Śrīkaṇṭhadatta's commentary by adding to it notes from
Ḍalhaṇa's commentary, etc. Jolly was led astray by Nārāyaṇa's ad-
ditions to the Kusumāvalī and held that it could not have been written
before the fourteenth century (Medicin, p. 7). A study devoted to this
Nārāyaṇa was written by Gode (St. I.L.H. 2, p. 176-181). Nārāyaṇa states
that he was a brāhmaṇa of nāgaravaṁśa stock and a son of Bhābhallā (prin-
ted text Kusumāvalī) or Bhāmalla (Gode, l.c., p. 176). The evidence collec-
ted by Gode points to Nārāyaṇa as the grandfather of Ananta who wrote a
work, called Kāmasamūha, in 1457. Gode assumed that Nārāyaṇa lived
about 1325-1400, but he departed from Hoernle's date of Vijayarakṣita
and took that date into account, though there was no need to do so.
In my opinion Nārāyaṇa may be assigned to the period 1360-1400. It
is not known to me whether there exist manuscripts of the Kusumāvalī


=== Page 38 ===
26                                      INTRODUCTION

without Nārāyaṇa's interpolations. The work is not quoted or referred
to by Niścalakara, though both Śrīkaṇṭhadatta and Niścalakara were
pupils of Vijayarakṣita.
    A different author, called Śrīkaṇṭha, who wrote the Amṛtavallī, is
quoted by Niścalakara several times (Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 137).
Śrīkaṇṭhadatta's date is closely dependent on that of Niścalakara; as
we have seen, the latter composed his Ratnaprabhā between 1110 and
1120. Śrīkaṇṭhadatta may have written his works in the same period
or somewhat earlier. It is not known with certainty who was the elder
of the two, but it appears reasonable to suppose that Śrīkaṇṭhadatta
was the senior pupil because it was he who completed the work of his
teacher. An indication pointing in the same direction may be that
Śrīkaṇṭhadatta wrote a commentary on the Siddhayoga, a work still
highly esteemed in his age, but soon to be replaced by Cakrapāṇidatta's
Cikitsāsaṁgraha, a commentary on which was written by Niścalakara.
A comparative study of the works of Śrīkaṇṭhadatta and Niścalakara
may throw more light on their mutual relationship.

    VĀCASPATI wrote a commentary on the Mādhavanidāna called Ātaṅka-
darpaṇa. In the introduction to this work the author states that his
father, Pramoda, was chief physician at the court of Hammīra, and that
his elder brother, Raiśarman, was one of the paṇḍits at the court of
Muḥammad Shāh (Aufrecht, Cat. Florentine Skt.Mss., nr. 345; Peterson,
Sixth Report, nr. 460, p. 35-36). Hoernle (Osteology, Introduction p. 17)
identified Hammīra as Amīr Muizzuddin Muḥammad, the celebrated
Muḥammad Ghori, who reigned in Delhi from 1193 to 1205.
    Vācaspati also observes that he has consulted the Madhukośa (Peter-
son, ibid.; Hoernle, ibid.), so he is later than Vijayarakṣita and Śrīkaṇṭha-
datta. Hoernle assigned Vācaspati to about 1260, twenty years after
the supposed date of Vijayarakṣita. The latter, however, lived much
earlier, as we have seen, and an accurate determination of Vācaspati's date
depends on the identification of the patrons of his father and brother.
If Hoernle is right as to the identity of Hammīra, Vācaspati may have
lived about 1220-1240.
    The complete text of the Ātaṅkadarpaṇa has been printed, together
with the Madhukośa (in the first edition of the Mādhavanidāna by Vaidya
Jādavji Tricumji Āchārya, Nirṇaya Sāgar Press, Bombay). Seeing that
it often repeated the Madhukośa, only fragments of it were printed in the
subsequent editions (see the Introduction to the fifth edition, 1955). I
am under the impression that these fragments too are often only repe-

CHAPTER ONE

THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS (CONSISTING OF)
THE ORIGIN, ETC. (PAÑCANIDĀNALAKṢAṆA)

1, 1 : Having paid homage to Śiva, who is the cause of the coming into
      being, continuance and absorption of the universe, who is the door
      to heaven and to liberation from transmigration and the refuge of
      the three worlds,

M :
(The maṅgalācaraṇa ¹ is addressed to Harihara²). After having reflected
upon the writings of the vaidyas ³ Bhaṭṭāra(haricandra), Jejuāṭa, Gadā-
dhara, Vāpyacandra, Śrīcakrapāṇi(datta), Bakula, Īśvarasena, Bhoja,
Īśāna, Kārtika(kuṇḍa), Sukīra and Sudhīra, and of Maitreya and Mādhava
who are the foremost among them, and having studied other scien-
tific works ⁴ as well, I have made this effort (of writing a commentary)...
I have started (to write) this (Madhukośa, i.e.) ‘Store of honey’ of ex-
planations, having collected explanations from various books, as a bee
collects little bits of the juice of flowers from various trees. In the course
of the commentary on (this) book also those (data on) origins (, etc.) are
written down, which have been made use of by Mādhava, (but) have
not been (explicitly) stated ...

1, 2 : This (book, called) ‘The ascertainment of diseases’, containing the
      secondary affections, precursory signals of death, origins and
      signs is, making use of the words of various sages, composed now
      in a succinct way on the request of accomplished physicians.⁵

1, 3 : This very (book) will enable physicians, lacking various treatises
      and possessing little intelligence, to discern a disorder with ease.

M :
The activity of prudent people is not (aroused) without indicating the
contents (of a book), the relation (between title and contents) and (its)
aim. Therefore, in order to point this out, (these) two stanzas are enun-
ciated ...
That book by which ascertainment of, (i.e.) knowledge about, diseases
(is acquired) with regard to their specificity as arising from wind, etc.,


=== Page 42 ===
30
THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS
as being curable or incurable, etc., is composed, (i.e.) written; 'by us' (has
to be supplied) ... (The expression 'containing the secondary affections,
precursory signals of death, origins and signs' points both to the con-
tents of the book and to the relation between the title and the contents).
A secondary affection is another morbid alteration, occasioned by ex-
citement of the morbific entity which starts the disease, as Caraka de-
clares: "An illness, added to an illness, which arises at a later time and
is not in disagreement with its commencement, is called a secondary
affection".⁶

A sign, inevitably pointing to death, is (called) a precursory signal
of death.

An origin is a ground, bringing about the production of a disease.
A sign is a ground indicating a disease; prodrome, symptom, thera-
peutic diagnosis and onset are denominated by this (term). (An 'etymo-
logical' remark is added).

Although the origin also indicates a specific disease, it is denominated
separately in order to substantiate the two kinds of causes as the ground
of production and the ground of apprehension. The terms secondary
affection, etc. will be dealt with in detail as the opportunity arises.

Mādhava says 'making use of the words of various sages' for the
reason that one may ask how the activity of prudent people (can be
aroused) regarding the instruction (about origins, etc.), because things
are thus that the essential nature of the origin, etc. of diseases, being
very subtle, is not an object of knowledge of someone who is not omni-
scient. With these (quoted words) the authoritativeness of the book (and)
its being an expedient to to (arouse) activity ⁷ has been stated. For sages
are called those superior men, who on account of the strength of their
supernatural faculties,⁸ (resulting) from austerities and yoga, are in pos-
session of all that knowledge which pertains to the three (divisions of)
time.

Because one may reflect that, if there were already another book of
this kind by someone else, this one would serve no purpose by reason
of the fact that (medical) practice would be known and so the object (of
the book) would already have been attained, for that reason he says
'(it is composed) now'. A composition of this kind, making use of the
words of various sages, is made now, for the first time, by me.

(It is made) in a succinct, (i.e.) condensed, way.

In that way the fault that it would not lead to activity in those with
a restricted (range of) thinking, by being too extensive, is avoided.

'On the request of accomplished physicians' is said for this reason,


=== Page 43 ===
THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS 31

that the book would be useless if one doubts whether, even when the
book has been written, any physician will occupy himself with it, be-
cause (it may be regarded) to have been made by a person who has not
been recognized (as an expert).
The meaning of 'request' is an entreaty with words like 'Be so kind
as to make a book to render assistance to us'; or it has the sense of an
order; in the latter case the author expresses his modesty.
He says 'lacking various books' because one may doubt if there will
be activity of those possessing little intelligence, by reason of the pro-
fusion of the words of the sages.
This very book will enable to discern a disorder, (i.e.) a disease, in an
easy way; 'it is an instrument (to discern a disorder)' should be sup-
plied.
These words indicate its purpose to be knowledge about diseases;
therapy has to be regarded as the result of this (knowledge). As has
been said in the Caraka(saṃhitā) : “First of all the disease should be
investigated and immediately following upon that the remedial agent;
thereupon the physician should employ a therapeutical measure with
which he is conversant” (Sū. 20, 20).
It is said : 'those possessing little intelligence' because one may raise
the following objection : knowledge about diseases will come about only
by the words of various sages; so what is the use of this book that is
dependent on those (words) ?
('Possessing little intelligence') means with a restricted (range of)
thought, for people with a great (range of) thought are competent to
study the various extensive books which are difficult to master, but

He says 'those lacking various books' considering that this very (book)

        Considering that there are five means of (getting) knowledge about an

        These five (means of getting knowledge) indicate, both dissociated and
        associated (with each other), an illness.
        Against the view that the (mentioned means), associated (with each

        a set of means to acquire valid knowledge is seen. The very fire which
        has been acknowledged by means of inference, may certainly (also) be
        known by direct apprehension and verbal authority. Further, being

        cannot remain indifferent to the opinion that an illness can be sub-

        One can ask for example how an origin may be averted if it is not

        been dealt with) in a condensed way” (U. 1, 25).¹²

(Caraka says) : “A fever by concerted action is incurable when all its
