1, 5a-c : The origin is indicated by the synonyms (instrumental) cause
              (nimitta), ground (hetu), underlying factor (āyatana), antece-
              dent (pratyaya), provenance (utthāna) and cause (kāraṇa).
                                                                  (A.h.Ni. 1, 3a-c).²⁸

M :
Among the (elements, consisting of) the origin, etc., the characteristics
of the origin which consists of a cause are enumerated, which set apart
(entities) of the same class and those of a different one ... The meaning
expressed by these (synonymous) words is : origin. (Nyāyasūtra 1, 1, 15
is quoted as an example of a series of synonyms). The question may be
raised : is it expressed by the accumulation (as a whole) or by each of
the (synonyms) separately ? (This objector may say :) the former (alter-
native) is not (the correct one) because an accumulation of words which


=== Page 47 ===
THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS 35

indicate one and the same meaning is not used; if the latter (alternative
were the correct one), liability to inaccuracy (would arise), because
*nimitta* (also) means omen, etc., *hetu* the agent effecting (a proposition ²⁹),
*āyatana* the seat (of a morbific entity, etc.), *pratyaya* the suffixes of the
present tense, etc., and *utthāna* the rising (of a star) and excretion.

(The answer is) : it is not like that, for the whole (series of words
consisting of) *nimitta*, etc. does not mean omen, etc. For that very rea-
son it is said ‘(the origin is indicated) by the synonyms’. They are not
at all synonyms of these (words in the case that they denote other con-
cepts), because words in a regular order and expressing the same mean-
ing are called each other's synonyms. Something which acts as an origin
can for that reason be expressed by the words *nimitta*, etc. if they are
synonyms. This enumeration of synonyms occurs for the sake of common
practice in science. The origin is characterized in a condensed way as
the ground of production of a disease, together with the way in which
this action is necessarily brought about (*itikartavyatā*). With regard to
those who consider the onset as the way in which this action is necessa-
rily brought about by a morbific entity, the expression ‘together with
the way in which this action is necessarily brought about’ (is employed)
in order to exclude (that view about) the onset, because (in their opinion)
there does not exist a way in which this action is brought about which
differs from that by a morbific entity. To those who consider the onset
as the emersion of an illness the (following) characterization (suffices) :
the origin is the ground of production of an illness. In both cases the
word ‘production’ serves to differentiate it (i.e. the origin) from the
ground of apprehension, (consisting of) the prodromes, etc.

This ground (i.e. origin) is of several kinds. With regard to it(s distinc-
tions) it is first of all of four kinds, as Haricandra says (in his comment)
on the chapter (of the *Carakasamhitā*) about the armamentarium (of a
physician) ³⁰ : “It is of four kinds according to its distinction into near
and distant, subordinate and predominant (grounds).”

Near (grounds) of excitement of a morbific entity are e.g. the com-
ponent parts of night, day, season and (the digestive process of) ingested
food; they are not linked to accumulation, etc.

A distant (ground is indicated) e.g. (by) : “Phlegm, accumulated in
the winter, brings about a phlegm disease in the spring.³¹” Or : a near
(ground) of fever is the indulgence in dry (substances), a distant one is
the anger of Rudra.

(A ground is) subordinate e.g. if it is too weak to bring about an ill-
ness, as Caraka says : “Or when the (specific entities, consisting of the


=== Page 48 ===
36 THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS

origin, etc.) are conform, (but) very weak, a morbid alteration is not the
result” (fr. Ni. 4, 4).³²
A predominant ground is e.g. poison, etc.
Or grounds are of three kinds, distinguished into inadequate conjunc-
tion of the senses with their objects, erroneous judgment and transfor-
mation (by time).³³ Inadequate conjunction of the senses with their ob-
jects (refers to) colours, tastes, etc., subject to absence of junction, junc-
tion beyond the proper measure and junction in an improper way; er-
roneous judgment (denotes) improper knowledge, etc.; transformation
(indicates) coldness, etc., arising from the individual nature of the sea-
sons and subject to absence of junction, etc. “In this very case it (i.e.
time) is the inner nature of demerit (as) a ground of disease” says Bhaṭṭā-
rahāricandra, because it also brings about suffering when ripened after
an interval of time. Cakra(paṇidatta) however declares its inner nature
to consist of erroneous judgment; erroneous judgment only is the root
of demerit, arising from the killing of a brāhmaṇa, etc., brought about
by improper knowledge; its relative strength need not be examined in
this instance because demerit is in every respect established as a cause
of disease.
(The ground) is of three kinds according to its distinction into a ground
of a morbific entity, a ground of an illness and a ground of both (morbific
entity and illness).
Grounds of morbific entities are e.g. the sweet (taste), etc., which is
caused by accumulation, excitement and appeasement, produced in accor-
dance with a (particular) season. The ground of a disease is e.g. the con-
sumption of earth as a cause of morbid pallor. Though earth surely
brings about excitement of a morbific entity, as said by Caraka : “A-
stringent (earth excites) the wind, saltish (earth) the bile, sweet (earth)
phlegm” (Ci. 26, 27cd), nevertheless only morbid pallor is started by the
morbific entities arising from it, and not another morbid alteration; so
it is the ground of an illness. A ground of both (morbific entity and
disease) is e.g. what is said about the wind-blood (disease) ³⁴ : “(The
combustive alteration arising) in someone riding on an elephant, horse
or camel and in someone eating ...”, etc.³⁵ This means that, although
in this case the generation of the illness is preceded by excitement of the
morbific entity, there is nevertheless causation of it, both with respect
to the illness and the morbific entity. A remedy that only eliminates the
illness should therefore not be employed in such a case, but (a remedy)
that is opposed to both (morbific entity and illness).
And it should not be said that an illness, being an effect, ceases by


=== Page 49 ===
THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS 37

reason of the very cessation of the (disturbance of the) morbific entity,
which is a cause. For that reason remedial substances have a fixed
faculty for each single case. For what other reason is an emetic procedure
that is (the) proper (means) to eliminate phlegm not employed in (cases
of) dimness of vision by phlegm ? As has been said in the Suśruta(sam-

be submitted to an emetic procedure, nor a person painfully oppressed
by morbid pallor.36”

This same (ground) is of two kinds according to its distinction into a
(ground) bringing about the production and a (ground) bringing about
the manifestation. With regard to this (distinction) an example of (a
ground) which brings about the production is the sweet taste, arising in
the winter, of phlegm; an example of (a ground) which brings about the
manifestation is the glowing heat of the sun in the spring, which makes
this very phlegm manifest; thus says Bhaṭṭāraharicandra. Making mani-
fest means in this case : setting in motion. (The ground) is of two kinds
according to its distinction into external and internal ones. With regard
to this (distinction) external (grounds) are : diet, behaviour, time, etc.
With a view to these (external grounds) Tiṣaṭācārya says : “From phy-
sical exercise, depletion, falling down (from something), breaking (some

become excited, (as well as) when rainclouds are arriving, when the food
has been transformed (by digestion) and during the afternoon. By pun-

alteration, by sharp and saline (substances), by wrath, fasting, glowing
heat (of the sun), sexual intercourse with women, sesame seed, linseed,
thick sour milk, surā, verjuice, āraṇāla, etc., during the digestion of the
ingested food, in the autumn and the summer, at noon and at midnight,
the bile of living beings will become excited. By heavy, sweet-tasting
and excessively oleaginous (substances), milk, confectionery (prepared)

of food) containing a great quantity of butter (sarpiṣprāpūra), at the
time (i.e. in the season) of snow-fall, at the beginning of the day, just
after the ingestion (of food) and in the spring, a general excitement of
phlegm comes about.37”

Internal (grounds) are for example the morbific entities and the cor-
ruptible (constituents of the body).

     (Morbific entities) are of two kinds according to their distinction into
chief and adjunctory ones. The chief one predominates, the adjunctory
one is not predominant. As Caraka says : “A chief one is independent,
its signs are manifest and its provenance and appeasement ³⁸ occur in
accordance with what has been said ; an adjunctory one, however, shows
the opposite characteristics” (fr. Vi. 6, 11). The purpose of this (distinc-

(morbific entity) should get a specific treatment that is not in disagree-
ment with the adjunctory one. That has been stated in the Caraka-

such a case from appeasement of the predominant one” (fr. Ci. 21, 40)³⁹;
a secondary affection is adjunctory.
     (Morbific entities are of two kinds) according to (their distinction into
those which agree with) the constitution and (those which) deviate (from
it) : it is troublesome to cure a wind disease in a person whose constitu-
tion is dominated by wind, but its cure is easy in persons with a con-

of) the characteristics of easy curability : “In case the (constituent) sub-
ject to corruption will not possess qualities comparable (to those of the
morbific entity) and in case the morbific entity (dominating the disease)
will not be (the same as the predominant one in) the constitution”
(Sū. 10, 11cd).

another seat, it generates, even if maintaining its proper measure, a
morbid alteration. As Caraka says : “When the wind, in a condition
with decline of phlegm, has carried away with itself the bile, which
maintained its natural state, (has moved it) from its seat, and spreads
over the limbs of the body, a cutting pain and a burning sensation of

of an increase (of bile) and not a different (kind of) corruption ; otherwise
there would occur no burning sensation at all. For a morbific entity that
maintains its own measure does not generate a morbid alteration.⁴⁰

may be) thus, it is nevertheless necessarily required for the sake of

decline; otherwise, being of the opinion that there is an increase of bile,
one ought to employ a purgative or bile-diminishing (procedure), which
is not suitable at all in this case, for (the bile) should be brought back
to its own seat. That which has been stated by Caraka : “Decline,

threefold mode of being of the morbific entities” (Sū. 17, 112ab), etc.,
refers to what usually occurs.”
(Morbific entities are distinguished) according to their modes of being :
modes of the morbific entities are the states of decline, increase, etc. As
has been said in the Caraka(samhitā) : “Decline, maintenance and in-
crease (with regard to their quantity constitute) a threefold mode of
being of the morbific entities; (as) another threefold (mode of being)
should be discerned (their moving) in an upward, downward and lateral
(direction) and (as) still another threefold one (their staying) in the
viscera, the branches, and in the vital points and junctures of the bones”
(Sū. 17, 112-113ab).

The modes of being consisting of their moving in an upward direction,

(type of) blood-bile a purgative procedure (should be employed) and in

etc., in which the morbific entities are moving in a lateral direction, a
therapy (should be employed) that is in accordance with what has been
said (upon this subject). Increased morbific entities give rise to painful con-

branches, and sometimes in the vital points and junctures of the bones. The
mode of being in which they stay in the vital points and junctures of
the bones is taught to be one single entity because it leads to a state
which is curable only with difficulty. The viscera (consist of) the recep-
tacle of undigested food, etc. ; the branches (consist of) blood and the
subsequent elements (of the body), together with the skin, according to
the meaning Caraka himself has given to this technical term.⁴²

with regard to their being accompanied by or being devoid of immature

ejection of saliva, loosening of impure matter, the inability to eat and
weariness are the signs of impurities accompanied by immature matter;
when they are devoid of immature matter the opposite (signs are pre-
sent)” (A.h.Sū. 13, 25; 27; 23cd; 24).⁴⁴ “Wind, accompanied by imma-
ture matter, will oppress the body successively by means of a confined
state (of the impurities), adynamia of the (transforming) fire, lassitude,
rumbling of the bowels, painful sensations, swelling and pricking pain;
when excited vehemently it may wander and seize (all the limbs) simul-
taneously; it becomes increased by oleaginous (substances), etc., at the
rising of the sun and of clouds, and at night. Devoid of immature matter
it is clear, dry, not accompanied by a confined state (of the impurities)
and attended by (only) slightly painful sensations; it becomes appeased
by (substances) with opposite qualities, specifically by those which are
oleaginous. Bile is bad-smelling, yellowish-green, brown, acid, solid and
heavy, when accompanied by immature matter; it should be declared
to bring about acid eructations and a burning sensation in the throat
and cardiac region. In a mature state it is slightly copper-coloured,
yellow, very hot, pungent as to its taste and non-solid; it should be
discerned that it is odourless and bestows appetite, force and (intensity
of) the maturating (fire). Phlegm, accompanied by immature matter, is
turbid, ropy and grumous and remains (sticking) to the throat; (in that
state) it is bad-smelling and harmful to (the feeling of) hunger and to
eructation. It should be discerned to be mature when it is frothy, lumpy,
pale, devoid of tough (constituents) and without any smell; being (en-
dowed with an) unfixing (ability) it brings about an unpolluted condition
of the mouth.” ⁴⁵

The purpose of this (distinction) is (that) a maturation-promoting
(agent should be employed) if (a morbific entity is) accompanied by im-
mature matter and an appeasing (agent) if it is devoid of immature
matter.

And these morbific entities, intimately connected with each other, are
of sixty-two ⁴⁶ types according to distinctions concerning more and
most ⁴⁷ (serious degrees of excitement), etc. Examples of those (distinc-
tions) are not written down here because (this commentary would be-
come too) extensive; they should be examined in Suśruta's chapter on

    The prodromes are mentioned immediately after the origin because

Specific (prodromes) are e.g. (as follows) : in the initial (stage) of a

It may be objected that (presence) to an extraordinary degree ⁵⁴
(means presence in) a developed state ; the consequence of that would
be that yawning, etc. are symptoms, because it is said (by Mādhava
later on) : “When this very (phenomenon) has reached a developed state,
it is called a symptom”. ⁵⁵

The answer is : in the same way as fatigue, etc. make (one) aware of
(the presence of) fever as one single entity, with the exclusion of other
diseases, without however indicating specific (distinctions) as to its
arising from wind, etc., from which it follows that those (prodromes)
are present in an undeveloped state, (in that way) yawning, etc. make
(one) aware of (the presence of) imminent wind fever, with the exclusion
of fever by bile, etc. ; without indicating however the specificity of
symptoms, consisting of their being occasioned by the dryness, coldness,
decline of the elements (of the body), covering (action) or other (parti-
cular characteristics of wind) ; by reason of this fact that they make (one)
aware of an undeveloped wind fever, yawning, etc. are certainly in an
undeveloped state ; that is the explanation (given) by Jejjaṭa, Vāpya-
candra, Mādhavakara,⁵⁶ Kārtikakuṇḍa, etc. Others, however, say that
yawning, etc. are designated as prodromes, even when they are in a
developed state and accompanied by numerous undeveloped prodromes,
as (in the case of) a pile of māṣa beans, (in the expression) ‘they walk,
provided with a parasol’, ⁵⁷ and so on.

And it is not thus that it is not distinct from a symptom because it is
present in a developed state, (for) it is said that a prodrome inevitably
makes (one) aware of an impending illness and a symptom of a present

one. In this (connection it is thus that) the specific prodrome remains

the prodromes), generated by a state of coalescence of morbific entities

prodromes are of two kinds, the generic prodrome is made mention of
(by Mādhava).

A prodrome is that, (e.g.) fatigue, etc., by which an ailment, (i.e.) a
disease, being about to arise, (i.e.) desirous of being produced on account
of the complete presence of the whole (of its causes), (but) not (yet)
governed by, (i.e.) not intimately connected with, the specific (charac-
teristics of a) morbific entity, (e.g.) the special kind of shivering, etc.,
occasioned by wind, etc., is characterized, (i.e.) known. With the words
‘it is an undeveloped sign’, (etc.) the specific prodrome is made mention
of. (A remark about the syntactical structure of the sentence follows).

A sign is a characteristic. Undeveloped (means) not exceedingly well-
developed and the ground with respect to this is its slightness, (i.e.)
minuteness, which means that it is not undeveloped by reason of its
junction with a covering (agent), etc. ‘(It is) in accordance with each
(particular illness)’ means that the very symptoms of a particular illness
are called its prodromes when they are in an undeveloped state.

Others, however, characterize the prodrome as follows : “That sign,
which is brought about by excited morbific entities residing in their (own)
seat and which makes (one) aware of an impending illness, is called a
prodrome.” ⁵⁸ That is not very suitable, because the prodromes of king-
ly consumption, (consisting of) the falling down of (blades of) grass and
hairs of the head, etc. and occasioned by the invisible (force),⁵⁹ are not
invariably concomitant. As Caraka says : “The (phenomenon that) in
(patients) with kingly consumption usually *ghr̥ṇas*,⁶⁰ hairs of the
head and (blades of) grass are falling down in foods and drinks and that the
hairs of the head and the nails are growing abnormally fast (..., that is
the set of prodromes ...)" (Ci. 8, 35).⁶¹

And this (phenomenon) does not arise from a morbific entity either
because there does not exist an intimate connection between morbific


=== Page 58 ===
46
THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS

entities and grass, etc., and a particular condition, not intimately con-
nected (with a morbific entity), is regarded to be unable to act as a
cause, because, by settling mutual connections in an uninterrupted series,
there would arise too far-reaching consequences (and) everything would
be the cause of everything.

Being of the opinion that the very competent Vāgbhaṭa has written
down the words ‘(that) by which’,⁶² comprehending all the prodromes,
whether arising from the invisible (force) or from a morbific entity, just
because he wishes to avoid (mentioning) a morbific entity with regard to
these, Mādhavakara has described the characteristics of prodromes in
the very way he (i.e. Vāgbhaṭa) did.

To put it shortly the characteristic (of a prodrome) is (as follows) :
‘a prodrome is a sign that only makes (one) aware of an impending
illness’. The word ‘only’ differentiates it from origin and therapeutic
diagnosis and from the onset which consists of the way in which the
action is brought about by a morbific entity, because the (terms)
belonging to this class make (one) aware of an illness which is (either)
produced (or) not (yet) produced.

For it is thus that an origin in the form of the consumption of earth
makes (one) aware of an impending morbid pallor and, if it occurs as
an adverse therapeutic reaction, an (actually) present specific illness;
therapeutic diagnosis, applied in the stage of the prodromes, procures
knowledge about an impending specific illness and, applied in the stage
of the symptoms, about an (actually) present specific illness; the onset
procures knowledge about an imminent specific illness by the produc-
tion and excitement of the prodromes at noon, etc., and about an
(actually) present specific illness by the excitement of the symptoms at
noon, etc.; that is the way in which they make (one) aware of an illness,
(whether it is) produced (or) not (yet) produced.

An objector may say that, when the specific (nature) of an illness that
has been produced can be accurately determined after remembering the
specific (nature) of its prodromes, the prodromes too make (one) aware
of an (actually) present illness, as stated by Caraka with regard to the
doubts about the (presence of) symptoms of blood-bile or an urinary
disease : “If a person passes urine, coloured turmeric-yellow or red, but
does not present the prodromes of urinary disease ...” (Ci. 6, 54ab), etc.

It is said as an answer to this (objection) : can a prodrome be observed
before the emersion of an illness or is this impossible ? In the former
(case) it verily makes (one) aware of an impending illness, in the latter
there would be no production of remembering at all by want of personal

experience.³³ If it is said (as an objection) that the prodromes, consisting

    If it be argued that the process of remembering is not a means of

    The same (statement) as about the process of remembering should be

about a jar, etc.; a sign, however, is not (of a) generic (character, but
characteristic of something).
    And the prodromes are verily the signs of an illness though it is not
(yet) present, in the same way as the coming up of specific clouds (is a
sign, indicative) of rain.
    That is all about the prodromes.

1, 7 : When this same (phenomenon, i.e. the prodrome) has reached a

M :
Although the onset is that which immediately follows upon the (stage

‘This same (phenomenon’ refers to) the prodrome itself. ‘A developed
state’ (means that it has) become perceptible. Does (the term) develop-
ment (mean that the set of prodromes develops) completely or (does this
occur only) fragmentarily ?
In the former case all fevers would be incurable, for Caraka has said :
“(The man in whom settle down) all the prodromes” (I.5, 4a), etc.; in
the latter case the consequence would be that prodromes like : “Yawning


=== Page 61 ===
THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS 49

to an extraordinary degree by wind, burning of the eyes by bile” (Su.U.
39, 27bd) etc., may also become symptoms.
(The answer to this question is that) it is not like that, by reason of
the fact that neither a complete nor a fragmentary (development) is
assented to, but the prodromes as such are (considered to be) signs of
an illness when they have developed, without having accurately deter-
mined their particularity, (i.e.) whether one or several (prodromes) are
present, (in the same way) as smoke as such makes (one) aware of (the
presence of) fire, without (having determined) its particularity, (i.e.)
whether it arises from grass or from leaves, etc.

When it has been established to be thus, a full development of the
whole (set of prodromes indicates) incurability, but otherwise curability
(is present).

The consequence is not that yawning, etc. are symptoms, for these
(exist) in a developed condition in an earlier (stage of the illness); (more-
over), because that which from an undeveloped state has reached deve-
lopment, is denominated as a symptom, and because these (prodromes)
cannot possibly be (called) symptoms, by reason of the fact that they
are accompanied by numerous other undeveloped signs, and because
prodromes and symptoms (do) not (occur) at the same time.

Īśvarasena, however, says : “The undeveloped own form of an illness
is its prodrome; that which has developed is its symptom”. That is not
right, because the (following) alternative cannot be maintained : for
thus (it has been said) : What is meant by ‘own form’? Does it express
‘itself as to its form’ ⁶⁸ or ‘its own form’ ⁶⁹ ? And (in case it expresses)
its own (form), (does that point to its own) quality or (its own)
effect ?

(With regard to ‘itself as to its form’ the answer is that the term)
‘own form’ is not correct, first because (this would be) the contradiction
of an action referring to that same thing as an object which is its
(svātmāni kriyāvirodhaḥ : e.g. even the best dancer cannot dance on his
own shoulders, a sword cannot cut itself). For a symptom is said to be
the cause of perception of an illness; if this (symptom) is said to be the
very own nature of an illness, the own nature of an illness would be
acknowledged from the own nature itself, and that is clearly the contra-
diction of an action referring to that same thing as an object which is its
subject. Neither is it (its own) quality, for it is impossible (to maintain)
that the black (colour) of the skin, nails, faeces, urine and eyes, etc.,
described by Caraka, ⁷⁰ is a symptom of haemorrhoids. This black (colour)
of the skin, nails, faeces, urine and eyes, etc., is not a quality of haemor-


=== Page 62 ===
50 THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS

rhoids at all for the (following) reasons : it does not rest on them ; quali-
ties are resting on the bearers of (those) qualities ; otherwise (there would
be) too far-reaching consequences (enabling one to call everything a
quality). Nor is it an effect, because (in that case) the consequence would
be that secondary affections, etc. would also be symptoms. If it be
argued that these (secondary affections) are signs of an illness, the cure
of which is difficult or which is incurable, (the answer is that) it is not
thus ; they are signs of incurability, etc. in itself, but not of the illness,
because they have become known already (in an) earlier (stage of the
illness) and have been mentioned as distinct (elements). That has been
said : “This (book, called) ‘The ascertainment of diseases’ containing the
secondary affections, precursory signals of death, origins and signs, is
composed (now)” (Mā.ni. 1, 2cd). If it is said (as an objection) that a
secondary affection is not the effect of an illness, but of the morbific
entity which is starting an illness, as has been said in the Suśruta(sam-
hitā) : “That, the root of which is this (previously produced illness) it-
self (tanmūla eva), is technically called a secondary affection” (fr.Sū. 33,
18), explained by the commentators (as follows) : “tanmūla is said (to
mean) : that, the root of which is this, which consists of the morbific
entity”, 71 (the answer is that) it is not thus. As soon as an illness, by
reason of improper conduct, has acquired strength by augmentation of
the morbific entity which is its root, it brings about a secondary affec-
tion ; therefore it has been said : ‘that, the root of which is this’. For that
very reason Caraka says : “Some diseases become appeased when they
have become the ground of (another) disease” (Ni. 8, 21ab), etc. It may
be said that really all these (meanings) are sometimes and to some degree
expressed by the term ‘own form’. Some are of the opinion that there
is no inaccuracy (in Īśvarasena’s statement) if things are thus. Never-
theless it would only be an established rule, but not a characteristic,
because one quality, comprehending all symptoms, would be absent,
and secondary affections would become (identical with) the own form of
an illness. For that reason the characteristic of a symptom is said to be :
that sign which only makes (one) aware of an illness which has (already)
been produced. The word ‘produced’ (is made use of) in order to differenti-
ate (a symptom) from a prodrome ; the word ‘only’ differentiates origin,
onset and therapeutic diagnosis (from the symptom), because the (latter)
make (one) aware of an illness which is either produced or not (yet)
produced. That has just been shown. The word ‘sign’ excludes the eye,
etc. To those who consider the onset to consist of the emersion of an ill-
ness, the word ‘sign’ differentiates the (onset from a symptom) ; for the


=== Page 63 ===
THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS 51

(onset) is (in that case) not a sign with respect to the knowledge of an
illness, but a cause (of this knowledge).

The synonyms of 'symptom' are made mention of for the sake of
common practice in science and in order to characterize (the symptom)
in the same way as the origin.

(An objector may say) : is it not thus, that an illness is known by
means of its symptoms and (knowledge about) an illness is not attained
at all without symptoms, because the very agglomeration of (symptoms,
consisting of) the inability to eat and so on, is (identical with) fever and
(the presence of) all the eleven symptoms, (consisting of) cough and so
on, is (identical with) kingly consumption?

The answer is that it is not thus. A specific (type of) coalescence be-
tween a particular morbific entity and corruptible (constituent) is an
illness in the form of fever, etc., and its effects are the inability to eat,
etc. Moreover, this very inability to eat, etc., are, each one separately,
symptoms and a collection of these (symptoms) is an illness, because a
collection is certainly different from its constituent elements, in the same
way as (this is the case with) a wood (consisting) of *khadira* trees.

Others, however, connect (this opinion) with the wish to express a
distinction, even in cases where there is none, as in examples like the
head of Rāhu or the body of a torso.⁷² The Nyāya experts, on the other
hand, do procure a distinction in those cases.⁷³

(An objector may ask) on account of Caraka's words : “A morbid
alteration is just suffering” (Sū. 9, 4d) : what is the position of a collec-
tion (of symptoms, consisting of) the inability to eat and so on, with
regard to suffering, which is a quality of the soul?

(The answer is) that it is not like that, because, according to the
'etymology' 'suffering is that which brings about suffering', the ground
of suffering, consisting of incongruity of the elements, etc., is accept-
ed to be the state of being an illness.

The inability to eat, etc. are certainly morbid alterations by means
of their own form, but when they are substantiating another (morbid
alteration), they are truly called signs. As Caraka says : “Those signs
of illnesses which, for the sake of knowledge, have been mentioned in
(this) summary, are also illnesses, but, when they are temporarily present,
they are rightly regarded as signs and not as ailments” (Ni. 8, 40).⁷⁴

1, 8-9 : The application of remedial agents, foods and rules of conduct,
contrary to ground and illness, providing the result of that
which is contrary (to ground and illness) and conducive to
well-being (8), should be known as therapeutic diagnosis of an
illness, which is traditionally called adequate (treatment). The
opposite (of it), adverse therapeutic diagnosis, is technically
called inadequate (treatment) with respect to the illness (9).

M :
Therapeutic diagnosis is dealt with … Grounds are external and in-
ternal; an illness is fever and so on. The application, (i.e.) the employ-
ment, of remedial agents, regimens of diet and behavioural rules, which
are, whether dissociated or associated, contrary to ground and illness,
providing, whether being dissociated or associated, the result of that
which is contrary to these two, (i.e.) leading to appeasement of a
disease by their special faculty, even when their peculiarities are the
same as those of the origin, should be known, when conducive to well-
being, as that which is called therapeutic diagnosis of an illness. Its
synonym is made mention of with the words : ‘this same (element)
is traditionally called adequate treatment.’ In the Caraka(saṁhitā) it
has also been said : “For the sake of adequate (treatment, i.e.) therapeu-
tic diagnosis” (fr.Sū. 11, 38). (The word *hi* is used to fill up a quarter of
the stanza).

(About) ‘conducive to well-being’ (we remark that) well-being is
characterized by cessation of a disease. Well-being is, for example, what
is indicated in common language when people say : ‘We have become
happy by liberation from toil’; conducive to well-being is that which
leads to well-being of that kind and brings it about uninterruptedly
during a proper length of time. The purport expressed by this is that
the drinking of cold water by a person with a recent fever,⁷⁸ accom-
panied by a burning sensation and thirst, is not (an instance of) thera-
peutic diagnosis, although it brings about temporary well-being.⁷⁹ In
this case ‘remedial agents, foods and rules of conduct’ (constitute) an
implicative expression; one should understand that place and time are
also indicated by it. For that very reason Vṛddhavāgbhaṭa has said,
after stating ‘that which is contrary to the illness’, etc. : “Place and time

are also indicated by it" (fr. A.s.Ni. 1, 12). Also Sudāntasena says :
"That which, being contrary to ground, illness, etc., is attended by well-
being, and (also) places, etc. (which are contrary to the ground, etc.),
should be known (to constitute) therapeutic diagnosis; when otherwise,
it is adverse therapeutic diagnosis."
    In a condensed way its characteristic is : "That, which is generated
by remedial agents, etc., and is attended by well-being, is therapeutic
diagnosis."
    The words 'remedial agents', etc. mean that the well-being, generated
by garlands, sandal, women, etc., is excluded. The words 'attended by'
are used to differentiate from it the temporary well-being generated by
something unwholesome.
    Moreover, this (stanza of the Nidāna) is a proper one to illustrate
(therapeutic diagnosis) by means of examples, but it is not a charac-
teristic (of it), because (the words) 'remedial agents', etc. (on the one
hand), and 'contrary to the ground', etc. (on the other), are unsuitable
for a characterization by their mutually confusing character. Therefore
the characteristic (of therapeutic diagnosis) is : 'therapeutic diagnosis is
the ground which properly appeases the suffering arising from an illness',
or : 'therapeutic diagnosis is adequate (treatment)', or again : 'thera-
peutic diagnosis is that which is generated by remedial agents and is
attended by well-being', for regimen of diet, behavioural rules, place,
time, reducing measures, etc., whether consisting of substances or not
consisting of these, are stated to be remedial agents in the Caraka(sam-
hitā).⁸⁰ And now (we give) examples (of the different forms of thera-
peutic diagnosis). (First of all) those which are contrary to the ground.
A remedial agent is for instance a hot remedy, like dry ginger, etc., in
(a case of) cold fever;⁸¹ as has been said : "The best of physicians appease
diseases brought about by heat by cold (measures), but diseases brought
about by coldness (need) a hot drug" (Ca.Vi. 3, 41). An example of food
is rice boiled in meat-broth, (prescribed) in a wind fever (arisen) from
fatigue.⁸² A rule concerning behaviour is for instance (the prescription
of) waking during the night in a case of phlegm which has arisen from
sleeping by day.⁸³ And now those which are contrary to the illness. A
remedial agent is for instance pāthā as an obstipating agent in diar-
rhoea;⁸⁴ in the same way śirīṣa destroys poison,⁸⁵ khadira skin diseases ⁸⁶
and haridrā urinary diseases.⁸⁷
    These (remedial agents) are not linked to a morbific entity, but ap-
pease the disease by their special faculty. Vāpyacandra, however, says :
"That substance, which eliminates illnesses like fever, etc., is also op-


=== Page 66 ===
54                                       THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS

posed to the morbific entity (of those illnesses), but it is distinct from
(a substance), opposed to a morbific entity, in the following way : that
(a substance), which is opposed to a morbific entity, does not necessarily
eliminate an illness; emetic and reducing measures for instance, (though)
being eliminative of phlegm, do not eliminate a visceral swelling by
phlegm, for it has been said : "When phlegm, (though) curable by re-
ducing measures, is the agent (which brings about) fever and visceral
swelling, reducing measures (do) not (constitute an) approved (therapy),
even when place, time, etc., are comparable (in such a case to those in
which reducing measures are beneficial)".⁸⁸ and also : "A person with
dimness of vision or visceral swelling should not be submitted to emetic
procedures, nor a person oppressed by morbid pallor or abdominal
disease".⁸⁹ "That which eliminates an illness, necessarily eliminates the
morbific entity (of it); appeasing the illness, it also appeases the mor-
bific entity which starts it; otherwise that disease would not be subdued
at all, for its cause would remain in the same condition."
Others say that this is not very logical, for the morbific entity in-
heres in (the disease) or is its instrumental cause; the absence of an
effect is, however, not exclusively connected with the absence of the
inherent (cause) or the instrumental cause, but also with the absence of
the non(-immediately) inherent cause; in the same way as the non-
existence of a jar (results) from the annihilation of the non(-immediately)
inherent cause, (consisting of) its connection with the series of (com-
ponent) parts,⁹⁰ in that way annihilation of a disease also (results) from
the annihilation of (a non-immediately inherent cause, such as) the con-
nection of onset and characteristics.
A morbific entity, however, ceases of its own accord or by means of
another therapeutical procedure. If it is accepted that (a remedial agent)
opposed to the illness necessarily brings about cessation of the morbific
entity, it would be difficult to demonstrate that it is distinct from (a
remedial agent) opposed to both (morbific entity and illness).
(An objector may ask) : Why is the elimination of a morbific entity
by emetic procedures, etc. prescribed in a morbid alteration started by
it, if a morbific entity is an instrumental cause? For abolishment of a
jar does not occur in case the stick, the potter, etc. are abolished.
The answer is : as long as an effect is lasting in an instrumental cause,
annihilation of the effect (results) from abolishment of the instrumental
cause. Morbific entities are usually of the same kind as the light (of a
lamp) that is annihilated when the wick and the oil are annihilated.
Food (which is contrary to the illness consists), for example, of lentils,

etc. as obstipating agents in diarrhoea.⁹¹ Conduct (contrary to the ill- ness) is e.g. strained evacuation in the retentive disease.⁹² Vāpyacandra says that conduct, contrary to the illness, also consists of spells, the bearing of (auspicious) herbs, oblations, offerings, voluntary vows, ex- piatory rites, sacrifices, obedience to the guru and the gods, etc.
And now (those) things which are contrary to (both) ground and ill- ness. A remedial agent (consists), for example, of the ten roots which eliminate both wind and swelling in a swelling by wind,⁹³ as has been said in the Caraka(samhitā) in the chapter about the six hundred pur- gative preparations, in that part of it beginning with ‘pātala’ until ‘these ten eliminate swellings’ (fr. Sū. 4, 16).⁹⁴ Food (consists), e.g., of diluted buttermilk in (cases of) grahaṇī (disorder) by wind or by phlegm,⁹⁵ and a thin gruel in fever arising from a cold wind,⁹⁶ for it destroys the wind by its hot potency and fever by its special faculty. As has been said in the Caraka(samhitā) : “They destroy fever by reason of their adequacy with respect to fever” (Ci. 3, 153c) and also in the Suśruta(samhitā) : “Gruel is always salutary in (case of) fever and diarrhoea” (U. 40, 158cd). Conduct is for instance waking during the night, which is (of a) dry (quality) and contrary to lassitude, in (a case of) lassitude arisen from sleeping during the day, which is (of an) oleaginous (quality).⁹⁷
And now (those things) with the result of that which is contrary to the ground. A remedial agent is e.g. a hot poultice,⁹⁸ productive of bile, in a swelling by an inflamed sore which shows a predominance of bile.⁹⁹ Food is e.g. (such food) which brings about combustive alteration in a swelling by an inflamed sore which is in (the stage of) maturation.¹⁰⁰ Conduct is e.g. causing terror in (a case of) insanity by wind.¹⁰¹
And now (those things) with the results of that which is contrary to the illness. A remedial agent (consists) e.g. (of) an emetic agent, (as) madana fruits, etc., in (a case of) vomiting.¹⁰² Food is e.g. milk (as) a purgative in diarrhoea.¹⁰³ Conduct is e.g. tickling (of the throat) in order to (provoke) vomiting in (a case of) vomiting.¹⁰⁴
And now (those things) with the result of that which is contrary to both ground and illness. A remedial agent is e.g. an unguent (made) from aguru,¹⁰⁵ etc. in (case) someone (is) scorched by fire ¹⁰⁶ or (the employ- ment of) poison in (a disorder by) poison.¹⁰⁷ Food is e.g. an alcoholic beverage, bringing about intoxication, in an alcoholic disorder, arising from the drinking of alcoholic beverages.¹⁰⁸ Conduct is e.g. physical exercise, in the form of crossing a water (by swimming), in a confused state of the wind generated by physical exercise.¹⁰⁹
(An objector may ask whether) it is not thus that in vomiting, arising

from a great amount of phlegm and in which an emetic procedure should
be employed, there would occur a disease, which remains for a long time,
or is of an ineradicable character, if no emetic procedure is employed,
and that the application of an emetic procedure is for that reason op-
posed to the morbific entity only. As has been said in the Suśruta(sam-
hitā) : "An emetic procedure is said to be salutary in (cases of) vomiting
which are provided with a great amount of a morbific entity" (U. 49,
16ab).¹¹⁰ Also in (cases of) diarrhoea accompanied by immature (matter),
there is opposedness to the ground only, because the immature (matter)
flows out by means of the purgative quality of milk. In the same way
there is opposedness to the ground only in cases of scorching by fire,
because the blood goes to another seat, by reason of its dissolution by a
hot therapeutical procedure; otherwise the blood, excited by the burning,
and staying at the same seat, would begin to be subject to a matu-
rative process. As has been said in the Suśruta(samhitā) : "Blood,
brought to excitement by fire, becomes vehemently excited in a creature,
afterwards its bile is also roused ¹¹¹ by that very impetus" (Sū. 12, 17).
A cold therapeutical procedure is prohibited in such a case because it is
a ground of a grumous condition of the blood. As Suśruta says : "For
cold water, by its natural condition, coagulates the blood to an extra-
ordinary degree; therefore well-being is brought about by something hot,
but never at all by something cold” (Sū. 12, 21); ‘it coagulates' (means
that) it brings about a grumous condition. In the same way a poison
derived from roots, which is endowed with a downward movement as its
own form, is opposed to the ground only (when it is applied) in (a dis-
order by) an animal poison, which is endowed with an upward movement
as its own form. As has been said in the Caraka(samhitā) : "When it is
said that poison destroys poison, the special faculty is the cause with
regard to that; that which regards the movement in an upward direction
or in a normal direction (i.e. downwards), is also ruled by its special
faculty" (Sū. 26, 69).
The meaning of this is as follows : it has been said 'it is ruled by its
special faculty' because one may ask what is the reason of this distinc-
tion regarding its (way of) movement although there are no specific kinds
of being a poison. Contrary to the ground only in the same way is, in an
alcoholic disorder brought about by an alcoholic beverage, the applica-
tion of the same alcoholic beverage (from which the disorder has arisen),
to which mātuluṅga, verjuice, etc. have been added, (as) prescribed by
Suśruta,¹¹² etc.; for an (alcoholic beverage) to which other substances
have been added is certainly different from the pure (beverage); or, in

an alcoholic disorder with wind (as its predominant morbific entity),
generated by a dry (alcoholic beverage, such as) *mādhvīka*, etc., the ap-

What has been said in the Suśruta(saṃhitā) : "In the same way as some-

Opposedness to the ground only is also present with regard to the
crossing of a water in (cases of) stiffness of the thighs;¹¹⁴ the heat of
the body, not going outside by the coldness of the water, dissolves, as
in the kiln of a potter, both fat and phlegm, which are lumped together
in the interior, and by physical exercise both these (elements) are de-

opposed to the ground, etc.

The answer (to this objection) is that, even if it were thus, (things
with the result of that which is contrary to a ground, an illness or both),
are shown to be separate (entities) by the masters in order to substantiate
subsidiary deviations of the peculiarities. That has also been stated in
the Caraka(saṃhitā) : "Therapeutic diagnosis is the application, attended
by well-being, of remedial agents, regimens of diet and rules of conduct,
which are contrary to ground and illness, or bring about the result of
that which is contrary to ground and illness” (Nī. 1, 10). A deviated state
of a peculiarity brings about appeasement of a disease, even when this
peculiarity is the same as that of a ground.

‘The opposite (of it) is adverse therapeutic diagnosis’ means that the
application of remedial agents, etc. is called adverse therapeutic diag-
nosis when it brings about suffering. Its synonym is spoken of with the
words ‘it is traditionally called inadequate (treatment) with respect to
the illness’. By the word illness the morbific entity should be understood
as well.

(An objector may ask) : Does adverse therapeutic diagnosis make (one)
aware of a specific illness or does it not ?
If one says that it does not do so it is useless to deal with it in (the
section on) the origins; if one is of the opinion that it does substantiate
(a specific illness) this (view) conflicts with (the statement) : 'the discern-
ment of diseases is traditionally said to consist of five (elements)' (fr.

signs by means of the good or adverse effects of therapeutic diagnosis"

Those are the characteristics of therapeutic diagnosis.

... The corruption of the morbific entities is of various kinds : it is

etc., that is called the onset. 'In accordance with the (particular manner

ward and lateral way of moving, etc. The two synonyms of onset are
mentioned for the sake of common practice in science and in order to

    Bhaṭṭāraharicandra says : "The words emersion and origination (in-
dicate that) also emersion (of an illness) is a cause of knowledge because
no knowledge exists about something which has not emerged." These
words express that (the emersion) is not (only), like the origin, etc., a
cause of knowledge as imparting knowledge, but (also) as an object of
knowledge.
    Others say that this is not correct because such a (view about the)
onset that compares it with light, the eye, etc., is not suitable in thera-
peutics. Further it is not a fixed rule that only something which has
emerged may be discerned, because an illness which has not (yet) e-
merged is knowable by means of its origin and prodromes, as (imminent)
rain, etc. (are knowable) by (the arrival of) clouds, etc. Moreover, when
what is expressed by the words 'it has emerged' is said to be different
from the emersion, rain, etc. are indeed different from an imminent
appearance (of rain). That, however, which does not emerge in any of
the three (divisions of) time, cannot possibly be known. Nevertheless,
the onset is not the emersion of an illness, because light, the eye, etc.,
would also be (elements) which have to be considered, in a similar way
as in (the concept of) emersion, and (also) because, without all those
(elements, i.e. light, the eye, etc.), knowledge would not exist.
    Therefore Bhaṭṭāraharicandra's view is (as follows) : "The onset is the
emersion of an illness, additionally characterized by the way in which
(this emersion) is brought about by a morbific entity and it is not its
mere emersion." Vāgbhaṭa, who says : "In accordance with the (parti-
cular manner of its) corruption", etc., has also declared the onset to be
the specified emersion of an illness. When things are thus, specific thera-
peutic procedures are obtained, as for instance the application of redu-
cing measures, maturation-promoting procedures, sudation, etc. in fever,
because it makes (one) aware that the receptacle of undigested food is
being corrupted, the (transforming) fire damaged, etc. Although such a
(concept of the) onset is reached by the very (use of the) term morbific
entity, and because these morbific entities have a subsidiary function,
(the onset) is nevertheless made into a separate (entity) for the very sake

of specific therapy, in the same way as the prodrome is (made an entity)
which is different from the symptom, although there is no specificity
with regard to it as imparting knowledge. Therefore the onset is the
emersion of an illness, additionally characterized by the way in which
(this emersion) is brought about by a morbific entity; only that is its
characteristic.

bile and phlegm.

(An objector may ask :) Is it not thus, that Caraka, with regard to
distinctions of the onset, has also mentioned the mode in the same way


=== Page 75 ===
                      THE FIVE CHARACTERISTICS                                  63

as the number ? (He says) for instance : “Illnesses are of two modes
according to their distinction into endogenous and adventitious ones”
(fr. Ni. 1, 12⁴) and : “There are three modes of blood-bile” (fr. Sū. 19, 3),
etc. In this connection it may be asked for which reason the mode is not
mentioned here.

The answer is that the term number includes the mode, because the
latter is invariably connected with number. The distinction between
mode and number is as follows : a mode is a manner and it only occurs
in (entities) of the same class by reason of their being accompanied by
some other quality (though they, as such, are not subject to change);
there exists for instance an upwards going manner in the entity (called)
blood-bile, though it remains the same (conceived as an entity). Number,
however, also occurs in all that which possesses distinctness; (one can
say), for example : there are four jars; there are eight fevers. In this
very case the mode is the manner and it cannot be applied to distinct
(things); for that reason a manner, attended by a quality of the cause, is
applied to illnesses which are distinct with regard to number, etc. The
Nyāya experts say likewise : “(The term) mode (is made use of) when
distinct entities are conceived by means of a common quality; number,
however, (is applied to) everything that may be called a distinct en-
tity”.¹⁴¹ the grammarians, on the other hand, explain : “A manner is
provided with something common, (but) a distinction does not refer to
(the occurrence of) common (qualities in the enumerated things)”.¹⁴²
thus it has been written by Vāpyacandra.

(An objector may say) : Is it not thus, that the way in which a fever
is known by the discrimination of each component (of the morbific en-
tities), etc., is not the way in which (it is known) by number ?

The answer is : distinctions as to the morbific entity of an illness are
known by means of the distinctions concerning number; as a conse-
quence of this, having got knowledge about fever, etc. as to their own
form, the specific type should be investigated for the sake of therapy
(by asking) : ‘which one (out of the total number) is this fever?’; the
specific type is found when that has become known; by way of such an
uninterrupted series the fact arises that number is a cause. If (an illness)
is just being produced and has emerged, being distinct with regard to
its morbific entity, then it is suitable to inquire about it (by asking) :
‘which one (out of the total number) is this one?’ For which reason (is
this question put forth)? For the sake of specific therapy.

That are the characteristics of the onset.

serves to differentiate (these entities) from the corruptible (constituents,

The distinction between a constitution and a disease is as follows : a
constitution does not bring about much trouble when unwholesome

ing about another disease, can do so only when its force has been aug-
mented by another origin. (The construction is : thus a disease arises
which is the origin of a disease). On this very subject examples are given
with the words ‘as for instance’, etc.
     ‘From both (diseases)’ (means) : from blood-bile and from fever.
     (Because) ‘suffering’ is said to be that which makes one suffer, suffering
is what brings about oppressing pain. According to Vāpyacandra this
word ‘suffering’ should be added to all (the terms), (i.e.) fever and the
subsequent ones, with change of the gender (as the case may require).
And also visceral swelling arises from haemorrhoids. From cough arises
decline ; ‘of the vital fluid and so on’ should be supplied. This decline
occurs as the ground of a disease. Because one may ask of which disease
(it is the ground), it is said : of desiccation, (i.e.) kingly consumption.
Some read here a different text which has been been explained by Haricandra,
etc. : “And desiccation also arises when decline and that which affects
the chest are the ground”.¹⁵⁹ This has the (following) meaning : decline
is kingly consumption ; that which affects the chest is a lesion of the
chest ; (a grammatical remark is made) ; when these are the ground,
desiccation, (i.e.) decline of the elements (of the body), arises.
     An objector may raise the question whether) it is not thus, that
Caraka, who has summarily described the whole origin as being three-
fold with the words : “Inadequate conjunction of the senses with their
objects”, etc. (fr. Sū. 11, 38) and who later declares that also a disease
is an origin, contradicts the summarized description of the threefold
origin as stated by himself.
     On this (question) some reflect (as follows) : that origin which has been
said to be threefold has all illnesses as its range, but this one (mentioned
above) has a fixed range in each case, as a consequence of which not all
diseases arise from a disease, but only some (particular) illness (arises)
from some (particular) disease ; that is really a fourth origin, called
disease. Others however say that, even when a disease is the origin of
a disease, this does not occur at all with exclusion of the threefold origin,
the consequence of which is that this (mentioned) fever does not start
blood-bile as long as its force is not augmented by inadequate conjunc-

tion of the senses with their objects, etc.; with regard to the production
of an illness the ground is therefore only threefold, directly or in-
directly.160

1, 19ab : First being isolated diseases, they are functioning as a ground
                     later on.
                                                                     (Ca.Ni. 8, 20ab).161

M :
Because (the question may be raised) whether these very diseases,
which have been mentioned as the origin of another disease, generate
a disease when they have been scarcely produced or immediately follow-
ing upon that (production), it is said : 'they, first being', etc. These ill-
nesses, first being isolated, (i.e.) independent, because they have not
acquired a ground of augmentation, are at first only diseases because
they bring about a painful condition; later on, when they have acquired
a ground of augmentation, they bring about that which is the aim,
(i.e.) the purpose, called generation of an illness, of a ground, (i.e.) an
origin, as fever for instance (generates) blood-bile.

1, 20   : but another one does not become appeased, though being a
                     ground as well.

                     which are the most difficult (to cure) in men.

M :
The diversity of that very illness, generating a disease, is dealt with ...
Thus, in the mentioned manner, intermixtures, (i.e.) assemblies of ill-
nesses, are observed, as for instance (when) nasal catarrh does not cease
and cough is produced, haemorrhoids do not cease and abdominal affec-
tion and visceral swelling occur. They are the most difficult (to cure)
because they generate suffering of many kinds and, usually, are obstruc-
tive to treatment.

With the words ‘therefore’, etc. is expressed that the mentioned five
(elements, consisting of the) origin, etc. have necessarily to be known
because they are the ground of success, characterized by cessation of
disease. (It is said) ‘outstanding’, (i.e.) great, success because the
(of this science covers) many (subjects). ‘Ascertainment’ is the origin, etc.
Now the qualities of wind, etc., as stated by Caraka, are written down
in order to know, with regard to the morbid alterations which will be
described, about an inherence (in a morbid alteration, the qualities of
which are) congruous with the natural state, an inherence (in a morbid
alteration, the qualities of which are) incongruous with the altered state,
etc. : “Wind is dry, cold, light, subtle, fluctuating, clear and harsh; it
is appeased by substances with contrary qualities. Bile is slightly
oleaginous, hot, sharp, liquid, acid, flowing and pungent; it is quickly
appeased by substances with contrary qualities. Phlegm is heavy, cold,
soft, oleaginous, sweet, solid and mucilaginous; its qualities become
appeased by contrary qualities” (Sū. 1, 59-61).¹⁰³

contrary to a) the ground, b) the illness and c) both ground and illness. He gives a long
list of examples which are almost identical to those found in the Madhukoṣa.

Ca.Ni. 1, 11 : "Onset, emersion and origination have the same meaning with regard to
an illness." Cakra comments : "Although the signs become apparent immediately after
the onset, nevertheless the onset is dealt with at the end (of the series) because it is of
little purpose in the examination of an illness ... With respect to it some say that it is
the emersion of an illness as such, occasioned by the function of the last cause (*antya-
kāraṇavyāpārajanya*). Being of the opinion that, although the onset does not make (one)
aware of an illness in the (same) way as the origin, etc. does, it is nevertheless not a
characteristic of a not (yet) produced illness, they describe that the production leads to
the perception of an illness. Others do not share this opinion. When it is different the
consequence arises that some specific (peculiarity) is learnt from the onset. It is not a
fixed rule that an illness is perceived only after it has been produced completely; as a
consequence of this a not (yet) produced illness is indicated as an impending one by its
origin and prodromes. Therefore the word onset expresses here the emersion of an ill-
ness, connected with the specific function of the morbific entity which generates the
illness (*vyādhijanakadoṣavyāpāraviśeṣayukta*); for that very reason 'origination' is men-
tioned as a synonym. For the origination is the participation of the productive cause
which extends as far as the generation of an illness (*utpādakāraṇasya vyādhijanana-
paryantam gamanam*). The onset certainly makes (one) aware of a specific (peculiarity)

       of an illness, as for instance by the onset of fever, (described in the statement) beginning
       with 'and, when it is excited and has entered the receptacle of undigested food' and
       ending with 'then it results in fever' (Ca.Ni. 1, 20), peculiarities of fever are acknow-
       ledged, consisting of the facts that it brings about corruption of the receptacle of undi-
       gested food, injury of the (transforming) fire, corruption of the nutrient fluid, etc. It
       should not be said that this bringing about of a corruption of the receptacle of undi-
       gested food, etc. (constitutes) a peculiarity of the morbific entities, (for) from that would
       result that peculiarities of causes only are understood by the term origin. As a conse-
       quence (of this reasoning) the peculiarity of the cause, consisting of a function of the
       morbific entity which generates the illness, is expressed by the word onset, which has
       been made a separate (concept) in order to make (one) aware of a specific (peculiarity)
       of an illness ..."
       ¹¹⁸ Aruṇa comments : “... Discrimination is the settling of each component, (i.e.)
       the examination of every single part, the effect of each one having to be inferred, of the
       morbific entities, which have been united, (i.e.) brought about together, in one illness ...
       As for instance : in this illness the excited wind becomes corrupted with one quality
       which is present in excess, sometimes the dry, sometimes the light, sometimes the cold
       (quality), or sometimes with two or three qualities which are present in excess. In the
       same way the bile, etc. ... Such an ascertainment with regard to the (morbific entity)
       is (called) discrimination. As a consequence of this the ways of excitement are not com-
       parable in all diseases. The qualities dry, etc. of wind, for instance, always lead to ex-
       citement, but sometimes there exists pre-eminence (prakṛṣṭatva), sometimes defecti-
       veness (nyūnatva) of some quality with regard to the bringing about of excitement.
       That is the very ground of the infinite number of maladies and therapies ... With regard
       to therapeutic diagnosis, consisting of restorative measures (saṁtarpaṇa) or depletion,
       of an illness, one may also ask whether it is attended by well-being when (applied)
       completely or when (applied only) partially ...” He remarks that the term number is
       used to indicate the special (asādhāraṇa) ways of production of an illness because these
       are not substantiated by another term. The ascertainment whether an illness arises
       from a couple of morbific entities or from concerted action is not covered by this con-
       cept, but is called discrimination by means of more and most (serious) degrees (of ex-
       citement).

FEVER (JVARĀ)

2, 1 : Fever, the source of which is the exhalation of Rudra,¹ whose
    violent wrath had been aroused by the disrespect of Dakṣa,²
    is traditionally said to be of eight kinds : it arises from one
    (morbific entity) separately, a pair (of morbific entities), close
    union (of all three morbific entities) or in an adventitious way.³

M :
    And now fever has to be spoken of first owing to its predominance
    over all diseases.⁴ Its predominance (arises) from (the fact) that it is
    the first one of all bodily diseases which has been produced, from its
    forcefulness, the fact that it brings about glowing heat of body, senses
    and *manas*, its necessary presence in birth and death ⁵ and its per-
    vasion of all living beings, whether stationary or locomotive. Other
    morbid alterations are not like that. As has been said in the Caraka-
    (saṁhitā), from : “Fever has formerly been stated by you, holy one,
    to be the predominant disease, bringing about glowing heat of body,
    senses and *manas*, the firstborn of all diseases, full of force ; (about the
    nature, etc.) of this constant enemy of living beings in their absorption
    and rising” (Ci. 3, 4-5ab), etc., up to : “Holy one, be so kind as to tell”
    (Ci. 3, 9d).⁶ Moreover (it has been said) : “When fever is entering a
    living being, nothing whatsoever is not afflicted by glowing heat”
    (Ci. 3, 31cd).
    In (the book of) Pālakāpya it has been said : “It is called *pākala* in
    elephants, *abhītāpa* in horses, *īśvara* in cattle, *jvara* in men, *pralāpa*
    in goats and sheep, *alasa* in camels, *hārīdra* in buffalo cows, *mṛgaroga*
    in deer, *abhīghāta* in birds, *indramada* in fish, *pakṣapāta* in flying in-
    sects, *akṣika* in beasts of prey”, etc. And at another place : “Of water
    (it is called) *nīlīkā*, of soil *ūṣara*, in a tree *koṭara*”, etc.⁷
    Its first production is made mention of with the words ‘by the
    disrespect of Dakṣa’. (A paraphrase of 2, 1ab follows).
    The exhalation (of Rudra) is taught to be a sign of wrath in this
    case ; for that very reason it has been said by Suśruta : “Arisen from
    the fire of Rudra’s anger as a source” (U. 39, 9a). The wrathful Rudra
    cast a glance with the third fiery eye between his eyebrows and from


=== Page 98 ===
86 FEVER (JVARĀ)

that (glance) a fiery arrow was formed. As Caraka says : “The Lord
cast a look with the eye between his eyebrows, burnt those Asuras
and emitted an arrow,⁸ which was glowingly hot by the fire of wrath
and which destroyed the great sacrifice” (Ci. 3, 20)... This story about
the production of fever should be read, with its particulars, in the
(section on) therapy of the Caraka(saṃhitā).⁹
With this (story, mentioned above), the anger of Rudra has been
stated to be the distant cause; if fever were not produced by that
(anger), it would be produced no more, owing to improper conduct,
nowadays; thus says Bhaṭṭāraharicandra.
This tale being inapplicable with regard to therapy, other commen-
tators explain it in another way : because anger is at the source of
(fever), it becomes clear that it consists of fiery energy, for wrath is
of a fiery nature. As Caraka says : “From wrath (excitement of) bile
(arises)” (fr. Ci. 3, 115d).
It results from this (statement) that in every fever a therapeutical
procedure should be used that is not in disagreement with bile. As
has been said by Vāgbhaṭa himself : “Without bile there is no heat
and without heat there is no fever; therefore one should avoid things
which disagree with bile, the more so when there is an excess of bile”
(Ci. 1, 16cd-17ab). For that very reason the Caraka(saṃhitā) teaches,
because of its maturation-promoting character, making use of (a sub-
stance with) a bitter taste which destroys bile in a case of fresh fever,
discarding (substances with) a pungent, acid and saline taste; accord-
ing to what has been said (by Caraka) : “Reducing measures, sudation,
time, a gruel and the bitter taste promote the maturation of morbific
entities which have not been altered by digestion, in a case of fresh
fever” (Ci. 3, 142cd-143ab).¹⁰ (Time means in this case a period of eight
days ¹¹). Others, however, say : (fever) has been shown to deserve wor-
ship because, having the anger of Rudra as its source, it is of a divine
nature. As Videha says : “Or, on the other hand, fever becomes ap-
peased at once by acts of worship”.¹²
In the Harivaṃśa its actual bodily form is said to be (as follows) :
“Fever has three feet, three heads, six arms and nine eyes; it has
ashes for a weapon, is fierce (like Rudra) and resembles all-destroying
time in the form of Yama” ¹³ (Harivaṃśa 2, 122, 71cd-72ab).
Fever is mentioned (by Mādhava) in a concise way, though it is
manifold ... Its eight types are explained ... That has (already) been
explained (in the discussion) about the onset.

FEVER (JVARA) 87

2, 2 : By improper regimen of diet and conduct the morbific entities,
residing in the receptacle of undigested food, after having
thrown outside the visceral fire, will give rise to fever, when
they follow the nutrient fluid in its course.14

M :

With the words 'by improper (regimen of diet)', etc. the onset is
dealt with.

Impropriety of articles of food is their employment when they dis-
agree with regard to the grounds, consisting of natural state, etc., of
the employment of articles of food. As Caraka says : "In this respect
there are the following eight underlying factors of the specific modal-
ities of food, viz. natural state, getting it ready, commixture, quantity,
place, time, standards about its employment and the person who en-
joys the food as the eighth (item of the series)" (Vi. 1, 21).

With respect to this (series) the natural state is the junction of sub-
stances with qualities such as heaviness and lightness, belonging to
their own nature, as for instance (the heaviness) of māṣa beans and
(the lightness) of mudga beans.15 Getting it ready is its preparation,
as, for instance, (the preparation) of parched rice-grain, which is light,
from vrīhi rice, which is heavy.16 Commixture (means) close union, as,
for instance, of milk and fish.17 Quantity (means) the determination of
the measure of a food substance 18 as to its components and as to its
total mass.19 Place is the region of production, occurrence, etc. of a
substance.20 Time (means time as) permanent motion and (time) in
relation to stages (of life, of a disease, etc.).21 Standards about the em-
ployment are fixed rules about the employment,22 as for instance : one
should only eat when one's food has been disintegrated.23 He who en-
joys the food is the man himself, who has been examined as to what
is adequate to him, (of which kind) his constitution is, etc.24

Impropriety of conduct is an undertaking, etc., not in accordance
with one's force.

With the words 'residing in the receptacle of undigested food' it
is substantiated that the morbific entities do not start a fever without
having reached the receptacle of undigested food. About the recep-
tacle of undigested food has been said by Caraka : "The region between
the navel and (the nipples of) the breast of a living being is traditionally
called the receptacle of undigested food" (Vi. 2, 17ab).
'After having thrown outside the visceral fire' (means that) the vis-
ceral fire itself, hurled away by the morbific entities and got outside,


=== Page 100 ===
88
FEVER (JVARĀ)

becomes apparent by its heat. The visceral fire is mentioned in order
to exclude the fire of the elements (of the body), etc. …
`Following the nutrient fluid in its course' (means) : intimately con-
nected with the nutrient fluid; (the morbific entities) necessarily pro-
duce fever after having corrupted the nutrient fluid. Jējjaṭa says :
“This is the onset of bodily fevers only, but not of the adventitious
ones; the latter bring about distress at first and become attended by
wind, etc. afterwards.”
For that very reason the onset of an adventitious (fever) is de-
scribed separately in the Suśruta(saṃhitā) : “The wind of bodily beings,
excited by fatigue, a lesion, or traumatic injury, will lead to a vehement
fever, after having occupied the whole body” (U. 39, 80cd-81ab). 25 In
this case the wind does not stay at all in the receptacle of undigested
food, but wanders through the channels which carry the nutrient fluid
in an upward, downward and lateral direction. In the Caraka(saṃhitā)
it is also said : “In that case the wind, arising from traumatic injury
and corrupting mainly the blood, brings about fever, accompanied by
distress, swelling, alteration of colour and pain” (Cī. 3, 113cd-114ab). 26
It may be objected that in an adventitious fever also heat is experienced
and that it has been said : “There is no heat without bile” (A.h.Cī.
1, 16c); from these (arguments it would follow that) an adventitious
(fever) is a bodily (fever) as well.
That is not correct, because its production (takes place) at a later
(point of) time. As has been said : “The adventitious one, bringing
about distress at the beginning, is the eighth (kind of) fever; having
been an isolated adventitious one for some time, it becomes attended
by the morbific entities later on” (fr. Ca.Nī. 1, 30). And moreover :
“An adventitious morbid alteration follows an endogenous one, and
an endogenous (morbid alteration) follows, when it has extraordinarily
increased, an adventitious one as well” (Ca.Sū. 19, 7ab). 27
It may be objected that with the words ‘by improper regimen of
diet’, etc. the onset has been stated to be one and the same and that
is not correct, for the onset is a distinct (kind of) conjunction; a dis-
tinct (kind of) conjunction is founded on distinctions of its constituent
elements and the constituent elements of the conjunction, (viz.) wind,
etc., are in this case of various kinds; from this (reasoning it follows
that) the onset will also be of various kinds, for the conjunction of
wind and bile is not the same as (the conjunction) of phlegm and bile.
The answer (to this objection) is that the onset is indeed of several
kinds, but these belong to one class because the corruption of the


=== Page 101 ===
FEVER (JVARA)
89

receptacle, etc. is said to be uniformly present in all cases; so the onset
of an adventitious (fever) can also be distinguished by distinct (kinds
of) conjunction.

Ā :
... "Food taken at the wrong time and beyond the proper quantity,
as well as that food which is inadequate and incongruous, is called an
improper diet".²⁸ A regimen of diet is improper when it disagrees with
regard to place, time, constitution, etc. and when it disagrees with
regard to commixture, as does (a mixture) of milk and fish. Improper
conduct is an undertaking which is not in accordance with one's force.
"The person who (tries to) perform an action, (though) being unable
to perform it, and he who does not perform it, (though) being able to
do so, are called persons with an improper conduct; one should always
avoid (such) persons"...²⁹

2, 3 : The disease in which obstruction (of the flow) of perspiration,
a general sense of glowing heat and also a seizing (pain) in the
whole body occur simultaneously, is designated as fever.
(Su.U. 39, 13cd-14ab).³⁰

M :
... Obstruction (of the flow) of perspiration (means that) the warmth
(of the organism) has no outlet.³¹ (A grammatical remark follows). That
has been said in the Caraka(saṁhitā) : "Bringing about glowing heat
of body, senses and *manas*” (Ci. 3, 4a); "A deviated state of the senses
should be known as a characteristic of a general sense of glowing heat"
(Ci. 3, 37ab); and moreover : "A deviated state of the mind, disinclina-
tion and languor are the characteristics of a general glowing heat of
the *manas*” (Ci. 3, 36cd).³²
A seizing (pain) in the whole body is a painful sensation in the whole
body.
It is said (that they occur) ‘simultaneously’, (i.e.) as an agglomera-
tion, because that is the characteristic of (fever); (this is made mention
of) because inaccuracy would arise in taking each of these (symptoms)
separately. Obstruction (of the flow) of perspiration occurs as a pro-
drome of skin diseases, a general sense of glowing heat in the disease
called burning and a seizing (pain) in the whole body in a wind disease
affecting the whole body.


=== Page 102 ===
90
FEVER (JVARĀ)

It may be objected that the (mentioned set of) characteristics is not
invariably concomitant, because in bile fever perspiration appears, and
in wind fever an incongruous start and lapse occur and there is erratic
seizing (pain) in the whole body.³³

Jejjaṭa, Kārtikakuṇḍa and others have answered this (objection),
saying that a settlement (is made in these cases) with reference to the
relation between a general rule and exceptions (to this rule). Others
say that this is not logical : the relation between a general rule and
exceptions (to it may be applied) to a mode, but not to a characteristic,
because this (latter use) would be a case of faulty definition by limi-
tation of the attributes (to only a portion of the disease defined) or
extension of the attributes (beyond that disease which is defined);
therefore perspiration means fire (in this case), according to the ‘ety-
mology’ : ‘one is perspiring by it’; its obstruction has an invariable
concomitance with the morbific entities. Although in wind fever, owing
to the fluctuating character of wind, an incongruous start and lapse
occur, nevertheless there is certainly found a seizing of the whole body
which has not become perceptible, because there is no cessation of the
corruption by the morbific entity, starting the fever, which stays in
the whole body; so inaccuracy does not occur.

In the Caraka(saṁhitā), however, the characterization of fever is :
“The typical sign of fever is the general glowing heat of body and
mind” (Ci. 3, 31ab).

It may be said as an objection that, on account of Caraka's words :
“A bodily fever arises first in the body, a mental one in the mind”
(Ci. 3, 36ab), it is not a (good) characteristic, because (fevers of) body
and mind are separate from each other. That is not right, because
the other symptom will necessarily arise after a very subtle interval
of time, in the same way as it is the characteristic of a substance
that it is provided with its qualities (after a very subtle interval of
time).³⁴

Ā :
... Instead of ‘obstruction (of the flow) of perspiration’ others read :
obstruction of the (natural) urges.³⁵ In that case obstruction of the
(natural) urges means that flatus, urine and faeces do not leave (the
body). That (reading) is unsuitable because faeces, etc. are evacuated in
bile fever; therefore that (reading) is a case of limitation of the attri-
butes (to only a portion of the class defined).

“There are eighty morbid alterations by wind, forty by bile and twenty

hotness, etc. in the (various) parts of the body, of the paroxysms, (i.e.)

Gadādhara, etc. explain (what is rendered by ‘inhibition of sneezing
and certainly dryness of the limbs’ as meaning) : sneezing, ⁴⁹ stiffness,

This is, however, considered to be an explanation based on inadver-

one word : sneezing-inhibition. For Vāgbhaṭa says : ‘‘Horripilation,
hypersensitivity of the parts of the body and the teeth, shivering,
suppression of sneezing, giddiness, confused speech, longing for warmth
and moaning ⁵⁰ occur in a fever by wind” (Ni. 2, 17cd-18ab). In the

has used the word ‘suppression’ in order to indicate restraint in each
particular context; as for instance in the (description of the) origins
of visceral swellings by wind : ‘‘Dry foods and drinks, incongruous and
excessive voluntary bodily movements and suppression of the (natural)
urges” (Ci. 5, 9ab), and also in (the description of) the characteristics
of fever with an internal impulse : ‘‘Suppression of the morbific entity
and the excremental matter” ⁵¹ (Ci. 3, 40b).
With this (exposition) has also been rejected the question of Kārtika-
kuṇḍa, who has his doubts about it: ‘‘How can, since sneezing is men-
tioned in (the description of) the characteristics of the liberation from
fever, this (sneezing) be a characteristic of (fever) ?”
Inflatedness is a condition, accompanied by a painful sensation, in
which the abdomen is filled with wind.
The words ‘pain in the head, cardiac region and limbs’ (are used) to
indicate a painful sensation which especially occurs in the head and
cardiac region, because the latter are enumerated (separately) and the
term ‘limb’ includes the head and the cardiac region.
Suśruta teaches that these (enumerated) symptoms are those which
are usually present; by the word ‘and’ should be understood all the
other (symbols), mentioned by Caraka.

the ruddy (colour) such as it is present in diarrhoea, etc., started by
wind, which is colourless, and redness as it occurs in a mixture (of
some substance) with turmeric powder. As to what has been said in
the Suśruta(saṃhitā) : “Giddiness (arises) from rajas, bile and wind”
