DIARRHOEA (ATIṢĀRA)
209

M :
     With the words ‘pravāhikā’, etc. mention is made of its symptoms,
distinguished according to (the morbific entities) wind, etc.
     Is it not right that it has (already) been said : ‘the increased wind
(pushes down) the accumulated phlegm?’ Why then is ‘(pravāhikā)
brought about by wind’ made mention of?
     The answer is : (wind) is designated because it is present in excess.
For which reason are (the types of pravāhikā) that arise from bile
and blood mentioned as well?
     The answer is that it has been said ‘of someone whose food consists
of insalutary things’, and a disagreeing diet brings about excitement
of bile and blood in that condition; and when these two (entities) as
auxiliary forces of the wind show their own signs later on, it (i.e.
pravāhikā) is designated by means of these two (entities).
     (About) ‘coming about by means of oleaginous and dry (substances)’
(we remark that pravāhikā) arising from phlegm comes about by means
of oleaginous (substances) and (that type) arising from wind by means
of dry (substances) and, on account of the word ‘however’, (those types)
arising from bile and blood come about by means of sharp and hot
(substances). ‘Signs’ are the characteristics, distinguished in accordance
with wind, etc. ‘Due order’ is the due order of therapy, with distinc-
tions in accordance with the immature and mature conditions.

3, 23 : Who passes urine in the proper way without (passing) stools,
               whose wind moves, whose (transforming) fire is inflamed and
               whose viscera are light, is someone whose abdominal ailment
               has become arrested.
                                                    (Su.U. 40, 162).⁵³

M :
     That by which the cessation of diarrhoea is characterized is made
mention of for the sake of excluding the incertitude (consisting of the
problem that) cessation of diarrhoea (may be based) on non-appearance
of impure matter due to a constrained condition (of the impurities) by
wind or the retentive disease. The person, whose urine appears without
(the simultaneous appearance of) faeces, and (in whom this occurs) in
the proper way, i.e. in the way it is properly performed and not in a
deficient way, (is referred to); (whose) wind goes (out), ‘by way of the
anus’ has to be supplied. ‘It has become arrested’ (means) : it has
ceased. ‘Abdominal ailment’ (means) diarrhoea, because it is the topic

(of this chapter). This (stanza) describes the break-up of the onset. For
in diarrhoea the onset is as follows : the liquid element, even that

anus; but in the case that it appears by way of the urethra, it does so
at the same time as the faeces.

CHAPTER FOUR

THE GRAHAṆĪ DISEASE (GRAHAṆĪROGA)

4, 1 : Even when diarrhoea has ceased, the (transforming) fire of
  someone whose fire is sluggish and who eats insalutary things,
  being brought into a still more corrupted state, may bring
  about a great corruption of the grahaṇī.
             (Su.U. 40, 167).¹

M :
  Immediately after diarrhoea the grahaṇī disease (is described) be-
  cause (both) have the same peculiarity, (consisting of) a flowing (out)
  of liquid (matter), and because (both) attend each other.
  Its onset is made mention of ... The word ‘even’ informs (us) about
  the fact that the grahaṇī disease may arise due to its own ground, even
  in the absence of diarrhoea. Others, however, explain that the word
  ‘even’ indicates (that it may occur) also in the case that the diarrhoea
  has not ceased.² The words ‘of someone whose fire is sluggish’ express
  that even the eating of insalutary things does not bring about a morbid
  alteration in a person whose fire is inflamed. For in the Suśruta(saṁ-
  hitā) it has been said : “Disagreeing (articles of food) will be inopera-
  tive in a person with an inflamed fire” (fr. Sū. 20, 22).³ ‘Still more’
  (means) : again,⁴ or to an extreme degree. (The expression) ‘more cor-
  rupted’ (is used) because it has been made corrupted already previously
  in diarrhoea. ‘It may bring about a great corruption’ (means) : it may
  bring about a complete corruption. This means that insalutary (foods)
  have to be avoided by someone whose diarrhoea has ceased, until he
  has acquired a strong (transforming) fire. For that very reason Suśruta
  says : “Therefore one should avoid (insalutary foods) in diarrhoea in
  the same way as when one has been purged, until one’s natural con-
  dition (has been regained) with respect to the morbific entities and the
  vital breath” (U. 40, 168).

Ā :
  ... What is this (organ) called grahaṇī ? “There are three (kalās),
  (those) of flesh, blood and fat (respectively), a fourth one of liver and
  spleen, moreover a fifth one of the bowels; a sixth one is thought to


=== Page 234 ===
220                                          THE GRAHAṆĪ DISEASE (GRAHAṆĪROGA)

be that holding the (transforming) fire; a seventh one is that holding
the semen; these are the seven *kalās* according to tradition” (Śāriga-
dharasaṁhitā 1, 5, 6-7ab) ...

4, 2-3 : This (*grahaṇī*), being corrupted by the extremely intensified ⁵
morbific entities, by one of them separately ⁶ or by all of them
together, releases the ingested food repeatedly in a quite im-
mature state (2) or in a mature state, accompanied by pain,
foul-smelling, at one moment being bound, at another moment
being liquid. People who know the Āyurveda call it the
*grahaṇī* disease (3).
                                                                  (Su.U. 40, 171-172). ⁷ ⁸
M :
        Preceded by the onset, the generic characteristics (of the *grahaṇī*
disease) are made mention of ... ‘Intensified’ (means) : extremely in-
creased. (A remark is made about the meanings of *mūrcchā*.)⁹ The
variant reading ‘surged’ ¹⁰ has that very meaning. (A paraphrase of 4,
2cd and the beginning of 4, 3 follows; some grammatical remarks are
made). ‘Accompanied by pain’ (means) : accompanied by piercing pain.
‘Foul-smelling’ (means) : with a bad smell. (The excremental matter)
is at one moment bound by (the action of) wind, at another moment
liquid by (the action of) bile. (The term) *grahaṇī* disease (means) a
disease (brought about) by the *grahaṇī*. And the *grahaṇī* is the basis
of the (transforming) fire. As Caraka says : “The *grahaṇī* is thought to
be the basis of the fire because it seizes the (ingested) food; ¹¹ it (is
present) above the umbilical region and is furthered by the support ¹²
(consisting of) the strength of the fire. It sustains the immature food
and emits it downwards ¹³ when it is mature” (Ci. 15, 56-57ab). More-
over, the following has been said in the Suśruta(saṁhitā) : “That one,
which is proclaimed to be the sixth *kalā*, called the bile-holding one,
staying between the receptacles of digested and undigested food, is pro-
claimed to be the *grahaṇī*” (U. 40, 169). A *kalā* is a boundary between
the receptacles of the elements; the meaning of ‘staying between the
receptacles of digested and undigested food’ means that it consists of
the receptacle of the food that is subject to the process of maturation.

Ā :
        ... It releases (the ingested food) ‘repeatedly’, (i.e.) many times. It
is also corrupted by bile, as fire (is corrupted) by heated water; for
that reason the term ‘morbific entity’ is used in the plural ...

4, 4 : Its prodromes are the following ones : thirst, inertia, decline of
force, combustive alteration of the food, maturation (of it) after
a long time and heaviness of the body.
(Ca.Ci. 15, 55).¹⁴

M :
The prodromes are dealt with ... ‘Combustive alteration of the
food’... (occurs) because of the sluggish state of the (transforming) fire,
and for that very reason maturation of that same food (takes place)
after a long time. ‘Heaviness of the body’ (is present) on account of
the fact that it is (filled) with immature matter.

4, 5-10 : Excited by pungent, bitter, astringent, extremely dry and
completely corrupted ¹⁵ foods, by a restricted diet, abstinence
from food, too much travelling, suppression of (natural) urges
and sexual intercourse (5), the wind brings about maladies,
after having covered the (transforming) fire.¹⁶
(Such) a person suffers when his food maturates, he shows a
maturation of a fermentative type, harshness of the body (6),
desiccation of throat and mouth, absence of hunger,¹⁷ thirst,
dimness of vision, tinnitus, frequently occurring pain in the
sides, thighs, groins and neck, *viṣūcikā* (7), oppressing pain
in the cardiac region, leanness, weakness, an altered taste,
shooting pain, an eager longing for (food of) all tastes and
asthenia of the *manas* (8).
When (the food) has been disintegrated and when it is being
disintegrated, inflatedness (occurs) ; when one has ingested
(food), one gets relief.
Such a man is uncertain (whether) a visceral swelling by wind
(is developing), a disease of the cardiac region or a (disorder
of the) spleen (9) ; he may, after a long time and accompanied
by suffering, again and again emit excrements that are liquid,
desiccated, thin, immature, accompanied by noises and
frothy, and he is tormented by cough and shortness of breath,
(when the *grahaṇī* disease arises) from wind (10).
(Ca.Ci. 15, 59-64).¹⁸

M :
With the words ‘pungent, bitter’, etc., the symptoms of *grahaṇī*
(disease) by wind are dealt with, preceded by (its) origins and onset.
‘Completely corrupted foods’ are foods which disagree by way of com-


=== Page 236 ===
222                                 THE GRAHAṆĪ DISEASE (GRAHAṆĪROGA)

mixture, etc. A variant reading of ‘by completely corrupted foods’ is
‘by foods which are cold,¹⁹ etc.’ A restricted diet is the eating of
slight amounts of food. The variant reading prāmṛta should be under-
stood (to mean) the taking of food when the (proper) time has passed.
‘Abstinence from food’ is fasting. The wind, excited by these causes,
having brought about a complete corruption of the fire, gives rise to
diseases. Reflecting : ‘Which maladies does it bring about ?’ he says :
‘(such) a person, when his food’, etc. ‘A maturation of a fermentative
type’ is an acid maturation; this occurs on account of the combustive
alteration of the food, generated by the sluggishness of the (trans-
forming) fire. ‘Harshness of the body’ is a scabrous state of the body
due to the desiccation by wind of the oleaginous substance staying in
the skin. ‘Dimness of vision’ is a sluggish state of the visual organ.²⁰
‘Pain’ is oppressing pain; this (word) is connected with the (series
of) words beginning with ‘the sides’. ‘visūcikā’ is the appearance of
immature food above and below. ‘Alteration of taste’ is a condition in
which the taste in the mouth is disagreeing. ‘Shooting pain’ is an op-
pressing pain in the anal region as if it were being cut to pieces. ‘An
eager longing’ is a desire, for (food of) all tastes, (i.e.) sweet (foods),
etc.; (a grammatical remark is made); and this occurs by means of a
corrupted condition of the inner organ, brought about by wind, or by
means of the great power of the illness. ‘Asthenia of the manas’ is
prostration. To ‘inflatedness (occurs), when it has been disintegrated
and when it is being disintegrated,’ should be supplied ‘(when) the
food (has been disintegrated)’. (About) ‘such a man is uncertain whether
a visceral swelling by wind (is developing), a disease of the cardiac
region or a (disorder of the) spleen’ (we remark that) he suspects these
(disorders) because (grahaṇī disease) is accompanied by oppressing
pains, like those occurring in visceral swelling by wind, etc.²¹ (He may
emit excrements which are) liquid, desiccated’ (means that the excre-
ments are) sometimes liquid, sometimes desiccated. ‘Thin’ (means) in
slight amounts.

Ā :
     The word ‘extremely’ is connected with pungent, bitter and astrin-
gent ... The groin is the juncture between hip and thigh ²² ... ‘Asthenia
of the manas’ is languor of the manas ...²³

4, 11-12 : By means of pungent and non-disintegrated ²⁴ (substances),
                      by those which bring about combustive alteration, by acid,


=== Page 237 ===
THE GRAHAṆĪ DISEASE (GRAHAṆĪROGA)                                   223

          by caustic (substances), etc., the bile, being present in abun-
          dance, damages, overwhelming ²⁵ it, the (transforming) fire,
          as hot water (extinguishes) a fire (11).
          (In such a case the patient), being of a yellow complexion,
          is made to flow (faecal matter) that is non-disintegrated, of
          a swarthy and yellow colour and liquid, while he is torment-
          ed by foul-smelling and acid eructations, a burning sensa-
          tion in cardiac region and throat, inability to eat and
          thirst (12).
                                                       (Ca.Ci. 15, 65-66) ²⁶

M:
    The symptoms of grāhaṇī disease by bile are dealt with, preceded
by (its) origins and onset ... '(Substances) bringing about combustive
alteration', (i.e.) generating combustive alteration, are vaṁśa shoots,²⁷
etc. Caustic (substances) are made from apāmārga,²⁸ etc.; caustics are
also yavaksāra,²⁹ etc., and moreover substances to which a caustic has
been added; a sauce, prepared with alkaline water, is eaten in Kāmā-
rūpa,³⁰ etc. The word 'etcetera' denotes saline, sharp and hot sub-
stances; the bile, increased by these (substances), overwhelming, (i.e.)
overpowering the fire, damages it. He says: 'as hot water (extinguishes)
a fire', for the very reason that one may ask: 'Is it not right that bile
is of a fiery nature or fire itself, and that it increases bile for that
reason? So why does it damage (the fire)?' (The answer is) : just as
water, even when it is provided with the quality 'hot', destroys fire,
in that way bile, (though) consisting of heat, yet damages the (trans-
forming) fire when its liquid component has increased.³¹
    To '(in such a case) the patient being of a yellow complexion is made
to flow (down)' should be supplied 'excremental matter'.

4, 13-16 : Having become excited on account of the enjoyment of
          food that is heavy, extremely oleaginous, cold, etc., on ac-
          count of taking too much food and of sleeping when one
          has scarcely ingested one's meal, phlegm damages the (trans-
          forming) fire (13).
          Suffering accompanies the maturation of the food of such
          a man; there are present sickness, vomiting, anorexia, a
          condition of the mouth (in which it seems covered) with a
          liniment, a sweet (taste in the) mouth, cough, spitting and
          nasal catarrh (14).

                                              (The patient) has the impression that his cardiac region is

                                          heavy; there occur corrupted and sweet eructations, and
                                          adynamia; libidinous feelings towards women are ab-

                                              There appear excretions which are loosened, combined

                                                                                                    (Ca. Ci. 15, 67-70).³²

M:
    Mention is made of the symptoms of *grahaņī* disease by phlegm,
preceded by (its) origins, etc. ... The word ‘etcetera' denotes (foods
that are) mucilaginous, sweet, etc. ‘On account of taking too much
food' is : on account of the taking of food beyond the (proper)
measure.
    Is it not a disagreeing statement to say : ‘It damages the (trans-
forming) fire on account of sleeping when one has scarcely ingested
one's meal ?'; sleeping should be understood here in the sense of
sleeping by day, on account of the fact that sleeping at night is a
ground of soundness; sleeping by day, however, animates the abdo-
minal fire by closure of the channels; for that very reason it is said :
"Sleeping by day is prescribed to persons with diarrhoea and disorders
of the process of disintegration (of the food)".³³
    The answer (to this objection) is : sleeping by day damages the
(transforming) fire by an exceedingly great increase of phlegm in per-
sons who have ingested a meal, but animates it in persons who have
not ingested a meal. As has been said : "One may cause to sleep by
day, according to inclination, people who abstain from food".³⁴
    'A condition of the mouth (in which it seems covered) with a liniment,
and a sweet (taste in the) mouth', (i.e.) a condition in which the mouth
(seems covered) with an unctuous substance, and in which it is sweet,
(occur) by means of phlegm itself'. ‘In a grumous condition' is : as
filled with a dense liquid.³⁵ 'An abdomen which is torpid' is an abdo-
men (the contents of which are) confined, in the sense of devoid of
movement, or torpid (means) stiff. ‘Heavy' is rigid. ‘Corrupted' is
morbidly altered. ‘Sweet eructations' are (eructations which are) sec-
ondarily characterized by sweetness. ‘Adynamia' is adynamia of the
(transforming) fire. ‘Absence of libidinous feelings towards women' is

the non-existence of lasciviousness with respect to women. (Excrements
which are) loosened, and combined with immature matter and phlegm;
that is the sense of the compound. 'Weakness' is inability.

Ā :
... 'Adynamia' (is adynamia) of the parts of the body. 'Loosened'
is : torn asunder; 'heavy excrements' are (excrements which are) a
little bound.

CHAPTER FIVE

HAEMORRHOIDS (ARŚAS)

5, 1 : One should know that haemorrhoids (occur) in the triad of anal
folds and are of six kinds : (they are brought about) by each of
the morbific entities separately, by the associated (morbific
entities), (they arise) from blood and they (are) innate.¹

M :
Haemorrhoids are made mention of... immediately after grahaṇī
disease because diarrhoea, grahaṇī disease and haemorrhoids attend
each other.
The etymology of ‘haemorrhoid’ is said to be : it crushes, (i.e.) it
harms, the vital breaths like a foe ² (Pāṇini 6, 3, 109 is referred to).
‘Innate (ones)’ are (those which have) arisen together with the body,
on account of the fact that the germinal part which starts the anal
folds has been brought into a corrupted condition.³ Those arising from
a pair of morbific entities have not been counted separately in this
case, since they are reached by an inherence (in a morbid alteration,
the qualities of which are) congruous with the natural state. For it has
been said in the Suśruta(saṃhitā) : “When in (a case of) haemorrhoids
the symptoms of two morbific entities are observed, one should discern
it as (a case of) combined action; and this combined action is of six
kinds” (Ni. 2, 22). The sixfold condition of combined action (means)
here (that there exist) three (kinds of) combined action by means of
couples consisting of wind, etc., and three other ones by means of the
same (morbific entities) when they are connected with blood. That one
arising from concerted action has been counted as a separate (item)
in the numeration, considering it to be reached by an inherence (in a
morbid alteration, the qualities of which are) incongruous with the
altered state, because it is connected with incurability, which is not
observed in those arising from one single morbific entity.
(About) the triad of anal folds (we remark that) the anal area measures
four digits and a half; the three folds, which are components of it,
established one above the other, resembling the convolutions of a
conch-shell, are called pravāhaṇī, visarjanī and saṃvaraṇī. In this


=== Page 245 ===
HAEMORRHOIDS (ARŚAS)                                                                231

   (area) the anal lip is half a digit (in measure). Suśruta has pointed out
that the first fold upwards of it occurs at a distance of one digit.
Moreover, it has been said in (the treatise by) Bhoja : “The anal lip
is called (that part measuring) one barley grain and a half from the
edges of the hair(y region); it is known that the first fold is at one
digit from the anal lip; the two other ones are proclaimed (to occur)
at distances of one digit and a half each.”
   This means that the second and third one are found at a distance
of one digit and a half (each).⁴

Ā :
     … ‘Innate’ means : arising from (one’s) lineage …

5, 2 : The morbific entities, after having made skin, flesh and fat
             completely corrupted, bring about sprout-like growths of flesh
             of diverse conformations in the (area of the) *apāna*, etc. These
             are called haemorrhoids.

                                                                                     (A.h.Ni. 7, 2).⁵

M :
     The very form of haemorrhoids is dealt with, preceded by the onset.
The words ‘skin and flesh’ include the blood, residing in skin and flesh,
in accordance with the bringing about of a discharge of blood, as it
has been taught in the (section on) therapeutics.⁶ The (area of the)
*apāna* is the anal region; by the word ‘etc.’ the nose, etc. are understood.
The specialists in internal medicine, however, require (that) the term
haemorrhoids (be applied only) to those (sprout-like growths) which
arise from the anal region, although an excess of flesh (also occurs) in
those arising from the nose, etc. (They require it) because there does
not exist in those (latter ones) an onset as described with the words
‘the fivefold wind’, etc., and there do not occur prodromes as described
with the words ‘a constrained condition’, etc.⁷ As Caraka says (in the
statement) beginning with ‘the penis’ up to ‘properly designated as an
excess of flesh’ (fr. Ca.Ci. 14, 6).⁸ Suśruta, however, has employed the
term haemorrhoids with respect to these (growths at other places of
the body), by reason of the common peculiarity of consisting of sprout-
like growths of flesh and of being curable by means of a cutting in-
strument, caustic or cauterization, in the same way as the oleaginous
substance from *sarṣapa*, etc. is designated as oil. This very view is
shared by Vāgbhaṭa, who reiterates (the opinion of) Suśruta.

M :
    Mention is made of the origin of haemorrhoids by wind ... Eating
    a restricted (amount of food) is (eating) a very slight (amount), (eating
    a slight (amount) is (eating an amount) the measure of which is defi-
    cient. Jejjaṭa, however, says that (a) restricted (diet means) : taking
    food when the (proper) time has passed. If pramṛta (instead of pramita)
    is read, it is said (to denote) grain, etc., the power of which has been
    annihilated.
    Others say that a restricted (diet) is the habitual use (of foods) with
    one (particular) taste. That is not a very suitable application (of this
    term). Does it mean (the habitual use) of pungent (substances), etc.,
    which bring about excitement of wind, or of sweet ones, etc., which
    bring about excitement of phlegm ?
    The first (alternative is) not (the right one) because pungent (sub-
    stances), etc. have (already) been enumerated in this very (stanza); as
    to the second (alternative), however, (it should be noticed that) the
    habitual use of sweet (foods), etc. verily brings about appeasement of
    wind and, moreover, it has been stated that weakness (arises) from
    the habitual use (of foods) with one (single) taste, but no increase of
    wind. Thus should be reflected about it.
    ‘Sharp’ is added to ‘alcoholic beverage’ as a specification, because
    mild alcoholic beverages, such as paiṣṭika, etc., appease the wind.¹¹
    ‘A cold place’ is a marshy place; ‘a cold time’ is the winter, etc. ‘Glow-
    ing heat’ is hot(ness); glowing heat (of the sun), though provided with

HAEMORRHOIDS (ARŚAS) 235

etc. (fr. Ci. 14, 7).²¹ Is it not right to say that the announcement of a
specific (type), with the words 'those arising from the three morbific
entities', is based on an inconclusive argumentation, because verily
all diseases arise from the three morbific entities, according to what
has been said : “A substance with (only) one taste does not exist nor
a disease arising from (only) one morbific entity; they are defined by
means of that one of the tastes and morbific entities which is present
in excess ?” ²² That is not right. According to the statement : “Wind,
bile and phlegm are coursing through the whole body” (fr. Ca.Sū. 20,
9), there occurs necessarily, when one (constituent) element, etc. has
been corrupted by a morbific entity, some kind of corruption with
respect to the other morbific entity residing in it, owing to the intimate
connection (that exists) between a corrupted (constituent) and a mor-
bific entity. Moreover it is thus, that the wind, when it has become
increased on account of its own causes, supplies, owing to its coldness,
force to phlegm which is cold and, owing to its lightness, to bile which
consists of fiery energy; bile (supplies force) to wind owing to its
pungency, and to phlegm owing to its liquidity; phlegm (supplies
force) to wind owing to its coldness, and to bile owing to its liquidity.
For that very reason it has been said : “No disease whatever arises
from one (single) morbific entity.” ²³ With this very view (in mind) it
has been said : “One excited morbific entity will bring about excite-
ment of really all of them.” ²⁴ In that case in which all three (mor-
bific entities) are excited on account of their own causes, the de-
signation '(arising from) three morbific entities' (is used); that is the
settled doctrine. (It should be used) in the same way everywhere.

the same way phlegm is of five kinds as well : “Chest, throat, head,
junctures, 91 receptacle of undigested food, nutrient fluid, fat, nose and
tongue are the seats of phlegm, (but) the chest (is its seat) in a very
special way.” 92 Thus it has been established that the three morbific
entities are of five kinds. 93

This is the fulfilment (of the requirements) with respect to the four
basic elements. And this (fulfilment) is possible when a remnant of
vitality has been left (in the patient).

¹ Ca. divides haemorrhoids first into two classes : those which are innate and those
which arise at a later time in life (Ci. 14, 5). The latter are distinguished into those arising
from wind, bile, phlegm, a combination of (two) morbific entities and concerted action
(Ci. 14, 11-20). At Ci. 14, 23 it is said, however, that haemorrhoids never occur without
excitement of all three morbific entities and that their type is determined in accordance
with the morbific entity which is prevalent. Haemorrhoids arising from blood are not
made mention of in the nidāna section of Ci. 14, but do appear in the section on therapy,
though in an ambiguous phrasing; Ci. 14, 38cd : "(Haemorrhoids, which are) discharging
and (those, which are) wet, are possessed of an abundance of blood and bile." Su. agrees
with Mā.ni. 5, 1. Su.Ni. 2, 3 : "There are six (kinds of) haemorrhoids, (those by wind,
bile, phlegm, blood and concerted action and (those which are) innate." Ḍa. observes :
"... Is it not thus, that by means of the very words '(those) by wind, bile, phlegm, blood
and concerted action and (those which are) innate' a number of six (kinds of haemor-
rhoids) has been obtained? So why is (their) number taught by the word 'six'? The
answer is : (it is done) in order to avoid that haemorrhoids generated by two morbific
entities are included in counting (the types). Although wind, etc., when having blood
as a basis, are the starting agents of bloody haemorrhoids, nevertheless the words
'(those) arising from blood' are used, metaphorically, in the same way as something
burnt by means of a fire with ghee as its basis is said to be burnt by means of ghee."
Gayadāsa comments : "... Is it not thus, that the accurate determination of a number
of six (kinds of haemorrhoids) is contradictory on account of the fact that it has also

been shown that there is a number of six (kinds of) haemorrhoids by a combination (of
two morbific entities) ? That has been stated (as follows) : “When in (a case of) haemor-
rhoids the symptoms of two morbific entities are observed, one should discern it as (a
case of) combined action; combined action is traditionally said to be of six kinds”
(Ni. 2, 22). The answer is that the meaning has been explained as follows : in those cases
in which concerted or combined action occurs with an inherence (in the morbid altera-
tion, the qualities of which are) congruous with the natural state, the number is not
made redundant according to the consideration : ‘an aggregate is not different from its
component parts’, because (cases of) combined action, the signs of which are those of
each single morbific entity as a (constituent) element, (i.e. those of) wind, etc., are in-
cluded in (the syndromes by) wind, etc. solely, as one (category) with respect to (their)
therapy. That has been stated in the Caraka(saṁhitā) : after saying “There are five
(kinds of) visceral swelling, (to wit those) arising from wind, bile, phlegm, concerted
action and blood” (fr. Sū. 19, 4), it is said on the other hand : “One should point out,
however, that the other visceral swellings, the signs of which are (of a) combined (charac-
ter), are three (in number), for the sake of the preparation of medicinal agents” (Ci. 5,
16). If, according to the words : ‘an aggregate is not different from its component parts’,
the inclusion of those arising from combined action in those arising from a single mor-
bific entity (to wit) wind, etc., does not occur, the statement ‘there are five (kinds of)
visceral swelling’ disagrees with the accurate determination of a number of five (types).
On the other hand others say : (it occurs) on account of the tracing back of the word
‘concerted action’ to its derivation... That (is) not (correct), because it has been de-
monstrated in the Caraka(saṁhitā), that haemorrhoids by combined action (do
exist).” (Compare this reasoning with the similar one in Cakra’s comment on Ca.Ci. 5, 16).

CHAPTER SIX

SLUGGISHNESS OF THE (TRANSFORMING) FIRE
(AGNIMĀṆḌYA),
DISORDERS OF THE PROCESS OF DISINTEGRATION
(OF THE FOOD) (AJĪRṆA),
VISŪCIKĀ, INTESTINAL INERTIA (ALASAKA)
AND RETARDATION OF EVACUATION (VILAMBIKĀ)

6, 1 : Sluggish, sharp, incongruous and congruous, of four types is
the abdominal fire, owing to excess of phlegm, bile and wind
and owing to a congruous state of these.¹

M :
On account of the fact that sluggishness of the fire, etc. are effects
of haemorrhoids, mention is made of these (conditions) ... The sluggish
(fire) is mentioned first because it is difficult to subdue. 'Owing to
excess of phlegm, bile and wind' should be connected with 'sluggish',
etc., in due order. 'Owing to a congruous state of these' (means) owing
to a congruous state of phlegm, etc. 'Congruous' means : not morbidly
altered, its ground being a congruous state of the elements. This
absence of a morbid alteration is included in the subject 'morbid al-
teration' in order to indicate that knowledge about morbid alterations
is directly connected with knowledge about natural states. The ab-
dominal (fire is expressly denoted) to differentiate it from the fire of
the elements (of the body) and that of the gross elements.²

6, 2 : An incongruous fire brings about diseases arising from wind,
a sharp one (diseases) arising from bile as a cause and a sluggish
one morbid alterations with phlegm as a source.
(Su.Sū. 35, 25).

6, 3-4 : In a person with a congruous fire a congruous quantity of
eaten (food) is digestively altered in a proper way; even a very
slight (quantity, however, is) not at all (digestively altered) in
a person with a sluggish fire; but in a bodily being with an
incongruous fire (3) (the eaten food) is sometimes properly
maturated and sometimes not digestively altered. Someone, in

SLUGGISHNESS OF THE FIRE                                                              265

whom the eaten quantity (of food), even when it is beyond
the proper measure, is easily digestively altered, should be
known as a person with a sharp fire. A person with a congruous
fire is said to be the foremost (among them) (4).³

M :
Mention is made of the symptoms of these (types of fire) by the
application of an unusual treatise...⁴
    ‘(An incongruous fire brings about) diseases arising from wind⁵, (i.e.)
any one of the eighty qualified ⁶ wind (diseases) and of the unqualified⁶
ones, (consisting of) fever, diarrhoea, etc.; in the same way (a sharp
fire brings about) any one of the forty qualified bile (diseases), burning,
sucking pain,⁷ etc.; in the same way (a sluggish fire brings about) any
one of the twenty qualified phlegm (diseases), inertia, etc. All these
morbid alterations should be looked for in the Caraka(samhitā), in the
very chapter on the great diseases.⁸
    ‘A congruous quantity’ (is) an adjusted quantity of food. ‘The
(eaten) quantity (of food), when it is beyond the proper measure’ is an
implicative expression; this (expression) should be understood to
characterize eating before the previous meal has been digested, and
eating heavy food, etc. as well. As has been said elsewhere : “That
fire is the most excellent one, by which a quantity (of food) beyond
the proper measure is maturated, even in a person whose previous meal
has not yet been digested, and heavy food of someone who eats though
he sleeps by day.”⁹ The word ‘sharp’ includes the person with an in-
cinerating fire, (for) only an extremely sharp fire is called incinerating.
As has been said in the Caraka(samhitā) : “In a man whose phlegm
has declined, the bile, being excited and following the wind (in its
course), renders, by its own heat, force to the fire in the seat of the fire.
Thereupon the fire, together with the wind, having acquired force,
may give rise to a general painful condition of the body. Having over-
powered the food, it quickly maturates it again and again on account
of its sharpness.¹⁰ Then, after maturating the food, it also maturates
the elements (of the body, consisting of) blood, etc. Thereupon it leads
a man to weakness, disorders and death. After ingesting food, one be-
comes appeased; having scarcely disintegrated it, one becomes breath-
less. Illnesses like thirst, cough,¹¹ a burning sensation, fainting, etc.
find their source in an extremely (sharp) fire” (Ci. 15, 217cd-221ab).¹²

6, 6 : Some say there is a fifth (type of) disorder of the process of
             disintegration (of the food), devoid of a morbific entity, and
             (in which) maturation (of the food occurs) on the (following)

M :
Mention is made of the disorders of the process of disintegration (of
the food) because a sluggish state of the fire and disorders of the process
of disintegration (of the food) are causally related to each other...
'By means of the three (morbific entities)', (i.e.) every single one (of
the morbific entities), phlegm, etc., in accordance with their number
(in this series). (About) 'due to a remnant of the *rasa*' (we remark) :
a remnant of the *rasa* is the remnant (set apart) for the *rasa*, (a gramma-
tical remark follows), as e.g. the wood (set apart) for the sacrificial
post (is called) the sacrificial post-wood; or, as Jejjāṭa holds : "By the
word *rasa* the food which possesses taste is intended by means of an
elliptical expression; by this word *rasa* the food which possesses taste
is designated; the remnant of it, which is characterized by the absence
of transformation, is the remnant of the *rasa*." ¹⁵
(An objector may ask :) Is it not true that, if things are like that,
there is no distinction between the latter and the immature, combus-
tively altered and constrained (types), because it necessarily occurs in
the form of any one of these, and that, moreover, there must occur
acid eructations, etc., which are the signs of these, and that, accord-
ingly, when an unpolluted condition exists with regard to the eructa-
tions, the consequence arises that the characteristics of the disorder
of the process of disintegration (of the food, arising) from a remnant
of the *rasa*, will not come forth? For it has been said in the Suśruta-
(saṃhitā) : "When no desire for food arises, though there exists an
unpolluted condition with regard to the eructations, and when one's
cardiac region feels heavy, it is proclaimed to be the fourth disorder
of the process of disintegration (of the food), accompanied by effusion,
(arising) by means of the remnant of the *rasa*” (Sū. 46, 503). Also,
Nāgārjuna says in the Ārogyamañjarī : "Absence of the desire for food,


=== Page 281 ===
SLUGGISHNESS OF THE FIRE                                                              267

etc., even when an unpolluted condition has been reached with respect
to the eructations, oleaginousness of the mouth, a painful condition
of the junctures and heaviness of the head, these are the characteris-
tics of the *rasa* of the sluggish (type of the) disorder of the process of
disintegration (of the food). When it has increased extremely, there
may also occur sickness, fever, fainting, etc., giving rise to a turmoil
of all ailments.”

Thus it is not; on account of the extremely slight amount of the
remnant of the food, though necessarily occurring in the form of the
combustively altered (type), etc., the consequence is not that eructations,
which correspond to it, arise, as in the case of the desire to ingest food
at an improper time. As Suśruta says : “When a very small amount
of immature matter, confined by the morbific entities and in a dis-
solved ¹⁶ condition, does not cover the path of the fiery energy,¹⁷
there occurs, even in a disorder of the process of disintegration, the
desire to ingest food; this (desire) kills, as a poison, the person with a
sluggish *buddhi*” (Sū. 46, 51).¹⁸ The characteristics of a remnant of
the *rasa*, arising from non-maturation of the food, have also been
stated in another treatise : “Disorders of the process of disintegration
(of the food) may be of four kinds, (of the immature, combustively
altered and constrained (type), and also (of the type arising from) a
remnant of the *rasa*; they arise from incomplete maturation of the
food. Gadādhara, however, says : “A remnant of the *rasa* is a remnant
with regard to the *rasa*; it is a remnant with regard to the *rasa* gene-
rated from the food, a component part of the food which has entered
it additionally, and is not perceptible, like the water which is present
in milk.” ¹⁹

But what then is the distinction between (the disorder from) a
remnant of the *rasa* and the immature type, etc. of the disorder of the
process of disintegration?

The answer is : the triad, consisting of the immature type, etc.,
arises from the food, but (the disorder from) a remnant of the *rasa*
arises from the *rasa* of the food, and designations according to (the
morbific entities), wind, etc., are not made in the latter because the
signs of wind, etc. are of a slight kind; distinctions are made according
to ground, characteristics and therapy.

(About the term) ‘disorder of the process of disintegration’... (we
remark that) disintegrated (means) matured; non-disintegrated is
the opposite (term), in the same way as black (non-white) (is the op-
posite of white). All disorders of the process of disintegration arise


=== Page 282 ===
268                                              SLUGGISHNESS OF THE FIRE

from the three morbific entities; it is explained that the designation
of one (particular) morbific entity is made by means of the signs of
that single morbific entity, which has unduly increased. For that
reason the causation of disorders of the process of disintegration has
been stated to relate to the three morbific entities, with the words
"From the drinking of an extreme amount of water", etc. 20 Excitement
of the triad of morbific entities also occurs on account of disorders of
the process of disintegration. As has been said in the Suśruta(samhitā) :
"From disorders of the process of disintegration a strong agitation of
the wind, etc. may arise." 21

(About) 'some (say there is) a fifth (type of) disorder of the process
of disintegration', etc. (we remark that) 'devoid of a morbific entity'
(means) not causing a corruption (consisting of) inflatedness, etc.
(About) '(in which) maturation (of the food occurs) on the (following)
day' (we remark that) food is maturated in a day and a night according
to the general rule; in case it is maturated, however, on the following
day, on account of a morbid factor, (consisting of) inadequacy with
respect to the measure and time (of the meal), etc., it is (called that type
in which) maturation (of the food occurs) on the (following) day. It is
distinguished from the former types by the fact that it does not bring
about inflatedness, etc., though maturation (occurs) with violation of
the time(-limit). The purpose of the (separate) denomination of this
(type) is that attention be paid to the time of maturation, because
ingestion of food is prohibited in a nocturnal disorder of the process
of disintegration.

(About 'a sixth one that is) of a natural kind and occurring daily'
(we remark that) 'of a natural kind' (indicates that) it does not give
rise to a morbid alteration. What is aimed at is the following : is the
ingested food at this very moment disintegrated or not? It is not
disintegrated at all because there is no rise of hunger, thirst, excretion
of impurities, etc., which are characteristics of disintegration. There-
fore non-disintegration is present, and this does not bring about in-
flatedness, etc.; so it is distinct from the former (types). And the pur-
pose of its (separate) denomination is the employment, for the sake of
maturation, of lying down on the left side, and other ways of (pre-
scribed) conduct. For it has been said in the Suśruta(samhitā) : "After
having ingested one's meal 22 and having walked a hundred feet, one
should lie down on the left side; one who has ingested his meal should
indulge in sounds, colours, tastes, sensations of touch and smells which
are agreeable to one's mind; by means of that (conduct) the food re-


=== Page 283 ===
SLUGGISHNESS OF THE FIRE 269

mains in the right condition” (Sū. 46, 487cd-488).²³ And in this case
food is not prohibited, being prescribed by (medical) science.
In the Caraka(saṃhitā), however, from : “The signs of this disorder
of the process of disintegration” (Ci. 15, 45a), up to : “It is a dreadful
food-poison” (Ci. 15, 46d),²⁴ the (type of) disorder of the process of
disintegration, called food-poison, is described. And it is explained that

arising from) a remnant of the rasa has not been described separately
(in the Carakasaṃhitā), being included in it (i.e. : in the food-poison
type).

Ā :
A remnant of the rasa is the non-maturated rasa which has been left
behind…

of) the disorders of the process of disintegration, because the latter

three (disorders, to wit) those of the immature, constrained and com-
bustively altered types, visūcī, intestinal inertia and retardation of
evacuation arise in accordance with their number (in this series)."
Bakulakara says that this is not correct. For retardation of evacuation
arises from the combustively altered type, if there is agreement with
its number (in the series), but it will be described (as arising) from
phlegm and wind. Therefore it is suitable (to assume that) the produc-
tion of visūcī, etc. is brought about by the three types of disorder of
the process of disintegration, in accordance with their source. For it
has been said : "A strong agitation of wind, etc. may arise from a
disorder of the process of disintegration." 35

6, 16-17 : (The disorder) of someone in whom the wind stagnates,
            pricking the limbs as with needles, (that disorder, arising)
            by means of a disorder of the process of disintegration, is
            called visūcī 36 by the vāidyas (16).
            It is not acquired by those with a restricted diet who know
            the traditional doctrines.
            Confused persons who have not subdued their minds and

M :
Mention is made of the 'etymology' of visūcī... The 'etymology' of
visūcī is as follows : "The wind, owing to its copiousness, pricks as
with needles." Disregarding the pricking pain as by needles, other
distinct kinds of painful sensations of several kinds also occur, as in
morbid pallor. As has been said in another treatise : "Owing to the
vehement excitement of wind, etc., it cuts 39 the limbs by distinct
kinds 40 of painful sensations of several types, as by needles; that is
why it is called visūcikā” (A.h.Sū. 8, 7cd-8ab).

‘Those knowing the traditional doctrines’ are those possessing know-

acquainted with knowledge about it. ‘Those who have not subdued
their minds’ are persons who have not subdued their senses. ‘Those

Ā :
… ‘Confused persons’, (i.e.) those who are unacquainted with what
should be eaten and should not be eaten, get it. (About ‘persons who
are cupidous with regard to eating’ we remark that) others read ‘per-

digested food occurs because corrupted matter and food are blended,
and because of excitement of the wind and the other (morbific entities).

6, 18 : Fainting, diarrhoea, emesis, thirst, piercing pain, giddiness,
cramp, yawning, a burning sensation, alteration of colour,
trembling and pains in the cardiac region occur in it (i.e. in
viṣūcī), together with a cutting pain in the head.
(Su.U. 56, 6).⁴¹

M :
Mention is made of the characteristics of viṣūcī... A cutting pain in
the head is a piercing pain in the head. Emesis and diarrhoea, occur-
ring together, are in this case a characteristic. In the Suśruta(saṃhitā)
the downwards moving type is included in (the disorder called) imma-
ture diarrhoea, and the upwards moving type in vomiting. In the
Caraka(saṃhitā), however, one reads : “One should know to be viṣūcī
that one, in which the morbific factor consisting of immature matter
has come forth upwards and downwards, and the symptoms of which
correspond to those which have been described” (Ca.Vi. 2, 11).⁴² From
this it follows that there exist an upwards moving type of viṣūcī, and
also a downwards moving type, because the immature type of diar-
rhoea has not been described in the Caraka(saṃhitā). It is explained
that the word ‘and’ ⁴³ indicates that a type that moves along both
pathways exists as well. One should consider the upwards moving
type to be distinct from the types of vomiting which arise from the
three morbific entities, because non-maturated food is vomited in it.

6, 19-20 : (In the case) that the lateral parts of the abdomen become
                  extremely swollen by obstruction, (in the case) that one
                  becomes breathless ⁴⁴ and moaning, ⁴⁵ (if) the restrained wind
                  moves about upwards ⁴⁶ of the lateral parts of the abdomen

M :
     Mention is made of intestinal inertia... (The lateral parts of the
abdomen) ‘become swollen by obstruction’ (i.e.) become inflated, be-
cause it will be stated presently that the impure matter is constrained.
‘One becomes breathless’, (i.e.) one becomes confused; ⁵⁰ ‘one moans’,
(i.e.) one makes the loud sound of someone who is afflicted. (The wind)
‘being restrained’, (i.e.) its downward course or (its motion) in the lateral
parts of the abdomen having been checked by the non-disintegrated
matter, moves upwards of (these parts), (i.e.) it goes upwards, to the
cardiac region, throat, etc. It is technically called intestinal inertia
because the (matter which constitutes its) morbific factor is solid. As
has been said in another treatise : “The food advances neither upwards
nor downwards, and is not digestively altered; ⁵¹ because it stays in
the receptacle of undigested food in an inert condition, this (disorder)
is traditionally called intestinal inertia” (A.h.Sū. 8, 6cd-7ab).

6, 21 : When the ingested food, corrupted by phlegm and wind,
                  comes forth neither upwards nor downwards in someone, the

M :
     Mention is made of retardation of evacuation... ‘Extremely difficult
to treat’ means that one should reject, (i.e.) avoid, (a patient suffering
from it).
     What is the distinction between intestinal inertia and retardation
of evacuation? We may ask this question, because both (diseases) are
comparable regarding the great strength of wind and phlegm and by
reason of the fact that habitually (immature matter) does not come

forth, neither along the upward nor the downward (path). The answer
is that in intestinal inertia violent piercing pains occur (and not in
retardation of evacuation), as has been said (A.h.Sū. 8, 10cd-11 is
quoted).⁵³

Ā :
... Instead of ‘corrupted’ (ingested food) some read : dissolved. This
very retardation of evacuation is described with the name ‘stick-like

restrain (the flow through) the channels and they stiffen, of their own

inertia quickly brings about the annihilation of the human body.” ⁵⁴ ⁵⁵

6, 22 : At what particular place the immature matter stays, at that
very place it may specifically give rise to a painful condition
by means of hosts of morbid alterations, the characteristics
of which are those of the morbific entity that has spread over
the body, and those which arise from immature matter.⁵⁶
(Su.U. 56, 10).

M :
After noticing *visūcī*, etc., which have arisen from a disorder of the
process of disintegration, mention is made of another effect of imma-
ture matter that is being generated from a disorder of the process of
disintegration... ‘Immature matter’ is the agent; at what particular
place it may stay, at that very place it may specifically give rise to a
painful condition; by this (statement) it is indicated that it brings
about a slightly painful condition at another place as well. By the use
of *yatra*, a word of the class called *sarvanāman*,⁵⁷ it is shown that im-
mature matter has a variable seat, like excited wind and the other
(morbific entities).
By means of what does it give rise to a painful condition ? By means
of hosts, (i.e.) multitudes, of morbid alterations. Of what kind are these ?
The characteristics of these are those of the morbific entity, excited by
its own cause, by which the body is overspread, (i.e.) pervaded; these
characteristics are pricking pain (by wind), a burning sensation (by
bile), heaviness (by phlegm), etc. Not only by these hosts of morbid
alterations, but also by those arising from immature matter, (i.e.)


=== Page 290 ===
276                                SLUGGISHNESS OF THE FIRE

absence of maturation, intestinal inertia, etc. (it may give rise to a
painful condition). It is said that by means of this stanza Suśruta has
included the disease, described in other treatises, called immature
wind,⁵⁸ because its characteristics are the same.

Ā :
     Immature matter is that which has not been properly transformed,
according to what has been said : “That which is not digestively altered
and has not been subject to the process of commixture, which is bad-
smelling, copious, mucilaginous and bringing about adynamia of all
the limbs, is called immature matter.” ⁵⁹
     At what particular place the immature matter, which is the agent of
the setting in motion and attraction of the wind, stays, (i.e.) remains
established on account of the alteration of its qualities, at that very
place it may specifically give rise to a painful condition, (i.e.) it may
painfully oppress. On account of the fact that desiccation, inflamma-
tory swellings, abscesses and other diseases, by means of sluggishness
of the fires of the elements of the body and the gross elements, have
their source in immature matter, its being a source of production has
been declared to be such as has been said (in the following statement) :
“Seven fires of the elements of the body and five of the gross elements
make, together with the abdominal fire, thirteen fires.” ⁶⁰ At what
particular place of one of the elements of the body the fire is sluggish,
at that very place may occur, with immature matter as its source, the
production of boils, etc.⁶¹

     6, 23 : That man whose teeth, lips and nails are brown, whose con-

M:

7, 1-2a : Worms are proclaimed to be of two kinds, as they are dis-
          tinguished into external and internal ones.
          They are of four kinds according to their distinction into
          those born out of external impure matter, out of phlegm,
          blood and faeces (1).
          They are of twenty kinds (distinguished) according to their
          names.
                                                    (A.h.Ni. 14, 42cd-43c).¹

M :
     Mention is made of the origins of (the disorders by) worms, imme-
diately after the disorders of the process of disintegration, because
the latter ones are the source of the former... Regarding these (worms),
there are external ones, which find their source in external impure
matter, (consisting of) the unctuous substance (produced) by the skin,
and internal ones, which find their source in the receptacle of undi-
gested food, etc.; these (worms) are said to be of two kinds if dis-
tinguished according to their location, and of four kinds if distinguished
according to their cause... External impure matter is said to be pers-
piration, etc., with which the body is daubed.² ... These same (worms)
are of four kinds, and, when distinguished according to their names,
of twenty kinds. Surpassing (the number of) twenty are the extremely
subtle worms which are innate and have been mentioned by Caraka,³
but these are not described in the paragraph on diseases (by worms),
because they do not bring about morbid alterations.⁴ Those worms
which are of twenty kinds, however, are said to be (related to) diseases,
because they generate fever, piercing pain, etc., by means of excitement
of the morbific entities.

Ā :
     Some are external, arising from the hair of the head, garments, etc.,
(viz.) lice, nits, etc., and others are internal. The source of the inter-
nal ones is immature matter, etc... Some of these specific names
are related (to each other), others are unrelated; they have been taught


=== Page 300 ===
286                                            WORMS (KRIMI)

by the early masters for the sake of common practice. Their names are
(as follows) : the two (kinds of worms), springing up from external
impure matter, are the lice and the nits; thep laces of their residence
are the hairs of the head and the garments. Those arising from phlegm
are (called) *antrāda*, *udarāveṣṭa*, *hṛdayāda*, *mahāguda*, *curu*, *darbha-
kusuma* and *sugandha*; in that way there are seven (kinds); their place
of residence is the receptacle of undigested food. Those arising from
blood are (called) *keśāda*, *lomavidhvamsa*, *romadvīpa*, *udumbara*, *saurasa*
and *mātr*; in that way there are six (kinds); they are seated in the
blood-carrying vessels. There are five (kinds of worms) springing up
from faecal matter : (their names are) *kakeruka*, *makeruka*, *sausrāda*,
*śaśūla* and *leliha*; their place of residence is the receptacle of digested
food. Thus there are twenty (kinds of worms).⁵

(type) is called bindukī; it is round and its source is the urine. The fifth (type) may be
(called) matkuṇā and brings about external secondary affections. The louse dwelling on
the head is white and is called śironivāsinī. The carmayūkā is (also) present on the subtle
skin of the eyes, and the yaṣṭikā on the hairs (of the body). By means of dry food, foods
(prepared) from wheat and barley, (foods prepared from) flour, treacle, wrong use of
milk, by lying down to repose by day, (dishes) accompanied by mucilaginous (substances),
by warmth and by indulging in glowing heat and water, by these (factors) arises, in the
receptacles of impure matter, the flock of worms, bringing about morbid alterations in
the viscera. They are taught to be of six kinds. I shall tell about their characteristics.
They spread, like serpents, through the organs which contain impure matter, in (that
part of) the visceral cavity in which phlegm (resides). Some are (called) pṛthumuṇḍa
('broad and bald'), others resemble an earthworm (kiñcuka), some resemble the sprouts
of grain, some are subtle, some are minute; (others) are known as sūcīmukha ('with a
mouth like a needle') and these bring about adynamia of the bowels. I shall tell about
their characteristics and therapy. Listen to me. Fever, or disease of the heart together
with piercing pain, emesis, moistening of the cardiac region, giddiness, suppression of
the appetite, alteration of colour, diarrhoea accompanied by frothy matter, growling
(sounds) in the abdomen, a sluggish state of the fire, thirst and a yellow colour of the
eyes arise in someone oppressed by kiñcukas. A feeling of pricking pain in the bowels
as by needles, or a bloody diarrhoea, in other cases (the sensation) that the liver is eaten
away or a vehement haematemesis, moisture in the mouth, inability to eat, rigidity, a
sluggiish state of the fire, shivering, hunger, thirst and fever should be known to be the
painful conditions (caused) by the worms (called) sūcīmukha. And now I shall tell about
the characteristics of those (which resemble) the sprouts of grain. These worms, staying
in the receptacle of impure matter, eat this impure matter vehemently. By those (worms)
there arise abscesses in the body and a cutting pain, roughness, leanness, a painful con-

CHAPTER EIGHT

MORBID PALLOR (PĀṆDUROGA),
JAUNDICE (KĀMALĀ),
KUMBHAKĀMALĀ AND HALĪMAKA

8, 1 : There are traditionally said to be five (kinds of) morbid pallor :
             three (kinds) by wind, bile and phlegm (separately), a fourth
             (kind) by concerted action and a fifth (kind) by the consumption
             of earth.
                                                      (Ca.Ci. 16, 3).¹

M :
     Subtle worms, arising from faecal matter, generate pallor; for that
reason mention is made of morbid pallor, immediately after the (chap-
ter on) worms... A disease, additionally characterized by pallor, is
(called) morbid pallor.² "What has been said in the chapter (called)
'On the eight abdominal diseases' of the Caraka(saṁhitā), (viz.) "There
are five (kinds of) morbid pallor" (fr. Sū. 19, 4³), and also the very
words of Caraka again : "There are traditionally said to be five (kinds)
of morbid pallor" (Ci. 16, 3a), indicate the curability of all the five
(kinds of morbid pallor), but not, as in the five (kinds of) insanity, the
incurability of that kind caused by concerted action"; thus says
Jejjaṭa. "(It is said) in order to exclude a deficient number;" thus
says Cakra(pāṇidatta).⁴

     Now it may be objected that (the type) arising from (the eating of)
earth does not occur in the Suśruta(saṁhitā), and also that (the eating
of) earth generates morbid pallor just by way of excitement of the
morbific entities, as has been said : “Astringent (earth brings about
excitement of) wind, salt-containing (earth excitement of) bile, and
sweet (earth excitement of) phlegm” (Ca.Ci. 16, 27cd); moreover the
consequence would be that the number of diseases would be endless,
if the distinctions with regard to origins were applied to the distinction
of diseases; and also (it is thus, that the type of morbid pallor) arising
from wind is occasioned by wind, excited by the several origins (of
its excitement, consisting of substances which are) dry, cold and so on.
     The answer (to this objection) is: also in the absence of specificity with
regard to the morbific entity from which it arises, mention is made


=== Page 311 ===
MORBID PALLOR                                                 297

(of a disease as a) separate (entity) in order to substantiate the speci-
ficity of its symptoms and therapy, as in enlargement (of the genitals)
by urine and by the bowels;⁴ Suśruta, however, has not made it (into
a) separate (entity) in the final paragraphs,⁵ with a view to abstaining
from diffusiveness. (Its) therapy, however, is in agreement with the
therapy of the morbific entities.⁶

8, 2 : The morbific entities of someone who indulges in physical
           exercise,⁷ acid (substances), saline (substances), intoxicating
           beverages, earth, sleeping by day and extremely sharp (sub-
           stances), after bringing about a corrupted condition ⁸ of the
           blood, convey pallor to the skin.⁹
                                                                   (Su.U. 44, 3).¹⁰

M :
Mention is made of the onset...¹¹ ‘Blood’ is an implicative expression,
by which Dṛḍhabala describes skin and flesh as liable to corruption
also.¹² Hārīta says that the nutrient fluid is also (liable to corruption).

Ā :
With the words ‘sexual intercourse’,¹³ etc. mention is made of the
origins of morbid pallor. From ‘extremely (frequent)’, (i.e.) outstand-
ingly (frequent) sexual intercourse, etc....¹⁴ ‘Sexual intercourse’
(means) indulgence in (sexual intercourse) with women; others read
‘physical exercise’. Because the plural of the word ‘saline (substance)’
(is used), caustic (substances) are also understood. ‘Sharp (substances)’
are rājikā, etc.¹⁵

8, 3 : A cracked skin, spitting out (saliva), adynamia of the limbs,
           the consumption of earth, swelling of the prominent part of
           the eyes, a yellow colour of faeces and urine and absence of
           digestive alteration are its harbingers, when it is imminent.
                                                                   (Su.U. 44, 5).¹⁶

M :
Mention is made of the prodromes... ‘A cracked skin’ is a condition
in which the skin is somewhat torn asunder. ‘The consumption of
earth’ is the desire to consume earth.¹⁷ ‘Swelling of the prominent part
of the eyes’ is swelling of the eye-balls... ‘Harbingers’ are prodromes.

298                                MORBID PALLOR

A :
        Others read ‘bursting open of the skin, spitting out (saliva) and
    adynamia of the limbs’; this (reading) has exactly the same meaning.
    ‘Spitting out (saliva)’ (occurs) by way of the mouth; it is called *thuga-
    thugi* ¹⁸ in common language.

8, 4 : The skin, urine, eyes, etc. have a dry, black and ruddy hue
    in morbid pallor by wind, and there occur pricking pain, trem-
    bling, obstructive abdominal swelling, giddiness, etc.¹⁹

M :
        Mention is made of the characteristics of that kind (which arises)
    from wind... The black and ruddy hue do not surpass the pallor in
    this case; otherwise it would not be a case of morbid pallor. As has
    been said in the Suśruta(saṃhitā) : “Just by reason of the fact that
    in all these (diseases) a pale condition is present in excess, (they are
    called cases of) morbid pallor” (U. 44, 4cd). By the word ‘etcetera’
    should be understood that cutting pain, piercing pain, etc. (are also
    present).

8, 5 : Someone whose urine, faeces and eyes are yellow, who is
    attended by a burning sensation, thirst and fever, whose faeces
    are loosened, and who has an extremely yellow hue, is a man
    with a morbid pallor by bile.²⁰

M :
        Mention is made of the characteristics of that kind (which arises)
    from bile... Is it not right to object that it is not suitable to speak
    of someone with morbid pallor from bile, on account of the very fact
    that morbid pallor is an effect of bile ?
        The answer (to this question) is : it is called ‘arising from bile’ be-
    cause it is occasioned by a very strong bile, which is not intimately
    connected with (one of) the other two morbific entities, in the same
    way as (one speaks of) blood-bile by bile.²¹

A :
        ‘Someone whose faeces are loosened’ is someone whose impure matter
    is somewhat liquid.

8, 6 : Someone with morbid pallor from phlegm presents effusion of
    phlegm, swelling, lassitude, inertia, an extreme degree of heavi-
    ness and a light colour of skin, urine, eyes and face.²²

M:
    Mention is made of the characteristics of that kind (which arises)
    from phlegm... Someone with morbid pallor from phlegm is addition-

8, 7 : Someone with morbid pallor by the three morbific entities, who
           is (moreover) attended by fever, anorexia, sickness, vomiting,
           thirst and weariness, who suffers from decline and whose senses
           have been damaged, should be abandoned.²³

M:
    It should be understood that (morbid pallor) by concerted action
    presents the very mentioned characteristics of (those kinds) arising
    from wind and the other (morbific entities), because there is an in-
    herence (in the morbid alteration, the qualities of which are) congruous
    with the natural state. For it has been said in the Caraka(samhitā) :
    “Of someone who indulges in all (kinds of) food, all the morbific en-
    tities, having become corrupted, bring about morbid pallor, arising
    from the three morbific entities, provided with the signs of (each of
    the) three (morbific entities), and very difficult to endure” (Ci. 16, 26).
    Mention is made of the fact that this very (type) is incurable if it is
    accompanied by secondary affections.²⁴ 'Someone whose senses have
    been damaged' is someone whose senses are unable to grasp their own
    objects.

Ā :
    Morbid pallor arising from the three morbific entities should be
    abandoned, which means that it is incurable if it is accompanied by
    these secondary affections.

            purities becomes excited.
            Astringent (earth) brings about excitement of the wind, salt-
            containing (earth excites) bile, and sweet (earth) phlegm (8).
            On account of its dryness earth brings about dryness of the
            nutrient fluid and the other (elements of the body), and of

            Being not digestively altered at all, it fills the channels and
            restrains them (9).
            After damaging the strength of the senses, the fiery energy,

             potency and vital fluid, it brings about morbid pallor that
             quickly annihilates (one's) force, colour and fire (10).
                                                        (Ca.Ci. 16, 27-29).²⁵

M :
        The onset of (morbid pallor) arising from (the eating of) earth is
made mention of... ‘Any one of the impurities’ (denotes) wind and the
other (morbific entities). ‘Salt-containing’ (earth designates earth)
containing a caustic substance. ²⁶ ‘On account of its dryness’, (i.e.)
on account of the raised quality of dryness, belonging to its natural
state. ‘Being not digestively altered at all’, (i.e.) not having reached
maturation at all by the visceral fire and the fires of the elements (of
the body).²⁷ ‘it fills and restrains the channels’, (i.e. those channels)
carrying the nutrient fluid and the other (elements of the body). ‘The
strength of the senses’ is the ability (of the senses) to grasp their own
objects. ‘Fiery energy’ is brightness according to Jejjaṭa, and heat
according to Cakra(pāṇidatta). ‘Potency’ (indicates here) the ability (to
perform one's functions). ‘Vital fluid’ is ‘that which, being the essential
constituent of all the elements (of the body), stays in the heart’, ac-
cording to Parāśara, and it is ‘the desire of overpowering others’
according to Jejjaṭa.

Ā :
        ... ‘Impure matter’ (denotes) wind and the other (morbific entities)...
The ground with respect to the excitation of the three morbific entities
by earth is shown with the words ‘astringent (earth)’, etc. ... ‘Salt-
containing (earth)’ is (earth) containing a caustic substance. ... ‘Being
not digestively altered at all’ on account of the fact that the dry
quality is raised, in agreement with its own nature. ‘Force’ is aptitude
with (regard to the functions of) the body.

9, 1 : (When) by extreme indulgence in warmth, physical exercise,
           grief, travelling and sexual intercourse, by sharp, hot, caustic,
           saline, acid and certainly by pungent (substances),¹

9, 2 : the bile has become combustively altered, it quickly combusti-
           vely alters, by means of its own qualities, the blood. There-
           upon blood comes forth, upwards, downwards or in both (direc-
           tions).
                                                            (Su.U. 45, 4cd-5ab).²

9, 3 : Being excited, it comes forth from the nose, eyes, ears and
           mouth upwards, from the penis, vagina and anus downwards,
           and from all the pores (of the skin) in which the hairs are seated.
                                                            (A.h.Ni. 3, 7cd-8ab).³

M :
       Blood-bile is made mention of, immediately after morbid pallor, on
       account of the fact that the former is, like the latter, occasioned by
       bile... ‘Sharp’ (means) possessed of a sharp potency, (like) *marica*,
       etc.; ‘hot’ (means) the glowing heat of a fire ; ‘caustic’ (substances are)
       *yavakṣāra*, etc., and those made from *ghaṇṭāpāṭalī*, etc. ; ‘combustively
       altered’ is : excited. ‘By means of its own qualities’, (i.e.) by those
       (qualities) mentioned in the statement : "Bile is sharp, liquid, foul-
       smelling," etc. (Su.Sū. 21, 11a). ‘It alters combustively’, (i.e.) it brings
       about excitement by means of the very qualities of itself, according
       to the saying : "Its combustive alteration (is of the same character)
       as that of bile" (Su.Sū. 21, 17d). ‘Thereupon (blood) comes forth’, (i.e.)
       bile and blood in the form of elements flow out, and not only blood,
       because (otherwise) the designation (of it as) blood-bile would be irre-
       levant. And when blood corrupted by bile is called blood-bile, one may
       (also) cling to the designation (of it as) bile-blood ; by way of this
       (reasoning) Suśruta has said that its explanation is : both blood and bile,
       in agreement with the compounds of the *dvandva* (type).
       Now it may be objected that it has been said in the Caraka(saṃhitā) :
       "Bile that has reached redness is is (called) blood-bile;" by way of this


=== Page 329 ===
BLOOD-BILE (RAKTAPITTA)                                                                    315

(reasoning) its explanation has been said to be : both blood and this
(red) bile, in agreement with the compounds of the *karmadhāraya* (type) ;
a triad of causes has been stated with respect to this, with the words :
“On account of its commixture with and corrupting of blood and its
generic similarity with it as to smell and colour, bile is called blood-bile
(in this case) by thoughtful (physicians)” (Ca.Ci. 4, 9).
How is it possible that there is no contradiction if things are like
that ?
(The answer is) : There is no contradiction in it, because in this case
also blood is coming forth; for when the blood, being corrupted and de-
positing its redness in the bile, combines with (the latter), blood itself
comes forth as well ; in this way the same meaning as that mentioned
above (is reached).
By way of this (reasoning) there is no fault in both ways of stating
the explanation (of the term blood-bile) : blood-bile (means) both blood
and bile, (and) blood-bile (means) both blood and this (red) bile.⁴

      ... 'Hot' (means) made glowingly hot by fire, or a substance (pro-
vided) with the quality hot. 'Caustic (substances)' are *yavakṣāra*, etc.,
and those made from *apāmārga*, etc... (When it is) extremely excited
(it comes forth) from both pathways, the upper and lower one, and
from all the holes (of the skin) in which the hairs (are seated).

Mention is made of that (kind arisen) from bile... 'With a yellowish-

hue and colour of the collyrium (called) sauvīra.⁸
Is it not right to ask why (a particular kind of) blood-bile (arising)
from bile is made mention of, if really every (kind of) blood-bile is
started by corrupted bile ?

The answer (to this question) is : this is right, but it is designated
as (arisen) from bile when bile, staying in its own seat and starting
blood-bile, is taken hold of by bile that is lodged in another seat, or
when bile alone, not being closely connected with another morbific
entity, is the starting (agent).
To this it may be objected that (a kind of blood-bile arising) from
bile alone does not arise at all, because he (i.e. Mādhava) will say
(presently) : "(That one) going upwards is combined with phlegm and
(that one) going downwards is attended by wind" (9, 7ab); a pathway
of that (kind, arisen from bile), has not been defined.
The answer (to this objection) is : when (blood-bile) has become


=== Page 331 ===
                                                               317
                                BLOOD-BILE (RAKTAPITTA)

combined with phlegm or wind, which have become perceptible (by
increase) due to their own causes, and which are bringing about their
own characteristics, it is designated as (arising) from phlegm, etc., but
not (in the case that it has become combined) by means of a relation-
ship to phlegm or wind which is attended by a relationship with regard
to its pathway. For that kind which is going upwards is necessarily
attended by phlegm as an adjunctory factor by reason of the great
power of the relationship regarding the pathway, and that kind which
is going downwards (is attended) by wind. And phlegm and wind do
not bring about their characteristics in that case, (in the same way)
as in the following instance : though bile brings about fever in the
autumn, attended by the adjunctory factor phlegm which is attended
by the great power of the season, that (type of) fever, being of a natural
kind, is nevertheless (called) bilious, as has been said : “And bile may
bring about (fever) in the autumn, with phlegm as its auxiliary force”
(A.h.Ni. 2, 5lcd).
     By way of this (reasoning it is thus, that) that (kind of blood-bile)
which is accompanied by the signs of one morbific entity is attended
by one morbific entity ; in the same way it should be understood with
regard to (those kinds) accompanied by the signs of two or three mor-
bific entities. Therefore both that kind going upwards and that one
going downwards (may be endowed) with the signs of one, two or
three morbific entities. By means of this (reasoning), (viz.) that the
pathway of (blood-bile arising) from bile has not been shown, that
which was said (as an objection) is excluded.⁹

Ā :
     ‘The colour of the eyes of a peacock's tail’ is like the colour of the
black colouring-stuff used in dyeing garments, made shining by means
of a gem coloured with black streaks ; thus Jejjāṭa and others say ;
this means : unctuous and black...

(condition) is incurable ?
It is not thus, because in this case the specified character (of its
blackness has been expressed) by the words ‘(present) to an extreme
degree’ : “it indicates in this case blackness present to a small degree”
says Jejjāṭa; or one should construe (this passage as follows) : that
blackness which has the hue of a ripe jambū fruit. ‘The mentioned
morbid alterations’ are shortness of breath, cough, etc.30 ‘Like the bow
of the Lord of the gods’ 31 (means : endowed) with various colours. ...
‘One will see even the atmosphere as a visible object’, (i.e.) one sees
though it is invisible, the atmosphere as a visible object; thus (this
passage) should be construed, because the eyes have suffered injury
from blood-bile; or (it means) one sees visible objects, (viz.) a jar, a
cloth, etc., and (also) the atmosphere, (endowed with a) red (colour).32...
‘Someone whose eructations are red and who sees (the visible objects
endowed with a) red (colour)’ may also mean : someone who sees that
his eructations are red.33

⁹ Cf. Cakra’s comment on Ca.Ci. 4, 11-13ab : “With a yellowish-red hue’ means :
pale red. ‘The colour of the eyes of a peacock’s tail’ is the colour of black garments,
etc., made shining by means of gandhaka (used) together with its core-wood. Now the
question may be raised whether (a kind of blood-bile arising) from phlegm does exist,

as bile is the starting agent in every kind of fever. In that very case in which it brings

its own characteristics, (in that case) it is, after dismissing the bile that has effected

is called blood-bile (arising) from bile. The designation (of a disease) with respect to its
morbific entity comes about by means of its characteristics and by nothing else. Therefore
blood-bile is designated as arising from whatever morbific entity, of which the charac-
teristics, generated by (the morbific entity), accompany it. In blood-bile by bile the bile
brings about its own characteristics in that one case only and not in other cases.
And also the following statement : blood-bile, brought about by bile only, has no (parti-
cular) pathway because it has been substantiated that blood(-bile) by wind moves down-
wards and (blood-bile) started by phlegm upwards; (that statement) is not correct for
this reason, that (blood-bile) by bile also possesses an upward and downward way of
moving; moreover, (blood-bile) by bile, when moving upwards, is accompanied by
phlegm on account of the great power of the pathway, and that (type) which moves
downwards is attended by wind on account of its relationship with a seat of wind.
And a morbific entity, attended by (another morbific entity) by reason of its relation-
ship with a (particular) pathway, is not at all (designated as) an adjunctory (morbific
entity) because it brings about its own characteristics; therefore that one, (by which

it is attended), is not referred to with the words : “(Blood-bile), attended by one mor-

10, 1 : From the restraint of (natural) urges and certainly from a
            state of decline, from rashness and from incongruous eating,
            from (this) tetrad of grounds the malady (called) consumption
            arises, which is (endowed) with the three morbific entities.¹

M :
        The origins of consumption (are made mention of), immediately
        following upon (the description of) blood-bile, because it has been said :
        the appearance of blood occurs among the symptoms of kingly con-
        sumption (arising) from bile.²

        The fourfold distant cause, being applicable in therapy, is discussed...
        ‘(Natural) urge’ (indicates) here (only the urge to pass) flatus, urine and
        faeces, and not all (the urges, to wit those) of yawning, etc., which are
        stated in (the chapter) on the non-restraint of the (natural) urges.³ As
        has been said in the Caraka(saṃhitā) : “When someone out of shame-
        fulness, disdain or fear, suppresses the urge (to pass) flatus, urine and
        faeces when it has arrived...” (Ci. 8, 20), etc. ‘From a state of decline’...
        by this (term) the grounds of decline of the elements (of the body) are
        understood, (consisting of) sexual intercourse beyond the proper meas-
        ure, abstinence from food, jealousy, despondency, etc. (About) ‘from
        rashness’ (we remark that) rashness, (consisting of acts like) the contest
        with a strong man, etc., is a cause (of consumption), because it is a
        ground of a lesion of the chest. (About) ‘from incongruous eating’ (we
        remark that) it is the employment (of foods) different from the twelve
        kinds of food set forth by Suśruta,⁴ by reason of the fact that this
        (incongruous eating) quickly obstructs the channels. For it has been
        said in the Caraka(saṃhitā) : “In those who use a mixed diet, consisting
        of foods and drinks of many kinds, in an incongruous way, the wind
        and the other (morbific entities), (having become) incongruous, generate
        dreadful ailments.⁵ Having obstructed the channels of the elements (of
        the body), got into an incongruous state by reason of the incongruity
        (of the food), the morbific entities favour the development of disease
