and so do not nourish the elements (of the body)” (Ci. 8, 28-29).⁶
“(Endowed) with the three morbific entities’ (indicates that) it arises,
being of only one kind, from the three morbific entities assembled
together, and (that) it is not of several kinds on account of distinctions
among its causes. As Suśruta says : “Because desiccation is thought of
as being of only one kind, (viz.) that one with the nature of concerted
action, the signs of the morbific entities settle down in it, according
to the (degree of) preponderancy (of each morbific entity)” (U. 41,
7cd-8ab).
And (what is the answer) if it be argued, since it is true that restraint
of the (natural) urges, etc. excites the wind : how is it possible that
consumption, which is generated by this (restraint, etc.), is (said to be
endowed) with the three morbific entities?
(In case of this objection) the answer is : it is said that by the very
excitement of wind excitement of phlegm and bile (occurs) as well, by
means of corruption of the (transforming) fire. By (the use of) the words
‘from (this) tetrad of grounds’ it is shown that, though the grounds are
innumerable, they are comprised in the mentioned tetrad.
It was Suśruta who made the association between the various words,
(consisting of) desiccation, etc., by which it is expressed. (He did so)
in the following (stanzas) : “It is denominated desiccation on account
of the complete desiccation of the nutrient fluid and the other (ele-
ments); wise people call it decline because it brings about decline of
the actions;⁷ owing to the fact that this ailment (once) occurred in
the moon, who is a king, some thoughtful (physicians) call it the king’s
consumption” (U. 41, 4-5). In Vāgbhaṭa(’s treatise), however, it has
been said : “King-consumption is the king of consumptions.” ⁸ (A
grammatical remark follows).

Ā :
‘Decline’ is decline of the elements (of the body), which arises from
several causes, (consisting of) sexual intercourse, abstinence from food,
discharge of blood, fasting, etc. (About) ‘from incongruous eating’ (we
remark that) it has been said : “(Eating) copiously, little or at an im-
proper time, that should be known to be incongruous eating” (Su.Sū.
46, 508cd).

10, 2 : When the trails of the nutrient fluid have been obstructed by
the morbific entities, with phlegm as their predominant one,
or also when the semen has gone into a state of decline in a


=== Page 344 ===
330                               KINGLY CONSUMPTION

        person who has indulged in sexual intercourse to an extreme
        degree, all the elements (of the body) go into a state of decline
        in an uninterrupted series; thereupon a man is subject to
        desiccation.
                                                     (Su.U. 41, 9cd-10).⁹

M :
        (Its) specific onset is described in order to show that consumption
        does not arise solely from the group of states of decline of the elements,
        but also from obstruction, etc. of the channels which carry the nutrient
        fluid, etc... When it would not be thus, the declined state of the ele-
        ments itself (would constitute) the disease, and not consumption.
        (With respect to the words : 'by the morbific entities with phlegm
        as their predominant one') it may be said that the triad of morbific
        entities is pointed to by the term ‘the morbific entities’; because phlegm
        is comprised in it as a specified (component, the question may be
        raised) why this same phlegm should be expressed (again) by another
        word.
        The reply (to this question) is : it is (a case) of analysis by means of
        the members composing it; it is a collection in the sense of a compound,
        in the same way as something consisting of many trees is (called) a
        wood. The extensive justification of (this) statement should be looked
        for in Jejjaṭa('s commentary) on the Suśruta(saṃhitā). The predomi-
        nance of phlegm should be understood (to be indicated) by the sluggish-
        ness of the fire, etc., which suffers disorder by the wind that is excited
        by the restraint of the (natural) urges, etc.
        ‘The trails of the nutrient fluid’ are the ducts carrying the nutrient
        fluid; in this case the word ‘etcetera’ should be considered to have been
        elided. Therefore, obstruction of the channels carrying blood, etc.,
        should also be understood (as aimed at). Or, since the nutrient fluid
        is the cause (of the production) of blood, etc., the very corruption of
        the nutrient fluid (is conducive) to corruption of the blood, etc.; thus
        says Kārtika(kuṇḍa). On this (subject) the following has been pointed
        out : because the nutrient fluid, which stays in the cardiac region,
        remains lodged in that same (seat) on account of the obstruction of
        (its) pathway and becomes morbidly altered, it flows out by way of
        the mouth. As Caraka says : “When the channels are obstructed, the
        nutrient fluid, staying in its own seat, becomes combustively altered,
        and it comes forth in many forms (from the) upper (pathway) by the
        impulse of coughing” (Ci. 8, 43). By this (statement) a process of de-


=== Page 345 ===
KINGLY CONSUMPTION 331

cline is shown that occurs in the normal way, because, since there is
decline of the nutrient fluid as an element (of the body), which acts as
a causative agent, a process of decline of blood and the subsequent
(elements), which are products of the nutrient fluid, is going on, due
to the absence of (a) nourishing (factor).

In order to show the reverse process of decline it is said ‘or also in
a person who has indulged in sexual intercourse to an extreme degree’.
When the semen has undergone decline, the elements (of the body),
constituting an uninterrupted series, (i.e.) being contiguous with each
other, are subject to decline : when for instance the semen has declined,
the marrow declines, when the marrow has declined, the bones are subject
to decline (and) in that way each (element) that precedes (in the series).

And if one objects, asking how it is possible that decline occurs of
elements that act as causative agents, owing to decline of semen that
is a product ?

(In that case) the answer is (as follows) : due to the decline of semen
the wind is excited. As has been said: “Excitement of the wind occurs
from decline of the elements (of the body) and (from obstruction) by
covering (its) pathway” (Ca.Ci. 28, 59ab). This wind desiccates the
marrow, due to its vicinity, and in the same way each preceding ele-
ment in its turn. The generation of effects in cases of immediate pro-
ximity has been shown, as for example in the desiccation of a piece of
wet soil by placing it near to a ball of iron made glowing hot by fire.

To the same effect are Suśruta’s words in (his) thesis on the circu-
lation of the nutrient fluid : “By an extreme increase each (element)
preceding (in the series) increases the next one (of the series) ; there-
fore it is salutary to diminish elements which have increased to an
extreme degree” (Sū. 15, 18).

About '(someone who is provided) with all (the signs)', etc. it may
be rightly asked, since all the symptoms are eleven (in number) and
the half of eleven is five and a half, which of the (many) symptoms
is present in the state of half (a symptom) or of what kind (this symp-
tom) is.

The answer (to this question) is : as there is no such thing as the
coming into being of the half of one (particular) symptom, only (a set
of) six symptoms can be understood (to constitute the intended) half
(number), on account of the fact that (this number) holds the best
position with regard to five or six symptoms (considered) as half (the
number of eleven).40

'When (the condition is) otherwise' (means) : when decline of
force and flesh is absent.

'When one is subject to decline (though) being a great eater' is (in
itself) one characteristic of incurability, as it constitutes a precursory
signal of death. 'Being oppressed by diarrhoea' is the second (charac-

consumption is someone whose life is dependent on (his) impure matter
(as a resource).41 'The testicles and abdomen being swollen' (consti-

testicles being curable by means of purgative procedures, treatment
disagrees (in this case). 'A light (colour of the) eyes', etc. are one by
one characteristics of incurability.

and should be tamed or another (animal), (trying to)
kill enemies by hurling rocks, pieces of wood, stones or
missiles (22), or reading with an extremely loud voice,
covering a long distance by running, crossing great
rivers ⁶³ (by swimming), or running (keeping pace) with
horses (23), making long jumps in an inconsidering way,
or dancing with quick motions,⁶⁴ or vehemently injured
(24), a lesion of the chest
by other formidable actions,
having developed, a powerful illness is stirred up, as well
as in someone who is extremely attached to women, or
who eats dry (articles of food), a slight amount (of food)
or a restricted amount (of food) (25).
The chest (of such a person seems to be) broken asunder
to an extreme degree, (seems to be) cut and becomes
painful everywhere ;⁶⁵ thereupon a feeling of pressure
arises in the sides, the body becomes subject to desicca-
tion, and shivering arises (26).
Gradually (such a person) is deprived of his potency,
force, colour, appetite and (transforming) fire, moreover
(there arise) fever, distressing sensations, dejection of the
mind, loosening of faecal matter and destruction of the
(transforming) fire (27).
In such a repeatedly coughing person phlegm, accompa-
nied by blood, comes forth,⁶⁶ which is corrupted, brown,
very bad-smelling, yellow, globose and copious (28).
Such a person with a lesion (of the chest) is subject to
an extreme decline ; (this occurs), moreover, due to de-
cline of the semen and the vital fluid.
(Ca. Ci. 11, 4-12ab).⁶⁷

M :
Lesions of the chest, together with their origins, are made mention


=== Page 356 ===
342                               KINGLY CONSUMPTION

of in the paragraph on desiccation, because the source of a lesion of
the chest is the very origin from which desiccation (arises, to wit)
inconsiderate actions, etc., and because the source of desiccation (may)
also (consist) of a lesion of the chest. ‘In someone who stretches (his
body)’, as a variant of ‘in someone exerting himself’, (means) : in
someone whose cardiac region is being expanded.
‘That should be tamed’, (i.e.) that deserves to be tamed, refers to
that same (already mentioned) strong bull, etc. ‘Or another animal’
(means) : an elephant, camel, etc. ‘In someone (trying to catch and)
check’ (means) : in someone (trying to restrain. ‘A rock’ is a rock (of
an) oblong (shape); ‘a stone’ is a piece of (flat) rock (of a different
shape); a missile is a specific kind of missile weapon, or a specific kind
of (contrivance), provided with an extreme force, to set rocks, etc. in
motion. ‘In someone (trying to kill enemies’ (means) : in someone
beating down (his) foes. ... To ‘in someone crossing great rivers’
should be supplied : ‘with one’s arms’. ‘Or in someone injured by
other formidable actions’ (points to) wrestling, etc. ; instead of ‘formi-
dable’ others read : valiant (actions), (i.e.) by foes. Among these causes
some should be understood to bring about exertion of the whole body,
some of the chest especially. ‘Illness (is stirred up’, i.e. the illness)
with the characteristics of a lesion of the chest ; or ‘illness’ (may denote)
the wind, according to the (following) tradition : “The morbific entities
may also be denominated by the term illness”, thus says Jejjaṭa.⁸⁸
‘The chest (seems to be) broken asunder’, (i.e.) feels broken as it were;
‘(seems to be) cut’, (i.e.) feels as torn asunder, as if divided into two
parts; the variant ‘(the chest) is combustively altered’ is unsuitable
by reason of the absence of a cause and because the commentators
have not expounded it. ‘Potency’ is power; ‘force’ is stoutness of the
flesh(y parts of the body). The variant ‘loosening of faecal matter on
account of the very destruction of the (transforming) fire’ means that
loosening of faecal matter comes into being, destruction of the (trans-
forming) fire being its ground; it is said that the word ‘(the) very
(destruction)’ expresses that loosening of faecal matter by destruction
of the fire also occurs in the absence of the great power of the illness.
‘Corrupted’ (means) subject to disorder; this very (term) is explained
with the words ‘brown’, etc. ‘Globose’ (means) : specifically composed
of globules; Jejjaṭa says (it means) confined. ‘Such a man ‘with a
lesion’, (i.e.) with a lesion of the chest, ‘is subject to decline’, (i.e.)
acquires desiccation of the elements (of the body). He is subject to
decline, not only from the lesion as such, but even more so from de-

(such a person) will vomit matter that is (of a) yellow, red, dark or ruddy (colour). (Such)
a man experiences an extreme glowing heat in his whole chest, and gasps for breath
because of this (sensation of) being (internally) consumed by fire; his mouth and breath
are bad-smelling and the colour (of his skin) and his voice are indistinct;" A.h.Ni. 3,

rise to coughing. By means of this (coughing) one may spit out phlegm, accompanied
by blood and (of a) yellow or brown (colour), desiccated, globose, stinking and copious,
by way of a painful throat and chest that feel (as if) cut asunder, (as if) being pricked
with sharp needles and in which one feels a piercing pain. Cutting pain in the junctures,
fever, shortness of breath, thirst, an altered state of the voice and trembling occur (in
such a person); he makes sounds like the cooing of a pigeon and experiences a piercing

maturating (fire), force and colour; in a person presenting (this kind of) decline, the urine
may be mixed with blood and there may occur a seizing pain in the back and iliac region;"

APPENDIX TWO
The Sanskrit medical authors and works quoted and referred to in
M., Ā., the notes and the appendices.

AGNIVEŚA was one of the six disciples of Ātreya Punarvasu; each
of them wrote a treatise (_tantra_) on _kāyacikitsā_ (internal medicine)
(Ca.Sū. 1, 30-33). The Agniveśatantra has not been preserved in its
original form, but the Carakasamhitā is the form it acquired after its
redaction by Caraka (and Dr̥ḍhabala). An Agniveśasamhitā is men-
tioned in some Ms. catalogues, but this must be the Carakasamhitā
(see New Cat.Cat. 1, p. 36). Puzzling is a Nidānasthāna ascribed to
Agniveśa (see Cat. Skt. Mss. N.-W. P. 1, p. 586-587). A text called
Añjananidāna is ascribed to Agniveśa, but certainly written by a later
author. Mukhopādhyāya states (H.I.M. 3, p. 520) that Śrīkanthadatta,
in his Vyākhyākusumāvali on the Siddhayoga, quotes stanzas from the
Agniveśatantra which are not found in the Carakasamhitā (these
stanzas are reproduced on p. 521). Agniveśa is once referred to in M.
(on 2, 66cd-74ab); this is really a reference to A.h.Ni. 2, 61-62a, where
Agniveśa's opinion on a certain subject, in contrast to that of Hārita,
is reported.

ARUNADATTA was a son of Mr̥gānkadatta, as indicated in the colo-
phons of his comm. on A.h. This comm. called Sarvāṅgasundarī or
Sarvāṅgasundarā, extends over the whole of A.h. and has been printed.
From a remark by Ḍa. on Su.Ka. 1, 30 it is clear that Arunadatta also
wrote a comm. on A.s. (see Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 131-132 and
Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 12); this comm. on A.s. has not been preserved.
Moreover, mention is made of a comm. on Su. by Arunadatta (see Cat.
Skt. Mss. N.-W. P. 1, p. 594-595 : Suśrutatikā by Arunadatta ; cannot
be procured for copying; old and apparently correct). It is uncertain
whether the medical author Arunadatta is the same as an author of
that name who is quoted as a lexicographer and grammarian. The
earliest work in which the latter is cited is Vardhamāna's autocomm.
on the Gaṇaratnamahodadhi, a work dated 1140 (Cat.Cat. 1, p. 30;
Gode, St.I.L.H. 1, p. 185; Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 13). This Arunadatta
is also quoted in Sarvānandavandyaghatiya's Tīkāsarvasva on the
Amarakośa, dated 1159 acc. to N.N. Das Gupta (IC 3, 1936-1937, p.


=== Page 404 ===
390
APPENDIX TWO

159-160), but dated 1180 acc. to Bhatt. (ABORI 28, 1947, p. 119;
Bhatt. refers to p. 34-36 of the Introd. to Puruṣottamadeva's Pari-
bhāṣāvṛtti, Rajshahi, 1946); moreover in Ujjvaladatta's Vṛtti on the
Uṇādisūtras of Pāṇini (New Cat.Cat. 2, p. 287), dated about 1250
(Gode, Introd. A.h., p. 8 : assigned by Aufrecht to circa 1250), and
finally in Rāyamukuṭa's comm. on the Amarakośa, dated 1431 (R.G.
Bhandarkar, Report on the search for Skt. Mss. in the Bombay pre-
sidency during the year 1883-4, p. 467).

In his article in IHQ Bhatt. remarks that the first and the second
Aruṇadatta may be identical; in his article in ABORI he states that
they are evidently identical, without adducing arguments to prove his
point. No other author made such a definite statement in this matter.
Acc. to Cordier (JA, t. 17, 1901, p. 186-187) Aruṇadatta may be
identical with a commentator on A.h. called Hāṭakāṅka (a fragmen-
tary Ms. of a comm. on A.h.Ni., said to be by Hāṭakāṅka, is described
in Burnell's Index to the Skt. Mss. in the Palace at Tanjore, p. 65
(5,384); an incomplete Ms., probably a copy of the Tanjore Ms., is in
the coll. Cordier of the Bibliothèque Nationale at Paris : see Filliozat,
JA, t. 224, 1934, p. 156, nr. 8; see about other Mss. : New Cat.Cat. 1,
p. 465), the comm. of which shows a close analogy to that of Aruṇa-
datta. This suggestion of Cordier cannot be correct because Aruṇa and
Hāṭakāṅka are frequently quoted as different authors in Śrīdāsa
paṇḍita's comm. on A.h.

Aruṇadatta's date was determined by Hoernle (Osteology, Introd.
p. 17) to be about 1220. This date was regarded as the correct one for
a long time, but Bhatt. has proved (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 130 ff.; see also
Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 13, footnote 1) that Hoernle's method in fixing
the date was wrong. The earliest writer to quote from Aruṇadatta is
Ḍalhaṇa (on Su.Ka. 1, 30). Ḍalhaṇa is generally assigned to about 1200,
so Aruṇa must be earlier. Vijayarakṣita, Śrīkaṇṭhadatta and Nīścala-
kara do not quote him, so his date may be somewhere between the
dates of these authors and 1200. Bhatt. fixes Aruṇadatta's date
(assuming that the first and second Aruṇadatta are identical) at about
1150 (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 132). If both authors are indeed identical, the
date is somewhat earlier : 1100-1120. Acc. to Bhatt. (ABORI 28, 1947,
p. 119) Nīścalakara was probably an elder contemporary of Aruṇa-
datta. N.N. Das Gupta says (IC 3, 1936-1937, p. 159 ff.) that Aruṇa-
datta was a Bengali, but he offers no proof to give force to that state-
ment. In Bhatt.'s opinion (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 132) Aruṇadatta lived in
the north, because he remarks that the practice of fellatio, current in


=== Page 405 ===
                                                                               391
                                APPENDIX TWO

the south, is not approved of. Acc. to Bhaṭṭ. again (ibid.), Aruṇadatta
indulges in advanced grammatical polemics and has interesting notes
on prosody and rhetoric from hitherto unknown sources. So it is not
improbable that Bhaṭṭ. is right in assuming that the first and the
second Aruṇadatta are identical.
      Cordier remarks (JA, t. 28, 1901, p. 154) that Aruṇa's most important
source was the comm. of Candranandana; this statement may be right
as there is indeed much affinity between the two comm.
      Aruṇadatta is quoted once in Ā. (on 2, 56-57), but this passage is
probably a later interpolation and has been put between brackets by
the ed. of the text. The quotations from Aruṇadatta in Śrīkaṇṭha's
comm. on the Siddhayoga are probably additions by Nārāyaṇa, a late
writer (after Ḍalhaṇa and Hemādri), who revised Śrīkaṇṭha's comm.,
as indicated in the colophon on p. 665 of the ed. of the work in the
Ānandāśrama Series.

      ĀŚVINĪKUMĀRASAṂHITĀ. Acc. to the New Cat.Cat. (1, p. 441) a work
called Dhāturatnamālā forms part of the Āśvinīkumārasaṃhitā. An-
other part of it, called Saṃnipātakaḷikā or Saṃnipātārṇava, is known
in some Mss. There seems to exist a comm. on the latter work by
Māṇikya, son of Padmanābha (New Cat.Cat. 1, p. 441). Acc. to Cordier
(Le Muséon, N.S. 4, 1903, p. 349-350) the Saṃnipātārṇava and Dhā-
turatnamālā are said to form part of the Āśvinīsaṃhitā, which is pro-
bably identical with the Āśvinīkumārasaṃhitā. A Ms. of the Dhā-
turatnamālā from the Āśvinīkumārasaṃhitā is described in Cat. Skt.
Mss. BORI, vol. 16, part 1, p. 133-134. A Ms. containing the saṃnipāta
chapter of the Āśvinīsaṃhitā is described in Cat. Skt. Mss. Madras,
vol. 23, nr. 13069, p. 8787. Acc. to Bhaṭṭ. (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 136)
Niścalakara remarks that Cakrapāṇidatta borrowed from the Āśvinī-
kumārasaṃhitā. Acc. to Gode (St.I.L.H. 1, p. 133) Candraṭa quotes
from the Āśvinīsaṃhitā in his Yogaratnasamuccaya. The work must
be rather old and should not be said to be a relatively late compilation,
as Hoernle thought it to be (JRAS, 1909, p. 861).

      ĀLAMBĀYANA must have been the author of a treatise of toxicology
(agadatantra), as appears from quotations by commentators. The
quotations have been partially collected by Mukhopādhyāya (H.I.M.
3, p. 760).

      ĀṢĀPHADHARMA, referred to by Vijayarakṣita on 1, 14cd-15ab as one
of the early commentators (pūrvatīkākāra), must be the same as


=== Page 406 ===
392                                          APPENDIX TWO

Āṣāḍhavarman, referred to as one of the early commentators (pūr-
vatīkṛt) by Cakra on Ca.Ci. 3, 217. In both cases he is mentioned
together with Svāmidāsa (Cakra puts him after Svāmidāsa and Vijaya-
rakṣita mentions Āṣāḍhadharma first). Āṣāḍhavarman and Svāmidāsa
undoubtedly belong to the group of the earliest commentators on Ca.,
because they are quoted by Jejjaṭa. Cakra's quotations from Āṣāḍha-
varman clearly indicate that the latter commented on the whole of
Ca., after it had been completed by Dṛḍhabala. In the Introd. to the
Lahore ed. of Ca. Āṣāḍhavarman and the author of the comm. called
Parihāravārtika are classified as two different commentators on Ca.
on p. 22, but on p. 26 the Parihāravārtika is said to have been written
by Āṣāḍhavarman. Cakra mentions the Parihāravārtika twice; in
Cakra's comment on Ca.Ci. 23, 137-139 both Āṣāḍhavarman and the
Parihāravārtika are quoted in such a context that indeed it may be
true that Āṣāḍhavarman's comm. on Ca. was called Parihāravārtika.

INDU was the author of a comm. on A.s., called Śaśilekhā. This comm.
has been preserved and printed for the greater part (from imperfect
Mss.). It is often quoted by Niścalakara as Indumatī (Bhatt., IHQ 23,
1947, p. 138-139). Indu also wrote a comm., called Śaśilekhā, on A.h.
(Gode, St.I.L.H. 1, p. 157, footnote; Gode is not quite sure about it,
but there seems to be no doubt, because the colophons of the Madras
Ms. are clear; see Gode about the particulars; a second Ms. of Indu's
comm. on A.h. may be present in the Adyar Library, see Gode, l.c.,
p. 154 footnote, and the Index of Skt. Mss. in the Adyar Library, p. 9,
nr. 55). It is not impossible that the commentator Indu is identical
with the author of a Nighanṭu, also called Indu, who is frequently
quoted by Kṣīrasvāmin in his comm. on the Amarakośa (see Vogel,
Introd. A.h., p. 15; N.N. Das Gupta, IC 3, p. 154; Gode, St.I.L.H. 1,
p. 159-160). Some are of the opinion that Indu, the commentator (and
possibly the author of a Nighanṭu), is identical with Indukara, the
father of Mādhavakara (N.N. Das Gupta, IC 3, p. 154 : not improbable;
refuted by Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 139, because Indu, the commen-
tator, belonged to Kaśmir, and Indukara, the father of Mādhavakara,
to Eastern India; Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 14 : based on very shaky
evidence). It is almost beyond doubt that Indu was a native of Kaśmir
(see Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 131; Gode, St.I.L.H. 1, p. 158 : Indu
gives terms current in Kaśmir for particular plants; Vogel, Introd.
A.h., p. 13). It is difficult to make definite statements about Indu's
date. If Indu, the commentator, is identical with the author of the


=== Page 407 ===
393
APPENDIX TWO

Nighaṇṭu, he is earlier than 1050 (see Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 15). In
any case he must have lived before Niścalakara, whose Ratnaprabhā
was written between 1110 and 1120, and after Bhaṭṭāraharicandra,
who is quoted by him (see Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 14; Gode, St.I.L.H.
1, p. 160-161). A more precise statement would be possible if Indu,
the commentator, were identical with the father of Mādhavakara;
this is, however, very improbable.
Tradition makes Indu the pupil of Vāgbhaṭa, but there is no reliable
evidence to support the tradition (see Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 13-14
and Vogel's footnotes). In my opinion it is even very improbable be-
cause Indu himself observes that there were already some commen-
taries on A.s. before he started writing the Śāśilekhā (see Gode, St.
I.L.H. 1, p. 155, footnote); at least one generation of commentators
on A.s. must have preceded him; so he cannot have been a direct
pupil of Vāgbhaṭa. It is clear, however, that Indu was acquainted
with both A.s. and A.h. (because he wrote a comm. on both texts;
A.h. is quoted in the comm. on A.s., see Gode : St.I.L.H. 1, p. 156).
The unsatisfactory conclusion is that Indu lived before 1050 and after
the composition of A.h. and A.s. There is still one point to be mentioned.
Acc. to Rudrapārāśava (the ed. of A.s. with Indu's comm.) Indu
quotes from the Kāśikāvṛtti on Pāṇini, composed about 650 (see Gode,
St.I.L.H. 1, p. 155-156). If correct, this fact is not of much avail in
fixing Indu's date, because the A.h. was composed about 600 and A.s.
was elaborated after that date.

ĪŚĀNA(DEVA) was a commentator on Ca. (Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p.
139), quoted by Vijayarakṣita, Śrīkaṇṭhadatta (on the Siddhayoga),
Vācaspati, Niścalakara and Nāganātha (in his Nidānapradīpa : Jolly,
Cat.Skt.Mss. München, nr. 381, p. 54-55; see Introd., Comm. on the
Nidāna, about Nāganātha). The full name, Īśānadeva, is used once by
Vijayarakṣita and also only once by Niścalakara, suggesting (acc. to
Bhatt., l.c.) that Deva was probably his family title. From the quotation
in M. and Ā. on 2, 34-36ab nothing definite can be deduced about the
nature of Īśānadeva's work.

ĪŚVARASENA is quoted by Vijayarakṣita, Śrīkaṇṭhadatta (on Siddha-
yoga 81, 52), Niścalakara (see Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 139) and Cakra.
The latter quotes him on Ca.Ci. 15, 92-93 and mentions him (as a
commentator on Ca.) on Ca.Si. 1, 20-22ab. From Cakra's remarks on
Ca.Si. 1, 20-22ab may be concluded that Īśvarasena lived after Dṛḍha-


=== Page 408 ===
394                                                     APPENDIX TWO

bala. He may have been later than Jejjaṭa because he is not quoted
by the latter; moreover, Cakra's list of commentators (in the comm.
on Ca.Si. 1, 20-22ab) impresses as being arranged in a chronological
order : the commentator, called Saindhava (who is already quoted by
Jejjaṭa) precedes Jejjaṭa and Īśvarasena is mentioned after Jejjaṭa.
If Bhaṭṭ. (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 139) is right in assuming that a particular
list of authors, given by Niścala, is put in a chronological order (see
also : Gadādhara), Īśvarasena was later than Vāgbhaṭa and Ravigupta
(author of the Siddhasāra) and anterior to Gadādhara.

KARAVĪRA was one of the seven disciples of Dhanvantari; he is called
Karavīra or Karavirya (Su.Sū. 1, 3). Each of these seven disciples is
supposed to have written his own treatise on surgery. Karavīra is
quoted once in M. on ch. 1-10; he is also quoted in Ā. (New Cat.Cat.
3, p. 177) and by Niścalakara (Bhaṭṭ., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 139).

KĀRTIKAKUṆḌA, often called Kārtika, was a famous commentator
on Su. He is quoted once in Cakra's Bhānumatī on Su.Sū. (Bhaṭṭ.,
IHQ 23, 1947, p. 140); he is often and respectfully quoted by Vijaya-
rakṣita, Niścalakara (Bhaṭṭ., ibid.) and Ḍa. Acc. to Śrīkaṇṭhadatta
(Kusumāvalī on Siddhayoga 12, 22-24) he preceded Vṛndakuṇḍa, the
author of the Siddhayoga. This view is refuted by Hoernle (JRAS,
1906, p. 287) on insufficient grounds. Bhaṭṭ. (l.c.) is of the opinion that
both Kārtikakuṇḍa and Vṛndakuṇḍa, as their common family title
proves, belonged to a *vaidya* family of Bengal.
It is interesting to notice that Kārtikakuṇḍa is very often quoted
by Ḍa.. but only on Su.U. Vijayarakṣita also quotes him on passages
from Su.U., except once (on 5, 43). From Ḍa.'s quotations and remarks
Kārtikakuṇḍa appears as a person with an independent mind and
many views of his own, often discarding stanzas from Su.U. or reading
them in a different way. From Śrīkaṇṭhadatta's comm. on Siddha-
yoga 12, 22-24 and 59, 30 it is evident that Kārtikakuṇḍa sometimes
adopted certain views on the authority of Vṛddhakāśyapa and other
old medical writers. Hoernle tried to establish (JRAS, 1906, p. 286-288)
that Kārtikakuṇḍa is identical with Bhāskara, mentioned in the in-
troduction to Ḍa.'s comm. on Su. as the author of a *pañjikā* on Su.
Hoernle thought he might be right because Kārtikakuṇḍa is not men-
tioned in Ḍa.'s introduction and Bhāskara is not quoted by Ḍa.
Hoernle was certainly wrong because Ḍa. states that both Gayadāsa
and Bhāskara wrote a *pañjikā* on Su., and, though Bhāskara is in-


=== Page 409 ===
APPENDIX TWO 395

deed never quoted by Ḍa., the latter frequently quotes the two au-
thors of a pañjikā (pañjikākārau) and the Bṛhat- and Laghupañjikā,
both separately and together.
About Kārtikakuṇḍa's date I offer as a hypothesis to be verified
that it may be in the range between Mādhavakara and Vṛndakuṇḍa,
if Śrīkaṇṭhadatta's remark on Siddhayoga 12, 22-24 is to be trusted,
and assuming that the series of commentators mentioned by Vijaya-
rakṣita on 1, 5d-6 is put in a chronological order (see : Vāpyacandra).
(See also about Kārtikakuṇḍa : Gode, IC 13, 1947, p. 199-208).

KĀŚYAPASAṂHITĀ, also called Vṛddhajīvakīyatantra and ascribed to
Vṛddhajīvaka, is an old medical work, which has been partially pre-
served in a single Ms., discovered by Haraprasād Śāstrī in Kāṭhmāṇḍū
at the end of 1898 (see H. Śāstrī's Report on the search of Skt. Mss.
during the years 1895-1900, p. 9). Cordier corrected Haraprasād Śāstrī's
statements about the Ms. (Le Muséon, N.S. 4, 1903, p. 322-323). A
fragment of the work has been preserved in a Chinese translation (see
P.C. Bagchi, IC 9, p. 53-64). The Kāśyapasaṁhitā has been edited,
with a long introduction in Sanskrit, by Paṇḍit Hemarāja Śarmā. The
Kalpasthāna of the work has been revised by someone called Vātsya
(see the colophon of the Kalpasthāna). Quotations from Kāśyapa occur
in many commentaries; an author called Vṛddhakāśyapa is also
quoted by commentators. The quotations found in Madhukośa,
Kusumāvalī and Nibandhasaṁgraha have been collected by Mukho-
pādhyāya (H.I.M. 1, p. 182). Acc. to the latter (l.c., p. 186-187) the
Ms. of the Kāśyapasaṁhitā is described by Burnell (in : A classified
index to the Skt.Mss. in the Palace at Tanjore, London, 1879-1880,
p. 70, Nr. 41); this is, however, an erroneous assertion for the work
described by Burnell, though called Kāśyapasaṁhitā, is a completely
different medical treatise of Tantric inspiration. A Ms. of a work called
Kāśyapiyaroganidāna is described by S. Kuppuswami Sastri (Cat.Skt.
Mss. Madras, vol. 26, nr. 13112). The Kāśyapasaṁhitā is a text that
especially deals with children's diseases. It is a remarkable fact that
quotations from the Bhālukitantra, met with in commentaries, are
sometimes very close to passages found in the Kāśyapasaṁhitā.

KṢĀRAPĀṆI was one of the six disciples of Ātreya Punarvasu; each
of them wrote his own treatise on kāyacikitsā (Ca.Sū. 1, 30-33). Kṣāra-
pāṇi's treatise was called Kṣārapāṇitantra, and not kāyacikitsātantra,
as is asserted in the New Cat.Cat. (5, p. 150). An (incomplete) list of


=== Page 410 ===
396                                          APPENDIX TWO

quotations from the Kṣārapaṇitantra has been collected by Mukho-
pādhyāya (H.I.M. 3, p. 561-564), who states that Kṣārapaṇi is quoted
by Śrīkanṭhadatta, Śivadāsasena, Candraṭa and Cakrapāṇidatta. To
this list should be added : Jejjaṭa, Vijayarakṣita, Niścalakara, Aruṇa-
datta, Dalhaṇa, Hemādri and Śrīdāsapaṇḍita. A very long quotation
(in verse) from Kṣārapaṇi's treatise is found in Candraṭa's comm. on
Tisaṭa's Cikitsākalikā (Mukh., H.I.M. 3, p. 562-564).

KHARANĀDA. The medical treatise by Kharanāda was known from
quotations only until the year 1938. During excavations at Navapura
near Gilgit in the summer of 1938 a fragment of a comm. on this work
was found by M. S. Kaul Shastri (see his Report on the Gilgit excava-
tion in 1938, Quarterly Journal of the Mythic Society, vol. 30, p. 1-12).
The comm. is called Khāraṇaṇdanyāsa and relates to a chapter on
pregnancy from Kharaṇāda's treatise (the chapter is called khuṇḍī-
kagarbhavakrānti; cf. the title of Ca.Śā. 3). Kaul Shastri dates the
Ms. fragment between the seventh and ninth century. Gode says in
an article about this fragment of the Khāraṇaṇdanyāsa (St.I.L.H. 1, p.
126-131) that he is inclined to fix 650 A.D. as the terminus before which
Kharaṇāda may have composed his work and about 850 A.D. as the
terminus before which the comm. was composed. A short time before
Kaul Shastri's Report was published Gode had written an article on
the references to Kharaṇāda's treatise (St.I.L.H. 1, p. 112-125). In
that article he concluded that Kharaṇāda's treatise had been composed
before 1150 A.D. Judging by the quotations no more could be said at
that time, acc. to Gode, though Kharaṇāda is also quoted by Jejjaṭa,
which leads to the conclusion that Kharaṇāda lived before 600. The
date of composition of the Kharaṇādasamhita is pushed back to a still
earlier date by the fact that Haricandra quotes it (see : Haricandra). In
the same article Gode stated that Kharaṇāda's treatise had assumed
so much importance in the 13th century that Keśava wrote his Siddha-
mantra to harmonize the mutually conflicting views of Caraka, Suśruta
and Kharaṇāda, as stated by Keśava himself. From Gode's study of
quotations from Kharaṇāda's treatise it became clear that Kharaṇāda
and an author called Khāraṇādi are identical and that the names
Kharaṇāda and Khāraṇādi were current in Bengal and Mahārāṣṭra
respectively.

The two quotations from Kharaṇāda in M. and Ā. are not found
among the collection of quotations from Hemādri's Āyurvedarasāyana
and Vopadeva's Siddhamantraprakāśa (a comm. on the Siddhamantra


=== Page 411 ===
APPENDIX TWO                                    397

by Keśava, the father of Vopadeva) in Gode’s first article. (See about
Kharanāda also : Haricandra).

GADĀDHARA. Acc. to Bhatt. (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 140) there are two
medical authors of this name. This statement is not correct, for it is
quite unknown whether the second Gadādhara, mentioned as the
father of Vaṅgasena, ever wrote a medical work. Bhatt. is right,
however, in distinguishing two persons called Gadādhara, mentioned
in medical treatises.
    1) A medical author Gadādhara is quoted or mentioned eleven times
in M. Judging by these quotations he seems to have been a commen-
tator on Su. Gadādhara is also quoted by Niścalakara who gives some
interesting details about him: “Gadādhara was of the Dāsa family and
preceded Cakrapāṇidatta, as clearly indicated by Niścalakara ; the latter
calls him once *antaraṅgagadādharadāsa*, which may mean that he
was a court physician” (Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 140). Stanzas
ascribed to Vaidya Gadādhara are quoted in the Saduktikarṇāmṛta of
Śrīdharadāsa, composed in 1205 (N.N. Das Gupta, IC 3, p. 159). Bhatt.
is sure that Gadādhara wrote a treatise called *Vaidyaprasāraka* ; as a
proof of this he quotes from Ms. P of the Ratnaprabhā : *vaidyaprasārake
gadādharādayas tu* (l.c.), which is not convincing, but he says elsewhere
(IHQ 23, 1947, p. 148) that the Vaidyaprasāraka by Gadādhara is
often quoted by Niścalakara. A work, called Vaidyaprasāraka, is
repeatedly quoted in Śrīkaṇṭhadatta’s comm. on the Siddhayoja (e.g.
on 4, 51; 11, 28; 37, 59). Gadādhara is quoted in the same comm.
(e.g. on 41, 51; 46, 4), but Śrīkaṇṭha nowhere indicates that the
Vaidyaprasāraka was written by Gadādhara. The Ms. of an anonymous
medical work, called Bṛhadvai-dyaprasāraka, is in the Coll. Cordier in
Paris (Cordier, Le Muséon, N.S. 4, 1903, p. 341 ; Filliozat, JA, t. 224,
1934, p. 162, nr. 161). Gadādhara is not quoted by Cakra (on Ca.),
Da., Aruṇa and He.; nor does Gayadāsa quote him on Su.Ni. If the
names of authors who wrote a comm. on Su. and who are mentioned by
Vijayarakṣita on 1, 5d-6 and 1, 11-13 are really put in a chronological
order, Gadādhara preceded Vāpyacandra and lived after Jajjaṭa (see :
Vāpyacandra). Bhatt. assumes (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 139) that a particular
list of authors, given by Niścala, is in a chronological order; if this
statement is correct, Gadādhara was later than Vāgbhaṭa, Ravigupta
(author of the Siddhasāra) and Īśvarasena and anterior to Govardhana
(author of a Ratnamālā and later than Mādhavakara), Cakrapāṇidatta
and Bakula.


=== Page 412 ===
398                                          APPENDIX TWO

2) Another Gadādhara, who was not of the Dāsa family (Bhatt,
IHQ 23, 1947, p. 140), was the father of Vaṅgasena. If my hypothesis
about Gadādhara 1) is correct, the father of Vaṅgasena is indeed a
different person, for Vaṅgasena's date is after that of Mādhavakara.

               GAYADĀSA, also called Gayin, wrote a comm. on Su., called Nyāya-
candrikāpañjikā, which covered the whole of Su. as the numerous
quotations show (Hoernle, JRAS, 1906, p. 293). Part of it has been
preserved; the comm. on the Nidānasthāna has been printed; the
comm. on the Śarīrasthāna is extant, for the greater part, in a Ms.
of the Cambridge University Library (Add. nr. 2491; see about this
Ms. : Jolly, ZDMG 58, 1904, p. 114-116 and Hoernle, JRAS, 1906,
p. 294). It is assumed that Gayadāsa was also the author of a comm.
on Ca. (Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 141; Renou et Filliozat, l'Inde Clas-
sique 2, p. 159), but this comm. is not extant. Gayadāsa is quoted
twice in M.; the quotation in M. on 2, 18-23 may refer to Gayadāsa's
comm. on Ca.; the quotation on 9, 11 refers to the comm. on Su.
Gayadāsa is one of Ḍa.'s chief authorities, often quoted by him. Ḍa.
refers once to the Nyāyacandrikā (on Su.Sū. 27, 26). In the introd.
to his comm. Ḍa. mentions Gayadāsa and Bhāskara as authors of a
pañjikā on Su. and often quotes and refers to pañjikākāra (in the
singular or dual), bṛhatpañjikā, mahāpañjikā and laghupañjikā, with-
out further specifications. It is not clear which of these pañjikās de-
signates the comm. by Gayadāsa. Moreover Ḍa. quotes (once, on U.
49, 19) a candrikākāra on Su. Bhatt. (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 141) assumes
that a comm. called Candrikā, often quoted by Niścalakara, is the
famous comm. on Su. by Gayadāsa, but he does not even try to give
evidence of this identity. Bhatt. (l.c., p. 154) quotes an interesting
passage from Niścalakara, which proves that Gayadāsa was the court
physician of a king of Bengal (ity etad gauḍeśvarāntaraṅgaśrīgayadā-
sena darśitam). Cordier (Le Muséon, N.S. 4, 1903, p. 333) had already
noticed that at the end of a Ms. of Gayadāsa's comm. on Su.Ni. the
latter is called an *antaraṅga* (see about this term : Cakrapāṇidatta).
At the end of the printed text the term *antaraṅga* does not occur.
               For a long time it was difficult to determine Gayadāsa's date. Jolly
stated (ZDMG 58, 1904, p. 116) : earlier than Ḍa. Hoernle remarked
(Osteology, Introd. p. 16) : not later than 11th century, and (ibid.;
JRAS, 1906, p. 291) : Cakrapāṇidatta and Gayadāsa may have been
contemporaries. It is possible to say something more about it now.
Important in narrowing the limits of the time in which Gayadāsa must


=== Page 413 ===
APPENDIX TWO                                                399

have lived is the fact that Jejjaṭa is quoted by him. Moreover, Gaya-
dāsa is referred to once by Cakrapāṇidatta, acc. to Bhatt. (IHQ 23,
1947, p. 154). Bhatt. (ibid.) arrived at the conclusion that Gayadāsa
can be placed about 1000 A.D. in the reign of one of the greatest
Pāla kings : Mahīpāla I (c. 988-1038 acc. to Majumdar, History of
Bengal I, p. 136). It is, however, not clear at all that Cakra (on Ca.Ci.
26, 293) refers to Gayadāsa ; he only speaks about a *candraikākṛt* on Su.
Therefore the problem remains whether Gayadāsa and Cakrapāṇidatta
were contemporaries or not. It is not without importance that Gaya-
dāsa is quoted by Vijayarakṣita, for the latter preceded Dalhaṇa. So
Gayadāsa’s date is somewhere between those of Jejjaṭa and Vijaya-
rakṣita.

     GUṆĀKARA. The author of this name, quoted once in M. (on 5, 31-32),
has played an important part in Hoernle’s efforts to fix the chronology
of a number of medical authors. Hoernle writes (Osteology, Introd. p.
17) : “Vijayarakṣita quotes Guṇākara who wrote the Yogaratnamālā
in 1239 A.D.” This fact established, in Hoernle’s opinion, the lower
limit for Vijayarakṣita’s date. In footnote 3 on p. 17 of Hoernle’s
Osteology it is made clear that the information about Guṇākara was
obtained by letter from Cordier. With regard to the date of Guṇākara
Hoernle refers the reader to Peterson’s Report, 1886-1892, p. XXVI.
Cordier possessed a manuscript of the Yogaratnamālā, also called
Āścaryaratnamālā (see Cat.Cat. 1, p. 283), ascribed to Siddha Nāgār-
juna, with a comm. by Guṇākara (this Ms. is now in the Coll. Cordier
of the Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris ; see Filliozat, JA, t. 224, 1934,
p. 160, nr. 95). The commentary was written in 1239-1240 by the Jaina
scholar Guṇākara (Cat.Cat. 1, p. 155 ; Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 132-133).
The Yogaratnamālā is a work on magical rites, incantations and sor-
cery and it is very improbable that Vijayarakṣita quotes from a com-
mentary on a work of such a kind. Moreover, Guṇākara is quoted,
together with Cakrapāṇidatta and Gadādhara, in order to explain a
medical technical term. Bhatt. (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 132-133) has contri-
buted a great deal to the elucidation of the problem. The three quota-
tions to explain the term *āṭopa* which are found in M. on 5, 31-32 were
traced by him in Niścalakara’s *Ratnaprabhā*, where they serve the
same purpose (the third quotation, taken from Gadādhara acc. to M.,
is said to be from a work, called *Candraikā*, in Niścalakara’s comm.).
In Niścalakara’s comm. another quotation from Guṇākara occurs,
again pointing to him as a medical author. Moreover, Bhatt. failed to


=== Page 414 ===
400                                                     APPENDIX TWO

find both quotations in two Mss. of Guṇākara's comm. on the Yoga-
ratnamālā. It is clear now that Hoernle was wrong and that Guṇākara,
quoted by Vijayarakṣita and Niścalakara, is not the Jaina scholar
but a medical author, who probably wrote a comm. on Ca. Guṇākara,
the medical author, is moreover quoted in Nāganātha's Nidānapradipa
(New Cat.Cat. 6, p. 58) and in Gopāladāsa's Cikitsāmṛta (New Cat.Cat.
6, p. 58; Bhaṭṭ., IHQ 24, 1948, p. 322).

GAUTAMA. A sage, called Gautama, is mentioned : Ca.Sū. 1, 8;
Ca.Ci. 14, 3; Ca.Si. 11, 4, but the author Gautama, quoted in M., must
have been a different person. A medical author, called Gautama, is
quoted in A.s. (Sū. 8, 125; the passage is quoted from A.s. by Hemādri
in his comm. on A.h.Sū. 7, 22cd-26). An author, called Gotama, is
quoted by Gayadāsa on Su.Śā. (Hoernle, JRAS, 1906, p. 302). Other
quotations are not known to me.

CAKRAPĀṆIDATTA. often called Cakrapāṇi or Cakra, wrote the follow-
ing works : 1) a comm. on Ca., called Āyurvedadīpikā or Caraka-
tātparyaṭīkā, which has been preserved and repeatedly printed; 2) a
comm. on Su., called Bhānumatī; this work has been partially (on
Su.Sū.) preserved and printed; acc. to Cordier (Le Muséon, N.S. 4,
1903, p. 332) a complete Ms. of the Bhānumatī forms part of a private
collection in Benares; from quotations in other comm., especially
Niścalakara's Ratnaprabhā, it is clear that Cakra's Bhānumatī covered
the whole of Su.; 3) Cikitsāsaṃgraha, a well-known and often printed
treatise on therapy; Niścalakara and Śivadāsasena wrote a comm. on
it; 4) Dravyaguṇasaṃgraha, a short work on materia medica, which
has been printed; Niścalakara and Śivadāsasena wrote a comm. on
this work too; 5) Śabdacandrikā; this work has not yet been printed;
Mss. of it are in the IO Library and the Oxford University Library;
acc. to Jolly (Medicin, p. 6) it is a collection of pharmaceutical and
botanical terms with their explanations; 6) Sarvasārasaṃgraha (Jolly,
Medicin, p. 6); this work too has not been printed; N.N. Das Gupta
(IC 3, p. 156-157) observes that this work may be by a later author,
also called Cakrapāṇidatta; 7) Vyāgradaridraśubhamkara, also known
as Śubhamkara; this work is quoted in Niścala's Ratnaprabhā and
was written before the Cikitsāsaṃgraha (acc. to Bhaṭṭ., IHQ 23, 1947,
p. 148); it is also referred to, as Vyagradināśubhamkara, in Gopāla-
dāsa's Cikitsāmṛta (Bhaṭṭ., IHQ 24, 1948, p. 318); 8) Muktāvalī,
mentioned in the New Cat.Cat. (6, p. 284) as a medical lexicon.


=== Page 415 ===
APPENDIX TWO                                                401

Cakra has given us information about his person at the end of the
Āyurvedadīpikā and Cikitsāsaṁgraha. He was a son of Nārāyaṇa who
was the superintendent of the kitchen ( _rasavatyadhikārin_ ) and a
minister of the king of Bengal ( _gauḍa_ ). His elder brother, Bhānu, was
a court physician ( _antaraṅga_ ). Cakra was born from a family of _vaidyas_,
bearing as a family name Lodhravali; this name is mentioned as one
of the eight aristocratic _vaidya_ families of Bengal by Bharatamallika
in his Candrapravbhā (p. 8, acc. to Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 128, foot-
note 6). Bhatt. (l.c., p. 134-135) rejects the current reading of the
colophon of Cakra’s Cikitsāsaṁgraha and favours a variant (warranted
by some Mss.; he refers to Peterson’s Ulwar Cat., p. 154), in which
Cakra states that he himself was the superintendent of the kitchen and
a minister of the king of Bengal. Bhatt. adduces as arguments that the
variant is stylistically faultless and that Nīścala was removed by some
length of time even from Cakra’s disciples, whose views are sometimes
criticized by Nīścala.
Cakra’s teacher was Naradatta and the Āyurvedadīpikā is based on
Naradatta’s interpretation of Ca. (see Introd. Āyurvedadīpikā).
Vṛnda’s Siddhayoga was the chief source of Cakra’s Cikitsāsaṁgraha
(as indicated by Cakra himself : Jolly, Medicin, p. 6). Nīścala carefully
records whether Cakra’s formulas are found in the Siddhayoga or ab-
sent from it. In Cakra’s time the Siddhayoga must have been the most
popular compendium on therapy in Bengal (see Cikitsāsaṁgraha,
_susthādikāra_ 16).
There is no doubt that Cakra was a native of Bengal. He is said to
have been a resident of the Virabhūma district of Bengal ( _vaṅga_ ) (see
Gul 1, p. 117; the statement is supported by a quotation from an
author called Jayadeva; no particulars about the latter are are given).
Śivadāsasena observes (on Cakra’s Cikitsāsaṁgraha, _susthādikāra_ 16)
that Nārāyaṇa, Cakra’s father, was a minister of king Nayapāla of
Bengal (1038-1055 acc. to Bhatt., l.c. p. 134, and Majumdar, History
of Bengal I, p. 144; 1040-1070 acc. to Gul 1, p. 117). Cakrapāṇidatta’s
date is usually fixed at about 1060 (Cordier, JA, t. 17, 1901, p. 182;
Hoernle, Osteology, Introd. p. 16), but Bhatt., being of the opinion
that Cakra himself was a minister of king Nayapāla, says that it can
now be definitely stated that Cakrapāṇi wrote his Cikitsāsaṁgraha in
the decade 1040-1050 (l.c., p. 135). Bhatt.’s arguments, referred to
above, are weak. I am of the opinion that the period in which Cakra
wrote his works should be fixed at about 1060-1075.
The meaning of the term _antaraṅga_ has been the subject of a study


=== Page 416 ===
402 APPENDIX TWO

by N.N. Das Gupta (IC 1, p. 684-686). The word *antaraṅga* is repeatedly
used, a.o. by Cakrapāṇidatta (whose elder brother was an *antaraṅga*),
Niścalakara and Śivadāsasena. Bhatt. translates *antaraṅga* as royal
physician (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 135). Śivadāsasena observes (on Cakra's
*Cikitsāsaṁgraha*, *susthādhikāra* 16) that the term designates a learned
physician of good family. See about the possible meanings and the
development of the use of the term N.N. Das Gupta's article.

CANDRANANDANA was the son of Ratinandana (Vogel, Introd. A.h.,
p. 15) or Ravinandana (New Cat.Cat. 6, p. 355; Cordier, JA, t. 17,
1901, p. 185) and a native of Kaśmīr (Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 15). He
wrote a comm. on A.h., called *Padārthacandrikā*, on the instance of
Śakunadeva (see Introd. *Padārthacandrikā*; New Cat.Cat. 1, p. 464).
This comm. has been preserved, at least almost completely (see Introd.
A.h., *sūcipatram saptamam*, about two Mss., covering together the
whole of the work, some stanzas of the last chapter excepted) and has
been printed partially (on *Sūtrasthāna*). The complete text of the comm.
is available in a Tibetan translation.

There is also a medical lexicographer called Candranandana, who
is frequently quoted in Kṣirasvāmin's comm. on the *Amarakośa*, esp.
in that part dealing with the *vanauṣadhivarga* (Vogel, Introd. A.h.,
p. 16, footnote 2; Gode, St.I.L.H. 1, p. 160). A Ms. of the work of
this Candranandana, called *Guṇanighaṇṭu*, is in the coll. Cordier in
Paris (Filliozat, JA, t. 224, 1934, p. 157, nr. 31). Acc. to Cordier (JA,
t. 17, 1901, p. 185) the work is called *Gaṇanighaṇṭu* (New Cat.Cat. 6,
p. 356 indicates: *Oṣadhinighaṇṭu* or *Gaṇanighaṇṭu*) and is a small
vocabulary of materia medica in 33 sections (*gaṇa*), mainly drawn
from A.h. (Cordier calls this work *Guṇanighaṇṭu* in his article in Le
Muséon, N.S. 4, 1903, p. 350). The identity of these two authors,
called Candranandana, is accepted by Cordier (l.c.), Bhatt. (ABORI 28,
1947, p. 119), Gode (St.I.L.H. 1, p. 160) and Bāpālāl G. Vaidya (Introd.
*Nighaṇṭu Ādarśa*, p. 37); Vogel (Introd. A.h., p. 16) has his doubts
about this question. New Cat.Cat. mentions also (6, p. 356) a work
by Candranandana called *Madanādinighaṇṭu*.
About Candranandana's date opinions differ. He may be identical
with the physician Candrābhinandana who is said to have assisted
Vairocana in translating the four Tantras (*rGyud bźi*, the classic of
Tibetan medicine) into Tibetan at the time of the Tibetan king Khri-
sroñ-ldeḥu-btsan (755-797) (Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 15-16; see also p.
16, footnote 1); this identity is a matter of doubt. Bhatt. (ABORI 28,


=== Page 417 ===
APPENDIX TWO 403

1947, p. 119) says that Candranandana lived in the middle of the 11th
century at the latest, because he is identical with the lexicographer
of the same name quoted by Kṣīrasvāmin. Cordier was of the opinion
that Candranandana was a contemporary of king Abhimanyu II of
Kaśmīr (Cordier, Catalogue 3, p. 472, acc. to Vogel, Introd. A.h., p.
15, footnote 8). Candranandana must in any case have lived before
the date of the translation of his comm. on A.h. into Tibetan. This
translation was made by Rin-chen-bzaṅ-po between 1013 and 1055.
The quotation from Candranandana in Ā. on 2, 56-57 is probably
a later interpolation and has been put between brackets by the ed.
of the text.

CANDRIKĀKĀRA. This authority, quoted in commentaries under the
name of Candrikākāra, has often been identified as Gayadāsa, who
wrote the comm. called Nyāyacandrikāpañjikā on Su. (see a.o. : Bhatt.,
IHQ 23, 1947, p. 141). Cordier supposed (Le Muséon, N.S. 4, 1903, p.
331) that a comm., called Carakacandrikā, might be Gayadāsa's
comm. on Ca.

One has to be careful in identifying the Candrikākāra or Candri-
kākṛt and his comm., for Cakrapāṇidatta refers to a comm. called
Candrikā, once clearly as a comm. on Ca. (Cakra on Ca.Sū. 27, 129)
and speaks also about a Candrikākṛt on Su. (Cakra on Ca.Ci. 26, 293).
Ḍa. once refers to a Candrikākāra as a commentator on Su. (Ḍa. on
Su.U. 49, 19), who does not agree with Cakra's comment on the stan-
za; I think that it is very improbable that Ḍa. refers to Gayadāsa in
this way, for he always quotes the latter either under his name or as
Pañjikākāra and (probably) as the author of the Bṛhatpañjikā. More-
over, the Candrikā which is quoted by Aruṇadatta, is acc. to Cordier
(JA, t. 17, p. 185) Candranandana's Padārthacandrikā. So the Candri-
kākāra, mentioned twice by Vijayarakṣita in M. on ch. 1-10, may not be
Gayadāsa, but some other commentator. The Candrikākāra, quoted in
M. on 2, 61cd-65, may be the author of a comm. on Su., but this is
not quite clear; the Candrikākāra quoted in M. on 10, 20 is, however,
evidently a commentator on Su.

CARAKA made a revision of the Agniveśatantra; the revised text
became known as the Carakasamhitā (see the colophons of Ca.). Some
scholars made rather definite statements about Caraka's date. On the
authority of the Chinese version of the Sūtrālamkāra, translated from
Sanskrit into Chinese in the 5th century, S. Lévi (JA, t. 8, 1896, p.


=== Page 418 ===
404                                             APPENDIX TWO

480-482) argued that he was the physician of king Kaniṣka. Jolly was
in doubt about this identification (WZKM 11, 1897, p. 164-166) and
so was Müller (JRAS, 1932, p. 803-808). Filliozat (in : Renou et Filliozat,
l'Inde Classique 2, p. 150) observes, however, that there is nothing to
invalidate this tradition; he goes on to assert that, even if the tradition
proves to be incorrect, this will not substantially alter the state of
affairs as to Caraka's date, because the tradition that he lived during
Kaniṣka's reign established itself at an early date; so Caraka probably
lived during the first century of our era. Hoernle was of the opinion
(JRAS, 1909, p. 857-893) that the Carakasamhitā, in its original form,
is anterior to the Nāvanītaka (which forms part of the Bower Ms.)
because at least twenty-five formulae found in the Nāvanītaka are
identical with formulae occurring in the printed editions of the Caraka-
samhitā and exclusively in those portions of it, which are attributed
to Caraka himself and not to Drḍhabala. Caraka's name, however, is
nowhere mentioned in the Bower Ms. Hoernle fixed Caraka's date as
lying between that of Kaniṣka and that of the Bower Ms., which he
dated in the second half of the 4th century. The Nāvanītaka, contained
in the Bower Ms., must have been composed some centuries before the
date of the Ms. (see Hoernle's article in JRAS, 1909). Hoernle thought
it might have been written in the 2nd or 3rd century. So Caraka's
date would fall between that of Kaniṣka and the 2nd or 3rd century.
Müller (JRAS, 1932, p. 809-810) disagrees with Hoernle and says that
the formulae found in both Nāvanītaka and Carakasamhitā do not
prove that the latter already existed when the Nāvanītaka was com-
posed. He is of the opinion that the Carakasamhitā was redacted in a
number of stages about the middle of the period 500-1000, but before
700. Mukhopādhyāya (H.I.M. 3, p. 610-613) is convinced that the
Carakasamhitā is a book of great antiquity, because Patañjali (un-
specified by Mukh.), who flourished in the 2nd century B.C., wrote a
comm. on it (he refers to a quotation found in Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa's Laghu-
mañjūṣā) and for other reasons too (l.c., p. 611-613). The arguments
used by Mukhopādhyāya to prove the great antiquity of Caraka are
repeated by Srivastava (Hist.Ind.Pharm., p. 44-47). (See also Hari
prapanna, Rasayogasāgara, Introd. p. 71-84). Rāy (Hist.Chem., p. 60)
tries to prove that Caraka should be placed in the early Buddhistic
era. In my opinion the best solution is to assume that Caraka's redac-
tion of the Agnivēśatantra already existed or was made in the first
two or three centuries of our era.
           Many commentators, among whom Vijayarakṣita, refer to and quote


=== Page 419 ===
APPENDIX TWO 405

from a text called the *kāśmīrapāṭha* of the *Carakasamhitā*. Vijaya-
rakṣita's reference (on 5, 27c) to the *kāśmīrān* who read Ca.Ci. 14,
171a differently, was discussed by Hoernle (JRAS, 1909, p. 890-891),
who thought that the Kaśmīr recension of Ca., referred to by Vijaya-
rakṣita, should with good reason be ascribed to Dṛḍhabala, and the
original form of the verse, adopted by Mādhavakara, to Caraka. Acc.
to Hoernle this implied that the Kaśmīr recension was not known to
Mādhava and that Dṛḍhabala was posterior to Mādhava. I do not see
why it should be thus, for the printed editions of Ca., which contain
Dṛḍhabala's recension, read the verse in the same way as Mādhavakara.
The other quotation by Vijayarakṣita from the *kāśmīrapāṭha* of Ca.
is identical with that in the printed recension of Dṛḍhabala. Hoernle
also deals with the Kaśmīr recension of Ca. in his Osteology (Introd.
p. 3): "The early commentators of the eleventh and thirteenth cen-
turies (e.g. Cakrapāṇidatta and Vijayarakṣita) often refer to a Kash-
mirian recension (*kāśmīrapāṭha*) when commenting on passages of the
earlier portion of the compendium, i.e. the portion written by Caraka
himself. The probability is that in all these cases the reference is to
Dṛḍhabala's revision of Caraka's work; for in references to the con-
cluding portion of the compendium, Dṛḍhabala, as a rule, is quoted
by name as its author." Mukhopādhyāya (H.I.M. 3, p. 637) disagrees
with Hoernle, drawing attention to the fact that Hoernle regards both
Caraka and Dṛḍhabala as Kashmirians, so that it is natural for com-
mentators to refer to Caraka's edition of the earlier part of the work
as the Kaśmīr recension. He further observes that this theory is based
upon a conjecture because nothing is known about Caraka's birth-
place and that the Kaśmīr recension may have been the work of a
Kashmirian physician, whose name is lost to us and who may have
been a different individual, neither Caraka nor Dṛḍhabala.

I tend to assume that Hoernle is wrong. Cakrapāṇidatta refers to
the *kāśmīrān* (on Ca.Ci. 3, 117 and 119; Ci. 25, 41) and the *kāśmīra*-
(*pāṭha*) (on Ca.Ci. 13, 112cd-113ab) in such a way that the impression
is created that not Dṛḍhabala's recension is referred to (Cakra's re-
marks on Ci. 3, 117 and 119 refer to passages incorporated in the text,
read by the *kāśmīrān* and adopted by Cakra; his remark on Ci. 25, 41
concerns a variant, adopted by the *kāśmīrāḥ*, but not read by Cakra;
also on Ci. 13, 112cd-113ab Cakra records a variant found in the
*kāśmīrāḥ*). All these remarks may point to a Kaśmīr school of inter-
preters of Ca., who adopted their own readings and variants of Ca.
This is not improbable because a number of schools of interpreters of

the gauḍa recension acc. to Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 153). It is for

JATŪKARŅA was one of the six disciples of Ātreya Punarvasu. He
wrote his own treatise on kāyacikitsā (Ca.Sū. 1, 30-33). From quota-
tions by various commentators it is clear that there must indeed have
existed a Jatūkarṇasaṁhitā. The quotations in M. also point to this.
Mukhopādhyāya (H.I.M. 3, p. 547-550) collected the quotations from the
Madhukośa, Śrīkaṇṭhadatta's Vyākhyākusumāvali on the Siddhayoğa,
Ḍa.'s comm. on Su. and Śivadāsasena's Tattvacandrikā on Ca. Jatū-
karṇa is also quoted by Jejjaṭa (his name is written there Jātukarṇa),
Cakrapāṇidatta (on Ca.), Aruṇadatta (who writes his name Jātukarṇa),
Nīścalakara, and in the Kairalī comm. on A.h.U.; Nīścalakara quotes
Jatūkarṇa very often in his Ratnaprabhā (Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p.
142). In Nīścala's time the Jatūkarṇasaṁhitā must still have been
available, for he consulted three old copies of it (Bhatt., l.c., p. 127).
Jolly says (Medicin, p. 129) that acc. to Cordier (in : Origines, évolution
et décadence de la médecine indienne, Annales d'hygiène et de méde-
cine coloniales, 1901, p. 77-89) fragments of Jatūkarṇa's work have
been discovered in Nepal (I have not been able to verify this statement).

JEJJAṬA. The orthography of the name of this author varies : Jajjata
(in the colophons of the preserved parts of his comm. on Ca.), Jarjaṭa
(A.s., ed. Trichur; see Bhatt., ABORI 28, 1947, p. 112, note 1), Jejjaṭa
(M.; Ā.; Gayadāsa on Su.Nī.; Cakra on Ca.; often in Ḍa.; He.; etc.),
Jejjaḍa (sometimes in Ḍa.), Jejjaḍa (Ms. A of Nīścalakara's Ratna-
prabhā; see Bhatt., IHQ, 23, 1947, p. 142), Jaijjaṭa (Su. with Ḍa.'s comm.,
ed. by Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara, 1889, acc. to Hoernle, JRAS, 1906, p.
285; Jolly, ZDMG 60, 1906, p. 414), Jaijjaṭa (Jolly, ZDMG 58, 1904,
p. 114, referring to Roth in ZDMG 48, 1894, p. 139, who reviews the
third ed. of Su. by Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara; Roth, however, writes
Jaijghaṭa) and Jaiyyaṭa (Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2, p. 427). Jaḍa, quoted
five times in the Ms. of Gayadāsa's comm. on Su.Sū., is identical with
Jejjaṭa (Jolly, ZDMG 58, 1904, p. 116 : Jaḍa may be the same as


=== Page 421 ===
APPENDIX TWO                                                                               407

Jejjaṭa; Jolly, ZDMG 60, 1906, p. 413-414 : “The supposition of this
identity, simultaneously put forward by Cordier and by me, proves to
be right”; in a study of the Ms. of Gayadāsa’s comm. on Su.Śā.
Hoernle arrived at the same conclusion : JRAS, 1906, p. 301).
    Jejjaṭa wrote a commentary on both Ca. and Su. (see M. on 2,
61cd-65 and on 10, 2; the comm. on Su. is referred to by Ḍa. in the
introduction to his comm. on Su.). Gayadāsa ascribes also a tantra
(textbook) to him (see Hoernle, JRAS, 1906, p. 301). His comm. on
Su. must have been the oldest comm. on this text, but has not been
preserved. The only one to whom it seems to have been accessible in
recent times is Rudrapārāśava, the editor of A.s. with Indu’s comm.
(Trichur, 1913-1926), who filled up a lacuna in Indu’s Śaśilekhā with
the text of the Nirantarapadī comm. on Su. by Jarjaṭa (vol. 2, p. 298)
and who printed many notes from Jarjaṭa’s comm. in the second and
third volume of his ed. of A.s. (see Bhatt., ABORI 28, 1947, p. 112,
note 1). The name of Jejjaṭa’s comm. on Su. was known to Dasgupta,
who writes (H.I.Ph., 2, p. 428) that it went by the name of Bṛhalla-
ghupañjikā. Dasgupta, however, is wrong. (It is possible that Das-
gupta copied Cordier who also held the opinion that Jejjaṭa’s comm.
on Su. was called Bṛhallaghupañjikā; see : Le Muséon, N.S. 4, 1903,
p. 334). In Ḍa.'s comm. on Su. the Bṛhatpañjikā and Laghupañjikā
are clearly referred to as two separate works (Ḍa. on Su.Śū. 45, 157)
and, moreover, as the works of two authors with an opinion on a
particular point that differs from that of Jejjaṭa (Ḍa. on the same
passage). Jejjaṭa’s comm. on Su. was consulted by Candraṭa before he
started writing his Suśrutapāṭhaśuddhi (as indicated by Candraṭa him-
self at the end of this text; see Introd. Ca., p. 13). It seems to have been
available at least up to the time of Vijayarakṣita and Ḍa., who quote
from it; even Hemādri refers to it in his introd. to the Āyurvedarasā-
yana.
    Jejjaṭa’s comm. on Ca., in a revised version by Haridatta, has been
partly preserved in a single manuscript, kept in the Government
Oriental Manuscripts Library at Madras. It has been printed, together
with Cakra’s comm. on Ca. (Lahore, 1940, 2 vols.) and is called Niran-
tarapadavyākhyā. The extant fragments extend from Ca.Ci. 13, 32 to
Ci. 5, 73; from Ci. 23, 161 to Ka. 1, 4 and from Sī. 3 to Sī. 7, 31. It is
evident from the quotations in Jejjaṭa’s comm. that a number of com-
mentators on Ca. preceded him.
    Jejjaṭa mentions in his comm. on Ca. that he was a pupil of Vāgbhaṭa.
His date depends on the identity and date of this Vāgbhaṭa. It is often


=== Page 422 ===
408                                       APPENDIX TWO

silently assumed that the latter is the well-known medical author who
wrote the A.h.; this assumption is not contradicted by the dates of
both authors. There are, however, divergent opinions about the time
in which Jejjaṭa lived : Haridattaśarman (ed. of Jejjaṭa's comm. on
Ca.) : sixth century (Introd. p. 20); Gul (1, p. 116) : ninth century;
Bhattacharyya (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 153) : about 875-900. Only Hoernle
noticed (JRAS, 1906, p. 292) that Jejjaṭa's comm. on Ca. was known
to Vṛndakuṇḍa who mentions it : Siddhāyoga 39, 33 (carake prāha
jaijjaṭaḥ). So Jejjaṭa must have preceded Vṛndakuṇḍa. Hoernle's con-
clusion is that this would refer Jejjaṭa to the seventh century at the
latest. If my hypothesis on the enumeration in a chronological list of
some authors by Vijayarakṣita on 1, 5d-6 and 1, 11-13 is correct (see :
Vāpyacandra), Jejjaṭa lived before Gadādhara. He is anterior to
Gayadāsa because the latter quotes him.

In the Gul ed. of Ca. (1, p. 117) it is said : “Jejjaṭa may have been
a Kashmirian as is suggested by the ending -ṭa of his name, common
among Kashmirians (e.g. Kaiyaṭa, Mammaṭa). More probably he was
an inhabitant of Sindh, because he studied under Vāgbhaṭa, though he
may have travelled from Kashmir to Sindh in order to study under
Vāgbhaṭa.” (Vāgbhaṭa, the author of the A.h., was indeed an inhabitant
of Sindh; see : Vāgbhaṭa). Haridattaśarman (Introd. Ca. with Jejjaṭa's
comm., p. 20) observes : “Some say that Jajjaṭa is identical with the
father of Kaiyaṭa; in the introduction to his comm. on the Mahā-
bhāṣya Kaiyaṭa says that he is a son of Jaiyaṭa. Others are of the
opinion that Jajjaṭa and Jaiyaṭa are different persons.” The identity
of Jejjaṭa with this Jaiyaṭa is rejected by Gul (1, p. 116).

I think that Jejjaṭa's date may be : about 600 (the age in which
Vāgbhaṭa lived), because he quotes Dṛḍhabala; moreover, Jejjaṭa
quotes Bhaṭṭāraharicandra who lived before 600; Jejjaṭa preceded
Vāpyacandra, who preceded Mādhavakara; so Jejjaṭa must have lived
before 700.

DALHAṆA wrote a comm. on Su., called Nibandhasaṃgraha, which has
been preserved and repeatedly printed. In the introd. he states that he
was a favourite of king Sahapāla and gives as his genealogy that he
was a son of Bharatapāla, son of Jayapāla, son of Govinda; Govinda
and Jayapāla are described as physicians; his family's home was in
the neighbourhood of Mathurā. Acc. to Hoernle (JRAS, 1906, p. 290)
he had his home in the north-west; acc. to Filliozat (in Renou et
Filliozat, l'Inde Classique 2, p. 159) he was a Kashmirian.

Ḍa.'s date must be : about 1200; Cakrapāņidatta is quoted once by
Ḍa. (on U. 49, 19); Ḍa. quotes from Śrīpati's Jyotișaratnamālā (on
Śā. 1, 11; see : Bhațț., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 132); Śrīpati wrote another
work, the Siddhāntaśekhara, about 1040 (see Introd. to Śrīpati's
Gaņitatilaka, p. 62-63, ed. H. R. Kāpaḍiā, Gaekwad's Oriental Series,
vol. 58). Ḍa. is quoted by Hemādri once (on A.h.Sū. 7, 40). (See also
Introduction : Vācaspati). Ḍalhaņa is not quoted in the Madhukośa,
nor by Niścalakara, which may indicate that the proposed date is
correct. He is repeatedly quoted in the Kusumāvali, but these quota-
tions were added by Nārāyaņa, the reviser of that comm. (see :
Śrīkaņțhadatta).

TISATA was a son of Vāgbhața (see Cat.Skt.Mss. BORI, vol. 16,
part 1, p. 86-87) and the father of Candrāța. He is the author of the
Cikitsākalikā, also called Yogamālā (Cat.Skt.Mss. BORI, vol. 16, part
1, p. 84-85). Tisața is quoted by Vijayarakṣita and must be prior to
the latter. It is of more importance, however, that Cakrapāņidatta
borrowed from the Cikitsākalikā as Niścalakara observes (Bhatt.,
ABORI 28, 1947, p. 124-125). So Tisața cannot have lived later than
the 10th century, though Filliozat (in Renou et Filliozat, l'Inde Clas-
sique 2, p. 160) places him in the 11th century. Bhatt. (ABORI 28,
1947, p. 125) assigns Tisața and Candrāța to the first half of the tenth
century. The Cikitsākalikā has been printed; Jolly has translated and
published the first part of it (ZDMG 60, 1906, p. 413-468).
    Tisața's son, Candrāța, wrote a comm. on the work of his father;
two versions of this comm. are known, one much more elaborate than
the other (see Jolly, l.c.). The comm. has also been partially translated
by Jolly (ibid.). Besides the comm. on the Cikitsākalikā Candrāța
wrote a revised version of Su., called Suśrutapāțhaśuddhi. The im-
portance of this work was already noticed by Hoernle (JRAS, 1906,
p. 293). Moreover Candrāța wrote a work called Yogaratnasamuccaya
in which many of his sources are specified, which is of importance for
the chronology of the authors and works quoted and referred to by
Candrāța (the authors and works quoted by Candrāța in the Yoga-
ratnasamuccaya have been studied by Gode : St.I.L.H. 1, p. 132-137).
Apart from the already enumerated works of Candrāța the New Cat.
Cat. mentions (6, p. 354) a Candrāțasāroddhāra and a comm. by
Candrāța, called Vaidyatrimśāțțīkā.

TODARA(MALLA) was a famous minister of the emperor Akbar (1556-


=== Page 424 ===
410                                     APPENDIX TWO

1605). Under his inspiration an encyclopaedic work, called Toḍarā-
nanda, was written. The medical part of this work is called Āyur-
vedasaukhya. Acc. to Gode (St.I.L.H. 1, p. 295) the Toḍarānanda was

notices (Cat.Cat. 1, p. 214) that Toḍaramalla, minister of Akbar and
