and Sāmāmbikā. See about Toḍara and his medical works : BDHM
Hyderabad 3, 1965, p. 151-160 and 210-219.

DĀRUVĀHA is an old medical authority, already quoted by Jejjaṭa.
He is mentioned twice in the Kāśyapasamhitā (Sū. 25, 3; Sū. 27, 3).

DṚḌHABALA was a son of Kapilabala (Ca.Ci. 30, 290) and was born
in Pañcanadapura (Ca.Si. 12, 39); an author on kāyacikitsā, called
Kapilabala, is quoted by Cakra on Ca.Sū. 7, 45-50. Pañcanada is men-
tioned in Kalhaṇa's Rājatarangiṇī (taraṅga 4, 248); it is said to be
situated near the confluence of the rivers Vitastā and Sindhu (Introd.
Ca., p. 11). Acc. to M. A. Stein it is a place called nowadays Pañcya-
nor; so Dṛḍhabala would have been a Kashmiriān (Introd. Ca., p. 11).
Jolly (Medicin, p. 11), however, says that Dṛḍhabala was born in the
Pañjāb (pañcanada). Hoernle (Osteology, Introd. p. 2-3 and footnote
p. 3) remarks : “There are several places called Pañcanada; anciently
one of them appears to have existed in Kaśmīr, near the confluence of
the rivers Jhelam (Vitastā) and Sindhu; its place is indicated by the
modern village of Pantzinōr, which lies close to what was the original
site of that confluence, before its removal to its present site, in the lat-
ter half of the ninth century, in the reign of king Avantivarman ; it is
this Kashmirian Pañcanada, which was probably the home of Dṛḍha-
bala. (See Dr. Stein's transl. of the Rājatarangiṇī, ch. 4, 248 and ch.
5, 66ff. The usual identification of Pañcanada with the Pañjāb is un-
tenable, for Dṛḍhabala clearly indicates a locality, *pura*, not a country,
as his home).” (See also the remainder of Hoernle's footnote on p. 3
about Cordier's erroneous identification of Pañcanadapura). Filliozat
(in Renou et Filliozat, L'Inde Classique 2, p. 150) holds the view that
Dṛḍhabala was a native of Kaśmīr. Dasgupta (H.I.Ph. 2, p. 426) is


=== Page 425 ===
                                    411
                            APPENDIX TWO

        in doubt whether Dṛḍhabala was born in Kaśmīr or in the Pañjāb.
        (See also Mukhopādhyāya, H.I.M. 3, p. 622-624; Gul 1, p. 96-99).
        Dṛḍhabala completed Caraka's revision of the Agnivēśatantra, as
        clearly indicated in the text of Ca. Dṛḍhabala states (Ca.Ci. 30, 289-290)
        that he has written the last seventeen chapters of the Cikitsāsthāna
        and the whole of the Kalpa- and Siddhisthāna. Dṛḍhabala also says
        that he has made use of many treatises to complete Caraka's work.
        Cakra comments on this passage and observes that the treatises re-
        ferred to are those of Suśruta, Videha, etc. It has long been a problem
        which are the seventeen chapters of Ca.Ci. redacted by Dṛḍhabala,
        because his name appears in only some of the colophons. His state-
        ment that he has written the last seventeen chapters does not solve
        the puzzle, because there are two ways of arrangement of the chapters
        of Ca.Ci. (see e.g. Hoernle, JRAS, 1908, p. 999-1001 ; Mukhopādhyāya
        3, p. 624-626; Gul 1, p. 101-103). The authors of the Gul ed. of Ca.,
        after studying the subject (Gul 1, p. 103-105), concluded that the
        authorship of only seven chapters out of the thirty of Ca.Ci. remains
        doubtful. Twenty-three chapters can definitely be assigned, either to
        Caraka (1-8; 14, 19 and 21, because they are quoted in the Nāvanītaka
        of the Bower Ms., which is anterior to Dṛḍhabala ; 24 and 25, because
        ascribed to Caraka by Jejjata), or to Dṛḍhabala (26, 27 and 28 are
        ascribed to Dṛḍhabala by Vijayarakṣita ; 15 is ascribed to him by
        Aruṇadatta ; 16, 17, 22 and 23 are quoted by Vijayarakṣita and as-
        cribed to Dṛḍhabala ; 29 and 30 are the last chapters in both orders of
        arrangement and have been redacted by Dṛḍhabala as stated in the
        colophons). (The order of the chapters is that of the ed. Gul and the
        ed. Nirṇaya Sāgar Press. See also the treatment of the problem by
        Hoernle, JRAS, 1908, p. 1001-1027 and by Mukhopādhyāya, H.I.M.
        3, p. 626-629). Dṛḍhabala not only wrote the mentioned portions of
        the Carakasaṃhitā but probably revised the whole, though it is very
        difficult to determine what he added to the text of Caraka or what
        was changed by him (see about this question : Hoernle, JRAS, 1908,
        p. 1001-1002; Mukhopādhyāya, H.I.M. 3, p. 633-636 ; Gul 1, p. 105-106).
        Dṛḍhabala's date has often been discussed. Filliozat (in Renou et
        Filliozat, l'Inde Classique 2, p. 150) is very cautious, saying that his
        date is uncertain, but that he is anterior to Cakrapāṇidatta because
        the latter quotes him. Hoernle, basing his statements on a rather com-
        plicated, but not convincing reasoning (see his Osteology, p. 14-16,
        and his article in JRAS, 1908, p. 997-1028), arrives at the conclusion
        that Dṛḍhabala is posterior to the authors of A.s., Mādhavanidāna


=== Page 426 ===
412 APPENDIX TWO

and Siddhayoga, because he incorporated portions of these texts in
the Carakasamhitā. The author of A.h., however, is posterior to
Dr̥ḍhabala acc. to Hoernle (Osteology, Introd. p. 14-15; JRAS, 1908,
p. 1016-1018). Dr̥ḍhabala should be dated, acc. to Hoernle (Osteology,
Introd. p. 16), between Mādhava (7th or 8th century) and the author
of A.h. (8th or 9th century). Many scholars argue that Dr̥ḍhabala must
have lived in the 8th or 9th century (Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2, p. 426;
Jaggi, p. 71; Müller, SA 30, 1937, p. 54; Kutumbiah, Introd. p. 29).
Mukhopādhyāya has examined Hoernle's arguments regarding Dr̥ḍha-
bala's date and seems to disagree with him, being of the opinion that
Dr̥ḍhabala preceded Mādhavakara (H.I.M. 3, p. 630-633). I agree with
Mukhopādhyāya that Vijayarakṣita's comment on Mādhavanidāna 22,
14 indicates that Mādhavakara was acquainted with Dr̥ḍhabala's
work. Hoernle's objection (Osteology, Introd. p. 14, footnote 1) that
it was Vijayarakṣita's aim to make an exegetical and not a chronological
statement does not convince me at all. This leads to the important
conclusion that Dr̥ḍhabala must have preceded Mādhavakara.

Another point of value in determining Dr̥ḍhabala's date is the fact,
which was unknown to Hoernle, that Dr̥ḍhabala is quoted by Jejjaṭa
(dated by Hoernle as living in the seventh century at the latest), who
preceded Vr̥ndakunḍa and, in my opinion, was anterior to Gadādhara
and Gayadāsa. The editors of the Gul ed. of Ca. agree with Hoernle
that Vāgbhaṭa, the author of A.h., must have lived after Dr̥ḍhabala,
because prose portions of Ca., redacted by Dr̥ḍhabala, appear in a
closely related versified form in A.h. (Gul 1, p. 100). The same editors
(Gul 1, p. 100) state that Vāgbhaṭa, the author of A.h., cannot have
lived later than the 4th century, because quotations from him are
found in the Kāṇḍarpika chapter of Varāhamihira (Br̥hatsamhitā,
adhyāya 76; ed. and transl. Subrahmanya Śastri, p. 600-602) who
lived in the 5th century and because Bhaṭṭāraharicandra, who flourish-
ed during the reign of king Sāhasāṅka (375-413), was a contemporary
of Vāgbhaṭa. They also hold the opinion that the lack of evidence of
any reference to Dr̥ḍhabala in the Nāvanītaka, composed in the first
part of the 4th century, provides the upper limit to Dr̥ḍhabala's date.
Their conclusion is that Dr̥ḍhabala can be put fairly somewhere between
the end of the third and the beginning of the fourth century. Their
argument regarding Bhaṭṭāraharicandra's date is open to doubt and
it is unknown to me whether A.h. is quoted by Varāhamihira, but
Varāhamihira's date is later, because his son wrote an astrological
treatise dated about 600 (Winternitz 3, p. 571). In my opinion Dr̥ḍha-


=== Page 427 ===
                         APPENDIX TWO                                413

bala’s date may be about 500 or earlier, because he preceded Mā-
dhava, Vāgbhaṭa, Jejjaṭa and Āṣāḍhavarman.

     DHANVANTARINIGHANṬU. This work is acc. to Zachariae (Die indi-
schen Wörterbücher, p. 38) older than the Amarakośa. Gode (St.I.L.H.
1, p. 160) notices that it is quoted in Kṣīrasvāmin’s comm. on the
Amarakośa (Kṣīrasvāmin’s date is acc. to Zachariae, l.c., p. 21 : 11th
century; acc. to Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 15 : second half 11th century).
Acc. to T. Chowdhury (Introd. Paryāyaratnamālā p. 9) the Dhanvan-
tarinighaṇṭu was utilized by Māṅkha (who wrote his Śrīkaṇṭhacarita
between 1135 and 1145 acc. to Winternitz 3, p. 53).
     The work is the oldest medical Nighaṇṭu that has been preserved.
Two recensions of it are known, comprising seven and nine chapters
respectively (Cult. and Hist. of the Ind. P. 4, p. 198). Amara may
have used some older version of the work than that which is extant;
one Ms. is known in which it is stated that the original work of Dhan-
vantari has been revised by someone called Kāśyapa (Hist. and Cult.
of the Ind. P. 4, p. 198, referring to : Devasthali, Descr. Cat. of Skt.
and Prkt. Mss. in the Libr. of the Univ. of Bombay, p. 113, no. 278).

     NĀGABHARṬṬATANTRA. From the quotation in M. on 2, 37-38 it is
clear that this is the name of a medical treatise. It is quoted by Nīścala-
kara as Nāgabhaṛṭṭatantra, Nāgabhaṭṭatantra or Nāgatantra (Bhatt.,
IHQ 23, 1947, p. 143). Nāgabharṭṛ is quoted once by Nāganātha in
his Nidānapradīpa (Jolly, Cat.Skt.Mss. München, nr. 381, p. 54-55).

     NĀGĀRJUṆA. There are many problems about medical works attri-
buted to Nāgārjuna. A long series of works, among which also non-
medical treatises, is ascribed to him (see Cat.Cat. 1, p. 283; 2, p. 61;
3, p. 61). Su.U. is said to have been revised (pratisamṣkṛta) by Nāgār-
juna (Ḍa. mentions a reviser of Su. in his comm. on Sū. 1, 1; Cakra
refers to a reviser in his Bhānumatī, but does not mention his name;
see also Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2, p. 425 and Cordier, Le Muséon, N.S. 4,
1903, p. 332). Gayadāsa quotes Nāgārjuna twice on Su.Nī.; the first
quotation is a variant of a stanza of Su.U. as read by Nāgārjuna, the
second quotation is said to be taken from a treatise called Nāgarjunīya,
which appears to be a work in verse related to Su. There seems to
have been a school of interpreters of Su., who were called nāgārjunīyāḥ
and who adopted particular readings of Su., rejected by others. (See
Cordier, Le Muséon, N.S. 4, 1903, p. 333, about the nāgārjunīyāḥ,


=== Page 428 ===
414                                           APPENDIX TWO

mentioned in Bhaṭṭa Narahari's comm. on A.h., called Vāgbhaṭa-
khaṇḍanamaṇḍana). The tradition that Su. was revised and completed
(by writing its Uttaratantra) by Nāgārjuna is accepted by Filliozat
(Renou et Filliozat, l'Inde Classique 2, p. 157) who says that this
reviser may be identical with the author of the Yogaśataka, which is
usually ascribed to Nāgārjuna. Filliozat is of the opinion that the
Yogaśataka is the medical compendium referred to by I-Tsing (see :
A record of the Buddhist religion, etc. by I-Tsing, transl. Takakusu,
p. 128); I-Tsing stayed in India from 672 to about 688 (Vogel, Introd.
A.h., p. 8); acc. to Filliozat's hypothesis this Nāgārjuna would have
lived in the sixth century. Hoernle (Osteology, Introd. p. 9) still sup-
posed that Nāgārjuna, the reviser of Su., might be the well-known
Buddhist patriarch of that name, who is said to have been a contem-
porary of king Kaniṣka. Another possibility mentioned by Filliozat
(Renou et Filliozat, l'Inde Classique 2, p. 157) is that Nāgārjuna, the
reviser of Su., may be the Nāgārjuna who lived at Daihak near Som-
nāth a hundred years before the age of al-Birūnī (see Sachau's transl.
of al-Bīrūnī 1, p. 189 : this Nāgārjuna was an authority on rasāyana,
i.e. the art of preserving youth and acquiring a long, healthy life); in
this case Nāgārjuna would have lived in the tenth century. The Nāgār-
juna mentioned by Vijayarakṣita as the author of a work called Ā-
rogyamañjarī may be the Nāgārjuna mentioned by al-Bīrūnī, though
this cannot be proved (a work called Ārogyamañjarī, is referred to
in Gopāladāsa's Cikitsāmṛta; see Bhaṭṭ., IHQ 24, 1948, p. 318). In
any case it seems probable that there was more than one author called
Nāgārjuna and that several works were attributed to an author of this
name in later times. Niścalakara often quotes Nāgārjuna (Bhaṭṭ.,
IHQ 23, 1947, p. 143) and mentions two of his works by name : the
Yogamañjarī (Bhaṭṭ., l.c., p. 146) and the Vārtāmālā (Bhaṭṭ., l.c.,
p. 148).
     See about Nāgārjuna : Filliozat, Class. doctr., p. 12-14; Rāy, Hist.
Chem., p. 116-118; Srivastava, Hist. Ind. Pharm., p. 83-90; Mukho-
pādhyāya, H.I.M. 3, p. 822-843.

     NIŚCALAKARA. This author must be treated here on account of the
great importance of his still unedited commentaries, which contain data
throwing light on a great number of points which would have remained
obscure without Niścala's information. Niścalakara wrote commentaries
on Cakrapāṇidatta's Cikitsāsaṁgraha and Dravvaguṇasaṁgraha. The
first comm. is called Ratnaprabhā. It has been studied carefully by


=== Page 429 ===
APPENDIX TWO                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         415

D. C. Bhattacharyya (New light on Vaidyaka literature, IHQ 23, 1947,
p. 123-155). Bhatt. remarks (l.c., p. 125) that Nīścalakara as a com-
mentator forms a class by himself, because he refers almost all his
quotations to their sources. Bhatt. holds the view that Nīścalakara was
of Bengal origin. His father was called Sadānandakara. The Kara
family is mentioned as one of the vaidya families of Bengal in Bharata-
mallika's Candraprabhā (p. 7-9; Bhatt., l.c., p. 129). From several in-
dications it is clear that Nīścala flourished at a time in which Buddhism
was still reigning supreme in Bengal. This would place Nīścala in the
last quarter of the 12th century at the latest. Moreover, Nīścala has
recorded an important clue to his date. He describes an audience given
by king Rāmāpāla to the king of Kāmarūpa. The panegyric epithets
in this description indicate that this king, who had a long reign of at
least 42 years, was still alive when Nīścala wrote his comm. Bhatt.
fixes Rāmāpāla's reign at 1078-1120 (Bhatt. is criticized by Majumdar:
History of Bengal I, p. 180-181) and is of the opinion that Nīścalakara's
Ratnaprabhā was written in the decade 1110-1120. Nīścalakara him-
self remarks that he wrote the Ratnaprabhā after the death of his
teacher, Vijayarakṣita, who was in charge of the royal hospital (āro-
gyaśālā); Nīścala was in charge of the royal harem.

Nīścala's date enables us to fix the dates of many authors and works
more accurately than before Bhattacharyya's study of the Ratna-
prabhā. This applies particularly to the dates of Nīścala's teacher,
Vijayarakṣita, and another pupil of the latter, Śrīkaṇṭhadatta.

PARĀŚARA was one of the six disciples of Ātreya Punarvasu. He
wrote his own treatise on kāyacikitsā (Ca.Sū. 1, 30-33). Jolly says
(Medicin, p. 125) that acc. to Cordier (in : Origines, évolution et déca-
dence de la médecine indienne, in : Annales d'hygiène et de médecine
coloniales, 1901, p. 82 and 84) fragments of Parāśara's work have been
found in Nepal. Parāśara's treatise is referred to and quoted by Vāg-
bhaṭa (A.s. Sū. 17, 19-20) and by many commentators. A short text,
called Takravidhi (Ms. coll. Cordier, Paris; see: Filliozat, JA, t. 224,
1934, p. 158, nr. 48) and a Takrakalpa (the same text as the Takra-
vidhi?, Ms. Bikaner nr. 1438), are ascribed to Parāśara. An important
text, called Vṛkṣāyurveda, is also attributed to Parāśara (see G. P.
Majumdar, Arch. int. d'hist. des sciences 4, 1951, p. 104-112), as well
as a text on husbandry, called Kṛṣipaddhati (Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, nr.
1274; Aufrecht's Cat.Skt.Mss. Cambridge, nr. R.15.87).


=== Page 430 ===
416                                           APPENDIX TWO

PĀLAKĀPYA. To this author is ascribed the Hastyāyurveda (ed. Ānan-
dāśrama Sanskrit Series, nr. 26, Poona, 1894). Haraprasād Śāstri has
tried to assign a very early date to the work of Pālākāpya : 5th or 6th
century B.C. (JBORS 5, 1919, p. 307-313). The work is quoted in
Kṣīrasvāmin's comm. on the Amarakosa; so it cannot be later than
the 11th century (see S. K. De's article about Pālākāpya in the D.R.
Bhandarkar Volume, publ. by the Indian Research Institute, Calcutta,
1940, p. 73-75); an analysis of the contents of Pālākāpya's treatise has
been given by Mukhopādhyāya, H.I.M. 2, p. 402-423.

PAUṢKALĀVATA was one of the six disciples of Dhanvantari ; each of
them wrote a surgical treatise (Su.Sū. 1, 3). Jolly (Medicin, p. 125)
states that acc. to Cordier (Origines, évolution et décadence de la
médecine indienne, in : Annales d'hygiène et de médecine coloniales,
1901, p. 82 and 84) fragments of his treatise have been discovered.

BAKULA or Bakulakara is probably identical with Vakulakara, one
of the chief authorities of Nīścalakara and profusely quoted in the
latter's Ratnaprabhā. Nīścala devotes a flowery panegyric to Vakula-
kara, which should prove (acc. to Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 147) that
Vakula was a close connection of Nīścala and may have been the uncle
of the latter once referred to in the Ratnaprabhā. Vakula's work was
called Sāroccaya (Bhatt., l.c., p. 149). He was later than (Bhatt., l.c.,
p. 147) or more or less a contemporary of Cakrapāṇidatta, and a Bengali
(Bhatt., l.c., p. 155). Vakula is mentioned as a commentator on Ca.
by Mukhopādhyāya (H.I.M. 3, p. 615) and in the Introd. to Ca. with
Jejjata's comm. (p. 22). Vijayarakṣita refers to him in M. on 6, 15 as
an author who does not agree with Kārtikakuṇḍa's interpretation of a
passage from Su.U. which indicates that he was a commentator on
Su. and that his date is after that of Kārtikakuṇḍa. A long passage
from a work in verse by Bakula is quoted by Śrīkaṇṭhadatta on Siddha-
yoga 20, 24-27 and said to be inspired by Jejjata's comments.

BRAHMADEVA is mentioned as a ṭippaṇakāra (writer of glosses) on
Su. by Da. in the introd. to his comm. He is repeatedly quoted in the
Kusumāvalī and by Da. and once by Hemādri (on A.h.Sū. 7, 40,
about maireya). The quotations have been collected and studied by
Gode (St.I.L.H. 1, p. 191-194), who assigns him to the period between
900 and 1100. Hoernle supposed that Brahmadeva might be posterior
to Gayadāsa, because Da. observes in his comment on Su.Sū. 18, 45


=== Page 431 ===
APPENDIX TWO 417
that Brahmadeva follows Gayadāśa's opinion, who says that the stanza
should be rejected as not belonging to the text of Su. Hoernle may
well be right on this point. It has not been stressed, as far as I know,
that Brahmadeva is mentioned by Cakra (on Ca.Ci. 3, 217) as an early
commentator on Ca. (he is the last one of the series of early commen-
tators on Ca. enumerated by Cakra : Bhāsadatta-Svāmidāsa-Āṣāḍha-
varman-Brahmadeva). His date must at least be earlier than that of
Cakrapāṇidatta. To Gode it was a problem that the quotations from
Brahmadeva's comm. on the Siddhayoga as occurring in the Kusu-
māvalī might not form part of the original version of Śrīkanṭhadatta's
work, but could have been added later by Nārāyaṇa Bhiṣaj, the reviser
of the Kusumāvalī. For that reason he had to date Brahmadeva be-
tween 900 and 1100. If all the references to Brahmadeva as a commen-
tator on Ca., Su. and the Siddhayoga apply to one and the same per-
son, his date should be between those of Vṛndakuṇḍa and Cakra-
pāṇidatta.

BHĀLUKI is said to have written a treatise on surgery (śalyatantra)
(Gul 1, p. 145). He is already quoted by Jejjaṭa, but his work has not
survived. Quotations from it are frequent in the works of many com-
mentators. In Śrīkanṭhadatta's time his work must still have been
available, for Śrīkanṭha informs us (on Siddhayoga 1, 151) that a
particular recipe is to be found in the Siddhiṣṭhāna of the Bhāluki-
tantra.

BHĀVAMIŚRA is the author of the Bhāvaprakāśa, of which the Bhāva-
prakāśanighaṇṭu forms an integral part. Bhāvamiśra was the son of
Miśralāṭakana, as indicated in the colophons of the work. Jolly ob-
serves (Medicin, p. 2-3) that Bhāvamiśra is said to have been a famous
physician in Benares. He also notes (ibid.) that a good Ms. of the
Bhāvaprakāśa is present in Tübingen and dated 1558-1559 (he refers to
Garbe's Verz. no. 153). In his opinion the work cannot be much older
than this Ms., because syphilis (phiraṅgaroga) and the drug used to
treat it (cobacinī) are made mention of in the Bhāvaprakāśa and both
disease and drug were imported into India by the Portuguese about
1535. Later authors agree with Jolly as to the date of the work. An-
other treatise by Bhāvamiśra, dealing with materia medica, is called
Guṇaratnamālā (Jolly, Medicin, p. 3; Eggeling, Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, p.
981; Filliozat, JA, t. 224, 1934, p. 157, nr. 32). Cordier mentions (Le
Muséon, N.S. 4, 1903, p. 350) a Mādhavanidānaṭippaṇi by Bhāvamiśra.

BHEDA- OR BHELASAṂHITĀ. This old text has fragmentarily been pre-
served in a single Ms. described by Burnell in : A classified index to
the Skt. Mss. in the Palace at Tanjore, p. 63, nr. 2 (10,773). The text
of this Ms. is mutilated and contains many scribe's errors (it has been
edited twice in an unsatisfactory way). A fragment of the Bheḍa-
saṁhitā was found in Tuyoq in East-Turkestan by von Le Coq ; it has
been studied by Lüders (Medizinische Saṅskrittexte aus Turkistan, in :
Aus Indiens Kultur, Festschrift für R. Garbe, 1927, p. 148-162 = H.
Lüders, Philologica indica, Göttingen 1940, p. 579). The fragment of
this paper Ms. dates probably from the 9th century. A second fragment
from a different Ms., found at the same place, may or may not belong
to the Bheḍasaṁhitā (Lüders, l.c.). The Bheḍasaṁhitā is in many
respects similar to Ca., though much more concise. There are, how-
ever, also so many dissimilarities that it is clear that Bheḍa represents
a separate branch of the school of Ātreya, to which both Ca. and
Bheḍa belong (see Filliozat in Renou et Filliozat, l'Inde Classique 2,
p. 151). Filliozat (ibid.) is of the opinion that the Bheḍasaṁhitā may
be older than Ca. Barua (IC 3, p. 190-194) dates it in the early Buddhist
period. Burnell was of the opinion that Bheḍa was a native of Gandhāra
because that country is repeatedly mentioned in the treatise (Mukho-
pādhyāya, H.I.M. 3, p. 528). Many quotations from Bheḍa have been
collected by Mukhopādhyāya (l.c., p. 529-534).

BHOJA. There is much confusion about the identity of one or more
medical authors called Bhoja, Bhojadeva or Bhojarāja. Medical com-
mentators distinguish between Bhoja and Vṛddhabhoja (e.g. Ḍa.). A
series of medical works is ascribed to Bhoja : Āyurvedasarvasva,
Cārucaryā, Rājamārtaṇḍa, Rājamṛgāṅka and Viśrāntavidyāvinoda
(Cat.Cat. 1, p. 41 and 2, p. 95; Cordier, JA, t. 28, 1901, p. 180). Bāpālāl
G. Vaidya mentions a Bhojarājanighaṇṭu (Introd. Nighaṇṭu Ādarśa 1,
p. 37). Filliozat says (in : Renou et Filliozat, l'Inde Classique 2, p. 159)
that Bhoja was a commentator on Su. Hoernle had already noticed
(JRAS, 1906, p. 286) that Bhoja is frequently quoted by Ḍa., by
Gayadāsa and by Cakrapāṇidatta in his Bhānumati in connection with
Su.'s views, and that his work does not appear to have been a comm.
on Su., but rather an independent textbook, for Ḍa. once describes it
as a *saṁhitā* and Gayadāsa once as a *tantra*. Acc. to Hoernle he may
well have been the famous king Bhoja of Dhārā (1018-1063 acc. to
Kṛṣṇamachariar). Cordier (JA, t. 28, 1901, p. 180) thought it not
improbable that at the court of this king medical works were composed


=== Page 433 ===
APPENDIX TWO
419

which appeared under his name. Jolly (ZDMG 58, 1904, p. 116) cau-
tiously remarked that the medical author Bhoja might well be different
from the famous king of that name, because a renowned physician,
called Bhoja, already appears in Buddhist texts. Bhatt. (IHQ 23, 1947,
p. 145-146) writes that it has hitherto been overlooked by all scholars
that there were three medical authorities of the name of Bhoja : 1) an
ancient *ācārya*, pupil of Divodāsa and a class-fellow of Suśruta (refer-
red to and quoted in Cakra's *Bhānumatī* and by Ḍa.); he is sometimes
referred to as Vṛddhabhoja (e.g. in Candraṭa's comm. on the *Cikitsā-
kalikā*, Lahore ed., p. 200); 2) an earlier king Bhoja, cited already by
Jejjaṭa and quoted by Candraṭa; this cannot be Bhoja of Dhārā, be-
cause Candraṭa preceded Bhoja of Dhārā; acc. to Bhatt. this king
Bhoja is evidently identical with the Paramāra king Bhoja of Citor
who reigned in 665; 3) Bhoja, the author of the *Rājamārtaṇḍa*. See
also about kings called Bhoja and works attributed to authors called
Bhoja : Introd. by E. D. Kulkarni to Śālihotra of Bhoja, p. 17-20.
    I feel unable to disentangle the problems about Bhoja. From the
quotations in M. it seems probable that he wrote a treatise that was,
at least in part, composed in verse.

MADANAPĀLANIGHANṬU, also called Madanavinodanighanṭu or short-
ly Madanavimoda, is a work attributed to Madanapāla, a king to whom
many works are ascribed (see Cat. Cat. 1, p. 425). The work was com-
posed in 1374, as indicated at the end of some of the Mss. (see R. Roth,
Madanapāla, in : Indische Studien 14, 1876, p. 398-401; Eggeling,
Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, p. 977-979). It is also recorded in some Mss. that
Madanapāla ruled at Kāṣṭhā (sometimes written Kāṭhā), a town
situated on the Yamunā to the north of Delhi (see Roth and Eggeling
about the details and the genealogy of this king). Not only in the time
of Roth, but also at the present time, this king Madanapāla is confused
with an earlier namesake of his (see e.g. Krishnamachariar, p. 849 :
“The inscriptions of this king are dated 1104-1109”).

YOGATARAṄGIŅĪ. This work is a compilation of which two versions
exist : the Bṛhad- and Laghuyogatarangiṇī. It was written by Trimalla-
bhaṭṭa, as stated in the introductory stanzas of the work. The author
was a son of Vallabha, grandson of Siṅgaṇa Bhaṭṭa, a Telugu brāhmaṇa
residing at Benares, and brother of Rāma and Gopa (Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5,
p. 956). Sinh Jee (A short history of Aryan medical science, second ed.,
London, 1927, p. 215) was of the opinion that the work had been


=== Page 434 ===
420                                         APPENDIX TWO

written in 1751. Jolly (Medicin, p. 2-3) remarks that the work must
be much older, because one Ms. dates from 1663 at the latest and there
exists a Ms., dated 1498, of another work by Trimallabhaṭṭa. Gode
(St.I.L.H. 1, p. 295) quotes H. D. Velankar (Cat. of BBRAS Mss. 1,
p. 59) on the subject of Trimallabhaṭṭa's date : "Trimalla quotes the
Vīrasimhāvaloka (written in 1383) in his Yogatarangiṇī and a Ms. of
his Dravyaguṇaśataślokī is dated 1499; Trimalla's date, therefore, falls
between 1383 and 1499."

YOGARATNĀKARA. The author of this medical compilation is un-
known; Sinh Jee (A short history of Aryan medical science, second ed.,
London, 1927, p. 215) says, however, that it is a work by Nayanase-
khara, a Jain priest, who wrote it in 1633. The oldest known Ms. dates
from 1746 (Jolly, Medicin, p. 2). The Yogaratnākara quotes a work
called Nirṇayasindhu, composed in 1611 (Jolly, ibid.) or 1612 (Gode,
Bhāratīya Vidyā 4, 1943, p. 154-156) by Kamalākarabhaṭṭa. The date
of composition of the Yogaratnākara must therefore lie somewhere
between 1611 and 1746. Gode (l.c.) was of the opinion that the work
was written between about 1650 and 1725, because it contains some
stanzas on the properties of tobacco, which, acc. to him, was first
seen in India at the Bījāpūr court about 1605; the incorporation of
tobacco in an Indian medical treatise must in Gode's opinion have
required about forty years; moreover, the proposed date is in harmony
with the fact that the Yogaratnākara refers to the works called Vaidya-
jīvana and Vaidyavilāsa, written by Lolimbarāja, who flourished to-
wards the end of the 16th century (Gode, l.c.; see also Gode's article :
Lolimbarāja and his works, St.I.L.H. 2, p. 79-96). Katre (Bhāratīya
Vidyā 12, 1951, p. 59-61) has proved, however, that the Vaidyavilāsa,
quoted in the Yogaratnākara, is not a work by Lolimbarāja but by
Raghunātha Paṇḍita and was composed in 1697. The conclusion is
therefore that the Yogaratnākara was written between 1697 and 1746.
A problem with the Yogaratnākara is that there are more works
bearing the same title. Niścalakara quotes from the Yogaratnākara by
Bhavyadatta, who is one of Niścala's chief authorities (Bhatt., IHQ
23, 1947, p. 146 and 148).

RAGHUNĀTHA SŪRI was the author of the Bhojanakutūhala, a treatise
about dietetics. He also wrote works of a non-medical nature. He lived
in the 17th century, was a friend of Rāmdās and enjoyed the patronage
of queen Dīpā Bāī, the wife of Ekoji Bhosala of Tanjore. See about


=== Page 435 ===
APPENDIX TWO 421

Raghunātha and his works : Introd. to Bhojanakutūhala, vol. 1, by
Mahādeva Śāstrī; Gode wrote several articles about this author and
his Bhojanakutūhala : St.I.L.H. 2, p. 380-390, 391-403, 404-415 and
425-434. The Bhojanakutūhala was composed between 1650 and 1685
acc. to Gode (St.I.L.H. 2, p. 425-434).

RĀJANIGHANṬU, also called Nighanṭurāja and Abhidhānacūḍāmaṇi,
is a work by Narahari, also called Narahara, Nṛhari and Narasimha
(Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, p. 977), pupil of Śrīkaṇṭha and son of Īsvarasūri,
an inhabitant of Kaśmīr. In the introduction to his work the author
states that he has consulted the Dhanvantarīyanighanṭu, Madanani-
ghanṭu, Halāyudha and various other works, but that he follows the
opinions of the Dhanvantarīyanighanṭu (see Cat.Skt.Mss. Madras, vol.
23, nr. 13254, p. 8928-8930 and Cat. Calc. Skt. Coll., nr. 69 and 70). It
is clear that the work is later than the Madanapālanighanṭu, dated
1374; this fact was already known to Aufrecht (ZDMG 41, 1887, p.
487-488). Acc. to Filliozat (Renou et Filliozat, l'Inde Classique 2, p.
162) it dates from the 14th century; Gode (St.I.L.H. 1, p. 388) dates it :
about 1450. Acc. to Garbe (Die indischen Mineralien, pref. p. 6),
Keith (Hist. Skt. Lit., p. 512) and Dutt Sharma (Cat.Skt.Mss. BORI,
vol. 16, part 1, p. 291) the work was composed about 1235-1250, which
cannot be correct. Garbe's argument for this date was that the author
refers to his patron, called Nṛsiṃha; Garbe identified this Nṛsiṃha
with king Siṃhadeva of Kaśmīr who reigned from 1235-1250. T.
Chowdhury (Introd. Paryāyaratnamālā) assumes that the work was
written about 1400, which may be correct.

RĀJAVALLABHANIGHANṬU, also called Rājāvallabhadravvyaguṇa. This
work has been ascribed, erroneously, to an author called Nārāyaṇa or
Nārāyaṇadāsa (Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, p. 961-962; Jolly, Medicin, p. 2;
Cat.Cat. 1, p. 263). It is really a work written by Rājavallabha, an
author of unknown date, and has been revised by Nārāyaṇadāsa, who
lived about 1760 (acc. to Umeśacandra Gupta, Vaidyakaśabdasiṇdhu,
Preface). The fact that the work has been revised by Nārāyaṇadāsa is
clearly indicated in the introduction and colophon of some Mss. (see
Cat.Skt.Mss.Calc. Skt. Coll. 9, nr. 67, p. 56 ff.). There are considerable
differences among the various Mss. and editions of the work (see the
descr. of the enlarged version in the Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, nr. 2718, p.
962 and of Ms. no. 24 of the coll. Jones of IO). Acc. to Bāpālāl G.


=== Page 436 ===
422                                                         APPENDIX TWO

Vaidya (Introd. Nighaṇṭu Ādarśa 1, p. 37) internal evidence leads to
the conclusion that the author hailed from Bengal.

VAṄGASENA is the author of a medical treatise called Cikitsāsāra-
saṁgraha, sometimes called Cikitsāmāharṇava or Cikitsātattvasam-
graha (Cat.Skt.Mss. BORI, vol. 16, part 1, nr. 82, p. 99-100). This
work is often quoted as Vaṅgasena, Vaṅgasenasaṁgraha or Vaṅgadatta.
Aufrecht (Cat.Cat. 2, p. 130) considers the Cikitsāmāharṇava by Vaṅ-
gasena as distinct from the Cikitsāsārasaṁgraha. Vaṅgasena describes
the diseases (and their therapy) in the order introduced by Mādhavava-
kara and must have lived after the latter, as has already often been
noticed (Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, p. 951; Jolly, Medicin, p. 5). Vaṅgasena
adheres to Mādhavakara's arrangement of diseases even more closely
than Vr̥ndakuṇḍa. Jolly was of the opinion (Medicin, p. 5) that variants
found in Vaṅgasena's text are sometimes better than Mādhavakara's
readings. Vaṅgasena was the son of Gadādhara, who had moved from
Kāñjikā to another place of residence that is not specified (Va. 1, 4).
This Gadādhara is considered by some to be identical with Gadādhara,
the commentator on Su. (N.N. Das Gupta, IC 3, p. 159 : not impro-
bable; refuted by Bhaṭṭ., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 140; see : Gadādhara).
N. N. Das Gupta says (IC 3, p. 159), without adducing data supporting
his statement, that the original place of residence of Vaṅgasena's
parents, Kāñjikā, may be the same as Kāñjivilli in Rāḍha (Western
Bengal). Jolly supposed already (Medicin, p. 5), like N. N. Das Gupta
later, that Vaṅgasena might hail from Bengal (on account of his name,
acc. to Jolly; on account of his name, original place of residence and
from internal evidence, acc. to N. N. Das Gupta).

Vaṅgasena's Cikitsāsārasaṁgraha is, as indicated at the end of the
treatise (Ed. Veṅkaṭeśvar Press, p. 1100), a revision of what was called
before Vaṅgasena's birth the Agastisaṁhitā (an author called Agastya
is quoted by Cakra on Ca.Sū. 1, 62-63ab; more than 200 medical works
in Tamil are attributed to Agastya : see Renou et Filliozat, l'Inde
Classique 2, p. 162-163). A comm. on Vaṅgasena's work, written by
Vaidyanātha, is mentioned by Aufrecht (Cat.Cat. 1, p. 548).

The date of Vaṅgasena has been studied by Jolly (Medicin, p. 5 :
he may have been a contemporary of the Sena dynasty of Bengal);
N. N. Das Gupta (IC 3, p. 159) : 13th century; Gode (St.I.L.H. 1, p.
325) : 12th century at the latest. Bhaṭṭ. discovered (IHQ 23, 1947, p.
147) that Nīścalākara quotes the Vaṅgasenasaṁgraha. So his date must
fall between those of Vr̥ndakuṇḍa and Nīścalākara. A Ms. of Vaṅ-


=== Page 437 ===
APPENDIX TWO 423

gasena's work, dated 1276, is in the Cambridge University Library
(see Cat.Skt.Mss. IO 5, p. 952) and a Ms. dated 1320 in the BOR
Institute (Cat.Skt.Mss. BORI, vol. 16, part 1, nr. 78, p. 94-95).

VĀGBHAṬA. Three works are ascribed to Vāgbhaṭa : the Aṣṭāṅ-
gahṛdayasamhitā, the Aṣṭāṅgasaṁgraha and the Rasaratnasamuccaya.
The last work of these three is certainly not by the same author as
the other two works (see Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 1, and Cordier, JA
t. 18, 1901, p. 148-150; Bhatt. has traced a quotation from Rasavāg-
bhaṭa in Candrāṭa's Yogaratnasamuccaya, see ABORI 28, 1947, p.
122).

It has long been a problem whether both other works have been
written by one author. Commentators often refer to the author of A.h.
as Vāgbhaṭa and to the author of A.s. as Vṛddhavāgbhaṭa, which led
to the assumption that A.s. is older than A.h. The questions whether
there have been one or two Vāgbhaṭa's and which of the two works is
older have often been discussed. The date to be assigned to the com-
position of the texts has also been a favourite topic in articles and
books on the history of Indian medicine. The discussions on these pro-
blems have recently been reviewed and summarized by C. Vogel (In-
trod. A.h., p. 1-10) and there is no need to repeat his work. His con-
clusion is in agreement with that reached by Hilgenberg and Kirfel
in the introduction to their translation of A.h. into German : A.h. is
older than A.s. and the process by which A.h. has been transformed
into A.s. must have been a gradual one. This last point is confirmed
by Bhatt.'s study of Niścalakara's Ratnaprabhā (ABORI 28, 1947, p.
112-127; IHQ 23, 1947, p. 123-155). Niścalakara frequently quotes
from a work called Madhyavāgbhaṭa, the text of which is intermediate
between A.h. and A.s., but not all the quotations from it can be
traced either to A.h. or to A.s. Bhatt. says (ABORI 28, 1947, p. 113)
that the existence of this Madhyavāgbhaṭa became known to scholars
for the first time with the publication of Śivadāsasena's comm. on
A.h., called Tattvabodha; Śivadāsasena quotes from Madhyavāgbhaṭa
as well as from Vṛddhavāgbhaṭa (identical with A.s. acc. to Śivadā-
sasena) and Svalpavāgbhaṭa (identical with A.h. acc. to Śivadāsasena;
Bhatt., ABORI 28, 1947, p. 113). It was unknown to Bhatt., as rightly
stressed by Vogel (Introd. A.h., p. 5, footnote 3), that Cordier already
knew about the existence of a text intermediate between A.s. and
A.h. (JA, t. 18, 1901, p. 150-151; this text has been partially published
as Bābhaṭa in Calcutta in 1873). Both Cordier and Bhatt. regarded the


=== Page 438 ===
424                                                               APPENDIX TWO

existence of the Madhyavāgbhața as a proof that A.h. had gradually
grown out of A.s.

    About Vāgbhața's life we only know what he has said himself (A.s.U.
50, 132-133) : he was a son of Simhagupta (in some Mss. : Sañghagupta),
who was a physician, and a grandson of Vāgbhața; his teacher was
called Avalokita and he was born in Sindh. If Vāgbhața, the author
of A.h., is identical with the teacher of Jejjața, something more may
be said about his birthplace. In two colophons of the fragments of
Jejjața's comm. on Ca. (not his comm. on Su., as erroneously stated
by Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 8, footnote 2) Jejjața calls his teacher Vāhața
(Vāgbhața's name is always spelled in this way by Jejjața and by
Indu) Mahājahņupati. Bhatt. observes (ABORI 28, 1947, p. 122) about
this appellation that it indicates that Vāgbhața was the chief of a
small kingdom in Sindh, which may be identical with Majhanda in the
Karachi district, about 50 miles north of Hyderabad in Sindh (see
Bhatt., l.c., and Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 8, footnote 2).

    About Vāgbhața's date much has been written. When we assume
that there has been only one Vāgbhața, the author of A.h., the problem
is not too complicated. Many scholars have connected Vāgbhața with
a person about whom I-Tsing (a Chinese pilgrim who stayed in India
from 672 to about 682) states that he lately summarized the eight
sections of medical science and made them into one bundle (see Vogel,
Introd. A.h., p. 8-9 and his references to the literature on the subject;
see also J. Nobel, JAOS, suppl. nr. 11, 1951, about I-Tsing's medical
knowledge). I think Vogel is right in adopting the view that the person
alluded to by I-Tsing must be Vāgbhața, which implicates me in dis-
agreement with Filliozat, who is of the opinion that I-Tsing most pro-
bably refers to Nāgārjuna, the author of the Yogāśataka. I-Tsing
enables us to determine the date of composition of Vāgbhața's A.h.
at about 600.

    There are some other points worthy of consideration with regard to
Vāgbhața's date. Filliozat observes (in : Renou et Filliozat, l'Inde
Classique 2, p. 158) that A.h. reproduces stanzas from the Yogāśataka.
Fragments of a Ms. of the Yogāśataka have been found in Central
Asia; the date of this Ms. has been fixed as the 7th century or some-
what later (Filliozat, l.c., p. 157). This implies that the text of the
Yogāśataka must be older; it may date from the period between 500
and 600 or earlier; so Vāgbhața may quote from it. Another point is
that the A.h., as to the arrangement of its sections, follows Su. as a
model; A.h. contains an Uttarastāna, as Su. has its Uttaratantra;


=== Page 439 ===
                                                        425
                               APPENDIX TWO

      moréover, there are so many similarities between the contents
and A.h.U. that A.h.U. must be later than Su.U. (Filliozat, l.c., p. 158;
Hoernle, Osteology, Introd. p. 14). A third point is that Vāgbhaṭa
must be later than Dr̥ḍhabala (Hoernle, Osteology, Introd. p. 14-15;
Hoernle, JRAS 1908, p. 1016-1018). Some stanzas of A.h. are taken
from that part of Ca. which has been redacted by Dr̥ḍhabala (see e.g.
Aruṇadatta's comment on A.h.Śā. 3, 62cd-63ab). In my opinion Dr̥ḍha-
bala's date is about 500 or earlier, so Vāgbhaṭa may indeed have
borrowed from him. A fourth point is that Mādhavakara has borrowed
from A.h.; Mādhavakakara has to be dated about 700, which again leads
to the conclusion that the date of composition of A.h. may be about
600. This date is further corroborated by the date of translation of a
lost medical Sanskrit work into Tibetan; this work, usually called
rGyud bźi in Tibetan, sometimes agrees rather closely with A.h. and
was translated during the reign of the Tibetan king Khri-sroṇ-ldehu-
btsan (755-797 acc. to Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 16, footnote 1; 728-786
acc. to Filliozat in L'Inde Classique 2, p. 158). With regard to to the date
of Vāgbhaṭa, it is of great importance that the A.h. is mentioned by
'Ali b. Sahl Rabban al-Ṭabari, a Persian physician who wrote a
medical treatise, called Firdaws al-ḥikma (Paradise of wisdom) in 849-
850 (A.h. is written aṣṭāṇhṛdy; see Siggel: Die indischen Bücher aus
dem Paradies der Weisheit; Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 10 and footnote 1
on p. 10 with references). The fact that the A.h. was so famous in Persia
at that time warrants the assumption that it had been written long
before 'Ali b. Sahl. All the available evidence points to about 600 as
the probable date of composition of the A.h.
      The A.s. must have evolved gradually after the A.h. had been written.
It is not known at what date the A.s. was completed. The only thing
which can be said with certainty is that the A.s. was complete in
Indu's time.

      VĀPYACANDRA, whose name is also written Bāspacandra, was a fa-
mous commentator on Ca., quoted by Vijayarakṣita, Śrīkaṇṭhadatta,
Niścalakara and Hemādri.
      From the quotations in M. it is clear that he commented on Ca. He
may also have written a comm. on Su.; M. on 1, 5d-6 points in that
direction; moreover, he is mentioned there in a series of names of
commentators on Su. : Jejjaṭa-Vāpyacandra-Mādhavakara-Kārtika-
kuṇḍa. The latter series, particularly on account of Mādhavakara's
position in it, may be in chronological order as well as the series of


=== Page 440 ===
426
APPENDIX TWO

authors of a comm. on Su., enumerated in M. on 1, 11-13 : Jejjata-
Gadādhara-Vāpyacandra. There are no data contradicting the sup-
position of an enumeration in chronological order. If this hypothesis
is correct, Vāpyacandra must have preceded Mādhavakara and have
lived after Jejjata and Gadādhara. It may be that this assumption is
confirmed by the list of authors mentioned by Vijayarakṣita in the
introduction to the Madhukośa; the first six names are probably ar-
ranged in the correct chronological order : Bhaṭṭāra(haricandra)-
Jejjata-Gadādhara-Vāpyacandra-Cakrapāṇi-Bakula. This argument is
weakened, however, by the series of authors which follows in the same
introduction; among these Īśvarasena is put after Cakrapāṇi and Ba-
kula, though he preceded Cakra (see : Īśvarasena). The order may have
been influenced by the metre of the stanza (vasantatilakā), or a second
list begins with Īśvarasena.

VIDEHA is the same as Nimi or Nemi, the lord of Videha (Videha is
Tirhut in the eastern part of Bihar : Hoernle, Osteology, Introd. p.
8; Müller, JRAS, 1933, p. 323). The lord of Videha is credited with a
śālākyatantra (on eye diseases and diseases of the ears, nose and mouth)
in Su. (U. 1, 5) and identified as Nimi by Da. (who says that the pas-
sage does not refer to other authors of a śālākyatantra, such as Karāla
and Bhadraśaunaka); Da. remarks that some identify the lord of
Videha as the famous king Janaka of Videha, but that this is refuted
by the author of the Brhatpañjikā (probably Gayadāsa) and that he
refutes it too on the authority of the latter. Nimi, the king of Videha,
is also mentioned in Ca.Sū. 26, 5; A.h. mentions Nimi : U. 11, 27;
U. 13, 16; U. 13, 100 and U. 30, 31. Quotations from Nimi, Videha and
Mahāvideha were collected by Mukhopādhyāya (H.I.M. 2, p. 339-350;
the quotations are drawn from Madhukośa, Kusumāvali, Nibandha-
samgraha, Tattvacandrikā and Bhāvaprakāśa; Videha is moreover
quoted by Cakra on Ca., Gayadāsa on Su.Ni., Niścalakara and Hemādri;
Vrddhavideha is quoted once by Niścalakara; Nimi is quoted by
Aruṇadatta). Vijayarakṣita's quotations from Videha seem to indicate
that his work did not deal with eye diseases only, but was of a broader
scope.

VRNDAKUNDA wrote the Siddhayoga, a treatise on therapy, also
called Vrndamādhava. The author calls himself Vrnda and his work
Siddhayoga. Śrīkaṇṭhadatta calls the author Vrnda in the colophons,
but in the introd. to the comm. Vrndakuntha (Ānandāśrama ed.). The


=== Page 441 ===
APPENDIX TWO 427

treatise is called Vṛndamādhava and Siddhayoga in the colophons of
the comm. The work follows the Rugviniścaya (by Mādhavakara) in
its arrangement as stated by Vṛnda himself (1, 2), though he devotes
a separate chapter to *jvarātisāra* (fever-diarrhoea), which is omitted
by Mādhavakara. Hoernle was of the opinion that Mādhavakara was
the author of the Siddhayoga and that it was clear that the Rugvi-
niścaya was only the first part of a larger work, the second of which
is the Siddhayoga (JRAS, 1906, p. 288-290). Hoernle was wrong. It is
known to us now that Mādhavakara wrote a therapeutic treatise, the
Mādhavacikitsita, which is different from the Siddhayoga by which it was
superseded, as the latter was by Cakrapāṇidatta’s treatise. Cakrapāṇi-
datta’s Cikitsāsaṁgraha was modelled upon the Siddhayoga. The model
of the Siddhayoga may have been the Mādhavacikitsita, but the Mādha-
vacikitsita has not yet been sufficiently studied to be certain about
this point. Vṛndakuṇḍa (more often called Vṛnda) is frequently quoted
by Niścalākara (Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 148).

The Siddhayoga must still have been a very popular work in Cakra-
pāṇidatta’s time as appears from a stanza at the end of the Cikitsā-
saṁgraha (*susthādihikāra* 16), but I do not see that it proves that Vṛnda
belonged to Bengal as Bhatt. states (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 154). Another
piece of evidence, however, clearly indicates that Vṛndakuṇḍa was an
inhabitant of Eastern Bengal : Bhatt. (IHQ 23, 1947, p. 155) quotes a
stanza from Bharatamallika's Candrapraphā in which it is said that
Vṛndakuṇḍa, who wrote a medical treatise, was a resident of Eastern
Bengal (*vaṅgabhūmikṛtāśraya*). Regarding Vṛnda’s date Jolly remarked
(Medicin, p. 7) that the Siddhayoga must have been written at least a
century before Cakrapāṇidatta, because it had probably become an
authoritative work in Cakra’s time ; he added that Vṛnda is later than
Vāgbhaṭa (quoted Siddhayoga 1, 27) and Mādhava (because the Rugvi-
niścaya is mentioned). Hoernle assigned to Vṛnda the same date as
that of Mādhava (7th or 8th century) because he thought that both
authors were identical (Osteology, Introd. p. 16). Acc. to Bhatt. (IHQ
23, 1947, p. 153; ABORI 28, 1947, p. 125) the date to be assigned to
Vṛndakuṇḍa is 975-1000. In my opinion this date must be lowered to
about 800-900, because Bhatt.’s date of Mādhava is wrong (see : In-
trod., Mādhavakara); moreover there is the fact that Brahmadeva, refer-
red to as an early commentator by Cakra, wrote a comm. on the Siddha-
yoga, which makes it probable that the gap between Vṛndakuṇḍa and
Cakrapāṇidatta is wider than assumed by Bhatt. Acc. to M. Z. Siddiqi
(Indo-Asian Culture 5, 1957, p. 279) the Siddhayoga is mentioned by


=== Page 442 ===
428                                   APPENDIX TWO

the Arabian historian (Ibn Wāḍih) al Ya‘qūbi, who lived in the second
half of the 9th century (Nicholson, p. 349), but this is doubtful in my
opinion because Ya‘qūbi writes about an Indian medical treatise called
Sindhshan (Siddiqi’s transcription), which should literally mean ‘purity
of success’ or ‘elixir of success’ (ṣafw al-nujh, transcribed by Siddiqi
as safwun najh; Ullmann, p. 105 : ṣafwat an-nuġh); Sindhshan may
be a reflection of the Sanskrit term Siddhisthāna, but if ṣafwat an-
nuġh may mean ‘elixir of success’ it is possible that Ya‘qūbi indeed
refers to the Siddhayoġa and that its date of composition should be
fixed at about 800. (See about the work called sindh(i)shān by Arab
authors : Dietz, p. 118; Stenzler, ZDMG 11, 1857, p. 327; Ullmann,
Die Medizin im Islam, p. 105).

VOPADEVA was a contemporary and protégé of Hemādri and a paṇḍit
to Mahādeva, a king of the Yādava dynasty of Devagiri. He was a
pupil of Dhaneśa and a son of Keśava, the author of the medical work
called Siddhamantra. Vopadeva was a prolific author; his medical
works are the following : 1) Śataślokī, with the autocomm. Śataślokī-
candrakalā, 2) Siddhamantraprakāśa, a comm. on the Siddhamantra,
written by his father Keśava, 3) a comm. on the Śāṅgadharasamhitā,
called Gūḍhārthadīpikā, 4) Hṛdayadīpanighanṭu (Cat.Cat. 1, p. 616).
In the Siddhamantraprakāśa Vopadeva states that his father learnt
Ayurveda from Bhāskara and that his grandfather was called Mahā-
deva. Keśava says that he was honoured by Simharāja. This Simharāja
is identical with Simhaṇa or Simhaṇa II of the later Yādavas of
Devagiri, who ruled from 1210 to 1247 (See Gode, St.I.L.H. 1, p. 116-
118). Keśava’s Siddhamantra will have been written during the reign
of this king. Vopadeva’s works have therefore to be dated in the latter
half of the 13th century.

ŚĀRṄGĀDHARASAMHITĀ. This work has been written by Śāṅgadhara,
the son of Dāmodara (as indicated in the colophons). As there exists
a comm. by Vopadeva on the work, it must have been composed be-
fore Vopadeva’s time (Jolly, Medicin, p. 4). Filliozat observes (Renou
et Filliozat, l’Inde Classique 2, p. 160) that the work is usually regarded
as dating from the 13th century, but that it may date from the 11th
century. Acc. to Dutt (M.M., Preface p. 14) the Śāṅgadharasamhitā
is the oldest work containing a detailed account of the calcination and
preparation of various metals. Acc. to Jivanram who published a criti-
cal edition of the work (Bombay, 1891), Śāṅgadhara used Vṛnda-


=== Page 443 ===
APPENDIX TWO
429

kuṇḍa's Siddhāyoga in the composition of his saṁhitā. Acc. to Burnell
(see Preface Vaidyakaśabdāsindhu) the author of the Śārṅgadhara-
saṁhitā is posterior to Maheśvara, who wrote the Viśvaprākāśa (dated
1111). His date must lie between those of Vṛndakuṇḍa and Vopadeva.
A difficulty with Śārṅgadhara is that there are various authors of this
name. Another Śārṅgadhara, son of Devarāja, was the author of a
medical work called Triśati, Vaidyavallabha or Jvaratriśati (Cat.Skt.
Mss. IO 5, nr. 2713, p. 960). This author was a Baḍa-nagara Gujarātī
brāhmaṇa (Cat.Skt.Mss. BORI, vol. 16, part 1, p. 112). Moreover a
Śārṅgadhara, son of Dāmodara, grandson of Rāghava and great-grand-
son of Hammīra Bhūpati of the Śākambharī country, composed an
anthology, called Śārṅgadharapaddhati, in 1363 (Kṛṣṇamachariar,
p. 386). Some identify the latter with the author of the Śārṅgadhara-
saṁhitā (e.g. Paraśurāma Śāstrī, ed. of the Śārṅgadharasaṁhitā, and
Umeśacandra Gupta, author of the Vaidyakaśabdāsindhu).

Besides Vopadeva there are three more authors of a comm. on the
Śārṅgadharasaṁhitā : 1) Āḍhamalla, who wrote the comm. called
Dīpikā; Āḍhamalla was, acc. to the introd. to his comm., a royal
physician to Jaitrasimha at Hastikāntapurī and a descendant of the
author Śārṅgadhara, who lived in Hammirapura in the country called
Śākambharī; he even claims to descend from Cakrapāṇidatta. 2) Kāśīrā-
ma, who wrote the comm. called Gūḍhārthadīpikā; at the end of the
work he says that he has composed it in the reign of Shāh Salīm (i.e.
Jahāngīr, 1605-1627). 3) Rudrabhaṭṭa, the son of the vaidya Koṇerī-
bhaṭṭa; he wrote a comm., called Āyurvedadīpikā, that closely resem-
bles Āḍhamalla's comm. (see Śārṅgadharasaṁhitā, Introd. by Paraśu-
rāma Śāstrī, p. 7-8).

ŚIVADĀSASENA was the son of Anantasena, son of Uddharaṇa, son of
Lakṣmīdharasena, son of Kākutsthasena, son of Sāhisena, who lived
at the court of king Śikhareśvara. This information is given by Śiva-
dāsasena himself at the end of his commentary on Cakrapāṇidatta's
Cikitsāsaṁgraha. At the end of his comm. on Cakra's Dravya-guṇa-
saṁgraha he says that his father was a royal physician to Bārbak Shāh.
Bārbak Shāh, Sultan of Bengal, reigned from 1457 to 1474 (Introd. Ca.
p. 16, referring to Stuart's History of Bengal) or from 1459 to 1476
(Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 125). Śivadāsasena's father lived at Mālāna-
cikā, as stated at the end of the comm. on Cakra's Cikitsāsaṁgraha.
From other indications in the same comm. it may be concluded that


=== Page 444 ===
430                                         APPENDIX TWO

Mālañcikā was a village in the Pavanāmaṇḍala of Varendra, a part of
Bengal (see Introd. Ca. p. 16, footnote 2).
    Śivadāsasena wrote four commentaries : 1) the Tattvapradīpikā on
Ca. (there is a Ms. of this work, containing the comm. on Sū. 1-27,
in the library of the Asiatic Society at Bombay, see Introd. Ca. p. 17;
acc. to the Introd. to the Lahore ed. of Ca. there exists elsewhere a Ms.
containing the comm. from the beginning up to Ci. 27); 2) the Tattva-

Cakrapāṇidatta's Cikitsāsaṁgraha (printed) and 4) a comm. on Cakra-

Śivadāsasena must have written his works about 1500. A Ms. of his
comm. on A.H.U. is dated 1526 (see Introd. Ca. p. 16, footnote 3).

ŚRĪDĀSAPANDITA is the author of a comm. on A.h., called Hṛdaya-
bodhikā (in certain Mss. it is referred to as Hṛdayabodhini). The au-
thor was a native of Kerala and gives the Malayālam equivalents of
technical terms. His teacher was called Vāsudeva, as indicated in the
introduction of the comm. Another pupil of the same teacher also
wrote a comm. on A.h., called Vyākhyāsāra. Śrīdāsa often quotes from
the latter. The Vyākhyāsāra and Hṛdayabodhikā are closely followed
by a Malayālam comm. on A.h., called Alpabuddhiprabodhana and
written by Śrīkaṇṭha. The ed. of part 2 of Śrīdāsa's comm. Narayana
Pillai, identifies this Śrīkaṇṭha with the teacher of Rāghava, author
of a comm. on the Yudhiṣṭhiravijaya. Rāghava was the teacher of
Śaṅkara, author of the Śrīkṛṣṇavijaya. Rāghava is mentioned in a
kāvya dated from the 15th century and Śaṅkara is referred to by an
author flourishing in the beginning of the 15th century; Śrīkaṇṭha may
have lived in the latter half of the 14th century. It may be tentatively
accepted that Śrīdāsapaṇḍita flourished earlier than 1300. (Extracted
from the Introd. by P. K. Narayana Pillai to part 2 of A.h. with
Śrīdāsapaṇḍita's comm.).

SUKĪRA is mentioned by Vijayarakṣita in his Introduction to the
Madhukośa. He is once quoted by Ḍa. (acc. to the Introd., p. 25 of
the N.S. Press ed., 1938; on the page indicated the name Sukira does
not occur and I could not find the name elsewhere in Ḍa.'s comm.
on Sū.).


=== Page 445 ===
APPENDIX TWO 431

SUDĀNTASENA is twice quoted by Vijayarakṣita in M. The quotations
point to his being the author of a work in verse that closely followed Ca.
He is repeatedly quoted by Niścalakara (Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 149).

SUDHĪRA is mentioned by Vijayarakṣita in his introduction to the
Madhukoṣa. He is quoted several times by Ḍa. (a.o. on Su.Ci. 1, 27ab;
Ci. 1, 72cd; Ci. 1, 74cd-75ab). From Ḍa.'s quotations it may be con-
cluded that he was a commentator on Su. Acc. to Haridattaśarman
(Introd. p. 22 of the Lahore ed. of Ca. with Jejjata's comm.) he was
a commentator on Ca., but there is no evidence to support this state-
ment.

SUŚRUTA. The original text of the Suśrutasaṁhitā, before its revision
and completion (by adding the Uttarātantra) by a pratisamskartṛ (sup-
posed to be Nāgārjuna), must be very old, because Suśruta is already
mentioned and quoted in the Bower Ms., dated between the 4th and
the 6th centuries (see Filliozat in : Renou et Filliozat, l'Inde Classique
2, p. 147 and p. 675-676; Hoernle thought that the date of the Bower
Ms. was 350-375). Some Indian authors ascribe a very early date to
Suśruta. Rãy (Hist. Chem., p. 61) says he was, acc. to a Buddhist
Jātaka (no particulars are given), a teacher in the University of Kāśī
in Buddha's times. Srivastava (Hist. Ind. Pharm., p. 57) dates him
somewhere between 1000 and 600 B.C. and notes that Kātyāyana, who
lived in the 4th century B.C., is said to have written about Suśruta in
his Vārtikas (Winternitz 3, p. 390 says that, as a working hypothesis,
it may be assumed that Kātyāyana, the author of the Vārtikas on
Pāṇini's grammar, may have lived in the 3rd century B.C.). Mukho-
pādhyāya (H.I.M. 3, p. 576) says that the latest limit which we can
assign to Suśruta is 600 B.C.; he also refers to Kātyāyana's Vārtikas,
in which it is said : suśrutena proktam sauśrutam. (See about the opinions
of a series of scholars : Mukhopādhyāya, l.c., p. 578-579). It is clear
that no more can be said than that the original Suśrutasaṁhitā must
have been composed in the first three centuries of our era at the latest.
A difficult problem is presented by the revision of the text. There
must have been a reviser, because Cakrapāṇidatta and Ḍalhaṇa refer
to him (Ḍalhaṇa calls him Nāgārjuna ; see Nāgārjuna). This reviser not
only added the Uttarātantra, but also made slight changes in the re-
mainder of the text, which is proved by the fact that the Uttarātantra
is referred to Su.Sū. 3, 3 and in other passages. The original text dealt
with surgery as its special object; the Uttarātantra deals with what is


=== Page 446 ===
432                                                       APPENDIX TWO

called *śālākya* (eye diseases and ophthalmic surgery, diseases of the
ears, nose and mouth) and internal medicine, called *kāyacikitsā*. About
the date of the revision nothing definite is known. Filliozat says (Renou
et Filliozat, l'Inde Classique 2, p. 147) that, if the reviser is indeed
Nāgārjuna and identical with the author of the Yōgaśataka, his date
is the 6th century, and, if he is the Nāgārjuna who lived a hundred
years before al-Bīrūnī, his date is the 10th century. Mukhopādhyāya
(H.I.M. 3, p. 574 and 581) thinks that Nāgārjuna may be the celebrated
Buddhist chemist, who is said to have been a contemporary of king
Sātavāhana (l.c., p. 574) and of king Kaniṣka who lived in the first
century B.C. (l.c., p. 581).

I think that the reviser of the Suśrutasaṃhitā may have lived before
Dṛḍhabala, i.e. before 500, because Cakrapāṇidatta says (see : Dṛḍha-
bala) that the redactor of the Carakasaṃhitā made use of the works of
Suśruta and Videha, which means that chapters on *kāyacikitsā* from
Su.U. were employed by Dṛḍhabala; the latter wrote a.o. the chapter
of the Carakasaṃhitā on *pāṇḍuroga* (morbid pallor) and this subject
is dealt with in Su.U. If this be true, the problem remains where the
reviser of Su. found his material. Another point is whether Cakra's re-
mark is trustworthy. Moreover it is probable that Dṛḍhabala did not
create whole chapters anew, but that the Agniveśatantra was still ex-
tant, completely or partially; the revision of this work, started by
Caraka, was completed by Dṛḍhabala.

Another point to be considered in relation to the Suśrutasaṃhitā is
a text called Vṛddhasuśruta by commentators. It has been assumed
(Hoernle, Osteology, Introd. p. 5 and JRAS, 1909, p. 879; Mukho-
pādhyāya, H.I.M. 3, p. 572) that the work referred to as Vṛddhasuśruta
is the Suśrutasaṃhitā before it had been revised. This, however, cannot
be true, because four quotations from Vṛddhasuśruta in M. and Ā.
(see list of quotations from Suśruta) are found in the Uttarataṇtra.
Other quotations from Vṛddhasuśruta, however, are untraceable in the
Suśrutasaṃhitā as it has come down to us. Many of the quotations
from Vṛddhasuśruta and the Sauśrutatantra have been collected by
Mukhopādhyāya (H.I.M. 3, p. 583-587). The problems concerning
Vṛddhasuśruta and the work called Sauśrutatantra by commentators
have not been studied sufficiently and need further elucidation.

SVĀMIDĀSA. This author is referred to in M. on 1, 14cd-15ab as one
of the early commentators (*pūrvāṭīkākāra*). He is also mentioned as
such by Cakra on Ca.Ci. 3, 217. Vijayarakṣita mentions Svāmidāsa


=== Page 447 ===
APPENDIX TWO 433

after Āṣaḍhadharma, Cakrapāṇidatta puts him before Āṣaḍhavarman;
therefore it is not not clear whether one of the two lists (Cakra : Bhāṣadatta-
ma-Svāmidāsa-Āṣaḍhavarman-Brahmadeva; Vijayarakṣita : Āṣaḍhadhar-
ma-Svāmidāsa) is in correct chronological order. Svāmidāsa is certainly
one of the group of early commentators on Ca. because he is quoted
by Jejjaṭa.

HARICANDRA or Bhaṭṭārahāricandra, sometimes only indicated by
his title of distinction, Bhaṭṭāra, was an early commentator on Ca.
He is already quoted by Jejjaṭa as a good commentator (Gul 1, p. 114;
Introd. Ca., p. 12; Introd. Ca., Lahore ed., p. 26). There is also a re-
ference to him in a Ms. containing part of a comm. on A.s. (Indu's
comm. on that work?) : “The ignorant one who attempts to understand
Caraka's thought without (consulting) Haricandra's commentary, is
(like) a man who wants to drink up (read *pātum* instead of *vātum*) the
ocean” (Cat.Skt.Mss. Madras, vol. 23, nr. 13071, p. 8789). Indu refers
to Bhaṭṭārakaharicandra several times; these references by Indu show
that he had not much respect for Haricandra's views (Gode, St.I.L.H.
1, p. 161). Candraṭa praises Haricandra in the beginning of his comm.
on Tīsaṭa's Cikitsākalikā : “As there exist the commentaries of Hari-
candra and of the very intelligent Jejjaṭa, it is presumptuous for an-
other man to comment on the Āyurveda” (Jolly, ZDMG 60, 1906, p.
426; Jolly's reading of the stanza is somewhat different; Gul 1, p. 113;
Introd. Ca., p. 13; Introd. Ca., Lahore ed., p. 19). Cakrapāṇidatta re-
marks (on Ca.Sū. 7, 46) that Vāgbhaṭa follows Haricandra's opinion
on a particular point. Maheśvara writes about him in the Viśvaparākā-
śakośa 1, 5 (composed in 1111 acc. to Winternitz 3, p. 413) : “He whose
name was Haricandra, whose behaviour was as agreeable as the moon,
held in a wholly unrivalled way the position of an irreproachable court
physician to king Sāhasāṅka and adorned the treatise of Caraka with
his own commentary” (Introd. Ca., p. 13; Introd. Ca., Lahore ed., p.
19; Gul 1, p. 114). Haricandra was one of Maheśvara's ancestors
(Krishnamachariar, p. 146-147). An author, also called Haricandra but
probably a different person, is mentioned by Bāṇa (Harṣacarita 1, 12)
as an important prose writer. This same Haricandra is referred to in
Vākpati's Gauḍavaha (stanza nr. 800). It is said that he wrote a romance
called Mālatī (Krishnamachariar, p. 146). He is also referred to in the
Saḍuktikarṇāmṛta by Śrīdharadāsa (compiled in 1260 acc. to Das-
gupta and De, in 1205 acc. to Krishnamachariar; see Banerji's ed. of
the work, stanza nr. 2130) and in the Subhāṣitāvalī by Vallabhadeva


=== Page 448 ===
434

APPENDIX TWO

(written between 1417 and 1467 acc. to Krishnamachariar, p. 387). A
third author, called Haricandra, was a Jain poet of the Digambara sect
and a son of Ārdradeva and Rādhā (Krishnamachariar, p. 146-147).
Finally, a poet, called Haricandra and living at the court of Bhillama
III of Devagiri, composed an inscription in 1205 (Krishnamachariar,
ibid.).

A small portion of Haricandra's comm. on Ca., called Carakanyāsa,
has been preserved in a single Ms. (see its description in the Cat.Skt.
Mss. Madras, vol. 23, nr. 13092, p. 8801-8802). The fragment contains
the comm. on Ca.Sū. 3 (acc. to Gul 1, p. 115 it contains the comm. on
Ca.Sū. 1-3 and 5). This very important fragment of the oldest comm.
on Ca. known to us has not yet been edited. Acc. to Bhatt. (IHQ 23,
1947, p. 149-150) Haricandra also wrote a revised version of the Kha-
ranādasamhitā (he refers to a remark by Indu in the Śaśilekhā ed.
Trichur, vol. 2, p. 368 and p. 372). Bhatt. is of the opinion that Hari-
candra wrote a *samhitā* of his own, quoted by Nīścala, which cannot be
identical with the Kharanādasamhitā from which Nīścala quotes sepa-
rately. Moreover, a passage from Nīścala's Ratnaprabhā proves that
Haricandra himself quotes from Kharanāda. Acc. to Bhatt. a recipe,
couched in an elegant verse, taken by Nīścala from Haricandra, must
be quoted from Haricandra's own *samhitā*; at the end of it a poetic
address to a king is found, which proves, acc. to Bhatt. again, that
Haricandra wrote his *samhitā* for his patron, king Sāhasāṅka.

Haricandra's date cannot be established with certainty. It is only
clear that he lived before Jejjaṭa, Indu, Candraṭa, etc. Many scholars
who have written on the subject assume that the medical author Hari-
candra is identical with the author of the same name, referred to in the
Harṣacarita and by Vākpati (see Gul 1, p. 112-115; Introd. Ca., p.
13; Introd. Ca., Lahore ed., p. 19; Bhatt., IHQ 23, 1947, p. 149-150);
others deny the identity or have their doubt about it (see references
in Krishnamachariar, p. 146). There is no evidence to prove the identity,
nor any evidence disproving it. With regard to Haricandra's date this
problem is of little importance. Haricandra lived before Jejjaṭa and
after the composition of the Kharanādasamhitā. It follows from these
data that he lived before 600. Crucial in fixing his date more precisely
is the identity of king Sāhasāṅka. The identity of this king, however,
cannot be determined with any certainty. The editors of the Gul ed.
of Ca., however, remark without adducing any proofs to support their
statements : "The date of king Sāhasāṅka has been fairly well estab-
lished as 375-413. King Sāhasāṅka is very often identified with Vikra-


=== Page 449 ===
APPENDIX TWO                                                                               435

ma, i.e. Candragupta II, but this identification is not justified. Vikra-
ma was the predecessor of Sāhasāṅka and Haricandra is not mentioned
among the ‘nine gems’ of Vikrama’s court. Thus Haricandra’s date is
the 5th century”. Though this reasoning has its weak points, the date
assigned to Haricandra is not unreasonable. In my opinion his date is
before 600 and it may be said that he probably lived between 400 and
600. It is not clear whether Haricandra wrote his comm. before the
Carakasamhitā had been completed by Dṛḍhabala. The quotations from
Haricandra in M. refer to parts of Ca., which are due to Caraka himself.
In order to establish Haricandra’s date with regard to to that of Dṛḍha-
bala all the quotations from Haricandra and the references to him
should be collected and studied. A cursory examination of Cakra’s
comm. on Ca. shows that Haricandra is referred to only once in that
part of Ca. which has been redacted by Dṛḍhabala (on Ca.Si. 12,
41cd-45ab); this reference gives the impression that Haricandra com-
mented on the whole of Ca. ; if this is correct, he is later than Dṛḍhabala.

HĀRĪTA. To Hārīta is ascribed the Hāritasaṃhitā, also called Ātre-
yasaṃhitā or Ātreyabhāṣitaṃ Hāritottaram. Hārīta says that he is a
disciple of Ātreya, but the work as it has come down to us seems to
be of a much later date than the other medical saṃhitās. Cordier had
not much respect for the work (Le Muséon, N.S. 4, 1903, p. 348-349)
and regarded it as a relatively late text of an apocryphal nature, though
he admitted that parts of it might be old. He was of the opinion (JA
t. 18, 1901, p. 180) that it must have been composed somewhat earlier
than the Mādhavanidāna and that its pariśiṣṭādhyāya has been added
later at an indeterminate date. Filliozat observes (Renou et Filliozat,
l’Inde Classique 2, p. 151) that the text as it has been preserved is a
revision of a relatively late date, but he stresses (JA, t. 225, 1934, p.
127, footnote) that the work is of more importance than Cordier ascribed
to it. The work is composed in verse on a plan different from that of
Ca. and Su. Quotations from Hārīta occur in many commentaries, but
can be traced only partially to the text printed as the Hāritasaṃhitā
(see : Mukhopādhyāya, H.I.M. 3, p. 811). A long series of quotations
has been collected by Mukhopādhyāya (H.I.M. 3, p. 551-555), acc. to
whom an author called Vṛddhahārīta is quoted in the Toḍarānanda
(I.c., p. 556).

HEMĀDRI wrote a comm. on A.h., called Āyurvedarasāyana, which
has been partially preserved (see about the Mss. : A.h., ed. Kuṇṭe,


=== Page 450 ===
436                                APPENDIX TWO

sūcīpatram saptamam). Hemādri was a son of Kāmādeva, son of Vāsu-
deva, son of Vāmana (Cat.Cat. 1, p. 768). He lived during the reign
of two Yādava kings of Devagiri : Mahādeva (1261-1271 acc. to Hist.
and Cult. of the Ind. P. 5, p. 335; 1260-1271 acc. to Cat.Cat. 1, p. 768
and Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 16) and Rāmacandra (1271-1309 acc. to
Cat.Cat.; Gode, St.I.L.H. 1, p. 112; Krishnamachariar, p. 120; Vogel,
Introd. A.h., p. 16). Hemādri was a prolific author and many works
of his hand are known. In the Caturvargacintāmaṇi he states to be in
charge of the state records of Mahādeva (Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 16).
In the introd. to his Ayurvedarasāyana he mentions the Caturvarga-
cintāmaṇi; from this introd. and a contemporary inscription he ap-
pears to have been the archivist and chief minister of Rāmacandra
(Vogel, Introd. A.h., p. 16; Gode, St.I.L.H. 1, p. 186-190). From these
data it may be concluded that Hemādri wrote his Ayurvedarasāyana
during the reign of Rāmacandra.

APPENDIX THREE

TECHNICAL TERMS

*aṁsa* — (upper) scapular region.

See on the interpretation of *aṁsa* and terms connected with it :
Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2, p. 286, n. 4 and p. 287, n. 2; Hariprapanna,
Rasayogasaṅgara, *upodghāta* p. 81-82 and 138; Hoernle, Osteology,
p. 133-141.

*agni* — (transforming) fire.

There are thirteen fires in the human body (Ca.Ci. 15, 38cd; A.h.Śā.
3, 70cd). Chief of all is the abdominal fire; the others are dependent
on it and subject to increase or decline when the abdominal fire in-
creases or declines (Ca.Ci. 15, 39). Each of the five gross elements
(earth, water, fire, wind and space) is provided with its own fire, which
has a maturative effect on the constituent of the ingested food belonging
to it (Ca.Ci. 15, 13 = A.h.Śā. 3, 59; Su.Śā. 46, 526; A.s.Śā. 6, 59),
following upon the separation of these constituents by the abdominal
fire (Cakra on Ca.Ci. 15, 13) or by the wind (A.s.Śā. 6, 59). Subsequently,
the earthy constituent of the food replenishes the earthy constituents
of the body, etc. (Ca.Ci. 15, 14 = A.h.Śā. 3, 60; A.s.Śā. 6, 59). Moreover,
there are the seven fires of the elements of the body. Each element is
transformed into the subsequent element of the series by its own fire
and the seventh element, semen, is transformed into an embryo (Ca.Ci.
15, 15-16; A.h.Śā. 3, 62-63ab; A.s.Śā. 6, 64-66) or into the vital fluid
(A.s.Śā. 6, 66). See : Bhish 1, Introd. p. 48-50; Kirfel, Die fünf Ele-
mente; Kutumbiah, p. 41 and 53; Müller, Grundlagen, p. 50-52, Zur
Feuerwertung, SA 37, 1953, p. 312-319.

*añga* — part of the body.

The body is divided into six (chief) parts : (1) the head (and neck),
(2) the trunk (*antarādhi* or *madhya*), (3) and (4) the two arms, (5) and
(6) the two legs (Ca.Śā. 7, 5; Su.Śā. 5, 3; A.h.Śā. 3, 1; A.s.Śā. 5, 3).
See : Müller, Wörterheft, p. 75, nr. 4.


=== Page 452 ===
438                                  APPENDIX THREE

*aṅgula* — digit.

See : Müller, Wörterheft, p. 75, nr. 5.

*añjana* — collyrium.

*añjana* usually denotes a substance applied to the eyelids as a cosme-
tic or medicine. It is often said to consist of antimony (MW; PW).
Really two different substances are used for the purpose : antimony
trisulphide (Sb₂S₃) or stibnite, and lead sulphide (PbS) or galena. The
two substances are often confused, as Watt observes (CP, p. 72) :
“Antimony sulphide (stibnite) is employed by the ladies as a cosmetic,
but much of the antimony sold for that purpose is really galena, which
is often confused with antimony,” see about galena : Watt CP, p. 707.
Vogel (A.h., p. 85, n. 1) had two samples of stibnite, bought in Indian
bazaars, analysed in Germany ; they turned out to consist of galena.

*añjana* is also confused sometimes with *rasāñjana* acc. to Dutt, who
writes (MM, p. 108, footnote) : “Galena or the sulphide of lead ore is
sometimes called *rasāñjana* in Sanskrit and some physicians in Bengal
use the lead ore or *rasāñjana* whenever this term occurs in a prescrip-
tion. In the Upper Provinces, however, *rasāñjana* is invariably trans-
lated as *rasot* in the vernacular. This, no doubt, is the correct practice.
The mistake on the part of the Bengali physicians probably occurred
from their not being acquainted with *rasot*, which is the produce of
plants indigenous to the Himalayan range;” Dutt, MM, p. 108 :
“*rasāñjana* is prepared by boiling together equal parts of a decoction
of *dāruharidrā* and milk, till reduced to the consistence of an extract.”
Nadk. says about antimony sulphide (2, p. 13, nr. 8) : “It is a ter-
sulphide of antimony purified by fusion and reduced to a black powder.
The powder is used as an application to the eyelids and eye-brows
especially by women in Upper India ;” about galena he observes (2,
p. 87, nr. 33) : “It is obtained from the mountains of Sauvira, a country
along the Indus, whence it derives its name (*sauvīrāñjana*). The sul-
phide of lead is of glimmering lustre and is an ore of lead, occurs in
cubic masses destitute of rays and is tabular in its crystalline arrange-
ment. *sroto’ñjana* or white *surmā* is produced in the bed of the Yamunā
and other rivers. It is, like the black *surmā* or *sauvīrāñjana*, used as
a collyrium for the eyes, but is considered inferior to the black *surmā*
or galena.” Five kinds of *añjana* are distinguished in the Rasaratna-
samuccaya (3, 101-112 ; ed. H.S.S.), a text referred to in Vśs and dealt
with by Ray (H.Ch., p. 175) : (1) *sauvīrāñjana*, which is smoke-coloured ;


=== Page 453 ===
APPENDIX THREE 439

Rāy : “It is mostly galena or sulphide of lead, though it is usually
translated as sulphide of antimony; it is said to be obtained from the
mountains of Sauvirā, a country along the Indus, whence it derives
its name;” Hindi comm. : stibnite; (2) rasāñjana, said to be endowed
with a yellow hue; Rāy : the extract of the wood of Berberis asiatica
(dāruharidrā); Hindi comm. : yellow oxide of mercury (HgO); (3) sroto’ñjana,
said to be astringent; Rāy : “Evidently stibnite or the native
sulphide of antimony; the word literally means ‘produced from a river’,
especially from the Yamunā;” Hindi comm. : antimony sulphide; (4)
pușpāñjana, said to be white; Rāy : unidentifiable; Hindi comm. : zinc
oxide (ZnO); (5) nīlāñjana; Rāy : undoubtedly stibnite (this may be
incorrect; compare Rāy, p. 151 : Rasendracūḍāmaṇi : lead is prepared
from nīlāñjana; Hindi comm. : lead sulphide.

Garbe (Ind. Mineralien) makes the following observations : (1) sauvirāñjana
(p. 54) : this is antimony sulphide; possibly the name was
transferred later to lead sulphate, because sauvirāñjana is already said
to be white in Bhā.pra.; the series of synonyms in Rn (varga 13, 214)
points to a substance of a black colour, i.e. antimony sulphide, which
is of a greyish colour and in its natural state greyish black and easy
to pulverize; (2) rasāñjana (p. 57-58) : the description in Rn (varga 13,
221-223) enables us to identify this substance with certainty as pre-pared
from slags of brass; the name was transferred later to a decoc-tion
of the roots of Curcuma; acc. to the Amarakośa (followed by PW)
rasāñjana is copper sulphate (tuttha), prepared by adding a decoction
of Curcuma (dārvikā); (Garbe is in error here, because dārvikā is a
synonym of dāruharidrā and not of haridrā); (3) sroto’ñjana (p. 58-59) :
this substance can only be identical with pure antimony on account of
the synonyms sauvirasāra and kapotasāra (Rn, varga 13, 226); Garbe
points to the erroneous observations in Dutt (MM, p. 74): “sroto’ñjana
is described as of a white colour and is said to be produced in the bed
of the Yamunā and other rivers. It is called saffed surmā in the ver-nacular,
and the article supplied under this name is calcareous or Ice-land
spar;” (4) pușpāñjana (p. 56) : the synonyms rītika, rītikusuma
and rītipușpa (Rn, varga 13, 224) point to the chief ingredient as brass;
the only possibility left is to explain pușpāñjana as a collyrium pre-pared
from calx of brass, in agreement with PW; in Bhā.pra. this
añjana is no longer mentioned and it must already have been out of
use for centuries; Dutt (MM, p. 74) is unable to identify the substance
and says : “I have not met with any person who could identify or
supply the drug;” (5) nīlāñjana (p. 54-55) : antimony sulphide.

anupāna — postprandial potion.

The term anupāna is used in two senses : (1) a fluid drunk in com-
bination with a remedial agent or after the taking of a medicinal sub-
stance; (2) a fluid drunk after eating a dish during a meal and at the
conclusion of a meal. See about the rules in relation to an anupāna :
Ca.Sū. 27, 319-328 and Cakra's comment; see also Da. on Su.Sū. 46,
419 and 438 and the article in Vśs.

apatarpaṇa — depletion.

Ca.Vi. 3, 43-44 : apatarpaṇa is of three kinds : (1) laṅghana, reducing
measures, used in disorders in which the morbific entities are of slight
strength; (2) laṅghanapācana, reducing and maturation-promoting
measures, used when the morbific entities are of moderate strength;
(3) doṣāvasecana, measures bringing about the effusion of the morbific
entities, resorted to when the morbific entities are present in copious
amounts. A.h.Sū. 14, 1cd-4cd : apatarpaṇa is synonymous with laṅ-
ghana; laṅghana is that which promotes lightness of the body; laṅ-
ghana is of two kinds : (1) śamana, (2) śodhana (the latter term corres-
ponds to doṣāvasecana). See Kutumbiah, p. 141.

apūpa — flour-cake.

OP (p. 8, 19, 36, 284) : a round, sweet cake of barley meal or rice
flour, baked in clarified butter on a slow fire; honey was added to
sweeten it. Vśs quotes from the Vaidyanighantu : “apūpas are made
from finely ground wheat, mixed with treacle and squeezed (after the
addition) of water; they are of a circular shape and (should be) baked
in ghee.” Ca. mentions apūpas of barley flour (Sū. 27, 265) and also
makes use of the terms pūpa (Sū. 27, 267), pūpaka (Sū. 27, 269) and
pūpalikā (Sū. 27, 267); Ca. describes pūpas of wheat flour (Sū. 27, 272)
and pūpakas made with milk and sugar-cane juice (Sū. 27, 269). Cakra
says (on Sū. 27, 267) that a pūpalikā is called cāpaḍikā (in common
language) and quotes a recipe for its preparation from (the treatise on
cooking by) Nala. The preparation of aphrodisiac pūpas and pūpalikās
is described Ca.Ci. 2², 10-12 (Kav p. 1080, footnote : those cakes that
have conical ends with the middle portion thicker are called pūpalikās;

OP, p. 290 : pūpalikās are small cakes of rice or wheat-flour, fried
in ghee, with ghee-filled inside and coated with treacle and saffron.

ways of baking. He. remarks that apūpas are thin and flat and pre-
