amla

The term amla has several meanings when used as a noun :
m. : (1) vinegar (MW; PW); (2) Oxalis corniculata Linn. (MW; PW);
(3) = amlavetasa (PW ; Śkdr); (4) = phalāmla; (5) = amlīkā (HK);
n : (1) = dhānyāmla = kāñjika (Vśs; Cakra on Ca.Ci. 29, 151); (2) =
takra (PW ; Śkdr ; Cakra on Ca.Ni. 2, 4); (3) = ghola (Vśs); (4) =
phalāmla; (5) the fruit of amlavetasa (Vśs); (6) the fruit of the
badara tree (Vśs); (7) = barbaracandana (Vśs).
Kaut. 2, 15, 18-19 (text p. 64; transl. Kangle p. 142; transl. J. J. Meyer
p. 141; transl. Sham. p. 101) distinguishes dravāmla, i.e. dadhi, dhā-
nyāmla, etc., and phalāmla, i.e. vṛkṣāmla, karamarda, āmra, vidalā-
malaka (i.e. vidala and āmalaka), mātuluṅga, kola, badara, sauviraka,
parūṣaka, etc. There is a group, called ‘the four acids’ (caturamla),
mentioned at Ca.Ci. 15, 111; Cakra observes that it consists of (1)
vṛkṣāmla, (2) amlavetasa, (3) dāḍima, (4) badara, but acc. to others of
(1) kapittha, (2) cukrikā, (3) vṛkṣāmla, (4) dāḍima, and that, in another
treatise, it is said to be composed of (1) vṛkṣāmla, (2) mātuluṅgāmla,
(3) badarāmla, (4) amlavetasa. See about the ‘five acids’ : Dn, varga 7,
57; Rn, varga 22, 28. See about the ‘phalāmla-pentad’ : Dn, varga 7,
53; Rn varga 22, 24.

ariṣṭa, m.

HB, p. 86, n. 52 : a medicated spirituous liquor, prepared from honey
and treacle with the addition of (unboiled) medicinal drugs, the whole

in which remedial agents have been boiled.” Cakra on Ca.Sū. 27, 182 :

ariṣṭa, riṣṭa, n. — a precursory signal of death.

Ca.I. 2, 5 : “A precursory signal of death, once arisen, never disap-
pears, except in death, and death does not occur without a precursory
signal as its harbinger.” Su.Sū. 30, 3 : “If someone presents a deviation
from the natural state of his body or mind this is, briefly stated,
(called) a precursory signal of death.” A.h.Sā. 5, 1-2ab : “A precursory
signal of death is a sure sign (indicative) of imminent death, in the
same way as a flower (is such a sign) with regard to to (the appearance of)
a fruit, smoke with regard to fire and the rising of clouds with regard
to rain. Death does not occur without a precursory signal and life is
impossible when such a signal has been observed.” A.s.Sā. 9, 3 : “In
both healthy and sick people who crave for another body, morbific
entities, having got beyond the reach of remedial agents and per-
vading the whole body, indicate the decline of life, as compact clouds
(indicate) rain, and generate suddenly an overthrow of the natural
state; that is, briefly stated, said to be a precursory signal of death.”
A great number of ariṣṭas is described : Ca.I.; Su.Sū. 29-33; A.h.Sā.
5 and 6; A.s.Sā. 9-12; Bhe.I.; Kā.I.; Hā. 2, 3-5. See : Filliozat, Ap-
pendix : Accadian, Greek and Indian medical prognostics; Jolly,
Medicin, p. 23-24; Kutumbiah, p. 99-106; Sinh Jee, p. 164-175.

This term is explained by Cakra on Ca.Ni. 1, 33 as deficiency of

asthi—bone.

There are said to be three hundred and sixty bones in the human

āgāradhūma

This term occurs Ca.Ci. 23, 51, Si. 7, 25 and Si. 9, 58, but is not
explained by Cakra. Its synonym grhadhūma is found Ca.Sū. 3, 5, Ci.

dictionaries make it to be the name of a plant. I do not know on what
authority. At Su.Ka. 1, 58 it is said to be dhūma āgārasambhavah, i.e.
'smoke produced in a house', that is, the soot deposited in the cob-

prescribed by Kavirāja. In Bengali it is called jhul and in Sanskrit

The latter is a wrong form of the Sanskrit alandhūma, 'thick smoke'
or soot."

ādāna — period of resorption.

visarga — period of emission.

See Ca.Sū. 6, 4-8; Su.Sū. 6, 7-8; A.h.Sū. 3, 2-7ab; A.s.Sū. 4, 5-8;
Kā.Khi. 7, 5-12; Hā. 1, 4, 21-31; Bhā.pra. 5, 329-339.
ādāna is that half of the year in which the sun moves to the north,
visarga the other half in which it moves to the south. ādāna consists
of the cool season, spring and summer, visarga of the rainy season,
autumn and winter. During visarga the moon is strong and during
ādāna the sun. In the period of ādāna the oleaginous constituents of
the earth are resorbed by the sun, leading to a predominance of dry
qualities and the dry (i.e. bitter, astringent and pungent) tastes, which
bring about weakness. In the period of visarga there is predominance
of the non-dry (i.e. acid, saline and sweet) tastes, which increase the
strength of men.

anāha — obstructive abdominal swelling.

This term has often been translated erroneously : Gul : constipation,
distension ; HSu, and HB, p. 125, n. 242: habitual constipation, consti-
pation ; MW : suppression of urine, constipation ; Vogel : constipation ;
more adequate is PW : Verstopfung des Leibes; the sense is too broad
in MW : epistasis (= acc. to Butterworths Medical Dictionary : sup-
pression of a secretion or discharge) and HK : Verstopfung.
anāha is defined : Su.U. 56, 20cd-21ab = Mā.ni. 27, 17 = Bhā.pra.
8, 31, 19 : “Gradually accumulated immature or faecal matter, greatly
confined by the wind which has deviated from its (normal) qualities,
(constitutes), when it does not come forth in its normal way, the morbid
alteration called obstructive abdominal swelling.” Defined in this way,
anāha means an obstruction of the bowels, either on a high or on a
low level. Obstruction on a high level (āmodbhava) is called pratyānāha :
Sārṅga 1, 7, 49. The characteristics of anāha are described by Vāg-
bhaṭa as follows : A.h.Ni. 11, 60 = A.s.Ni. 11, 49 (Ki. 11, 48) : “A
vehement abdominal inflatedness, with a very ferocious pain, accom-
panied by distension and (arisen) by obstruction of the wind (in its)
upward and downward (course), that (condition) is declared to be ob-
structive abdominal swelling.” Sometimes the term is used in a broader

     Acc. to Watt (CP, p. 1053) *ālākta* is washed lac (*lākṣā*) ; acc. to Dutt

udaśvit
PW : zwei Theile Buttermilch mit einem Theile Wasser. MW : a
mixture consisting of equal parts of water and buttermilk. Dutt, MM,
p. 283 : butter-milk mixed with half its bulk of water. Kav p. 538 :

upadrava — secondary affection.

PW : Symptom (sowohl eine hinzukommende Krankheitserscheinung
als Krankheitszufall überhaupt). MW : a supervenient disease or one
brought on whilst a person labours under another. Bhisb : sympathetic
disease, morbid affliction, unfavourable symptom. Filliozat (Fragm.
koutch.) : maladie intercurrente. Gul : complication, sequela, affliction.
HK : Folge-erscheinung. HSu : troublesome disease. Jolly : schlimmer
Zufall. Vall : complicazione. Vogel : sequela. It is very difficult to find
an adequate term to render the sense of upadrava. Translations like
‘complication, intercurrent disease and supervenient disease’ are in-
adequate because an upadrava is a secondary development of the pri-
mary morbific process. The term is explained in the following passages :
Ca.Ci. 21, 40 : "A secondary affection is a disease in itself, (of a) major
or minor (character), arising at a later time than the (originally present)
disease and dependent on (that) disease. It is technically called a
secondary affection as it arises after a disease. In such a case the
(original) illness is predominant and the secondary affection has the
(same) qualities as that illness. It usually becomes appeased when the
predominant (illness) is appeased. It is, however, more painfully op-
pressing because, as it is produced later on, the body is (already) being
vexed by illness. Therefore a secondary affection should be attacked
promptly.” Cakra comments : " ... (The words) 'arising at a later time
than the disease', (which mean) : arising during the middle course of
the disease, differentiate (a secondary affection) from a sign that is
produced together with the disease. Although there are signs which
sometimes arise at a later time than the disease, these (are) not (signs
said to) arise at a later time than the illness, strictly speaking, as they
usually arise together with the disease; therefore they are not of the
nature of secondary affections. (The words) 'dependent on (that) dis-
ease' (mean that their) cause is comparable to that of the disease be-
cause they are occasioned by excitement of the morbific entity starting
the disease ... 'A disease in itself' designates the secondary affection


=== Page 462 ===
448 APPENDIX THREE

dealt with by the word disease, separately from the illness which is
its root. In this way it is differentiated from (that) stage of an illness
which arises at a later time ... A stage of an illness has the very form
of the illness which is the root (of the secondary affection) because it
is something which necessarily occurs, but a secondary affection does
not necessarily occur. Although some illnesses, started by morbific en-
tities with a great force, already join secondary affections at their pro-
duction, and the term secondary affection does not refer to (a disease
that is) simultaneously produced, those maladies which arise as sec-
ondary affections are in that case nevertheless called secondary affec-
tions and rightly so, though produced together with (the predominant
disease). In the true sense of the word, however, (those diseases which)
arise simultaneously do not present the characteristics of secondary
affections, but (only) those which arise in such a case as an intermixture
(of diseases) .” Fr. Su.Sū. 35, 18 : “The illness, arising at a later time,
which is added to a previously produced illness, is a superinduced one
(aupasargika) ; such an (illness), the root of which is that (previously
produced illness) itself, is technically called a secondary affection.”
A.h.Sū. 12, 60d : “Those (dependent diseases) which arise later on are
secondary affections.” Kā.Sū. 27, 57cd-58a : “That malady which
arises later, by the (same) cause as that one arisen previously, is called
a secondary affection.” Hā. 3, 2, 17 : “That illness which is added to
an illness is called a secondary affection; those people who have
a secondary affection are to die, those without it will live.”

*eṇa*

See also : *hariṇa*.
PW : *eine Antilopenart* (schwarz und mit kurzen Beinen). MW : a
species of deer or antelope (described as being of a black colour with
beautiful eyes and short legs). Kav, p. 169 : the black antelope. Nadk.
2, p. 143 : *Antilope cervicapra* Linn. Vās : = *hariṇa* : a particular kind
of black deer. Bpn, *māmsavarga* 10 : it is of a black colour. Rn, *varga*
19, 417 : it is also called *pṛṣata* (spotted antelope). Ma.nigh., *varga* 12,

antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*). Ḍa. on Su.Sū. 20, 5 : it is the black deer (*kṛṣṇa-

6, 43 : it is of a black colour and also called *kamala*. He. on A.h.Sū. 6,
43 : it is of a black colour.

It is clear that *eṇa* is usually regarded as a black antelope ; only Cakra
and Rn consider it a spotted antelope. The animal called *eṇa* is pro-
bably the male of *Antilope cervicapra* (Linnaeus, 1758), the black buck
or Indian antelope. It is an elegant animal of a striking colour and
with beautifully spiralled horns. The coat of the males begins to turn
black when they are three years old. The darkening of the coat varies
in intensity ; it may remain a dark brown colour, especially in southern
India. Besides *Antilope cervicapra* two other antelopes occur in India :
the nilgai or blue bull, *Boselaphus tragocamelus* (Pallas, 1766) and the
four-horned antelope, *Tetracerus quadricornis* (Blainville, 1816). See :
Prater, The book of Indian animals, p. 270-273.

*kaṣāya*

    This term is often, but in many cases erroneously, translated by
    decoction. It has a very broad sense in Ca. Five kinds of *kaṣāya* are
    enumerated at Ca.Sū. 4, 7 : (1) *svarasa* : the juice pressed out from a

    by boiling medicinal plants or parts of these with water over a fire;
    (4) *śīta* : a cold infusion made by crushing a medicinal plant and keeping
    it in boiled water for a night; (5) *phāṇṭa* : a hot infusion, made by
    pouring hot water on a crushed drug. These five *kaṣāyas* are mentioned
    by Da. in his comment on Su.Sū. 37, 12. They are also described at
    A.h.Ka. 6, 8-11. At A.s.Ka. 8, 9-13 they appear with partially different
    names : (1) *niryāsa* (= *svarasa*), (2) *kalka*, (3) *niryūha* (= *śṛta*), (4) *śīta*,
    (5) *phāṇṭa*. In the Kāśyapasamhitā seven kinds of medicinal prepara-
    tions are described which correspond to seven types of *kaṣāya*. They are
    enumerated at Khi. 3, 35-43ab : (1) *cūrṇa* : a powder, (2) *śītakāṣāya* :
    prepared by pouring cold water on a crushed drug, (3) *svarasa*, (4) *abhi-
    śava*, which seems to correspond to a *śīta* in Ca., (5) *phāṇṭa*: made by
    having the water boil once, (6) *kalka*, (7) *kvātha* (= *śṛta*). The five
    *kaṣāyas* are also enumerated at Śāṛṅga 2, 1, 1 : (1) *svarasa*, (2) *kalka*,

kāñjika — fermented rice-water.

PW : saurer Reisschleim. MW : sour gruel, water of boiled rice in a
state of spontaneous fermentation. Dutt, MM, p. 12 : "kāñjika is a
sour liquid produced from the acetous fermentation of powdered paddy.
Two seers of powdered paddy grown in the rainy season are steeped
in eight seers of water and laid aside in an earthen pot for fifteen
days and upwards, when the mixture undergoes acetous fermentation.
The resulting fluid is called kāñjika or dhānyāmla, that is, the acid
produced from paddy. kāñjika is a clear transparent fluid with an acid
taste and vinous smell." Vās : sour gruel, the water of boiled rice in a
state of spontaneous fermentation; Caraka (says) : "After putting into
a vessel quickly ripening rice (āśudhānya) which has been pounded,
(as well as) young radishes (bālamūla) which have been cut into pieces,
to the measure of one prastha (= 1/4 of an āḍhaka) and throwing one
āḍhaka of water into that vessel, one should keep the mixture until it
has become acid; (then) it is known as kāñjika, which is everywhere
honoured;" Atrīsamhitā 11 : "After taking one tulā of ṣaṣṭika grains
that have been boiled and distributing them properly, throwing them

*kāñjika* — fermented rice-water.

PW : saurer Reisschleim. MW : sour gruel, water of boiled rice in a
state of spontaneous fermentation. Dutt, MM, p. 12 : “*kāñjika* is a
sour liquid produced from the acetous fermentation of powdered paddy.
Two seers of powdered paddy grown in the rainy season are steeped
in eight seers of water and laid aside in an earthen pot for fifteen
days and upwards, when the mixture undergoes acetous fermentation.
The resulting fluid is called *kāñjika* or *dhānyāmla*, that is, the acid
produced from paddy. *kāñjika* is a clear transparent fluid with an acid
taste and vinous smell.” Vśs : sour gruel, the water of boiled rice in a
state of spontaneous fermentation; Caraka (says) : “After putting into
a vessel quickly ripening rice (*āśudhānya*) which has been pounded,
(as well as) young radishes (*bālamūla*) which have been cut into pieces,
to the measure of one *prastha* (= 1/4 of an *āḍhaka*) and throwing one
*āḍhaka* of water into that vessel, one should keep the mixture until it
has become acid; (then) it is known as *kāñjika*, which is everywhere
honoured;” *Atrisaṃhitā* 11 : “After taking one *tulā* of *ṣaṣṭika* grains
that have been boiled and distributing them properly, throwing them
into a *droṇa* (a sort of wooden vessel) full of water, one should keep
this (mixture), carefully covered, for seven (days and) nights; one should
remove from it all the (rice-)paste; (the resulting fluid) is called *kāñjika*
(or) *āraṇāla*.” *kāñjika* was not only prepared from rice, but also from
*jūrnāhva* and *kodrava* (Da. on Su.Sū. 45, 214). *dhānyāmla* is usually
synonymous with *kāñjika* (Da. on Su.Sū. 45, 214; He. on A.h.Sū. 5,

12 : *dhānyāmla* is prepared from powdered *śāli* rice, *kodrava*, etc.);
Bho.ku. 1 (p. 123 : *kāñjika*; p. 125 : *dhānyāmla*) : idem. Compare
*Śārṅga* 2, 10-12ab. See : Ainslie 1, p. 461-463.

(the animal called) *trikaṇṭaka* is a particular type of the latter.” The

called a chameleon on account of its change of colour. *Calotes versicolor*
is, acc. to the Imp. Gaz. (1909, vol. 1, p. 268-269), the commonest
agamoid lizard, found all over India and known as the ‘bloodsucker’
in southern India; males of this lizard assume brilliant colours in the
breeding season, red and black predominating. The correct name of
this animal is *Calotes versicolor* (Daudin, 1802).

**kṛsara** = *kṛsara*; m., m.pl., f. (-*ā*).

*guṇa* — treacle.
See : *śarkarā*.

*guṇa* — quality.

There are five series of qualities (Ca.Sū. 1, 49). The first series con-
sists of the objects of the senses : sound, touch, colour, taste and smell.
The second series consists of twenty qualities, arranged as ten pairs of
opposites (Ca.Śā. 6, 10 and Cakra on Ca.Sū. 1, 49) : *guru* (heavy) —
*laghu* (light); *śīta* (cold) — *uṣṇa* (hot); *snigdha* (oleaginous) — *rūkṣa*
(dry); *manda* (sluggish) — *tīkṣṇa* (sharp); *sthira* (solid) — *sara* (flowing);
*mṛdu* (soft) — *kaṭhina* (hard); *viśada* (clear) — *picchila* (mucilaginous);
*ślakṣṇa* (smooth) — *khara* (harsh); *sthūla* (gross) — *sūkṣma* (subtle);
*sāndra* (viscid) — *drava* (liquid). Su. enumerates twenty-four qualities
(Sū. 46, 514-525ab), though it is said that they are twenty in number :
*śīta-uṣṇa*; *snigdha-rūkṣa*; *picchila-viśada*; *tīkṣṇa-mṛdu*; *guru-laghu*;
*drava-sāndra*; *śukṣa* (desiccated)-*ślakṣṇa*; *karkaśa* (scrabous)-*viśada*;
*sugandha* (fragrant)-*durgandha* (bad-smelling); *sara-manda*; *vyavāyin*
(diffusive)-*vikāsin* (relaxation-promoting); *āśukārin* (quickly acting)-
*sūkṣma*. The third series is summarily designated as *buddhi* (thought)
(Ca.Sū. 1, 49); acc. to Cakra this term implies special types of *buddhi*,
such as *smṛti* (remembrance), *cetanā* (consciousness), *dhṛti* (self-control),
*ahaṁkāra*, etc. The fourth series (Ca.Sū. 1, 49) is that ending with
*prayatna* (exertion); it consists of *icchā* (desire), *dveṣa* (aversion), *sukha*
(well-being), *duḥkha* (suffering) and *prayatna* (exertion) (see Ca.Śā. 1,
72ab). The fifth series is that beginning with *para*; the items of this
series are enumerated at Ca.Sū. 26, 29-30ab : *paratva* (superiority),
*aparatva* (inferiority), *yukti* (proper application), *saṁkhyā* (number),
*saṁyoga* (commixture), *vibhāga* (disunion), *pṛthaktva* (separate exis-
tence), *parimāṇa* (measure), *saṁskāra* (preparation) and *abhyāsa* (habi-
tuation). These ten terms are explained in the subsequent stanzas and
extensively commented upon by Cakra. See : Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2,

p. 360 and 369-371; Gul 1, p. 466-469; Kutumbiah, p. 37-38 and
113-114; Müller, Wörterheft, p. 95-96, nr. 76.

*gairika*

Dutt, MM, p. 96-97 : red and yellow ochre; red ochre is a silicate of
alumina coloured with oxide of iron; Nadk. 2, p. 7-11 : kaolinum, a
native white aluminium silicate; p. 95 : a clay found in lead and iron
ore and containing an excess of oxide of iron over any other clay;
there are two varieties : bole (yellow) and red ochre; the red ochre
contains more iron than the bole; Rāy, H.Ch., p. 201 : haematite,
which is red and often hard, and limonite, which is yellow or brown;
both occur in the form of ochres.
Ochre is a native earth coloured with hydrated iron oxide; it is of
two kinds, one having a clayey basis, while the other is a chalky earth.
Haematite is ferric oxide (Fe2O3); much of it occurs in a fine-grained
earthy form (red ochre); limonite, or brown iron ochre, is a natural
hydrated ferric oxide (Fe2O3 . H2O), impure and with a variable water
content.

*godhā*

A *godhā* is a varan and not an iguana, nor an alligator. PW describes
it correctly as a large kind of lizard (eine grosse Eidechsenart). MW is
wrong in saying that it is an iguana (either the gosamp or the alli-
gator); neither the iguana nor the alligator is found in India, and the
animal called *gosāmp* is a varan. The *godhā* has been rightly identified
as a varan by Hoernle; he writes (Bower Ms., p. 154, n. 374) : “godhā
or ‘Monitor’ is a name applied to several large species of lizard of the
genus *Varanus*, called by the Natives of India *gosāmp*, and by Euro-
peans miscalled ‘iguana’. They are looked upon as especially choice
food by the people who eat them. They are not any species of *Lacerta*,
which does not occur in India. So I am informed by Dr. Alcock, Super-
intendent of the Indian Museum.” In an important article by H.
Lüders (Von indischen Tieren, ZDMG 96, 1942, p. 23-81) much atten-
tion has been given to the *godhā* (p. 23-50). Lüders proves that the
*godhā* must be a varan. He says that four species of the genus *Varanus*
occur in India: *Varanus monitor*, two smaller species: *Varanus griseus*
and *flavescens*, and *Varanus salvator*, the largest species, nowadays
only found in N.E. India and Ceylon; *Varanus griseus* may be the
śvetagodhā and *Varanus flavescens* the *kapilagodhā*, both mentioned


=== Page 478 ===
462                               APPENDIX THREE

by Varāhamihira (Bṛhatsamhitā 54, 13 and 69); *Varanus salvator* is
probably the *jalajagodhã*, because it is often found in trees along
rivers and escapes into the water when alarmed; the other species are
called *sthalajagodhã*. The names of the varans mentioned by Lűders
are, acc. to Mertens (R. Mertens, Die Familie der Warane, 1942) :
*Varanus (subgenus Indovaranus* Mertens, 1942) *bengalensis* (Daudin,
1802); *V. (subgenus Psammosaurus* Fitzinger, 1826) *griseus* (Daudin,
1803); *V. (subgenus Empagusia* Gray, 1838) *flavescens* (Hardwicke et
Gray, 1827); *V. salvator* (Laurenti, 1768). In my opinion it is not
clearly established that *V. griseus* is the *śvetagodhã*; *V. griseus* is only
found at the periphery of the Indian peninsula and moreover *V.
bengalensis* may be of a yellow colour (its colour varies between yellow
and almost black); *V. flavescens* may be the *kapilagodhã*, but its colour
(yellowish) is not characteristic of the species. Much confusion about
the *godhã* is found among the commentators on medical texts. Cakra
(on Ca.Sū. 27, 38) says that a *gaṇḍaka* is a particular kind of *godhã*,
but Lűders (l.c., p. 56, n. 3) is of the opinion that *gaṇḍaka* designates
the rhinoceros. Ḍa. says (on Su.Sū. 46, 109) that the *godhã*, as well
as the *ghaḍiyāla*, is a particular kind of *kumbhīra*; Lűders (l.c., p. 70)
is of the opinion that *kumbhīra* always designates a crocodile, of which
there are three kinds in India : *Crocodylus palustris palustris* Lesson,
1831, *Crocodylus porosus porosus* Schneider, 1801, and *Gavialis gange-
ticus* (Gmelin, 1789); the latter is called *ghaṛiyāl* (l.c., p. 35 and p. 70).
See about synonyms of *godhã* : Ḍn, varga 6, 39; Ṛn, varga 19, 17;
Ma.nigh., varga 12, 109. See also : Ainslie 2, p. 263-264. See about
varans : R. Mertens, Die Familie der Warane (Varanidae), 1942; Liste
der Warane Asiens und der Indo-Australischen Inselwelt mit systemati-
schen Bemerkungen, 1959; J. Rotter, Die Warane, 1963. (*Varanus
monitor* is a nomen rejiciendum).

ghūṇa
See ch. 1, n. 60. Pr 820 : a ghuṇa is a wood-eating worm.

ghṛta — ghee.
See ch. 1, n. 19. ghṛta, ājya, sarpis and havis are synonyms acc. to
Pr 836; Dn, varga 6, 144; Rn, varga 15, 202; Ma.nigh., varga 8, 127;
Bpn, ghṛtavarga 1. In ancient times the enumerated terms were not
synonymous; see J. Gonda, The savayajñas, p. 199-200.

ghṛtapūra
(The term sarpisprapūra, found in the quotation from Tisata's Cikit-
sakalikā in M. on Mā.ni. 1, 5a-c, is probably a synonym of ghṛtapūra).
PW : Butterkuchen. MW : a sweetmeat (composed of flour, milk,
coconut and ghee). OP, p. 286 : a cake prepared with fine wheat flour
mixed with milk and fried in ghee; it is then coated with sugar; it is
also called havipūra. OP, p. 145, n. 2 (quotation from Śrīkaṇṭhadatta's
comm. on the Siddhayoga) : a havipūra, called ghevara in common
language, is made by squeezing fine wheat-flour (godhūmapaṭaśuddhikā)
with milk, frying it in a copious amount of ghee and adding white
sugar to it. Ḍa. on Su.Sū. 46, 293 : wheat-flour, squeezed with milk,
coconut and white sugar, plunged into ghee and fried, is the best kind
of ghṛtapūra; in common language it is called ghevara. Ma.nigh., varga
11, 62cd-63 : powdered wheat, squeezed with milk, strained, provided
with a copious amount of ghee and thereupon mixed with white sugar,
is taught to be a ghṛtapūra when karpūra and marica are added to it.
Vās (after giving a recipe similar to that of Ḍa.) : another way (to pre-
pare it) is as follows : take finely powdered wheat and add very clear
ghee to it to such an amount that (the flour) will lump together; then
one should squeeze it in milk; when it has become a soft mass one
should pour ghee into the vessel; when it has been well moistened,
making much noise, and has become hot, one should pour off (the fluid);
the ghṛtapūra will then rise until it has filled the vessel; whatever part
of it assumes a coppery colour should be immersed in a paste of candied
sugar. Bṛhad-yo.ta. describes various kinds of ghṛtapūra (taraṅga 16,
201-207). Bpn gives the recipe to make a pūrikā (kṛtānnavarga 48-50).

*cāturjāta*
Consists of *elā, tvac, patra* and *nāgakeśara* (the latter is also called

*caya*
I.e. accumulation, and (*pra*)kopa, i.e. excitement, of a morbiſic en-
tity are distinguished as different forms of *vṛddhi*, i.e. increase, of a
morbiſic entity. A.s.Sū. 20, 8 : increase is of two kinds : accumulation
and excitement. Ḍa. on Su.Sū. 21, 18 : accumulation is increase in a
compact form (*saṁhatirūpa*), excitement is increase in a dissolved form
(*vilayanarūpa*). The stages of the process of excitement are described
more fully : Su.Sū. 21. See : Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2, p. 335, n. 3; Gul 1,
p. 572-582 ; Kutumbiah, p. 71 and 85.

*cāṣa*
PW : der blaue Holzhäher, *Coracias indica*. MW : the blue jay.
Bhish : the blue jay; acc. to some : a kingfisher. Cakra on Ca.Sū. 27,
36 : = *kanakavāyasa* (variant : *kānanacaṭaka*). Ḍa. on Su.Sū. 29, 29 :
= *karatāṣa*. Ḍa. on Su.Sū. 46, 74 : a *cāṣa* has wings of the colour of
sapphire and is called *karatāśana* in common language. Aruṇa on
A.h.Sū. 6, 49 : = *kīkīdivī*.
The bird, designated in PW as *Coracias indica*, is called now *Coracias*
*benghalensis indica* Linnaeus, 1766. Probably *cāṣa* is *C. benghalensis*
(Linnaeus, 1758); two subspecies of this bird are common in northern
resp. southern India : *C. benghalensis benghalensis* Linnaeus, 1758 and
*C. b. indica* Linnaeus, 1766. It is a striking Oxford-and-Cambridge blue
bird with rufous-brown coloured breast and pale blue abdomen and
vent; in flight the dark and pale blue portions of the wings flash as
brilliant bands (see : Handbook of the birds of India and Pakistan 4,
p. 116-119); the subspecies *C. b. affinis* Horsfield, 1839, found in
eastern India, is darker and deeper coloured than *benghalensis* or
*indica* (see : Handbook 4, p. 119-120). See about the many species of
kingfishers found in India : Handbook 4, p. 68-98.

*cukra*
See *śukta*. Ḍa. on Su.Sū. 42, 11 and 45, 210 : *cukra* = *śukta*.

*takra* — diluted buttermilk.
PW : Buttermilch zur Hälfte mit Wasser gemischt (nach den Lexico-
gr. drei Theile Buttermilch mit einem Theile Wasser). MW : butter-
milk mixed with (a third part of) water. Dutt, MM, p. 283 : butter-

(*tuvara*) as to its taste; that, however, which is produced by churning

and (still) contains the fatty constituents while no water is added, is

it is of two kinds (again) : containing the fatty constituents or not

of water, and *takra* when it contains one fourth of water. Dravya gūṇa,

traditionally called *mathita* when it is not mixed ; the watery upper

but others say (it is *takra*) when half of it is water. Bpn, *takravarga*

*udaśvit* and *takra* ; *ghola* contains the fatty constituents and is devoid

tuents ; when one fourth of it consists of water, it is *udaśvit* and when
half of it is water, it is (called) *takra*. Bṛhad-yo.ta., *taraṇga* 23, 4cd-
7ab : the foremost among the sages, Suśruta and so on, have pro-

*ghola* contains the fatty constituents while no water is added, *mathita*
is devoid of the fatty constituents, but no water is added to it ; *takra*
is said to contain one fourth part of water and, as to *udaśvit*, half of
it consists of water ; Divodāsa, etc. have said that *takra* consists of

dadhi — thick sour milk.
        PW : saure Milch ; MW : coagulated milk, thick sour milk (differing
        from curds in not having the whey separated from it). Dutt, MM, p.
        283 : dadhi or curdled milk is prepared by adding some acid or a little
        curdled milk as a ferment to milk previously boiled; in the course of
        twelve hours the whole of the milk thus acted upon is changed into
        a more or less thick, acidulous, jelly-like mass. Cakra on Ca.Sū. 27,
        228 distinguishes three kinds of dadhi : mandaka, i.e. milk already
        subject to the process of alteration but not yet coagulated; jāta, when
        it has just coagulated and is of a sweet and somewhat acid taste;
        sujāta, when it is of a manifestly acid taste. Aruṇa on A.h.Sū. 5, 29cd
        distinguishes three varieties of dadhi : mandajāta (= mandaka), when
        the acid taste has not yet become manifest, samyagjāta, when the acid
        taste is manifest, and atijāta, when the acid taste has become excessive.
        Ma.nigh., varga 8, 88 enumerates four kinds of dadhi : thickened
        (styāna), completely thickened, somewhat thickened milk and mandaka.
        Bpn, dadhivarga 3-9 distinguishes five kinds of dadhi : manda, when
        the (acid) taste has not yet become manifest and the milk has only
        somewhat coagulated; svādu, when it has coagulated, is of a sweet
        (svādu) taste and not yet manifestly acid; svādāmla, when it is viscid
        and sweet, with an astringent after-taste; amla, when the sweet taste
        has disappeared and the acid taste has become manifest, and atyamla,
        when it has become excessively acid. Bho-ku. 1, p. 135 enumerates
        the same five varieties as Bpn and so does Bṛhad-yo.ta., taraṅga 22,
        3-9. The fatty constituents of dadhi are called dadhisāra or dadhisneha.

dhamanī — duct.
    There are twenty-four ducts in the human body acc. to Su.Śā. 9,
3-10, A.h.Śā. 3, 39-40ab and A.s.Śā. 6, 28-33, but their number is two
hundred acc. to Ca.Śā. 7, 14 and Kā.Śā. See : Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2,
p. 344-352; Kav p. 470, note; Filliozat, p. 160-162 (Fr. ed. p. 130-132);
Kutumbiah, p. 23-30 and 49-50; Müller, Wörterheft, p. 106, nr. 106;
Seal, p. 208-218.

dhātu — element (of the body).
    Seven elements of the body are distinguished : rasa (nutrient fluid),
rakta (blood), māṁsa (flesh), medas (fat), asthi (bone), majjā (marrow)
and śukra (semen). These elements are transformed into each other in
the order given. During the process of transformation they are separated
into a pure portion (prasāda) and waste matter (kiṭṭa). Each element
has its own type of waste matter (see mala). Both prasāda and kiṭṭa
may be called dhātu when they maintain their proper measure and
serve to maintain a healthy state. Moreover, there is the essential
part of the food (āhāraraśa), which is also separated into a pure portion
and waste matter, both called dhātu when present in their proper
measure. Impure matter (mala) is a synonym of waste matter (kiṭṭa)
and styled maladhātu when present in a congruous measure. The three
morbific entities (doṣa) are called dhātu when they are in a balanced
state. See about dhātu : Ca.Sū. 28, 4; Ca.Ci. 15, 15-35; Su.Sū. 14, 3-20;
Su.Sū. 15; Su.Sū. 16, 3-6; Su.Sū. 21, 3-4; A.h.Sū. 1, 13; A.s.Sū. 1, 31.
Besides the mentioned (chief) elements (of the body), a series of seven
additional elements (upadhātu) is discerned. This series consists of :
milk (stanya), the menstrual discharge (rajas), muscle-fat (vasā), sweat,
teeth, the hair and the vital fluid (ojas). Milk is the upadhātu of the
nutrient fluid, the menstrual discharge that of blood, etc. See : Śārṅga
1, 5, 16-17 and Bhā.pra. 3, 210-212. See about dhātu : Dasgupta,


=== Page 487 ===
APPENDIX THREE 471

H.I.Ph. 2, p. 319-320 and 322-324 ; Gul 1, p. 551-558 ; Jolly, Medicin,
p. 41-42 ; Kutumbiah, p. 34-36, 40-43 and 57-61 ; Müller, Vom Körper-
aufbau, p. 310-317, Ueber indische Vorstellungen von der Verdauung,
p. 203-223, Wörterheft, p. 106-107, nr. 107, Dhātu, PHMA, Heft 7,
1961, p. 3-23, Ueber verschiedene Ergebnisse, p. 106-107 ; Nobel ;
Sinh Jee, p. 91-96.

dhānya — grain and pulse.
    dhānya is divided into a number of categories; there are several
systems of classification : Ca.Sū. 27 : (1) śukadhānya : awned grain,
(2) śamīdhānya : pulse; Su.Sū. 46 : (1) śāli (i.e. śāli, ṣaṣṭika and vrīhi),
(2) kudhyānya (every kind of grain and pulse, except rice); A.h.Sū. 6
and A.s.Sū. 7 : (1) śūkadhānya, (2) śimbīdhānya (= śamīdhānya); Rn,
pariśiṣṭa, varga 16 : (1) śūkadhānya, (2) śimbīdhānya, (3) tṛṇadhānya
(grass-like kinds of grain, considered to be of an inferior quality);
Ma.nigh., dhānyavarga (10), 2-3ab : (1) śāli (raktasālyādi), (2) vrīhi
(ṣaṣṭikādi), (3) vaidala (mudgādi), (4) tṛṇadhānyaka = kṣudradhānya =
kudhyānya, (5) śākadhānya (yavādi); Bpn, dhānyavarga : (1) śāli, (2) vrīhi,
(3) śūkadhānya, (4) śimbīdhānya, (5) kṣudradhānya = kudhyānya =
tṛṇadhānya.

pūga(phala) — betel-nut.

The betel-nut is the seed of the palm Areca catechu Linn. It contains
a mixture of alkaloids; the principal ones, chemically closely related,


=== Page 491 ===

are arecaidine, arecoline, gavacinė and guvacoline. Arecoline is a

almost without parasympathicomimetic action. See : Ainslie 2, p. 268-

PW : Reisschleim, Reiswasser. MW : rice gruel or any drink mixed

mentioned are not very clear, Ḍa. quotes another opinion on the sub-

gruel from an unidentified source and also the definition of a scum
and a thin gruel according to others. He. remarks on the same passage :

When in paste, they should be mixed with the rice, and the whole

*prabhā* — lustre (of the skin).

Ca.I. 7, 14-15 describes three qualities of the skin : a) *chāyā*, the
shade, which depends on the other two qualities and is of five kinds,
viz. related to space, air, fire, water or earth; b) *varṇa*, the colour,
c) *prabhā*, the lustre, originating from the fiery element and of seven
kinds : red, yellow, white, brown, yellowish-green, pale and black.
Ca.I. 7, 16 characterizes these qualities as follows : “The shade over-
comes the colour, but the lustre reveals it; the shade is noticed when
near, but the lustre reveals itself from a distance.” Hoernle, Bower Ms.,
p. 174, n. 472 writes about *chāyā* as follows : “The word *chāyā* has
several meanings. In its widest sense it signifies the general appear-
ance of a person, in point of figure, size, colour and lustre; and any
morbid or unnatural change in these respects is an indication of ap-
proaching death. The 'reflection' of one's appearance with regard to


=== Page 495 ===
APPENDIX THREE                                                                             479

    `samsthāna` or ‘figure’ and `pramāṇa` or ‘size’ as cast in sunshine, water
    or a mirror, is called `praticchāyā`. `chāyā`, in a narrower sense, is dis-
    tinguished from it as the appearance of a person in point of `varṇa` or
    ‘colour’, and `prabhā` or ‘lustre’. Thirdly, `chāyā` signifies the mere `varṇa`
    or ‘colour’ (as different in kind : viz., red, yellow, white, blue, green,
    fallow and black, altogether seven), as distinguished from its `prabhā`
    or ‘light’ or ‘lustre’. The presence of ‘colour’ can be recognised from a
    distance by its ‘light’, but whether it is of this or that variety (red,
    yellow, etc.) can only be distinguished when near. Finally, `chāyā` is
    used in the sense of ‘morbid appearance’ just as `tṛṣṇā`, ‘thirst’, has
    also the sense of ‘morbid thirst’.”

    `prabhāva` — special faculty.

    This concept is treated Ca.Sū. 26, 67-73ab : “When one characteris-
    tically observes (in a medicinal substance) a generic similarity of taste,
    potency and digestive alteration and yet specificity of (its) actions,
    one traditionally calls this its special faculty. (For example) : `citraka`
    is regarded to be pungent (in taste), pungent with regard to its digestive
    alteration, of a hot potency (and useful in treating diarrhoea); `dantī`
    is the same (as to the enumerated qualities), but it purges a human
    being by its special faculty. Poison is said to kill poison; (its) special
    faculty is the cause of that (action); the action (of stimulating move-
    ment) in an upward direction and in the natural direction (i.e. down-
    wards) is ruled over by the special faculty. The manifold action of
    gems (and herbs) which should be worn (on the body) is brought about
    by their special faculty; special faculty is said to be inconceivable
    (`acintya`). Thus have been duly illustrated digestive alteration, potency
    and also special faculty. One (medicinal) substance performs (one) ac-
    tion by its taste and another one by its potency, another (medicinal)
    substance (does so) by its quality, digestive alteration and special
    faculty. When taste, etc. are in a congruous state with regard to their
    force, (the due order of their) inborn force (`naisargikam balam`) is (as
    follows) : digestive alteration displaces taste, potency (displaces) both
    (taste and digestive alteration) and the special faculty displaces (all of)
    these.” Cakra comments : “... That effect, which cannot accurately
    be determined by (considering it) as an effect of taste, etc. is pointed
    out as being brought about by the special faculty. For that very reason
    it has been stated that the special faculty is said to be inconceivable;
    this means that it is inconceivable as an effect of taste, potency and


=== Page 496 ===
480                                                                                    APPENDIX THREE

digestive alteration. He (i.e. *Caraka*) gives many examples because this
very (concept) is difficult to understand ..."
A.h.Sū. 9, 25 and A.s.Sū. 17, 25cd-26ab are identical with Ca.Sū. 26,
27cd-33ab. A.h.Sū. 9, 26-27ab = A.s.Sū. 17, 45-46ab : "The specific
action which occurs when taste, etc. are in a congruous state, arises
from the special faculty. Though *dantī* is comparable to *citraka* as to
taste, etc., it has a purgative action; the same applies to *mṛdvīkā*
(grapes), (when compared) with *madhuka* (liquorice), and ghee is, (com-
pared) with milk, a stimulant of the (transforming) fire;" Aruṇa com-
ments : "The special faculty of a substance is its very nature, out-
standing above qualities such as taste, potency, digestive alteration,
etc." See also *Śārṅga* 1, 2, 21cd-23ab = Bhā.pra. 1, 6, 246cd-248.
The term *prabhāva* is also used in a more general sense, designating
the power (*śakti*) of a medicinal substance and of an illness (see Ca.Vi.
1, 12-24 and Cakra's comment). See : Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2, p. 362-366;
Kutumbiah, p. 114-116; Sinh Jee, p. 116-117.

*pramāṇa* — a means of acquiring valid knowledge.

Ca.Vi. 8 describes four means of acquiring valid knowledge : (1) di-
rect apprehension (*pratyakṣa*) : 8, 39; (2) inference (*anumāna*) : 8, 40;
(3) comparison (*aupamya*) : 8, 42; (4) trustworthy tradition (*itihya*) :
8, 41. See : Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2, p. 373-377; Gul 1, p. 459-463; Kutum-
biah, Gener. Introd. p. 24-25, and p. 93-95.

*phalāmla*

See also *amla*. Vās : the group of fruits characterized by an acid
taste. Cakra on Ca.Ka. 1, 12 : the juice of *dāḍima*, etc. Ḍa. on Su.Sū.
46, 420 : *bījapūra*, etc.

*babhru*

PW and MW : a kind of large ichneumon; any ichneumon. Vās : =
*nakula* (ichneumon). Kohl (Asiatica, Festschr. Weller, 1954, p. 374) :
*nakula* = *Herpestes griseus* or *Mungo mungo*. [Both *Herpestes griseus*
and *Mungos mungo* are obsolete names : *Herpestes edwardsi lanka*
(Wroughton, 1915) = *H. griseus* Kelaart, 1852; *H. edwardsi edwardsi*
(Geoffroy, 1818) = *Mungos mungo ellioti* Wroughton, 1915; *H.*


=== Page 497 ===
APPENDIX THREE 481

edwardsi nyula (Hodgson, 1836) = *Mungos mungo moerens* Wrough-
ton, 1915; *H. edwardsi ferrugineus* Blanford, 1874 = *Mungos mungo*
pallens Ryley, 1914]. *Cakra* on Ca.Sū. 27, 35 : it is an exceedingly
hairy dog (*kukkura*) in *Parvatopakaṇṭha*; acc. to others it is a large
*nakula*. *Cakra* on Ca.Sū. 30, 77 : a large *nakula*. A.h.Sū. 6, 48, *Arunā* :
= *jāhaka*, acc. to others = *nakula*; *Candra* : = *nakula*; *He* : =
*accabhalla*.

It is generally assumed that *babhru* and *nakula* designate Indian
species of *Herpestes* (mongoose) and there is no reason to doubt this.
Six species of *Herpestes* are found in India : *Herpestes edwardsi*
(Geoffroy, 1818), *H. auropunctatus* (Hodgson, 1836), *H. vitticollis*
Bennett, 1835, *H. fuscus* Waterhouse, 1838, *H. urva* (Hodgson, 1836),
and *H. smithii* Gray, 1837. The largest species is *H. vitticollis*. Very
common are the rather large common mongoose, *H. edwardsi*, and the
much smaller small Indian mongoose, *H. auropunctatus* (see Prater,
The book of Indian animals, p. 96-105).

*basti*

An instrument, made from the bladder of an animal, with a syringe
attached to it, used to bring medicated substances into the rectum,
urethra and vagina. Dutt, MM, p. 17 : “A tube with a membranous
bag tied to its end. The bag was recommended to be made of the blad-
der of some animal, such as a bull, goat, etc. It was filled with the fluid
to be injected and tied to one end of a tube, about eight inches long
and with a tapering rounded extremity for introduction into the rec-
tum. Injections into the urethra and vagina were thrown in by similar
contrivances, the tubes being adapted in length and thickness to the
passages for which they were intended.” The term *basti* also designates
the fluid content of the instrument. There are two kinds of *basti*, dis-
tinguished with respect to the kind of fluid used : (1) *anuvāsana*, also
called *snehābasti* : an oleaginous enema; only oleaginous substances
are used for it; (2) *āsthāpana*, also called *nirūha* : a corrective enema;
other liquids, besides oleaginous substances, may be used for it; there
are two kinds of *āsthāpana* : a) *basti* in a restricted sense, designating
a clyster per anum, b) *uttarabasti*, designating a fluid brought into the
urethra. See about the application of *bastis*, their classification and the
rules about their use : Ca.Sū. 3-5; Su.Ci. 35-38; A.h.Sū. 19; A.s.Sū. 28;
Bhe.Si. 5-8; Kā.Sī. 2; Kā.Sī. 5-8; Kā.Khi. 8; Hā. 4, 3. See : HB, p.
105, n. 142; Jolly, Medicin, p. 26-27.

**bisa — mṛṇāla**

See also *śālū*(ka). There is much confusion about the exact mean-
ing of these terms, as is clearly visible from the material collected:
PW : *bisa* : Wurzel­schoss, Untergrundstengel des Lotus; die jungen
Wurzelschosse des Nelumbium und einiger Nymphaeen (namentlich N.
*edulis* [N. lotus Linn. = N. edulis DC.] so wie die im Boden befind-
lichen Theile des Stengels werden mit Vorliebe gegessen (Roxb.), und
scheinen schon in frühester Zeit als Leckerbissen gegolten zu haben;
*mṛṇāla* : die essbare röhrige an den Knoten mit Fasern besetzte Wurzel
der Lotusarten. MW : *bisa* : a shoot or sucker, the film or fibre of the
water-lily or lotus, also the stalk itself or that part of it which is under-
ground (eaten as a delicacy); *mṛṇāla* : the edible fibrous root of some
kinds of lotus, a lotus-fibre, fibre attached to the stalk of a water-lily.
Bhish : *bisa* : bulb of the lotus plant; *mṛṇāla* : the upper stem of the
lotus plant; vol. 1, p. 525, footnote : certain authorities aver that the
inner lining or membranous fibres of a lotus-stem are called *bisa*, the
outer covering being known as *mṛṇāla*. Dutt, MM, p. 110 : *mṛṇāla* is
the leaf-stalk of Nymphaea lotus Linn., N. stellata Willd. and N. rubra
Roxb. HB, p. 166, n. 435 : *bisa* is the root-stalk or scape, i.e. that
part of the stalk which is embedded in the ground down to the roots;
hence *bisagranthi* is the same as *padmamūla*, i.e. properly, the knots
of the underground stalk; it is opposed to *mṛṇāla*, the above-ground,
or leaf-stalk. HK : *bisa* : grobe Lotusstengel; *mṛṇāla* : Blattstengel
von *kamala* = *padma*, feine Lotusstengel. See also : Bosch, De gouden
kiem, p. 9; id., The golden germ, p. 23 ff.

Besides *bisa* and *mṛṇāla* the following terms are used to designate
parts of a lotus or water-lily : (*padma*-, etc.) *kanda, tantu, nāla* and
*mūla*, moreover *śālū*(ka) and *bisāṇḍa*.

Pr 676 : *mṛṇāla* = *padmamūla*; 677 : *bisa* = *padmakanda*; 678 : *nāla*
is (the stalk) to which the flowers, etc. are attached (*puṣpādibandhana*).
Dn, varga 4, 161 and Rn, varga 10, 258 : *bisa, mṛṇāla* and *padmanāla*
are synonyms. Rn, varga 10, 258 : *padmatantu* = *bisa*. Ma.nigh., varga
3, 83 : *bisa* = *mṛṇāla*; *padmādimūla* = *śālūka*. Su.Sū. 46, 464 enumer-
ates *mṛṇāla, bisa* and *śālūka* as three separate items; Ḍa. observes :
*mṛṇāla* = *padmanāla, bisa* = *bhisāṇḍaka, śālūka* is well known. Ḍa.
comments on Su.Sū. 46, 298 : *bisa* is the root (*mūla*) of *padma*, but
others say that it is the gross stalk (*sthūlapadmanāla*); *mṛṇāla* is the
gross offshoot of the root of *padma* (*padmamūlāt sthūlaprarohaḥ*), but
others say that it is the fine stalk (*sūkṣmam nālam*); Ḍa. on Su.U. 54,


=== Page 499 ===
APPENDIX THREE 483

14 : *bisa* = *bisāṇḍaka*. A.h.Sū. 6, 91, Aruņa and Candra : *mṛṇāla* is
of two kinds, fine and gross; the fine one is (called) *mṛṇāla* (in its pro-
per sense), the gross one *bisa*; He. : *mṛṇāla* is the fine and *bisa* the gross
root of *kamala*. It is difficult to determine the meaning of the mentioned
terms with certainty and the commentators are of little help on ac-
count of their disagreeing opinions. Nevertheless there are some terms
which may be assigned to a part of a particular type of plant with
some degree of accuracy. The genus *Nymphaea* possesses creeping root-
stocks; the rootstock of N. *lotus* Linn. is tuberous, short, erect and
roundish, that of N. *stellata* Willd. is ovoid, short and acute; Nelum-
*bium* *speciosum* Willd., however, has a slender, elongated, much-
branched and creeping rhizome, sending out roots at the nodes (see
Cooke 1, p. 26-28; Duthie 1, p. 33-35; Hooker 1, p. 114-115). From
these data we may infer that *padmakanda*, *bisāṇḍaka* and *bhisāṇḍaka*
designate the rootstock of species of Nymphaea. It may be that *bisa*
refers to the rootstock of Nymphaea and *mṛṇāla* to the slender rhizome
of Nelumbium, but this is not certain; another possibility is that *bisa*
designates the gross and *mṛṇāla* the fine parts of the rhizome of Nelum-
bium, or *mṛṇāla* is a term for the roots sent out from the nodes of the
rhizome, and this does not exhaust the number of possible interpreta-
tions. *nāla* probably means the stalk of the leaves and flowers of Nym-
phaea and Nelumbium. Acc. to Rau (Asiatica, Festschrift Weller,
1954, p. 511) Indian poets distinguished species of Nymphaea from
Nelumbium.

madya — intoxicating beverage.

Dutt, MM, p. 273 : all fermented and distilled liquors causing in-
toxication are called madya or madirā in Sanskrit. OP, p. 75 : strong
liquors are called madya. See the article madya in Vśs. Su.Sū. 45, 170,

madhu — honey.

Several varieties of honey are distinguished : Ca.Sū. 27, 243-244 :
“mākṣika, bhrāmara, kṣaudra and pauttika are the (four) classes of
honey; mākṣika is the best of these and bhrāmara is especially heavy;
mākṣika has the colour of (sesame) oil, pauttika that of ghee, kṣaudra
is monkey-coloured and bhrāmara is said to be white.” Cakra remarks :
mākṣikās are tawny (bees); bhrāmaras are well known; kṣaudra is made
by small (kṣudra) makṣikās; puttikās are large, tawny makṣikās. Su.Sū.
45, 133 : “The eight classes of honey are : pauttika, bhrāmara, kṣaudra,
mākṣika, chātra, arghya, auddālaka and dāla.” Da. remarks : (1) puttikās
are large, tawny makṣikās; others say that puttikās are makṣikās of a
black colour that resemble maśaka (a maśaka is a stinging gnat or
fly); (2) bhrāmaras are well known; (3) kṣudrās are completely tawny,
very small makṣikās; (4) makṣikās (in a restricted sense) are large and
of a tawny colour; others say that they are exceedingly small; (5) that
(kind of honey) which is made (in a nest) of the form of a parasol (or :
mushroom, chatraka) by (makṣikās) of a yellow and tawny colour,
called baga in common language, in the forests of the Himālaya and in
those of Mālava, is called chātra; (6) that (honey) which is produced
from the flowers of the madhūka trees in Jaratkārvarāśrama (‘Jaratkāru’s
hermitage’, the name of a locality), is arghya honey, called śvetaka
(white) by the people of Mālava; others say that arghya is produced by
(makṣikās) called arghā, which have sharp mouth-parts (tīkṣṇatuṇḍa),
are of a yellow colour and resemble ṣaṭpadas (‘six-footed’ animals);
(7) the uddālakas are very small, monkey-coloured kīṭas which usually
accumulate honey (called auddālaka) in termitaries; (8) dāla : a dala
is a petal (patra) and (the honey) which is present on (these petals) is

(called) dāla, but others say that completely tawny, very small makṣi-

accumulated in the interior of the cavities of trees by very small
makṣikās which look like pieces of sapphire (indranīladalala), is called
dāla. Thus has been told, in due order, the production of this (honey)
of eight varieties. mākṣika is of the colour of (sesame) oil, bhrāmara is
said to be white, kṣaudra has a tawny colour, pauttika resembles ghee,
chātra is slightly yellow, arghya is tawny, auddāla resembles gold and
dāla is slightly yellow.” See also Hā. 1, 18, 1 and 8; Bpn, madhuvarga
6-24; Rā.va.nigh., pariccheda 3, 333-338; Bṛhad-yo.ta., taraṅga 29,

honey-bees in India : (1) Apis dorsata Fabr.; this is probably the
bhramara; (2) Apis indica Fabr., a smaller species; one of its names
is ṣatpada; (3) Apis florea Fabr., the smallest species, about the size
of the domestic fly.

marman — vital point.

    The vital points are one hundred and seven in number. See about
    these : Ca.Śā. 7, 14; Su.Śā. 6; A.h.Śā. 4; A.s.Śā. 7. Ca. distinguishes
    three principal vital points, called mahāmarman : head, heart and
    bladder (Ci. 26, 1-3), but also enumerates six principal vital points
    (Śā. 7, 9). A.s. makes mention of seven principal vital points (Śā. 5,
    59-60). Kā. remarks (śārīrasthāna) that head, heart and bladder are
    the three principal vital points. See : Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2, p. 352;
    Filliozat, p. 163-164 (Fr. ed. p. 133-134); Kutumbiah, p. 146-155.

mala — impurity.

    The impurities are described : Ca.Sū. 28, 4 : the ingested food is
    separated into a pure portion (prasāda) which is called rasa, and waste
    matter (kiṭṭa); the rasa of the food (āhārarasa) is transformed into the
    element rasa (the nutrient fluid), and so on (see : dhātu); the āhārarasa,
    the element rasa and each of the subsequent elements have their own
    form of waste matter (kiṭṭa), called impure matter (mala); these im-
    purities consist of : sweat, urine, faeces, flatus (vāta), bile, phlegm, the
    impurities of the ears, eyes, nose, mouth, pores of the hairs and genera-
    tive organs, the hairs of the head, the beard, the body-hair, the nails,
    etc. Ca.Ci. 15, 18-19ab : the waste matter of the food consists of faeces
    and urine, that of the nutrient fluid is phlegm, of blood it is bile, of


=== Page 505 ===
APPENDIX THREE 489
flesh it is the particular impurities (svamala, i.e. those of the ears, eyes,
nose, mouth and generative organs), of fat it is sweat, of the bones it
consists of the hair of the head and the body-hair, of marrow it con-
sists of the fatty substance of the eyes and the skin. Ca.Sā. 6, 17 :
impure constituents of the body are those which bring trouble to the
body; they consist of : the excretions (upadeha) which come out of the
various openings of the body, elements which have become putrescent
(paripakva, i.e. overripe), excited wind, bile and phlegm and all the
other constituents present in the body, of whatever kind they may be,
that injure it; all those (constituents) are designated as impure matter.
Su.Sū. 46, 528a and 529 : faeces and urine are the impurities (derived)
from the food; the impurities of the elements (of the body) are, in due
order, phlegm, bile, the impure matter of the openings (of the body),
sweat, nails and body-hair, and (finally) the impure matter of the
and the fatty substance of the skin. (Su.Sū. 46, 529 = Śārṅga 1, 5,
15 = Bhā.pra. 3, 209). A.h.Sā. 3, 61cd and 63cd-64ab : the transparent
part of the waste matter of the food is urine, the dense part consists
of faeces; the impurities of the elements (of the body) are, in their due
order, phlegm, bile, the impurities of the openings (of the body), sweat,
nails and body-hair, the fatty matter of the excretions of the eyes and
the skin and (finally) the vital fluid (as the impurity of the element
semen). A.s.Sā. 6, 65-66 : the transparent part of the waste matter of
the food is urine, the dense part consists of faeces; the impure matter
of the nutrient fluid consists of phlegm and lasikā (serous fluid), of
blood it is bile, of flesh it consists of the impurities of the ears, eyes,
nose, mouth, pores of the hair and generative organs, of fat it is sweat,
of the bones it consists of the hairs of the head, the body-hair and the
nails, of marrow it consists of the impure matter of the eyes and the
fatty substance of the skin; the essential part of semen is the vital
fluid; because (semen) is very pure, it has no impure matter; others
say that the essential part of semen is the germ (of the embryo).

Another series of impurities is enumerated : Śārṅga 1, 5, 13-14 : the
following impurities arise from the seven elements (of the body), in
their due order : the water of the tongue, eyes and cheeks (arises from
the nutrient fluid), the colouring bile (from the blood), the impure
matter in the ears (arises from flesh), the impure matter of the tongue,
teeth, armpits, penis, etc. (from fat), nails (arise from the bones), the
impure matter of the eyes and the oleaginous matter in the mouth
(arise from marrow) and pustules (piṇḍikā) (arise from semen). Different
again is the enumeration found Manusmṛti 5, 135. The term mala may

medaka
    PW and MW : spirituous liquor used for distillation. Dutt, MM, p.
274 : the liquor distilled from rice receives different names according
to its consistency; the clear transparent fluid which floats on the top
is called prasannā; that below it, is called kādambarī; jagala is a

prasannā is the scum of surā; kādambarī is more dense than (prasannā);
the portion lower than (kādambarī) is called jāṅgala (= jagala) and
medaka is more dense than jagala (compare Śāriṅga 2, 10, 5-6; see :
surā). Cakra on Ca.Sū. 25, 49 : medaka is śvetasurā, called jagala.
Aruṇa on A.h.Sū. 5, 68 : medaka is the lower part of jagala, and jagala

Kangle p. 177; transl. J. J. Meyer, p. 186-187; transl. Sham. p. 132-
133) : medaka is prepared with one droṇa of water, half an āḍhaka
of rice and three prasthas of kiṇva; Kaut. 2, 25, 27 : the formula for
the requisite spices (sambhāra) to be added to medaka is : five karṣas
of each of (the following items) : pāṭhā, lodhra, tejovatī, elavāluka,
madhuka, madhurasā, priyaṅgu, dāruharidrā, marica and pippalī.

maireya
    PW : ein aus Zucker und andern Stoffen bereitetes berauschendes
Getränk. MW : a kind of intoxicating drink (acc. to Suśr., Sch. a com-
bination of surā and āsava). Dutt, MM, p. 274 : a sort of spirituous

of both āsava and surā, put in one vessel, should be known (after it

Su.Sū. 45, 170, Da. : mention is made of that āsava which has a three-
fold matrix and is called maireya; maireya, taken in that sense, arises

492                                APPENDIX THREE

when *surā* and *āsava*, prepared separately and mixed together, are
made to ferment again; *surā* is prepared from flour (*surā paiṣṭī*); *āsava*

*yūkā* — louse.
    Rn, *pariśiṣṭa, varga* 19, 31-32ab : a *yūkā* is a *kīṭa* of the hair of the

*rasa* — taste.

Six tastes are distinguished in classical Indian medicine : *madhura*
(sweet), *amla* (acid), *lavaṇa* (saline), *kaṭu* (pungent), *tikta* (bitter) and
*kaṣāya* (astringent). See about the tastes, their combinations, actions,
etc. : Ca.Sū. 26; Su.Sū. 42; Su.U. 63; A.h.Sū. 10; A.s.Sū. 18; Bhe.Sū.
12; Bhe.Vi. 1; Kā.Khi. 6; Bhā.pra. 6, 170-194. See on the subject of
the tastes : Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2, p. 357-360; Jolly, Medicin, p. 25-26;
Kutumbiah, p. 37, 114-115, 118-119; Lüders, Medizinische Sanskrit-
texte aus Turkistan; Müller, Grundlagen, p. 52-54, Grundsätze, p. 36-
49, Eigenwertungen, p. 66-72, Vorstellungen von der Verdauung, p.
198-203, Wörterheft, p. 129, nr. 173; Nobel; Sinh Jee, p. 101-103.

*rasaudana* — rice boiled in meat broth.
      About boiled rice (*odana*), the various ways it may be prepared and

*roga* — disease.
      See : *vyādhi*.

*rocana* — appetizing.
      Aruṇa and Candra on A.h.Sū. 5, 30: *rocana* is that which, like *ghṛta*
      *pūra*, etc., gives appetite (*rocate*), but does not destroy (the disorder
      called) inability to eat (*aruci*); *rociṣṇu* means : acting as an appetizer,
      and is applied to substances which, at the end of a meal, give appetite
      again to persons who were already satisfied; there are also substances,
      like *paṭola* leaves, which are not appetizing but yet destroy *aruci*
      (*arucighna*).

*laṅghana* — reducing measures.
      PW : Fasten. MW : fasting, starving system. Gul : lightening therapy,
      starvation. Kav p. 399 : anything that lightens or attenuates (the aggra-
      vated humours). Ca.Sū. 22, 9ab : “Everything that brings about light-
      ness of the body is traditionally called *laṅghana*.” Ca.Sū. 22, 18 : “Re-
      ducing measures consist of the four types of purificatory procedure,
      (being subject to) thirst, (exposure to) the wind and the heat (of the
      sun), maturation-promoting measures, fasting and physical exercise.”
      See also : *apatarpaṇa*. See : Kutumbiah, p. 138-141.

meat of a round shape or a variety of confectionary usually having a

lavana — salt.

Several kinds of salt are distinguished :
(1) saindhava, rock-salt; it is found in deposits in Sindh and the
Pañjāb (Watt CP, p. 963-965).
(2) sauvarcala, sonchal salt; acc. to Nadk. (2 p. 100), who quotes
N. N. Sen Gupta on this subject, it is a dark coloured salt made by
dissolving common salt in a solution of crude soda and evaporating it;
acc. to Rāy, p. 228-229, it is saltpetre; acc. to Cakra on Ca.Sū. 27,
303 and Ḍa. on Su.Sū. 46, 313 it is also called black salt (kālalavaṇa);
Dn, varga 7, 67 calls it rucaka.
(3) biḍa or viḍa; this is an artificially prepared black salt; see Nadk.
2, p. 98-99 about the methods of preparing it; Ḍa. remarks on Su.Sū.
46, 313 that it is an artificially prepared salt, made by heating (and
evaporating a solution consisting of) a mixture of the paste of (the
plant called) prasāraṇī and common table-salt (bhaktalavaṇa).
(4) audbhida; Nadk. 2, p. 100-101 : it is a saline efflorescence on
reh lands (see Watt CP, p. 51); acc. to Cakra on Ca.Sū. 27, 303 it is
called utkārikā; Ḍa. says on Su.Sū. 46, 313 that it is made by evapo-
rating, either by the heat of the sun or by fire, an alkaline water that
comes out of the earth (this may refer to subsoil brine and brine-
springs; see about these Watt CP, p. 965-967).
(5) sāmudra(ka), sun-dried sea salt; Cakra remarks on Ca.Sū. 27, 304
that it is made on the shores of the southern sea (see Watt CP, p. 969,
about Madras salt).
(6) romaka; this is the salt from the Sambhar lake near Ajmer; it is
also called śākambharīya; Ḍa. remarks on Su.Sū. 46, 313 that it comes
from the śākambharī region and that others say its origin is the rumā
lake.
(7) pāṁsuja; Nadk. 2, p. 101 : salt manufactured from saline earth;
Cakra says on Ca.Sū. 27, 304 that it originates from the eastern sea;
Aruṇa remarks on A.h.Sū. 6, 149, where it is called pāṁsūṭṭha, that it

*lāja*, m. pl. — parched grain.
PW : geröstetes Korn. MW : fried or parched grain (esp. rice grain).

*lekhana* — attenuating.
PW : in Fluss bringend. MW : attenuating. Bhish : liquefying, at-

Bhā.pra. 6, 224 : “That which desiccates the elements (of the body)
or the impurities and scrapes them away is called *lekhana*.”

*vāruṇī*
PW : Branntwein. MW : a partic. kind of spirit (prepared from hog-
weed mixed with the juice of the date or palm and distilled), any
spirituous liquor. Dutt, MM, p. 273 : the fermented juice of the palm
and date trees. HB, p. 80, n. 18 : *vāruṇī* is the liquor made by fermenting
the sap of the palmyra and date palms (the *tāla* or Borassus flabelli-
formis, and the *kharjūra* or Phoenix sylvestris), commonly called
‘palm-wine’; it is mentioned in the Vāruṇī Jātaka (I, 120) as a kind
of spirits, dearer than *surā*, or spirits of rice. OP, p. 301 : a strong
liquor prepared by fermenting the juices of palm fruit and dates.
Sārṅga 2, 10, 7ab : *vāruṇī* is the fermented juice of *tāla* and *kharjūra*
(see also Āḍhamalla's remarks). Ma.nigh., varga 8, 170 : *vāruṇī* is
thought to be prepared with *punarnavā* and ground *śāli* rice. Bpn,
*samdhānavarga* 24 : *vāruṇī* is said to be prepared with ground *punar-
navā* and *śāli* rice; the (liquor) prepared by fermentation of the juice
of *tāla* and *kharjūra* is also (called) *vāruṇī*. A.h.Sū. 5, 68, Candra : the
upper transparent (part, i.e. the) scum of *surā* is called *vāruṇī* or

*vipāka* — digestive alteration.

There are divergent opinions on the subject of *vipāka* : Ca.Sū. 26,
57cd-58 : “Usually it is thus that substances with a pungent, bitter


=== Page 516 ===
500
APPENDIX THREE

and astringent taste become pungent by digestive alteration, acid sub-
stances (remain) acid, savoury substances become sweet and saline ones
sweet as well.” Cakra points to the word ‘usually’, because there are ex-
ceptions to these rules; he defines *vipāka* as that quality which is pro-
duced at the time of completion of the contact of the ingested food
with the abdominal fire. A.h.Sū. 9, 20-21 agrees with Ca.Sū. 26, 57cd-
58 : “Usually savoury and acrid (*paṭu*, = *lavaṇa*) substances become
sweet by digestive alteration, acid substances (remain) acid, and bitter,
irritant (*ūṣaṇa*, = *kaṭu*) and astringent ones become pungent;” *vipāka*
is defined (Sū. 9, 20) as follows : “When, owing to the contact with
the abdominal fire, another taste arises at the end of the transformation
of the tastes, one traditionally calls this digestive alteration.” A.s.Sū.
17, 17-20 agrees with A.h. and Ca., but adds that three degrees of the
transformed tastes should be distinguished : slight, moderate and pre-
ponderant; moreover it mentions the divergent view of Parāśara who
was of the opinion that acid substances are acid after digestive altera-
tion, pungent substances pungent and the remaining four (sweet, bitter,
astringent and saline substances) sweet. Su. differs from Ca., A.h. and
A.s.; Su.Sū. 40, 10-12 : “Some say that digestive alteration is (the)
predominant (quality of a substance). Why (do they say so) ? Because
there is a proper and improper digestive alteration. All ingested sub-
stances generate, when properly or improperly altered by digestion, a
quality or a fault (*doṣa*). Others say with regard to this (subject) that
digestion (occurs) with regard to the tastes. Some want it to be of
three kinds : sweet, acid and pungent. That, however, is not suitable
because there is, on account of the qualities of the gross elements, no
acid digestive alteration different from that of immature matter; for
bile, when combustively altered, reaches an acid condition, because of
its fiery nature. If it would be thus, (that there is an acid digestive
alteration), there would also be a saline digestive alteration, for phlegm,
when combustively altered, reaches a saline condition. Some say that
a sweet (substance) is sweet (after digestive alteration), an acid one
acid and so on ... Others say that weak (tastes) come under the control
of strong ones (during the process of digestive alteration). An establish-
ed doctrine does not arise in that way and therefore the question re-
mains unsettled. According to traditional doctrine there are only two
kinds of digestive alteration : a sweet and a pungent one. Of these,
that one called sweet is heavy and that one called pungent, light. In
this respect (the five gross elements, i.e.) earth, water, fire, air and
space, are (regarded as) composed of two groups on account of simi-


=== Page 517 ===
APPENDIX THREE                                                          501

larities of their qualities (and characteristics of) heaviness or lightness;
earth and water are heavy, the remaining ones light. Therefore diges-
tion is only of two kinds. (The following stanzas) pertain to this (sub-

qualities of water and earth appear in excess, the digestion is said to
be sweet; with regard to substances in which, when being digested,

vīrya — potency.
         Potency is described : Ca.Sū. 26, 62-65 : “Some say that potency is

of eight kinds : soft, sharp, heavy, light, oleaginous, dry, hot and cold;

potency, for every action is brought about by potency.” Su.Sū. 40, 5 :

brought about by potency. That which is called potency is described
by him as being in conformity with this meaning only when applied
to (the qualities) heavy, etc., which are essential ones in the whole of
the qualities, displaying great power, and by reason of the fact that
they are the foremost to be designated and the very first to be per-
ceived. On these grounds that (which is called vīrya) is declared not to
refer to taste, etc., because (the latter) are of an opposite nature,
though (the qualities heavy, etc.) are present in them. Others say that
potency is of two kinds only, hot and cold, and that even a substance
of a manifold nature surpasses never at all the two great forces (called)
agnī and soma, as the universe (never surpasses) that which is manifest
and not manifest.” See about vīrya also : A.s.Sū. 17, 11-16; Śārṅga 1,
2, 17cd-18; Bhā.pra. 6, 238. See : Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2, p. 361-366;

vyādhi — illness.

The following synonyms are used to designate disease : ātaṅka,
ābādha, āmaya, gada, jvara, duḥkha, pāpman, yakṣman, roga, vikāra
and vyādhi (see Ca.Ni. 1, 5; Ca.Ci. 3, 11; A.h.Ni. 1, 1). Acc. to Filliozat
(Kumāratantra, p. 73, n. 3) roga means pain, not illness, and vyādhi
corresponds to disease. Filliozat observes that roga and vyādhi are
clearly distinguished in medical treatises; roga points to a local lesion
and vyādhi to a general affection; the sense of roga is near to morbid
symptom and that of vyādhi to syndrome. In the Madhukośa, however,
and in many medical texts and commentaries, roga and vyādhi are
used as synonyms, as well as ātaṅka, āmaya and gada. Sometimes roga
is a synonym of ruj or rujā and means pain; the latter two terms may
also occur denoting disease; vikāra is often used in a broader sense than
roga and vyādhi and refers to a morbid process in such cases. See also :
Müller, Wörterheft, p. 131, nr. 178 (roga) and p. 137-138, nr. 198
(vyādhi).

śarkarā — (ground) sugar.

śarkarā is one of the products of the sugar-cane, which are called,
as a group, ikṣuvikāra or ikṣuvikṛti. Several of these substances are
distinguished:

1) the juice, divided into two or more varieties : a) obtained by
chewing, b) obtained by mechanical pressure, c) obtained by mechani-
cal pressure but having stood for a time (paryuṣita) (only Bhā.pra.),
d) the boiled juice (Su.; Dravyaguṇa; Bhā.pra.)
2) the inspissated juice (phāṇita; Bpn, ikṣuvarga 21 : sugar-cane
juice which by boiling has become somewhat inspissated but is still
liquid to a considerable degree); phāṇita is called kṣudraguḍa in Ca.
(Sū. 27, 239); kṣudraguḍa(ka) as a synonym of phāṇita is mentioned :
Ḍa. on Su.Sū. 45, 159, Aruṇa on A.h.Sū. 5, 47 and Ma.nigh., varga 9, 13.
3) treacle (guḍa); there are differences of opinion about guḍa; usu-
ally it means sugar-cane juice that has become very thick by boiling
(Ḍa. on Su.Sū. 45, 159), but Bpn, ikṣuvarga 24-25 says : sugar-cane
juice which has become firm like a clod of clay by boiling it a long time is
called guḍa, but in Gauḍadeśa guḍa is called matsyāṇḍī; several varie-
ties of guḍa are distinguished : Ca.Sū. 27, 239 : a) sugar-cane juice
boiled down to one fourth, b) one third, c) half of its original quantity,
d) washed guḍa; Su.Sū. 45, 160-161 : purified (pure white) and not
purified (of a dark colour); A.h.Sū. 5, 47cd-48 : a) washed, b) not
washed, c) old and d) fresh; Dravyaguṇa, aikṣavādivarga 7-9 : a) wash-
ed, b) not washed, c) somewhat old; Bpn, ikṣuvarga 26-27 : a) old and
b) fresh.
4) crude sugar (matsyaṇḍikā, matsyaṇḍī); Bpn, ikṣuvarga 22-23 des-
cribes it differently : sugar-cane juice which has become thick by
boiling and contains only a small quantity of liquid is called matsyaṇḍī,
because it flows slowly (mandam yat syandate).
5) candied sugar (khaṇḍa).
6) ground sugar (śarkarā, also called śvetā, sitā, sitopalā; Bpn, ikṣu-
varga 30 : śarkarā or sitā is very white and looks like gravel). Sugar
was, as well as from the sugar-cane, also obtained from honey (madhujā)
and from yāsa (also called yavāsa, equated by the commentators with
the plant called durālabhā) (Cakra on Ca.Sū. 27, 241; He. on A.h.Sū.
5, 50ab); some sources mention a kind of sugar obtained from flowers
(Ma.nigh., varga 9, 13; Bpn, ikṣuvarga 31). See about these products
of the sugar-cane and other kinds of sugar : Ca.Sū. 27, 237-242; Su.Sū.
45, 157-167; A.h.Sū. 5, 44-53; Dravyaguṇa, aikṣavādivarga 1-14;

Ma.nigh., varga 9, 10-20; Bpn, ikṣuvarga 16-32. See also : Ainslie 1,

śāllaki

śāllaki, śāllakī, śāllaka and śalyaka mean : porcupine. PW remarks
(s.v. śalyaka) that it is a porcupine distinguished from another type
called śvāvidh. Not all the texts, however, maintain this distinction :
Ma.nigh., varga 12, 40 says that a śāllaka is also called śvāvidh; Bpn,
māṁsavarga 51 does not distinguish them either. The commentators
and nighaṇṭus are not of much help in identifying this animal; usually
only one or more synonyms are enumerated : Ca.Sū. 27, 38, Cakra :
a śāllaka is a mahāśakalin, called śālaka (in common language). Su.Sū.
46, 78, Ḍa. : a śalyaka is a vajraśakala, called śālā in common language.
Pr 802 : a śālūka (variants : śāllaka, sallaka) is (also called)śālalin
and śālin. Rn, pariśiṣṭa, varga 19, 3 : a śalyaka is (also called) śalyamṛga
and vajraśukti. Ma.nigh., varga 12, 40 : a śāllaka is (also called) śālalin,
śvāvidh, medhā, śūcini and kharā. Bpn, māṁsavarga 51 : a sedhā is (also
called) śalyaka and śvāvidh. Only Ḍa. (on Su.Sū. 46, 78) makes a re-
mark about the form of the animal and says that it resembles a large
godhā. Acc. to Seal (p. 191) śāllaka means a porcupine and śvāvidh a
hedgehog. Acc. to Gul a porcupine is called śvāvidh (vol. 6, Animals
and birds, p. 78, nr. 110) and a hedgehog kūrcikā (p. 66, nr. 60). Three
species of porcupine are found in India; the most common species is
*Hystrix indica* Kerr, 1792; *H. hodgsoni* (Gray, 1847) is found only in
the central and eastern Himālayas, Assam and lower Bengal; the third
species, *Atherurus macrourus* (Linnaeus, 1758), found in lower Bengal
and Assam, is an uncommon animal (see : Prater, The book of Indian
animals, p. 215-217; Fauna of India, Mammalia, second ed., vol. 3,
Rodentia, part 1, p. 288-313). The most common hedgehogs of northern
India are *Hemiechinus auritus* (Gmelin, 1770) and *Paraechinus micro-
pus* (Blyth, 1846) (see : Prater, p. 166-167). The śāllaki, resembling a
large godhā acc. to Ḍa. cannot be a porcupine or hedgehog; it may be
tentatively identified as the Indian pangolin, *Manis crassicaudata*
Gray, 1827 (see : Prater, p. 301-303).

*śāli*
    Dutt, MM, p. 269 : rice reaped in the cold season. Kav p. 50 : *śāli*
is red paddy, i.e. the paddy that is gathered at the end of autumn;

when still unhusked and belongs to (the season of) winter; others say
that it is white, both unhusked and husked, and that it belongs to
(the season of) winter. Kaut. 2, 24, 12 (text p. 77; transl. Kangle p.
172; transl. J. J. Meyer p. 179; transl. Sham. p. 128) : both *śāli*
and *vrīhi* rice belong to the class of seeds called *pūrvavāpa* (to be
sown first, i.e. at the beginning of the rainy season.)

śukta = cukra — verjuice.

PW : jedes durch Fermentation mit Pflanzenstoffen gewonnene saure
Getränk, saurer Reisschleim u.s.w. MW : anything fermented or be-

or cukra is thus prepared : take of treacle one part, honey two parts,

fermentation (abhiśuta) during one month, six months or a year,
either mixed with cirbhiṭa, ervāruka, joints of the sugar-cane, mango
fruits or āmalaka, or pure (without the mentioned additions), constitutes
the śukta group. Su.Sū. 45, 210, Ḍa. : śukta is also called cukra, as has
been said : “The whey, etc., which, together with treacle, kṣaudra
honey or kāñjika, has been put in a clean vessel (and kept in a heap
of grain for three days, is called śukta or cukra” (= Pr 1652-1653); it
is, together with sugar-cane juice, madhūka flowers, pīlu, etc., (but)
without anything astringent, subjected to fermentation; others say
that the fermented juice of tubers, etc. is also (called) śukta. Su.Sū.

śāḍava

    PW : Zuckerwerk mit Früchten u.s.w. (die richtige Form ist khāṇḍa-

`saṃdhi` — juncture.
    The number of junctures in the human body is said to be two hundred

*sīdhu, śīdhu*.

See ch. 1, n. 127 about *sīdhu* prepared from boiled and unboiled

(Su.Sū. 45, 186), made, acc. to Ḍa., from a decoction of *vibhītaka* (=

Ḍa., that treacle should be added, others are of the opinion this should
not be done. e) *śarkara* (Su.Sū. 45, 183; *Dravyaguṇa, madyādivarga* 13),
made, acc. to Ḍa., from refined sugar (*guḍaśarkarā*) or candied sugar
(*khaṇḍaśarkarā*).

*surā*

The term *surā* has a very broad sense in Ca. (see Ca.Sū. 27, 179-195)
and is applied to an alcoholic beverage together with its scum (*maṇḍa*);
the scum of *surā* is called *madirā* (see Cakra's comment); several bever-
ages, called *sīdhu* in Su., are included in Ca.'s concept of *surā*; Ḍa.
mentions separately (Sū. 27, 190) a variety of *surā* made from barley.
Ḍa. remarks (on Su.Sū. 45, 175cd-176ab) that *surā* is of a red colour
and somewhat turbid from the paste of ground *kiṇva* (ferment). The

varieties of surā, mentioned in Su., are : a) śvetā (Sū. 45, 176-cd-177ab);
