surāsava
PW : ein durch Maischen unreifer Fruchtkörner gewonnener Brannt-
wein. MW : beer or spirituous liquor produced by the fermentation of
unripe corn. Ca.Sū. 27, 187, Cakra : (an āsava) in (the manufacture of)
which surā takes the place of water; a similar remark is made by Ḍa.
in his comment on Su.Sū. 45, 187cd-188ab.

soma and agni
Phlegm (kapha) is often said to be of the nature of soma (saumya)
and bile (pitta) of the nature of agni (āgneya). See e.g. Ca.Sū. 12, 11-12;
A.h.Sā. 3, 90 and 96. See moreover on this subject : Kirfel, Die fünf
Elemente; Kutumbiah, p. 64; Müller, Wörterheft, p. 82, nr. 30 and
p. 148, nr. 236.

sauvīra — a partic. type of collyrium.
See : añjana.

sauvīra
PW : saurer Gersten-, Reis-, oder Weizenschleim. MW : sour gruel.
Dutt, MM, p. 12 : other grains besides paddy are sometimes used for
acetous fermentation (see : kāñjika); if the husked grains of barley
are boiled and steeped in water, the resulting acid liquor is called
sauvīra. HK : saurer Gerstenschleim. OP, p. 181, n. 4 : sour gruel pre-
pared with husked cereals. Dn, varga 6, 251 : sauvīra is made from
barley and wheat. Rn, varga 15, 297 : sauvīra is made from wheat.
Ma.nigh., varga 8, 204cd : sauvīraka is made from unboiled or boiled,
husked grains of barley. Bpn, samdhānavarga 8 : sauvīra is made from
unboiled or boiled, husked grains of barley, and also from wheat
according to some authorities (the same statement occurs Bho.ku. 1,
p. 124). Śārṅga 2, 10, 11cd : sauvīra is the product of fermentation
of husked and boiled grains of barley. Ca.Sū. 25, 49, Cakra : sauvīra


=== Page 533 ===
APPENDIX THREE                                 517

is prepared with husked barley. The preparation of sauvīraka (=
sauvīra) is described in detail : Su.Sū. 44, 35-40ab.

stambhana — obstipating (agent).

PW : stopfend. MW : a styptic or astringent. Dutt, MM, p. 6 :
stambhana or constipators are medicines which from their drying,
astringent and cooling qualities, and from their easy digestibility, in-
crease the air and retain the secretions. Bhish : a constipator. Gul :
astringent, styptic. HB : a styptic medicine. Ca.Sū. 22, 12ab : “stam-
bhaña is that which immobilizes what is moving and stabilizes that
which is fluctuating.” Va. 96, 12 = Śāriga 1, 4, 12cd-13ab = Bhā.pra.
6, 222 : “That which on account of its dry, cold, astringent and easily
maturating (qualities), brings about (an increase of) wind, is (called)
stambhana.” Su.Sū. 42, 10, Ḍa. : stambhana is that which immobilizes
the limbs, or that which makes firm what is soft. A.h.Sū. 5, 29cd,
Aruṇa : it is the opposite of bhedin and a synonym of grāhin; He :
it is the same as grāhin.

snāyu = snāva — cord.

There are nine hundred cords in the human body. See about these :
Ca.Śā. 7, 14; Su.Śā. 5, 29-36; A.h.Śā. 3, 17; A.s.Śā. 5, 79-85. See :
Chakraberty, p. 33-34; Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2, p. 352; Müller, Wörter-
heft, p. 149, nr. 239.

srotas — channel.

Ca. uses the term srotas in a very broad sense, including sirā, dhamanī,
nāḍī, etc. (see Vi. 5, 9). This view is made mention of : A.s.Śā. 6, 50.
Su.Śā. 5, 10 : there are nine channels, opening outwards, in men : the
ears, the eyes, the mouth, the nostrils, the anus and the urethra; in
women there are three more : (the openings) of the nipples of the breasts
and the vagina. For another meaning of the term srotas in Su. see :
Śā. 9, 12. A.h. distinguishes two classes of channels : a) the first class
consists of the two nostrils, ears and eyes, the anus, mouth and ure-
thra; in women there are three more : the nipples of the breasts and
the vagina; b) the thirteen innner channels, which are the abodes of
life and carry the breath, the elements of the body, the impurities,
water and food (Śā. 3, 40cd-42ab). The latter are of the same colour as
the element (they carry); they are round, gross or minute, of an elon-


=== Page 534 ===
518                                      APPENDIX THREE

gated form and like ramifications (of a plant) (Śā. 3, 43). A.s. says
that the channels are innumerable (Śā. 5, 95), but enumerates also the
two classes of channels, mentioned in A.h. (Śā. 6, 34-47). Kā. (Śā.)
distinguishes two classes of channels : subtle and gross ones; the gross
channels are nine in number : two below and seven above; subtle
channels are the navel and the pores of the hairs. See : Chakraberty,
p. 65-68; Dasgupta, H.I.Ph. 2, p. 344-352; Hariprapanna, Rasayoga-
sāgara, upodghāta p. 168-169; Müller, Wörterheft, p. 149-150, nr. 240;
Seal, p. 208-216.

sveda — sudation.

There are several methods of sudation. These are described : Ca.Sū.
14; Su.Ci. 32; A.h.Sū. 17; A.s.Sū. 26; Bhe.Sū. 23; Kā.Sū. 23; Hā. 4.
4. See also : Dutt, MM, p. 19-20; Jolly, Medicin, p. 27-28; Kutumbiah,
p. 128.

haṭṭa
     This word may be related to haḍḍa, which is a synonym of asthi acc.
to Dn, varga 6, 369. Acc. to Dn again, ekārthāni nr. 18 (p. 435), haṭṭa-
vilāsinī is a synonym of nakha (nail).

hariṇa
     PW : Gazelle (Antilope cervicapra, Molesw.). MW : deer, antelope.
Bhish : a red deer, a spotted deer. HK : Gazelle. Kav p. 169 : the com-
mon variety of the spotted deer. Acc. to many sources a hariṇa is a
deer of a coppery colour (Cakra on Ca.Sū. 27, 46 and Ca.Ci. 3, 191;
Su.Sū. 46, 57b; Da. on Su.Sū. 20, 5; He. on A.h.Sū. 6, 43).
     The term hariṇa is applied to a number of different species of deer;
Cakra on Ca.Sū. 27, 46 : pṛṣata = citrahariṇa, mṛgamātṛkā = hariṇa-
jāti, kurāṅga = hariṇabheda, gokarṇa = hariṇaviśeṣa, ṛṣya = nīlāṅdo
hariṇaḥ, cāruṣka = hariṇabheda, etc.; see also Cakra on Ca.Sū. 5, 5.
The term hariṇa may be used to designate the female of Antilope cervi-
capra (Linnaeus, 1758) (see : eṇa), but it is often loosely applied to
animals of related species (Antilopinae and Cervidae). The animals
mentioned by Cakra are identified as follows : a) pṛṣata : the spotted
deer or chital, Axis axis (Erxleben, 1777) = Cervus axis Erxleben,
1777 (Gul, vol. 6, Animals and birds, p. 55, nr. 19); PW : die gespren-
kelte Gazelle; MW : the spotted antelope; Bhish : the porcine deer?;

b) mṛgamātṛkā: the hog deer, *Axis porcinus* (Zimmermann, 1780) (Gul,
p. 75, nr. 95); MW: a kind of red-coloured hare-like deer; c) *kurāṅga*:
this may be *Muntiacus muntjak* (Zimmermann, 1780) = *Cervus muntjak*
Zimmermann, 1780; d) *gokarṇa*; PW and MW: *Antilope picta* (Pallas,

harita(ka) — vegetables.

The term *harita(ka)* is usually rendered by : (green) vegetable, (green)
potherb. (PW; MW; HB; Kav). It designates, however, a restricted
group of vegetables and potherbs : Cakra on Ca.Sū. 8, 20 : *haritaka* is
fresh ginger (*ārdraka*), etc.; Da. on Su.Sū. 19, 16: the group, called
*haritaka*, consists of *kuṭhera, śigru, surasa, sumukha, āsurī, bhūstṛṇa*,
*mūlaka* and *cukrikā*; A.h.Sū. 7, 32, Aruṇa and Candra : *haritaka* con-
sists of *mūlaka, kuṭhera*, etc.; He. : (it consists of) that series of pot-
herbs, which begins with *mūlaka* and is enumerated in the section on
potherbs.

haritāla — orpiment (As₂S₃).

See about this substance : Ainslie 1, p. 499-504; Dutt, MM, p. 41-44;
Garbe, Ind. Mineral., p. 48; IRM 1, p. 118-119; Nadk. 2, p. 20-23;
Watt CP, p. 92-93. See about its synonyms and properties : Pr 434;
Dn, *varga* 7, 119-127; Rn, *varga* 13, 58-60; Ma.nigh., *varga* 4, 27; Bpn,
*dhātvādivarga* 127-131.

haridrā — turmeric.

Turmeric is the rhizome of *Curcuma longa* Linn.; the powder made
from the rhizome is of a yellow colour; it is used in dyeing, in medicine
and as a constituent of condiments. The yellow colour arises from cur-
cumin (diferuloyl methane) and other related pigments, some of which
have been isolated and chemically characterized. See : Chopra, Indi-
genous drugs, p. 325-327; Steinegger und Hänsel, *Lehrbuch der Phar-
makognosie*, p. 403.


=== Page 536 ===
APPENDIX FOUR

SANSKRIT NAMES OF PLANTS
AND THEIR BOTANICAL EQUIVALENTS

*Introduction*

Except in a rather restricted number of cases the botanical identi-
fication of plants mentioned in Sanskrit texts has always presented
many problems. The number of disagreeing identifications, and above
all the number of botanical names met with in the literature, has
shown a steady increase in the course of time. This situation makes
it expedient to collect the data scattered in the more important books
on the subject and to arrange them systematically. The collection of
references in this glossary, dealing with all the plants mentioned
in the translation, notes and Appendices may be useful to others, the
more so because many books on the subject have no adequate index;
moreover, a great number of printing errors, inaccurate transcriptions
of Sanskrit terms, etc., are frequent obstacles, diminishing the reliability
of no small number of works. The omission of author's names after
scientific names of plants is a very common occurrence and this un-
happy practice, adopted in the Sanskrit-English dictionary of Monier-
Williams, often leads to confusion, as will appear from the glossary.
The botanical names in this glossary have been checked, without
any exception, by help of the Index Kewensis, the only work con-
taining all the names of phanerogamous plants, and the nomenclature
and synonymy have been set up in agreement with it. The name given
by the Index Kewensis as the valid one has been put first, followed
by the synonyms. There are, however, some exceptions to this general
scheme. Deviations from the Index Kewensis occur whenever pre-
scribed by the International Code (ed. 1972) in its list of nomina con-
servanda; names of species found in that list have been adopted.
These changes are indicated by a reference to the International Code.
Names put between square brackets are not found in the Index; in
the majority of cases this means that they are invalid or erroneous,
but there are exceptions. Invalid names are usually those between
square brackets when followed by a single author's name after the
Latin name. When two author's names occur, the first one being put


=== Page 537 ===
APPENDIX FOUR                                                                521

between round brackets, the name of the plant may be valid or inva-
lid. I refrained from decisions regarding the validity of this type of
names, prescribed by the International Code, by reason of my in-
sufficient knowledge of botanical taxonomy and the complicated chro-
nological problems which beset the field of nomenclature. In many
cases, however, I tried to supply the synonyms necessary to construct
the names in the way prescribed by the Code or to check those put
between square brackets.
     Names of varieties have been put between square brackets too when
not recorded in the Index; for the greater part they are not found
in the latter; whenever possible, i.e. whenever the botanical literature
was accessible to me, I referred to botanical works in which the parti-
cular variety is described.

elavālu(ka)
Much confusion exists concerning this substance as will become
apparent from the material collected :
(1) Bpn, karpūrādivarga 120 : it is also called kapitthathvac (the bark
of kapittha). Acc. to the Hindi comm. (p. 262-263) the substance is
described somewhere in Bhā.pra. as resembling kańkola and smelling
like kuṣṭha. In the same comm. three different identifications are made


=== Page 547 ===
531
APPENDIX FOUR

mention of : a) PRUNUS CERASUS LINN., b) GISEKIA PHARNACIOIDES
LINN., c) MUKIA SCABRELLA ARN. (Index Kewensis : MELOTHRIA
MADERASPATANA COGN. = MUKIA SCABRELLA ARN. = MUKIA MADERA-
SPATANA M. ROEM).
(2) DWH 2, p. 105-107 : GISEKIA PHARNACIOIDES LINN.; p. 105 :
“This plant is called in Sanskrit *vālu̥ka* and *elavālu̥ka* on account of
the number of large raphides contained in the leaves, and which give
them the appearance of being full of sand (*vālu̥*).” (Raphides are
minute intracellular crystals, usually of an acicular form).
(3) Gul : cherry tree (PRUNUS CERASUS LINN.).
(4) HB, p. 21 : GISEKIA PHARNACIOIDES LINN.; ibid., footnote 70 :
“*elavālu̥* is mentioned Su.Sū. 38, 14, where Ḍa.’s comm. explains it as
a reddish powder (*harivālu̥ka*), resembling that of the seeds of the
*kr̥ṣṇagandhā* (*kr̥ṣṇagandhikaphala*). The latter is a name of the horse-
radish tree or *śigru* or *śobhāñjana*,” ibid., p. 91, footnote 74 : “In
the Phar. Ind. (= DWH) 2, p. 105, it is wrongly identified with *vālu̥ka*;
the seeds, supplied to me by a native druggist, seem to be simply those
of chickweed.”
(5) HK : quotes the identifications of PW and Hoernle.
(6) Kav, p. 37 : a kind of red powder made of some seeds obtainable
of every native druggist, not identified; p. 294 : a fragrant powder of
a bark sold under that name; it is believed to come from the Spice
Islands; p. 642 : Gaṅgādhara takes it as implying *tejavala*, a kind of
wood apparently dry but juicy within; it is brought from Nepal.
(7) KB 2, p. 1187-1188 : GISEKIA PHARNACIOIDES LINN.
(8) MW : the fragrant bark of FERONIA ELEPHANTUM (*kapitthattvac*);
a granular substance (apparently a vegetable of a reddish-brown
colour, used as a drug and perfume).
(9) PW : the fragrant bark of FERONIA ELEPHANTUM (*kapitthattvac*),
used medicinally.
(10) V 7, p. 67 : GISEKIA PHARNACIOIDES.
(11) Vās : name of a perfume; a red powder sold under that name;
the seed of some plant.
(12) Ḍa. on Su.Sū. 38, 14 (printed ed., different from Hoernle’s text) :
“a reddish powder (*harivālu̥ka*), resembling the black, fragrant *katpha-
la*.” *katphala* is usually identified as MYRICA NAGI THUNB.

elā

Two kinds of *elā* are distinguished : 1) *su̥kṣmailā* or *kṣu̥drailā*, the
small cardamom, and 2) *sthu̥lailā* or *br̥hadelā*, the large cardamom.

elāvāluka

       This term occurs Kaut. 2, 25, 27 (text p. 79; transl. Kangle p. 178;
transl. J. J. Meyer p. 187; transl. Sham. p. 133). Sham. renders it by
SOLANUM MELONGENA, without any comment. J. J. Meyer takes it as
the fragrant bark of FERONIA ELEPHANTUM (elāvāluka), but remarks
that the reading elāvāluka makes it probable that one should translate :
elā and vāluka (i.e. harivāluka, the fragrant bark of kapittha); Kangle
translates : cardamomum, vāluka. Acc. to Vśs elāvāluka is a synonym of
elavāluka.

*barbaracandana*

Dn, varga 3, 9 : *barbarīkā* is a white, odourless type of *candana*;
Rn, varga, 12, 17: *barbaraka*, (also called) white *barbaraka*, is (a kind of
*candana* that is) fragrant; a synonym (see Dn and Rn) is *barbarottha*,
explained in PW as white sandalwood.

*barbarikā*

Is not recorded in the dictionaries; see *vanabarbarikā*.

vidālāmālaka

This term occurs Kauṭ. 2, 15, 18 (text p. 74 ; transl. Kangle p. 142 ;
transl. J. J. Meyer p. 141 ; transl. Sham. p. 101) ; (see App. 3 : amla).
Sham. is of the opinion that it is a synonym of āmalaka ; J. J. Meyer
(p. 141, footnote 7) is unsure about the meaning of the word ; he seems
to prefer to take the word as a compound and remarks that vidala
(acc. to the dictionaries) designates BAUHINIA VARIEGATA, but acc. to
Gaṇ. the pomegranate (dāḍima). In my opinion the word vidālāmālaka
is a compound and the first member is vidala or vidalā.
vidala : (1) BAUHINIA VARIEGATA LINN. (MW ; Vśs : = raktakāñcana) ;
       (2) B. PURPUREA LINN. (Vśs : = raktakāñcana) ;
       (3) the seeds of PUNICA GRANATUM LINN. (Vśs).
vidalā : (1) IPOMOEA TURPETHUM R. BR. (MW ; Vśs) ;
       (2) = sātalā (Vśs ; variously identified, but acc. to Vśs.
            EUPHORBIA NERIIFOLIA LINN.);
       (3) the bark of PUNICA GRANATUM LINN. (MW).
The best solution is to read vidala and to take it in the sense of
dāḍima (PUNICA GRANATUM LINN.) because the pomegranate is usually


=== Page 617 ===
APPENDIX FOUR 601

enumerated as one of the fruits called phalāmla. (Kangle also trans-
lates: pomegranate).

    (2) a kind of ANDROPOGON (MW; PW).


=== Page 628 ===
APPENDIX FIVE

*Medical annotations*

The interpretation of Āyurvedic Sanskrit texts from a medical point
of view is a field that has been neglected by non-Indian scholars. Many
Indian authors, on the other hand, readily equate disorders described
in the Sanskrit texts with syndromes and diseases recognized in modern
medicine. As I shall point out, many of these identifications are
doubtful.

As soon as one makes any attempt to connect the clusters of symp-
toms enumerated in the Sanskrit texts with entities called syndromes
and diseases in Western medicine, a great number of problems emerges.
First of all it may be useful to stress that the course of a disease is
thought of in Indian medicine as a continuous process of development.
A disease is something that gradually is made manifest. Prodromes
(pūrvarūpa) develop into full-fledged symptoms (rūpa). Secondary
affections (upadrava) are consequences of the basic morbid process.
At the end of this process recovery takes place or fatal signs (ariṣṭa)
appear, foreboding death. The stages of this evolutionary process are
delineated. Each stage is characterized by a cluster of signs. In many
cases the enumeration of these signs occurs in the form of verses, more
easy to remember than statements in prose. These verses, however, do
not allow free presentation of the characteristics, in accordance with
their importance; so it is inadmissible to regard the sign heading the
list as the central one. Secondly one should always remember that the
listed signs depend on the morbific entity (doṣa) or group of morbific
entities which is thought to be involved. Each of these is provided
with a fixed set of qualities and effects. Analysis of the groups of symp-
toms may therefore proceed from within, by determining which of the
components of the morbific entity or entities have been selected in a
particular disease. In order to achieve this aim the Indian medical
system must be mastered. In addition, the medical texts must be
studied comparatively, because the order of the symptoms, their num-
ber and the terms which are employed vary from one treatise to another.
If one proceeds in this way the problem remains as to what extent
empirical considerations and actual observations were important in
delimiting diseases and establishing their symptoms and course. On


=== Page 629 ===
                                                              APPENDIX FIVE                                                              613

reading the texts one cannot help receiving the impression that the
diseases distinguished and the symptoms enumerated are not based only
on theoretical considerations, but also on observation of facts. In many
cases, however, it is difficult to ascertain which signs may have been
met with in patients and which are stated for the sake of theory. To
this general rule there is one exception. It is repeatedly observed by
commentators that one or more of the symptoms of a particular
disease does not fit into the theoretical frame, but is nevertheless pre-
sent. Such a symptom is called *vikṛtiviṣamasamavāyārabdha* (see Madhu-
*kośa* on 2, 14-15ab); this difficult term expresses that the symptom
referred to cannot be explained theoretically as an effect of one of the
morbific entities involved. This type of symptoms may be considered
to have been really observed.
    It seems therefore legitimate to try to find out how far the described
syndromes correspond to real diseases which may have been encounter-
ed by the ancient Indian physicians. In the annotations which follow
I make a first attempt in this direction. It should be borne in mind,
however, that it is only possible to put forward a number of sugges-
tions, because I have no personal experience in the field of tropical
medicine.

                                                               Chapter 2

    In Indian medicine fever is regarded as the principal disease and is
dealt with first. It is designated as *jvara* in medical treatises; the cor-
responding term in older texts (*Atharvaveda*) is *takman*. (See about
*takman*: Filliozat, The classical doctrine, p. 119-121; Grohmann, In-
dische Studien 9, p. 381-423; Karambelkar, The Atharva-Veda and
the Āyur-Veda, p. 278-291; Müller, Der *takman* des Atharva-veda,
Artibus Asiae 6, 1937, p. 230-242; id., Wörterheft, nr. 94, p. 101-102;
see about *jvara* several publications by Müller : Grundlagen, p. 72-73;
Eigenwertungen, p. 27-29; Wörterheft, nr. 92, p. 100-101; Ueber ver-
schiedene Ergebnisse, p. 111-112).
    The concept of fever is broad and includes fever arising from the
smell of herbs (2, 28), emotional states (2, 28-29), magic (2, 29) and
possession by evil spirits (2, 30). The set of its prodromes (2, 4-5) re-
sembles the symptoms encountered when the body temperature is ris-
ing. The general signs of fever (2, 3) are not typical of all fevers, as
already observed by Vijayarakṣita. The descriptions of fever by wind,
etc. (2, 8-17) are vague and may include a number of infectious
diseases, such as enteric fevers and brucellosis. Chakraberty never

theless equates fever by wind with the cerebrospinal type of pernicious
aestivo-autumnal fever (p. 212), fever by bile with the bilious remittent
type of subtertian malaria and with blackwater fever, also known as
malarial haemoglobinuria (p. 210 and 213), and fever by phlegm with
influenza (p. 213). The general picture of fever by concerted action
(2, 18-23) is complicated. This *saṁnipātajvara* is often said to be typhoid
(*Yādavaśarman*; Dinānāth; Chakraberty, p. 215; Chakraberty takes
typhoid in such a wide sense that it includes all the eruptive fevers);
Filliozat (BSHM 30, 1936, p. 21-29) interprets *saṁnipātajvara* as “les
états typhoïdes et comateux”, though it has more features in common
with louse-borne typhus or a combination of relapsing fever and typhus
(the latter two frequently coexist). The many types of fever by con-
certed action described in the texts (*Madhukośa* on 2, 18-23 and the
notes) are for the greater part not clear, so it is only possible to put
forward suggestions as to some of these. The fever called *abhinyāsa*
(the “depressing” fever) or *hatāujas* (the fever “in which the vital
fluid has been damaged”) may be viewed as including a.o. uraemic
states. A cardio-pulmonary syndrome may be designated by *vibhu* (the
“all-pervading” or “powerful” fever), an affection of the lungs and the
liver (the pulmonary form of subtertian malaria ?) by *phalgu* (the
meaning of this word is not clear : reddish ?, weak ?); *makari* (named
after the *makara*, an aquatic animal, or after the ocean, sometimes
called *makarin*) may be some form of cystopyelonephritis; *visphuraka*
(the “quivering” fever) is not clear, nor the types called *śīghrakārin*
(the “swiftly acting” fever) and *kapphaṇa* (the meaning of this word
is not known). In many texts each of the thirteen fevers by concerted
action has its own name; though the diseases described escape a re-
liable identification, it may be useful to add some notes on the meaning
of their names. *babhru* is called after the animal bearing this name,
which is a mongoose, or after the colour of its coat, which is deep
brown; the meaning of *bhallu* is not clear; *āśukārin* is “quickly acting”;
*kampana* means “trembling”; *yāmya* may be connected with Yama,
the god of death, and mean “deadly”; *pākala* may be related to *pāka*,
“inflammation”; *krakaca* means “saw”; *vaidārika* is the fever that
“tears asunder”; *karkoṭaka* is the name of a plant and the fever called
thus may derive its appellation from the rough surface of the fruits
of this plant; *sammohaka* is named thus after one of its symptoms,
*sammoha*, i.e. “complete mental confusion”; the term *kūṭapākala* sug-
gests a fever with the highest degree (*kūṭa* is the top of a mountain)
of inflammation (*pāka*); *śūlagātra* designates that the limbs feel cold

615

in this disease; *tandrikā* is related to *tandrā*, which means “lassitude”,
*pralāpaka* and *pralāpin* to *pralāpa*, “confused speech”, *raktaṣṭhivin* to
*raktaṣṭhivana*, “spitting of blood”; *bhugnanetra* and *bhugnadṛś* indi-
cate that the eyes are distorted (*bhugna*); *jihvāka* points to the pro-

the main seat of the disease described; *antaka* means “deadly”;
*rugdāha* is called thus after the painful (*ruj*) and burning (*dāha*) sensa-

position of mental confusion in the described syndrome; *karṇaka* and
*karṇaka* point to the ears (*karṇa*) as the special seat of the affection;
*kaṇṭhakubja* is a fever in which the throat (*kaṇṭha*) is “crooked” (*kubja*);
*kumbhīpāka* may be called thus because inflammation (*pāka*) of a cavity
(*kumbha* means a jar), especially the nasal cavity, is present in it;
*proruṇūva* is unclear (the verb *pra-ūrṇu-* means “to cover”); *antardāha*
designates a sensation of inner burning as the chief symptom; *daṇḍa-

difficult term, connected with the burning sensation (*dāha*) and the
feeling as if animals (*hariṇa* can be a synonym of *eṇa*) move about on
one’s body, occurring as symptoms in this fever; *hāridraka* points to
the turmeric-yellow (*hāridra*) colour of the skin, etc. in this disease;
*ajaghoṣa* indicates that the patient can only produce sounds (*ghoṣa*)
like a he-goat (*aja*); *bhūtahāsa*, meaning “the laughter (*hāsa*) of an evil
spirit (*bhūta*)”, emphasizes an important feature of the illness; *yantrā-
pīḍa* is also a descriptive term, meaning “painful oppression (*āpīḍa*)
by a mechanical contrivance (*yantra*)”; *saṁnyāsa* usually designates a
complete loss of consciousness, but is employed in a different sense to
describe the fever called thus; *saṁśoṣin* usually means “completely
desiccating”, but has a different sense in this fever. The thirteen fevers
by concerted action are not uniformly described in the various treatises
and in some cases there must have been confusion of particular types.
The fever called *krakaca* in the *Kāśyapasaṁhitā* goes by the name of
*pākala* in Vangasena’s treatise and the Bhāvaprakāśa; the reverse is
true as well; *pākala* of the *Kāśyapasaṁhitā* corresponds to *krakaca* in
Vangasena and the Bhāvaprakāśa.

The swelling at the root of the ear arising at the end of a fever by
concerted action (2, 25) may be a parotitis, as Grohmann (Indische
Studien 9, p. 398) already observed. Parotitis is frequent as a compli-
cation of louse-borne typhus; it may also occur in severe cases of scrub
typhus, in louse-borne relapsing fever, etc.


=== Page 632 ===
616                                                                  APPENDIX FIVE

     In Indian medicine the concept of irregular fever (viṣamajvara) means
that a fever which has been present for a certain number of days
breaks off to make its reappearance at a later point of time (2, 31cd-
32ab). It does not indicate that the fever presents an irregular course;
on the contrary, it presents itself, as a rule, at regular intervals of time.
viṣamajvara should not be translated by malarial fever (Jolly, Medicin,
p. 72), nor by malarial remittent fever (Yādavaśarman and Dinānāth),
firstly because not all irregular fevers are malarial in origin and second-
ly because it is impossible to determine whether the fevers described
are of a remittent or intermittent type. Continuous fever (saṃtatajvara)
(2, 34) lasts for fixed periods of time, a statement which may be based,
at least partially, on experience; leptospirosis, also called seven-day
fever, is one of the diseases which may be designated in this way,
though one or more relapses occur in it. Double quotidian fever (sata-
taka) (2, 35) is not a continuous fever (as erroneously indicated by
Yādavaśarman); its inclusion in the group of irregular fevers proves
that the group as a whole cannot be regarded as forms of malaria.
Double quotidian fever may be identified as the typical fever of
leishmaniasis (kala-azar) (Chakraberty p. 211; Sudarśanāśāstri); the
initial fever presents as a rule a double remission in the twenty-four
hours. This only occurs in one other tropical fever, subtertian malaria
(by Plasmodium falciparum): a double crisis may occur in this disease,
with a drop of temperature — a false crisis — when the fever has
attained its apparent fastigium, followed by a fresh rise, which is then
succeeded by a true crisis; this phenomenon has been attributed to
the presence of two generations of parasites in the blood, one of which
matures somewhat later than the other. Quotidian fever (anyedyuṣka)
(2, 35) is found in malaria and in other diseases. It occurs when there
is a double infection with two maturation cycles of Plasmodium vivax
or P. ovale; such double infections usually synchronize within a week
and then follow the classic tertian pattern. A quotidian fever may also
arise in subtertian malaria; in enteric fevers the temperature is some-
times of an intermittent, quotidian type; in many other disorders fever
of a quotidian type occurs, resembling malaria : pyelonephritis, chole-
cystitis, amoebic abscess of the liver, etc. Tertian fever (tṛtīyaka) (2,
36) occurs in tertian malaria by Plasmodium vivax or P. ovale. In
enteric fevers the temperature may show a perfect tertian periodicity
throughout; this has also been seen in meningococcal septicaemia.
Quartan fever (caturthaka) (2, 36) is found in quartan malaria from
Plasmodium malariae. In enteric fevers again there may occur a per-


=== Page 633 ===
APPENDIX FIVE 617

fect quartan periodicity, as well as in meningococcal septicaemia. Re-
versed quartan fever (caturthakaviparyaya) (2, 39), usually called double
quartan fever (Yādavaśarman; Dinānāth; Sudarśanaśāstrī) may be
seen in multiple infection with Plasmodium malariae; the same applies
to reversed tertian fever (tṛtīyakaviparyaya) (Madhukośa on 2, 39),
sometimes called malignant tertian (Dinānāth). The type of fever
called vātabalāśaka (2, 40), incorrectly identified as influenza by Cha-
kraberty (p. 207), looks like a condition that may arise from a number
of disorders, e.g. cirrhosis of the liver with advanced hepatic failure
and ancylostomiasis with chronic anaemia. (See about balāśa and
vātabalāśaka : Grohmann, Indische Studien 9, p. 395-401; Filliozat,
The classical doctrine, p. 117-119; Jolly, Medicin, p. 72; Karambelkar,
p. 214-227; Müller, Wörterheft, nr. 141, p. 119). The fever that goes
by the name pralepaka (2, 41) may be connected with chronic pulmonary
tuberculosis; it has been identified with pneumonia (Jolly, Medicin, p.
73; Chakraberty, p. 206) and is sometimes called hectic fever (Yāda-
vaśarman, Dinānāth), which is probably inadequate.

The regular course of a fever, with shivering at the beginning,
followed by a sensation of warmth, was well known in Indian medicine
(2, 45). An aberrant type is also described, in which a peripheral
vascular failure develops (2, 46); this occurs in algid malaria, the
prognosis of which is bad (2, 46).

The strong fever making partings in the hair of the head (2, 67cd-
68ab) may designate a fever with drenching nocturnal sweats, as seen
for example in amoebic abscess of the liver.

Chapter 3

The concept of diarrhoea (atīsāra) in Āyurveda is theoretically based
on an increase of the watery element in the body, leading to a flow
(sāra) of faecal matter beyond the proper measure (3, 4). In practice this
does not work out. The stools need not be liquid in order to classify
the disorder as a case of diarrhoea (3, 6). More importance is attached
to altered qualities of the stools generally and a raised frequency of
their evacuation (3, 7-8). A series of factors is enumerated by which
diarrhoea may come about (3, 13). Some of these are really elements
furthering the appearance of intestinal disorders : a faultive diet, un-
cooked food, corrupted water, intestinal parasites, etc. The connection
between fear and diarrhoea is well known. Other facts are more diffi-
cult of evaluation. The diarrhoea caused by grief, as described in Indian


=== Page 634 ===
618                                            APPENDIX FIVE

medicine, presents peculiar characteristics. The drinking of a too great
quantity of water may have been associated with diarrhoea on account
of Indian medical theory. Stagnation of the natural urges as a cause of
diarrhoea may refer to the phenomenon that diarrhoea is preceded by
constipation in many cases, which was known to the ancient Indian
physicians (3, 5).

The frequent evacuation, accompanied by pain, of small amounts of
faecal matter (3, 6) usually points to a diarrhoea originating in the
colon; this would agree with the Indian view in which the third and
last stage of the digestive process is thought to be dominated by wind.
The diarrhoea from bile (3, 7ab) is of a composite nature. The diarrhoea
from phlegm (3, 7cd) may designate e.g. the various types of the mal-
absorption syndrome, in which stools of a light colour are evacuated.
In the most acute and fulminating forms of bacillary dysentery the
mucus in the stools may be mingled with a large amount of altered
blood and the evacuations come to resemble "meat washings"; this
agrees remarkably well with the severe character of the disease de-
scribed in 3, 8. The diarrhoea from grief (3, 9-10) is an indistinct entity;
the stools resemble *kākaṇantī*, i.e. *guñjā* seeds (the seeds of Abrus pre-
catorius Linn.), which are usually bright scarlet and black. The state-
ment that floating stools are characteristic of maturity (3, 12-13), i.e.
of a completed digestive process, is remarkable, because stools of this
kind are seen in all disorders associated with steatorrhoea. Many types
of diarrhoea were regarded as incurable (3, 14-17); the enumerated
characteristics of the stools, considered to indicate a bad prognosis,
are not typical of specific diseases; the diarrhoea in which the stools
resemble "meat washings" (compare 3, 8) recurs again here; mature
*jambū* fruits (Syzygium cumini Skeels) are black and juicy and stools
resembling these may point to any disorder in which loss of blood
occurs into the gastro-intestinal tract; offensive stools, smelling of de-
composing blood, are e.g. evacuated in amoebic dysentery, etc. Diar-
rhoea caused by some intercurrent disease, e.g. dysentery, has often
been the cause of death in patients with a chronic debilitating illness
(3, 19).

The bloody diarrhoea, described as related to that caused by bile
(3, 20) appears as a secondary development of intestinal disorders, in
which bleeding from the distal part of the bowels may occur. The
disease, called *pravāhikā*, is usually identified as dysentery (Jolly,
Medicin, p. 75; Yādavaśarman; Dinānāth); the description (3, 21)
points to disorders with irritation of the large bowel, including the


=== Page 635 ===
APPENDIX FIVE
                                                                               19
bacillary dysenteries. In severe cases of diarrhoea, especially in
the secretion of urine may be suppressed; recovery is marked by
passage of some turbid, highly coloured urine, followed by a “cri
diuresis” (3, 23).

*Chapter 4*

The *grahaṇī* disease is a chronic diarrhoea; the term should not be
rendered by sprue (Yādavaśarman; Dīnānāth), because a chronic diar-
rhoea may occur in many disorders. The imaginary organ in which the
disease finds its origin is the *grahaṇī*, the seat of the digestive fire
(Hariprapanna, Rasayogasāgara, *upodghāta* p. 143, equates it with the
mucous membrane of the small intestine, which is not supported by
the texts and an inadmissible modern interpretation). An increased
frequency of evacuation, accompanied by pain, with varying characters
of the stools, is typical of the disease (4, 2-3). Its prodromes mainly
consist of signs indicating a faulty digestion (4, 4).

Several disorders may be comprised by the *grahaṇī* disease, such as :
tropical sprue, pellagra, ancylostomiasis, amoebic dysentery, chronic
bacillary dysentery, tuberculous enteritis, etc. Some of the symptoms
enumerated are frequently met with in some of these diseases : fer-
menting stools (4, 6) in tropical sprue and pellagra, a ravenous appetite
(4, 8) in ancylostomiasis, etc.

*Chapter 5*

Haemorrhoids (*arśas*, pl. *arśāṁsi*) arise from the three anal folds,
according to Indian medical tradition (5, 1; Madhukośa; notes). It is
not at all clear what is meant by these folds. Hariprapanna (Rasayoga-
sāgara, *upodghāta* p. 144) identifies them as the plicae transversae recti,
which disagrees with their description in the texts, because the two or
three transverse folds are found higher up in the pars ampullaris recti.
Kutumbiah (p. 31) calls them spiral grooves, which again is contra-
dicted by the texts, in which it is distinctly stated that the folds are
structures with a lateral elevation. The anulus haemorrhoidalis may
be one of the folds, but the number three defies explanation, unless
the musculus sphincter ani internus and externus are also regarded as
folds. The series of symptoms described as accompanying haemor-
rhoids and the disorders enumerated as their sequelae (5, 12-15) may
really be syndromes in which haemorrhoids can develop secondarily.


=== Page 636 ===
620                                              APPENDIX FIVE

Conditions furthering the appearance of haemorrhoids are characterized
by an increased hydrostatic pressure in the portal venous system
(portal hypertension). The most frequent cause of such a condition
in tropical and subtropical countries will be cirrhosis of the liver and
primary hepatic carcinoma. Some of the mentioned signs may point
to cirrhosis : patients with cirrhosis seem likely to develop tubercu-
losis and pneumonia (5, 13); cough and shortness of breath occur in
cardiac cirrhosis (5, 13); in biliary cirrhosis many patients develop a
striking melanotic pigmentation of the skin (5, 14); cirrhosis of the
liver leads to splenomegaly (5, 15).

The ancient Indian physicians, unable to discern the underlying
causes of the appearance of haemorrhoids, tried to make a classifica-
tion based on their form and other qualities. Some additional informa-
tion will help the reader to understand what is said in the text. The
fruits of *bimbī* (Coccinia indica Wight et Arn.) are bright scarlet berries;
because the lips of women are often compared to them, a synonym of
*bimbī* is *oṣṭhopamaphalā*, i.e. (the plant), the fruits of which resemble
lips. A *kharjūra* fruit is a date. The fruit of *karkandhū*, as well as of
*kola* and *badarī*, is some kind of jujube (the fruit of species of Zizyphus);
jujubes are drupes, varying in form, size and colour, with a stone in
their interior. The fruits of *kārpāsī* and *vanakārpāsī* (species of Gossy-
pium) are capsules; the seeds are clothed with cotton wool. The form
of the flowers of the *kadamba* is explained in the *Madhukośa* (and in
one of my notes). *siddhārthaka* and *sarṣapa* are kinds of mustard seed.
*gojihvā* is the name of some plants with prickly leaves (see App. 4).
The fruits of *karkoṭa* (Momordica cochinchinensis Spreng.) are cucum-
ber-like, but ovate and pointed, and are covered with conical points.

One of the described syndromes in which haemorrhoids appear (5,
16-18) bears some resemblance to clonorchiasis (an infection with a
trematode, Clonorchis sinensis, inhabiting the bile-ducts); in this
disease fever occurs and a chronic diarrhoea is established with re-
curring attacks of jaundice; other hepatic disorders associated with
diarrhoea and jaundice may be involved as well.

The signs of haemorrhoids from phlegm (5, 19-23) cannot be attri-
buted to particular diseases with any certainty, though one may think
e.g. of lymphogranuloma venereum. The qualities of the haemorrhoids
described are clear for the greater part. Some additional remarks may
be useful. The fruits of *karīra* (species of Capparis) are fleshy berries,
with many seeds, imbedded in pulp. The fruits of *panasa* (Artocarpus
integrifolia Linn.f.) are very large; they contain reniform seeds about


=== Page 637 ===
APPENDIX FIVE                                           621

the size of a nutmeg, enveloped in a thin, smooth, leathery sheath and
lodged within the fleshy eatable part of the fruit. A vaṁśa sprout is
a bamboo sprout. The seeds of guñjā (5, 25) (Abrus precatorius Linn.)
are bright scarlet and black. The young shoots of the vaṭa (5, 25)
(Ficus benghalensis Linn.) are pubescent.
     Some of the syndromes described suggest carcinoma of the rectum
or colon (5, 25-27ab ; 5, 27cd-28) and chronic hepatic disorders (5, 29-30).
     The ancient Indians regarded haemorrhoids as a manifestation of
grave disorders, probably rightly so in many cases, for they were aware
of the fact that haemorrhoids may be associated with serious diseases,
as appears from the list of prodromes (5, 31-32) and other statements
(5, 33-34).
     The prognosis of haemorrhoids was thought to be related to their
localization (5, 35-37). The conditions in which haemorrhoids have a
bad prognosis (5, 39-41) resemble those found in advanced hepatic
failure by cardiac cirrhosis, biliary cirrhosis, etc., accompanied by
many symptoms caused by the primary disease and by a great number
of complications.
     The growths occurring on the penis (5, 42), included in the concept
of haemorrhoids, may be condylomata acuminata and those arising in
the umbilical region (ibid.) mollusca contagiosa.
     The polypous growths near the anus, called warts (carmakīla), can
not be identified. The disorders mentioned in the Ataṅkadarpana on
5, 44 are of various kinds; lesions destroying the penis or vulvar region
occur in granuloma inguinale.

Chapter 6

     In this chapter disturbances of the process of digestion are dealt
with, apart from those, associated with a chronic diarrhoea, which be-
long to the domain of the disease of the grahaṇī. The disturbances de-
scribed first consist of sluggishness of the (transforming) fire (6, 2-3)
(agnimāndya; Yādavaśarman : dyspepsia; Dinānāth : anorexia, hypo-
chlorhydria and achylic dyspepsia; Sudarśanaśāstrī : dyspepsia) and
other types of inadequacy of the (transforming) fire (6, 2-4), followed
by the disorders of the process of disintegration (of the food) (6, 5-
14) (ajīrṇa; Yādavaśarman : indigestion; Dinānāth : dyspepsia, in-
digestion; Sudarśanaśāstrī : indigestion). Nothing definite can be said
about the syndromes described; they consist of slight gastro-intestinal
disturbances, usually called indigestion or dyspepsia, terms which have


=== Page 638 ===
622                                              APPENDIX FIVE

no sharply defined meaning, or are symptoms of some more serious
disease, which may be of many kinds.
     The serious illness called _viṣūcī_ or _viṣūcikā_ is usually equated with
cholera (see Jolly, Medicin, p. 75; Chakraberty, p. 238; Yādavaśarman;
Dinānāth), though there are insufficient arguments for doing so. From
the descriptions of _viṣūcī_ (6, 16-18) one may deduce that it is a grave
disorder, mainly characterized by vomiting and diarrhoea. Many cases
of cholera must have been diagnosed as _viṣūcī_, but other diseases as
well, such as the choleraic form of bacillary dysentery, choleraic and
dysenteric forms of subtertian malaria, etc.
     Two more syndromes are distinguished : intestinal inertia (6, 19-20)
(_alasaka_) and retardation of evacuation (6, 21) (_vilambikā_). The disease
called intestinal inertia suggests a variety of disorders, e.g. subacute
and chronic colonic obstruction, ascites and peritonitis of whatever
origin, etc. Retardation of evacuation points to a chronic obstruction
of the bowels, as seen in carcinoma of the colon.
     About the secondary affections of _viṣūcī_ (6, 25) I want to observe
that none of these is characteristic of cholera; insomnia is a feature in
enteric fevers and dysuria may be a distressing symptom in bacillary
dysentery.

Chapter 7

Though the “worms” described in this chapter are mainly parasites,
they are called worms in the translation, because the range of the word
_kṛmi_ or _krimi_ by which they are designated is larger than the meaning
of the term “parasite”; moreover, the ancient Indians did not clearly
distinguish between the several phyla of invertebrates and the de-
velopmental stages of many of these animals.
     All the texts consulted enumerate twenty kinds of worms, with the
exception of the Hāritasaṃhitā, which counts only thirteen different
types. External and internal worms are distinguished in Ca., A.h.,
A.s. and Hā., not in Su. and Bhe. The internal ones are thought to
arise from blood, phlegm and faecal matter in Ca., A.h. and A.s.,
while in Su. all the worms are regarded as arising from these sub-
stances. Their classification and names agree to a very large extent in
Ca., A.h. and A.s.; Su. adheres to a different scheme. Mādhava follows
the lead of A.h. A survey of the classification of the worms and their
names is given in the table on page 625.
     Some studies have been devoted to the worms in Āyurvedic literature


=== Page 639 ===
APPENDIX FIVE
                                                                    623

and in the Atharvaveda (R. R. Kashyap, Parasitology in the Atharva-
veda, IC 2, 1935-36, p. 93-113; Müller, Indische Würmerkrankheiten,
Gesnerus 21, 1964, p. 14-22).
    The names of the worms are not always clear, as indicated in the
notes, and their identification, in so far as they are no imaginary
creatures, proves to be even more difficult. The worms, said in the
Suśrutasaṁhitā to arise from faecal matter, are identified by Chakra-
berty (p. 235) as follows : ajāva, i.e. slow-moving : Ascaris lumbricoides;
vijāva, i.e. agile : flagellates; kīpya, i.e. creeping : trematodes or flukes;
trippya (instead of cīpya), i.e. stealing : hookworms; gaṇḍūpada, i.e.
knotted feet : species of Taenia, tapeworms; curu, i.e. thread-like :
Oxyuris vermicularis, the threadworm; dvimukha, i.e. two-mouthed :
Trichuris trichiura, the whipworm. These identifications, proposed
without arguments by Chakraberty, are arbitrary and partly unten-
able, because flagellates, for example, are invisible to the naked eye.
It seems fairly certain that a yukā is a louse; lice are found on the
hairs of the head and the clothes (7, 2); so both Pediculus humanus
capitis, the head-louse, and P. humanus corporis, the body-louse, were
known. Nits were designated by the term likṣā; pipīlikā, though com-
monly used to denote ants, conveys the same sense as likṣā in the
Carakasaṁhitā (Cakra on Ca.Sū. 19, 4 : pipīlikā = likhyā). A clear
description of the crab-louse (Phtirus pubis), chiefly living on the hairs
of the genital and inguinal regions, is absent; it may have been known
as cipița, which means flat or flattened, because it is distinguished
from other lice by its broad and flat body. The matkuṇā mentioned in
the Hāritasaṁhitā may be the bed-bug of the tropics, Cimex hemi-
pterus (rotundatus).
    Ascaris lumbricoides (Linnaeus, 1758), the 'round worm', is proba-
bly designated as udarāveṣṭa (“throttling the abdomen”) or udarāda
(“eating the abdomen”), for it is said to resemble a gaṇḍūpada, i.e.
an earthworm (7, 8-9); it may be the gaṇḍūpada of Suśruta and the
kiñcukasamnibha, i.e. "resembling an earthworm" of the Hāritasaṁ-
hitā; it is certainly not a tapeworm, as indicated in the dictionaries
(PW : Bandwurm; MW : tapeworm).
    Tapeworms may have been called antrāda, i.e. “bowel-eater”, be-
cause the latter is said to resemble a broad leather thong (7, 8-9); the
proglottides of species of tapeworms of the genus Taenia may have
been designated as pṛthumuṇḍa, i.e. “broad and bald”, in the Hārita-
saṁhitā.
    Enterobius vermicularis (Linnaeus, 1758), formerly called Oxyuris


=== Page 640 ===
624
                                                                APPENDIX FIVE

        _vermicularis_, the ‘threadworm’, must have been known, for worms
crawling out of the anus and producing itching of the anal region
are described (Madhukóṣa on 7, 13-16); itching of the anus occurs when
female threadworms are depositing their eggs in enormous numbers
near the anus, as well as on the passage of an ascaris. The name of
the threadworm cannot easily be deduced from the descriptions, but
it may be the worm called _leliha_, i.e. “constantly licking”. _Trichuris_
_trichiura_ (Linnaeus, 1771), the ‘whipworm’, may also have been
known, because hyperinfection with these worms eventually results in
rectal prolapse, in which the worms may actually be seen attached to
the prolapsed bowel. Both the male and the female of this organism
have a rather long attenuated anterior portion, which may have given
rise to the name _sūcīmukha_, i.e. “having a mouth like a needle”, found
in the Hāritasāṁhitā.
        The term _kuṣṭhaja_, i.e. “arising from _kuṣṭha_” (a skin disease), oc-
curring in the Suśrutasaṁhitā, need not be fanciful. This worm may
actually denote the larva of _Chrysomyia bezziana_, a true myiasis-
producing fly, never breeding in dead but always in living tissues. It
is frequently found in India, where it appears to have a predilection
for human beings, the female laying her numerous eggs in the nasal
cavity or in tissues from which offensive discharges emanate. Patients
with a chronic discharge from nose or ears, and with lepromatous
leprosy, are attacked (Manson, p. 767). The fantastic names carried
by some worms, e.g. _lomadvīpa_ or _romadvīpa_, i.e. “having islands of
body-hair”, may refer to larvae of flies inhabiting the intestinal canal.
Already over twenty species of diptera are recognized; the larvae of
which have been found in or expelled from the intestinal canal (Manson,
p. 769). The commonest is _Calliphora vomitoria_, the larva of which is
endowed with circles of little spines (see Manson, p. 769, fig. 231); its
name _lomadvīpa_ appears very apt.
        The symptoms ascribed to the presence of worms are vague; some
of them may certainly occur in infections with worms ; diarrhoea is
common in trichuriasis; intermittent intestinal colic (_śūla_, i.e. “pier-
cing pain”) is the most common complaint in ascariasis, etc.; itching
of the anal region in infections with _Enterobius vermicularis_ has al-
ready been referred to.

Chapter 8

“Morbid pallor” (pāṇḍuroga) comprises anaemia, jaundice and other
disorders associated with an altered colour or pigmentation of the skin.
It is not correct to translate pāṇḍuroga by anaemia, as often occurs
(Gulabkunverba translation of the Carakasamhitā; Yādavaśarman;
Dinānāth; Sudarśanaśāstri), and certainly not by jaundice (as in Bhi-
shagratna’s translation of the Suśrutasamhitā); this has already been
pointed out by Müller (Eigenwertungen, p. 36, note 148). Hilgenberg
and Kirfel rendered the term by “Bleichsucht” and Hoernle (The
Bower Manuscript), correctly, by morbid pallor. The diseases described
in the chapter on morbid pallor are at least partially related
to the illness called hariman in the Atharvaveda (see about hariman;
Karambelkar, The Atharva-Veda and the Āyur-Veda, p. 205-214;
Müller, Die Gelbsucht der Alt-Inder, Janus 34, 1930, p. 177-
189).

The syndrome described as morbid pallor caused by wind (8, 4) is
rather obscure; it may be related to several disorders : tropical sprue
with anaemia, in which the patient is generally dark or muddy in
complexion because of a generalized hypermelanosis and complains of
dyspeptic distension of the abdomen; many patients with biliary cir-
rhosis of the liver develop a striking melanotic pigmentation of the
skin; in leishmaniasis the skin often acquires a strange earthy-grey
colour, which has given rise to the native name, kala-azar, i.e. “the
black disease”. Morbid pallor from bile (8, 5) suggests jaundice of a
non-obstructive type, accompanied by fever, as may occur in a great
number of disorders. Morbid pallor from phlegm (8, 6) may represent
several syndromes in which a chronic anaemia is found. Morbid pallor
arising from the three morbific entities (8, 7) resembles a chronic pro-
tein deficiency, associated with hypomelanosis and wasting and easily
leading to complications.

Much has been written about the eating of earth (8, 8-10) as a result
of or as a habit leading to anaemia. From recent studies it has become
clear that the ingestion of earth interferes with the absorption of iron
and produces an iron-deficiency anaemia (The Lancet, 18th April 1970,
p. 826, where references are given). The eating of earth can be a symp-
tom of ancylostomiasis (Manson, p. 278), which is frequent in India;
this infection with hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator
americanus) may give rise to severe anaemia.

Anaemia leads to oedema (8, 11) when present to a serious degree;


=== Page 643 ===
APPENDIX FIVE
in ancylostomiasis with chronic anaemia the stools may sometimes
contain small flakes of blood-tinged mucus (8, 11).
The disease called kāmalā (8, 16-18) is usually equated with jaundice
(Jolly, Medicin, p. 87; Hilgenberg and Kirfel; Gulabkunverba trans-
lation of the Carakasamhitā; Yādavaśarman; Dinānāth; Sudarśana-
śāstrī). Particular forms of jaundice are described as morbid pallor
from bile (8, 5), but kāmalā is a more pronounced form of it; it may
include obstructive jaundice, though the clay-coloured faeces occur-
ring in that syndrome are not mentioned. A more accurate description
of obstructive jaundice is found at Ca.Ci. 16, 124cd-128ab (note 39).
When kāmalā has been present for some time and does not decrease
in intensity, it is called kumbhakāmalā (8, 19ab); the serious state to
which it may give rise (8, 21cd-22ab) is suggestive of advanced hepatic
failure caused by cirrhosis or an amoebic liver abscess.
The disease called halīmaka (8, 22cd-23) is sometimes interpreted as
chlorosis (Yādavaśarman; Dinānāth; Sudarśanaśāstrī), which is ina-
dequate, because it is a serious illness. Its description may point to a
severe chronic anaemia, associated with jaundice; in jaundice the
coloration of the skin varies greatly in intensity, from a barely detecta-
ble light yellow to a greenish or even brownish colour. Finally it should
be mentioned that the best enumeration of the symptoms met with
in more serious degrees of anaemia is found in the Carakasamhitā (note
19, the generic characteristics of morbid pallor : Ca.Ci. 16, 13-16).

Chapter 9

The disease called “blood-bile” (raktapitta) does not fit into any
modern medical concept. It comprises all disorders in which loss of
blood, or matter supposed to be “blood-bile”, occurs through the
openings of the body (the eyes and the pores of the hairs are also
regarded as openings of the body). It includes haematemesis, haemo-
ptysis, melaena, lower bowel bleeding, anal bleeding, gross haematuria,
metrorrhagia and vaginal bleeding, nasal bleeding, loss of blood from
the ears and the eyes, generalized bleeding from the gastro-intestinal
tract, general disorders with numerous subcutaneous haemorrhages,
the discharge of bilious fluid through the mouth, the throwing up of
purulent sputum, etc.
Blood-bile from phlegm (9, 5ab) does not seem like a haemorrhage;
it may refer to blood-streaked sputum, usually produced by a hard
forceful cough. Blood-bile from wind (9, 5cd) may point to the sputum
627


=== Page 644 ===
628
                                                                     APPENDIX FIVE

of bacterial pneumonia and to haemoptysis. Blood-bile from bile (9,
6-7ab) may represent haematemesis (blood coming from the stomach
may be brown or black) and bilious vomiting (blood-bile resembling the
urine of a cow).
       The characteristics which indicate a bad prognosis (9, 12) are sug-
gestive of a great variety of disorders; stinking purulent sputum is
thrown up e.g. in bronchiectasis and abscesses of the lung; a faecal
odour after protracted vomiting indicates low obstruction of the small
bowel or peritonitis, etc.

Chapter 10

       The disease called yakṣman, consumption, or rājayakṣman, kingly
consumption, was identified as phthisis pulmonalis by Wise (p. 321)
and, following his lead, by many others (Yādavaśarman : phthisis,
consumption, pulmonary tuberculosis; Dinānāth : idem; Jolly, Medicin,
p. 88, is more critical : Auszehrung und Lungenschwindsucht, i.e.
cachexia and phthisis pulmonalis).
       The texts make clear that the disease has a much wider range and
may be viewed as comprising the whole series of conditions, of what-
ever origin, between physical exhaustion and cachexia.
       A disease of the name yakṣma is already referred to in the Atharva-
veda (Karambelkar, The Atharva-Veda and the Āyur-Veda, p. 195-200;
Müller, yakṣma, MIO 4, 1956, p. 278-313; idem, Die Medicin im Rg-
Veda, Asia Major 6, 1930, p. 352-357). Müller has repeatedly observed
that (rājā)yakṣma(n) is not identical with pulmonary tuberculosis and
that many disorders are included in the term (see also : Eigenwertungen,
p. 24-26), especially in old texts like the Atharvaveda. Filliozat rightly
says (The classical doctrine, p. 100) that rājayakṣma denotes the ca-
chexia resulting from various consumptive diseases, among which we
may recognize pulmonary tuberculosis.
       The three cardinal signs of kingly consumption (10, 5) only indicate
a disease of the lungs, accompanied by fever. The other symptoms
(add. stanza and 10, 6-7) make clear that haemoptysis is a feature of
this illness, which may point to pulmonary tuberculosis, but also to
a number of other disorders, such as pulmonary infarction, bronchi-
ectasis, mitral stenosis, etc.; the affection of the larynx and the diar-
rhoea mentioned may occur in tuberculosis.
       The disease called “a lesion of the chest” (10, 21-29ab) (urahkṣata)
is sometimes identified as pulmonary cavitation (Yādavaśarman ; Dinā-


=== Page 645 ===
APPENDIX FIVE                                                          629

nāth), suggesting a tuberculous origin; Jolly (Medicin, p. 88-89) was
more prudent, calling it wounds in the chest (Wunden in der Brust.
Pneumonie ?). The description of the disorder is not suggestive of pul-
monary tuberculosis; the very bad-smelling sputum that is coughed
up by the patient rather indicates some other involvement of the lungs.
The states of desiccation (10, 20) (śoṣa) and decline (10, 30) (kṣaya)
represent a wide variety of disorders.
